## 1. Kiṁchanda Jātaka
## The Reason for Enjoying by Day and Suffering by Night

The Introductory Story: While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, spoke this Kiṁchanda Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Kiṁchando kimadhippāyo," concerning the observance of the Uposatha.
2: That word is true. One day, many laymen and laywomen, who had come to listen to the Dhamma and were seated in the Dhamma hall having observed the Uposatha, were asked by the Omniscient Buddha, "Lay followers, are you observing the Uposatha?" When they replied, "Yes, Venerable Sir, we are observing it," the Buddha said, "You lay followers have done a good deed by observing the Uposatha. In the past, people obtained great wealth and retinue as a result of even a half-day Uposatha." Being requested by those lay followers, he brought forth the past.
3:
At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī, seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, went forth as a hermit. Having built a leaf hut in a delightful spot by the lower Ganges, he lived by gathering wild fruits. One day, a ripe mango, as large as a great water jar, fell from a mango grove into the Ganges and was carried by the current toward the ascetic's bathing place. While washing his face, he saw it coming down the middle of the river, swam out to get it, and brought it to his hermitage. He placed it in the fire-room, sliced it with a small knife, and ate just enough to sustain himself. He covered the rest with banana leaves and ate it day after day until it was finished. Once it was gone, he could not eat any other fruits. Bound by the craving for that taste, he thought, 'I will eat only such a ripe mango,' and went to the riverbank. Looking at the river, he made a firm resolve: 'I will not rise until I get a mango,' and sat down. There he sat without food for one, two, three, four, five, or six days, withering in the wind and sun, watching for a mango. On the seventh day, the river deity, reflecting on the situation, realized: 'This ascetic, overcome by craving, has sat looking at the Ganges for seven days without food. It is not right not to give him a ripe mango; if he does not get one, he will die. I shall give it to him.' She came and stood in the air above the Ganges, and speaking with him, she uttered the first stanza:

1. "With what desire, with what intention, do you sit alone in the heat? What are you longing for, what are you seeking? For what purpose, O Brahmin?"

[In this context: 'Desire' means inclination. 'Intention' means thought. 'Sit' means stay. 'Heat' means summer. 'Seeking' means searching. 'Brahmin' is used to address the ascetic because he has gone forth. This is what is meant: 'Brahmin, with what intention, thinking what, longing for what, seeking what, and for what purpose do you sit on this bank of the Ganges, looking at the river?']

Hearing this, the ascetic spoke nine stanzas:

2. "Like a great water-carrying jar of ample girth, such was that ripe mango, supreme in color, fragrance, and taste.
3. Seeing it carried by the current in the midst of the pure water, I grasped it with my hands and brought it to my fire-dwelling.
4. Then, placing it on banana leaves, I myself sliced it with a knife and ate it; it removed my hunger and thirst.
5. Having my distress removed, yet now that it is gone, I find no delight in any other fruits, though I endure the suffering.
6. Surely, death will wither me away; that mango whose fruit is delicious, of the highest sweetness, and delightful to the mind—the one I pulled from the great waters of the ocean-like river as it floated by.
7. I have told you everything, the reason why I fast; I sit by this delightful river, which is wide and filled with many large-finned fish.
8. Now you, too, tell me about yourself, you who do not flee but stand before me. Who are you, O beautiful one? For what reason have you come here, O lady of the lovely waist?
9. You shine like a well-polished gold plate, or like a tigress born on a mountain slope. Among the goddesses, those who are attendants to the gods,
10. And those women in the human world who are endowed with beauty—none is equal to you in form, neither among the gods, the Gandhabbas, nor in the human world. I ask you, O lady of golden limbs, tell me your name and your kin."

Story of the Past: Lay disciples, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, he ruled righteously and was full of faith. He was diligent in giving alms, observing the precepts, and keeping the Uposatha. He also encouraged his ministers and others to engage in almsgiving and other meritorious deeds.

The King’s chaplain (purohita), however, was a corrupt and deceitful judge, like one who eats the flesh from the backs of others. On the Uposatha day, the King called his ministers and said, "You all should observe the Uposatha."
4:
The chaplain did not observe the Uposatha.

Then one day, after having judged a case crookedly and taken a bribe, the chaplain came to serve the king. The king asked the ministers, "Are you observing the Uposatha?" and then asked, "Teacher, are you also observing the Uposatha?" The chaplain told a lie, saying, "Great King, I am observing it," and then descended from the palace.

Then, an official asked the chaplain, "Teacher, is it not that you are not observing the Uposatha?" The chaplain replied, "I only ate in the morning. When I reach home, I will rinse my mouth and observe the Uposatha. I will not eat at night and will keep the precepts during the night. In this way, I will be observing a half-day Uposatha." When the official said, "Very well, Teacher," the chaplain went home and did as he had said.

Again, one day, while the chaplain was sitting in the court of judgment, a certain virtuous woman was presenting her case. Being unable to leave for home, she thought, "I shall not let my observance of the Uposatha be neglected." As noon approached, she made an effort to rinse her mouth. At that moment, a bunch of well-ripened mangoes was brought to the chaplain.
5:
11. "O Brahmin, you who sit by the delightful Kosikī river..."

11-12. "O Brahmin, O sage who has abandoned evil. You sit by the delightful Kosikī river. I am a goddess who dwells by my own power in a mansion within that river of fierce currents. Many rivers flowing from mountain caves, filled with various clusters of trees, flow into it during the rainy season. They regard me as their chief."

13. "Furthermore, many forest waters, carrying currents of emerald-green water, and many rivers that bring delight to the Nagas, fill me with their waters."

14. "Those rivers constantly carry many kinds of fruits: mangoes, rose-apples, mountain jackfruits, kadamba fruits, palm fruits, and figs."

15. "Whatever fruit falls into the water from the trees growing on both banks, that fruit undoubtedly follows the current and comes under my control."

16. "O wise one, O ruler of men, listen to my words. Do not delight in excessive attachment. O wise king, having understood my words, restrain that attachment."

17. "O Royal Sage, promoter of the kingdom's welfare, I truly do not consider you wise, for though you are in the prime of life with flourishing flesh and blood, you desire death because of your craving for a fruit."

18. "O Sage, when one is under the power of craving, the Fathers (Brahmas), the deities, and the Gandharvas know of it. And those self-restrained, ascetic sages in the world who possess divine vision—they all undoubtedly know it. Even their glorious attendants know it."

Knowing the woman's observance of the Uposatha, the chaplain gave her the mangoes, saying, "Eat these mangoes and keep the Uposatha." The woman did as the Brahmin said. This giving of mangoes was the Brahmin's meritorious deed.

Later, after the Brahmin died, he was reborn in the Himalayan region by the banks of the Kosikī river in a three-league mango grove. He awoke in a beautiful golden mansion on a magnificent, decorated bed, like one waking from sleep. He was surrounded by sixteen thousand nymphs of noble appearance and adornment.
6:
That Brāhmaṇa enjoyed such glorious prosperity and happiness only at night. This is true. For that Brāhmaṇa, the result was consistent with his kamma as a Vemānika Peta (mansion-dwelling ghost). Therefore, at dawn, he had to enter the mango grove. At the moment of entry, his divine body vanished, and he took a form eighty cubits tall, like a palm tree. His entire body burned, appearing like a flame-of-the-forest tree in full bloom.

On each hand, there was only a single finger. His fingernails were the size of large hoes. With those nails, he would scrape and pull out the flesh from his own back to eat. Falling into painful agony, he would wail loudly and suffer.

At sunset, that body would vanish, and his divine body would reappear. Sixteen thousand adorned nymphs, carrying various musical instruments, would surround him. Enjoying great prosperity, the Brāhmaṇa would then ascend to his celestial palace in the delightful mango grove.
7:
19. Having known thus, the wise one knows all dhammas, the destruction and the passing away of life.
Evil does not accumulate for that man, if he does not intend for the death of another.

20. O you who are recognized by the assembly of sages, thus known as a blessing to the world, O beautiful one.
With unnoble conversation, you desire to cause an evil deed.

21. If I shall die on your bank, O goddess of beautiful form.
Without doubt, blame will come to you when I am dead.

22. Therefore, O goddess of slender waist, protect yourself from evil deeds.
Let not all the people blame you later when I have died.

He spoke these four verses.

19. O Goddess (Devadhītā). Just as I know all wholesome dhammas (subbacadhamma) and the passing away (cavana) which is called the destruction (viddhaṃsana) of life (jīvita). For that wise person (vidū) who stands having known in this way, if he does not strive (na ceteti) for the killing (vadhāya) of another person, evil (pāpa) does not increase (na cīyati).

20. O Goddess, who is designated as good by the assembly of sages (isipūgasamaññāte). I know you (taṃ) thus (evaṃ) as the welfare of the world (lokyā) by far-distancing yourself from evil. O beautiful Goddess (satī) who speaks words of blame improperly (anariyaparisambhāse), you (tvaṃ) are causing (jigīsasi) an evil deed (pāpakammaṃ).

21. O Goddess endowed with great and beautiful complexion (puthusussoṇi). If (sace) I (ahaṃ) shall die (marissāmi) on your bank (tīre). If I die because of not obtaining the mango, blame (asiloko) will surely (asaṃsayaṃ) reach you (taṃ).

22. O Goddess with a slender waist and broad hips (sumajjhime). Therefore (tasmā hi), you (tvaṃ) should indeed guard (rakkhassēva) against evil and blameworthy actions. When I (mayi) have died (mate), let not (mā) all (sabbo) the people (jano) blame (pakuṭṭhāyi) you (taṃ) afterwards (pacchā).

That Brahmin, as a result of having given a mango to a woman observing the Uposatha, received a mango orchard three leagues in size. However, as a result of being corrupt and taking bribes in judging cases, he had to pluck and eat the flesh of his own back. Due to the merit of a half-day Uposatha, he enjoyed celestial pleasures at night, surrounded by sixteen thousand celestial nymphs.
8:
At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī, seeing the faults in sensual pleasures, renounced the world to become an ascetic. He built a hermitage in a pleasant area downstream of the Ganges and lived by the practice of gathering alms.

Then one day, a ripe mango the size of a large water jar fell from that mango orchard into the Ganges. Floating with the river's current, that mango reached the front of the ascetic's hermitage. While the ascetic was washing his face, he saw the mango floating in the middle of the river. He swam out, took it, and brought it to his hermitage. He kept it in the fire-hall, sliced it with a small knife, and ate only enough to sustain himself. He covered the remainder with banana leaves and continued to eat it day after day until it was finished.

When the mango was gone, he was unable to eat any other large or small fruits. Bound by the craving for taste (rasataṇhā), he thought, "I will eat only that ripe mango." He went to the riverbank, watched the river, and made a resolution: "If I do not get the mango, I will not rise."

That ascetic remained there on the riverbank without food for six days, becoming withered by the wind and the heat of the sun. Then, on the seventh day, the river goddess, reflecting on the situation, realized: "This ascetic, following the lead of craving, has been without food for seven days while watching the river. It is not proper to not give a ripe mango to this ascetic. If he does not get the mango, he will die. I shall give it to him." Having thought thus, she went and stood in the sky above the Ganges, desiring to speak with the ascetic.
9:
Hearing the words of the goddess, the ascetic wished to inform her of the circumstances.
Then, the water-goddess wished to inform the ascetic of the circumstances.
Then, the ascetic wished to inform the goddess of his own circumstances.
Hearing those words, the goddess spoke these five verses:

23. 'O you who endure the unendurable, I have understood this matter regarding the mangoes. I give both myself and those mangoes to you. You have abandoned the sensual pleasures that are difficult to give up and are established in peace and righteousness.'

24. 'He who, having abandoned a former bond, remains in a later bond, practices unrighteousness, and his evil increases.'

25. 'Come, I shall lead you there; be free from concern. I shall bring you to the cool grove; dwell there without anxiety.'

26. 'O tamer of enemies, behold that grove echoing with birds intoxicated by the nectar of flowers—cranes, peacocks, divine birds, koḷaṭṭhimadhusāḷikā birds. Here, flocks of swans warble, and cuckoos rouse themselves.'

27. 'Here are mango trees with branches bent at the tips, resembling threshing floors of straw. There are kosamba, salala, and nīpa trees, with fruits hanging like ripe palmyra fruits.'

23. O ascetic who endures what is hard to endure (avissahasāhī). I have understood (aññātaṃ) this (etaṃ) reason for the sake of the ripe mango. You (yo tvaṃ), having abandoned (pahāya) the sensual objects (kāmaguṇe) such as gold, flowers, the white parasol, and the golden palace, which are difficult to give up (duccaje), have attained (adhiṭṭhito asi) virtue (sīla), called peace (santi) because it calms evil conduct, and the practice of righteousness (dhamma). I (ahaṃ) give (dadāmi) to you (te) both myself (attānaṃ) and that mango (taṃ ambaṃ), leading you (nayantī) and embracing you (āliṅgetvā) to the mango grove (ambavanaṃ).

24. O ascetic (bho tāpasa), he who (yo), having abandoned (hitvā) a former bond (pubbasaññogaṃ), stands (ṭhito) in a later bond (pacchāsaṃyojane), is said to practice (carati) unrighteousness (adhammañceva), and for him (assa), evil (pāpañca) increases (pavaḍḍhati).

25. O ascetic (tāpasa), come (ehi). I shall lead (pāpayissāmi) you (taṃ). Be (bhava) truly free from concern (appossukko) regarding the ripe mangoes. I (ahaṃ) shall bring (upānayāmi) you to the cool (sītasmiṃ) mango grove. Dwell (viharāhi) there without anxiety (anussuko).

26. O tamer of enemies (arindama), behold (passa) that divine mango grove echoing (abhināditaṃ) with birds (vakkaṅgehi) intoxicated by the nectar of flowers (puppharasamattehi). Cranes (koñcā), peacocks (mayūrā), and divine birds (ete diviyā) such as the koḷaṭṭhi and suvaṇṇasāḷikā birds dwell (vasanti) in this mango grove. Flocks of swans (haṃsapūgehi ca) make it echo with their warbling (kūjitā). Cuckoos (kokilā), while warbling (vassantiyo), make themselves known (pabodhare).

27. O tamer of enemies (arindama), in this mango grove (ettha), there are mango trees (ambā) with branches bent at the tips (vippasākhaggā) due to the weight of fruit, resembling threshing floors of straw (palālakhala-sannibhā) because of the mass of blossoms. There are also kosamba, salala, and nīpa trees with fruits hanging (vilambino) like ripe palmyra fruits (pakkatāla).

Having thus praised the mango grove, the goddess left the ascetic there, saying, 'Eat the mangoes in this grove and satisfy your craving,' and then she departed.
10:
The ascetic, having eaten the mangoes and satisfied his craving for them, rested. While wandering through the mango grove, he saw that peta experiencing suffering but was unable to say anything. However, at sunset, seeing the peta-asurakāya enjoying divine splendor surrounded by a troupe of dancers, he wished to ask the reason and spoke these three verses:

28. 'O divine being, wearing garlands, a diadem, and divine ornaments, adorned with divine limbs and anointed with divine sandalwood, you enjoy yourself at night. But by day, you experience [great] pain.'

29. 'These sixteen thousand goddesses who serve you—there are sixteen thousand of them. You possess such great power, marvelous and hair-raising.'

30. 'What deed did you do in the past? What evil, bringing suffering to yourself, did you commit among humans, such that you now eat the flesh of your own back? What is that evil?'

28. O divine being (devaputta), you (tvaṃ), wearing divine garlands (mālī), wearing a divine diadem (tiriṭī), adorned with divine ornaments (kāyūrī), being endowed with divine limbs (aṅgadī), and anointed with divine sandalwood (candanussado), enjoy (paricāresi) divine pleasure at night (rattiṃ). But by day (divā), you experience (vedesi) great suffering (vedanaṃ).

29. Those sixteen thousand goddesses (tāni soḷasitthisahassāni) who (yā imā) serve (paricārikā) you (te) exist (santi). Thus (evaṃ), you are (asi) one of great power (mahānubhāvo), marvelous (abbhuto) and hair-raising (lomahaṃsano).

30. In the past (pubbe), what deed (kiṃ kammaṃ) did you perform (akari)? Having committed (karitvā) what evil (yaṃ pāpaṃ) among humans (manussesu) that brings suffering to yourself (attadukhāvahaṃ), do you now (idāni) eat (khādasi) the flesh of your own back (attano piṭṭhimāṃsāni)? What (kiṃ) is that evil (taṃ pāpaṃ)?

The peta, recognizing the ascetic, said: 'Does your majesty not know me? I am your majesty's chaplain (purohita).'
11:
"I enjoy this happiness at night as a result of the half-day Uposatha I observed depending on you, Great King. However, I suffer great misery during the day as a result of the evil deed of bribery I committed. This is true; you appointed me to the seat of judgment, and because I acted dishonestly and took bribes, I was like one who eats the flesh of others' backs. Due to the result of that evil deed, I suffer this misery during the day." Wishing to inform the ascetic of this matter, he spoke these two verses:

31. Having received the Vedas, I was obsessed with sensual pleasures.
I lived for a long time to the detriment of others.

32. One who is a back-biter, thus tears and eats.
Just as I today eat the flesh of my own back.

31. Venerable ascetic, I learned the Vedas but was greedy for the objects of desire and the defilements of desire. Venerable ascetic, for a long time, I acted to the detriment and destruction of myself and others.

32. Venerable ascetic, whoever is a back-biter, or speaks slanderous words, that person, just as I now eat my own back-flesh, so too must they tear and eat their own back-flesh.

After saying this, the peta asked the ascetic, "Venerable sir, why have you come here?" The ascetic explained everything in detail.

"Venerable sir, will you stay here now, or will you go?" he asked. "I will not stay here; I will go back to the hermitage," he replied. Hearing this, the vimānika-peta said, "Very well, venerable sir, I will constantly serve you with ripe mangoes." Having transported him to the hermitage by his psychic power, he obtained a promise, "Please stay in this hermitage without weariness," and from then on, he constantly served him with ripe mangoes. The ascetic, eating those ripe mangoes, performed the preliminary work for the kasiṇa, developed the meditative absorptions (jhāna) and higher knowledges (abhiññā), and was reborn in the Brahma realm.

The Teacher, the All-Enlightened One, having brought this Dhamma teaching to the lay devotees and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, some became Stream-enterers (sotāpanna), some Once-returners (sakadāgāmī), and some Non-returners (anāgāmī). How did he identify the Jātaka? "Lay devotees, at that time, Uppalavaṇṇā was the river goddess, and I myself was the ascetic." Thus he identified the Jātaka.
12:
## The Result of Taking Bribes: Rebirth in the Peta Realm

The Kiṃchanda Jātaka is concluded.

## 2. Kumbha Jātaka

## The Origin of Intoxicating Drinks

The Teacher, the All-Enlightened One, who disciplines the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Kumbha Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Ko pāturāsi," concerning five hundred women who were friends of the lay devotee Visākhā and were drinkers of intoxicants.

This is the story: When a drinking festival was proclaimed in Sāvatthī, those five hundred women, while their husbands were celebrating the festival, prepared strong liquor, saying, "We shall celebrate the festival." They went to Visākhā and said, "Friend, let us celebrate the festival." When she replied, "This is a drinking festival; I do not drink liquor," they said, "You give alms to the Buddha; we, however, will celebrate the festival."

Visākhā agreed, saying "Very well," and sent those five hundred women friends away. She then invited the All-Enlightened One, gave a great offering of alms, and taking many flowers and perfumes, went to Jetavana Monastery in the evening, surrounded by those five hundred women, to listen to the Dhamma.

Those women, however, went with Visākhā while still drinking liquor. Standing at the gateway, they drank more and then approached the Teacher along with Visākhā. Visākhā paid homage to the Teacher and sat in a suitable place.

Among the five hundred women, some danced in front of the Teacher. Some sang songs. Some swayed their hands. Some swayed their feet. Some engaged in quarreling.

To cause a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in those intoxicated women, the All-Enlightened One emitted a dark blue ray from his eyebrows. Deep darkness occurred. Those women were greatly terrified, fearing death. Because of that, their intoxication vanished. The All-Enlightened One then vanished from his seated throne and stood on the summit of Mount Sineru. He emitted a ray from his uṇṇālomā hair, which was like the rising of a thousand moons and a thousand suns.

Standing on the summit of Mount Sineru, the Teacher, in order to cause spiritual urgency in those women, spoke this verse:

What laughter, what joy, when the world is constantly burning?
Shrouded in darkness, why do you not seek a lamp?
13:
He spoke this verse:

'O lay devotees! When the world is constantly burning with the fires of passion and so forth, why is there laughter? Why is there joy? Shrouded by the darkness of ignorance, why do you not seek the lamp of wisdom?'

At the conclusion of this verse, those five hundred women were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The Omniscient Buddha arrived and sat upon the Buddha's seat in the shade of the Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭī). Then Visākhā paid homage to the Buddha and asked, 'Venerable Sir, from what time did this drinking of intoxicants, which destroys shame and fear, first originate?' Desiring to explain this matter to Visākhā, the Omniscient Buddha brought forth a story of the past.

Visākhā, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, a hunter named Sura, a resident of the kingdom of Kāsi, went to the Himalayas (Himavanta) to search for goods such as ivory and yak-tails.
14:
In those Himalayas, there was a certain tree that grew tall, and at a height of a man, it branched into three. Between those three branches, there was a hollow the size of a large jar. When it rained, that hollow became filled with water. Surrounding that tree were yellow myrobalan trees (harītakī), emblic myrobalan trees (āmalakī), and pepper vines (marica). The ripe fruits of those yellow myrobalan, emblic myrobalan, and pepper trees fell into that hollow. Near that tree, wild rice grew of its own accord. Parrots took the ears of rice from that field, sat on the tree, and ate them. The fallen grains and husks of the rice they were eating also fell into the hollow of the tree. Thus, that water, being cooked by the heat of the sun, became a liquid the color of blood. During the summer, flocks of thirsty birds came and drank that water; they became intoxicated, fell at the foot of the tree, slept for a while, and then flew away chirping. The same happened to dogs, monkeys, and other animals on the tree.

The hunter, seeing this, thought: 'If this water were poison, these creatures would die. However, they sleep for a while and then go wherever they please. This water is not poison.' He took a little, drank it himself, and became intoxicated. He then felt a desire to eat meat. He lit a fire and killed partridges, chickens, and other birds that had fallen at the foot of the tree due to intoxication. He roasted the meat over the embers and stayed there for a day or two, dancing with one hand and eating the roasted meat with the other, while drinking that water.

Not far from that tree lived an ascetic named Varuṇa. On other occasions, the hunter had visited that ascetic. Then the hunter thought: 'I will drink this beverage together with the ascetic.' Having filled a bamboo tube and taking it along with roasted meat, he went to the leaf-hut and said, 'Venerable Sir, please drink this.' Both of them drank it while eating the roasted meat. Because it was discovered by Sura the hunter and Varuṇa the ascetic, that beverage came to be known as 'Surā' and 'Varuṇā'.

Those two, Sura the hunter and Varuṇa the ascetic, thought, 'This is a means of livelihood.' They filled bamboo tubes, carried them on a shoulder-pole, went to a border town, and informed the king: 'The makers of a beverage have arrived.'
15:
33. "Who are you appearing in the sky of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven,
Illuminating the night like the moon?
Rays emanate from your body,
Like the lightning called Satayata in the firmament."

34. "You move through the air where the wind is stilled,
You go and stand in the sky.
Is your psychic power well-developed and established,
Even like that of the deities who do not travel on foot?"

35. "Standing there, having traversed the sky on foot,
Who are you? Tell me this matter, O Brahmin.
You say, 'Buy this jar.'
Tell me, O Brahmin, what is the purpose of this jar of yours?"

33. "O Brahmin, from where have you come? Have you appeared in the sky, having come from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven? Like the moon illuminating the night, rays emanate from your body like the lightning called Satayata in the firmament."

34. "O Brahmin, you move through the sky where the wind is severed; you go and stand in the air. Is it that you possess well-developed psychic power, established like that of the deities who do not travel by foot?"

35. "O Brahmin, who are you, standing there having traversed the sky? Tell me this matter. You say to me, 'Buy this jar.' Tell me this matter; what kind of jar is this of yours?"

The King had them summoned. Sura the hunter and Varuṇa the sage offered the liquor to the King. The King drank twice or thrice and became intoxicated. For the King, that liquor was only enough for a day or two.

Then he asked the hunter and the sage, "Is there any more liquor?" When they replied, "There is, Great King," he asked, "Where is it?" They said, "It is in the Himalayas, Great King." He said, "If so, bring it." The hunter and the sage went and brought it a second time. Thinking, "We will not be able to go and bring it constantly," they noted the ingredients of the liquor. Starting with the bark of that tree, they put in all the ingredients and manufactured the liquor in the city.
16:
The faults of this pot are not few. Hear the many evils contained within this pot.

The townspeople drank the liquor, became negligent, and fell into misery. The city became as if desolate. The liquor-making hunter and ascetic fled from that city and reached the city of Vārāṇasī. They informed the king, "The liquor-makers have arrived." The king summoned them and provided provisions. They made liquor in Vārāṇasī as well. In Vārāṇasī, too, destruction occurred just as before. They fled from Vārāṇasī and reached the country of Sāketa. From Sāketa, they reached Sāvatthī. At that time, a king named Sabbamitta reigned in Sāvatthī.
17: That king, after providing hospitality and support to the hunter and the ascetic, asked, "What do you desire?" When they said, "We desire the roots and bark which are the ingredients of liquor, fine rice powder, and five hundred large jars," he had all of those provided. The hunter and the ascetic put the liquor into the five hundred large jars. Fearing that mice might drink it, they tied a cat to each jar to guard them. When the liquor matured and overflowed, the cats drank the liquor that leaked down the sides of the jars, became intoxicated, and fell fast asleep. Mice came and ate the ears, noses, teeth, and tails of those cats and went away. The ministers reported to the king, "The cats drank the liquor and died." The king, thinking, "These two, the hunter and the ascetic, must have prepared poison," had the heads of the two men cut off. Those two died lamenting, "O Great King, it is very sweet!" After killing them, the king ordered, "Break the liquor jars." When the cats' intoxication wore off, they got up and went about playing and frolicking. Seeing the cats going about in that way, they reported it to the king.
18: The king thought, "If it were poison, those cats would have died. It must be exceedingly sweet and excellent; I shall drink that liquor." He had the city decorated and a pavilion erected in the palace courtyard. Sitting on the royal throne with a well-constructed white umbrella in the decorated pavilion, surrounded by a host of ministers, he made an effort to drink the liquor. At that time, Sakka, the King of Devas, was surveying the world of men to see who was diligent in serving their parents and fulfilling the three kinds of right conduct. Seeing the king sitting there about to drink the liquor, he thought, "If this king drinks the liquor, and if he drinks it in this way, the entire Great Island of Jambudīpa will be ruined. I will act in such a way that the king will not drink the liquor." He placed a pot full of liquor on the palm of his hand, assumed the form of a Brahmin, and appearing in the sky in front of the king, said, "Buy this pot!" King Sabbamitta, seeing Sakka standing in the sky and speaking in that manner, asked, "Brahmin, where do you come from?" and wishing to converse with him, said: ## 35. Gradually, the practice of drinking liquor spread throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.

The Exposition of the Kumbha Jātaka is finished.

## 3. Jayaddisa Jātaka
## On Supporting One's Parents

While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Jayaddisa Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Cirassaṃ vata me," concerning a monk who supported his mother and father.

The story of the present is the same as that in the Suvaṇṇasāma Jātaka.

Specifically, the All-Knowing Buddha said, "Monks, in the past, wise men gave up golden garlands and the white parasol to support their parents," and he brought forth the story of the past.

The Story of the Past: Monks, in the past, in the city of Uttarapañcāla in the kingdom of Kapila, a king named Pañcāla reigned. His chief queen conceived and gave birth to a son.

In a previous life, a rival woman had become angry and made a wish, "May I be able to eat every child born to you," and was reborn as a Yakkhiṇī. At that time, she found an opportunity and, while the queen was looking, took the infant, who was like a lump of raw flesh, and went away, crunching and eating him. She did the same at the birth of the second son.

At the third birth, when the queen entered the delivery chamber, they surrounded the house and kept a firm guard. On the day of the birth, the Yakkhiṇī came and took the child again. The queen cried out loudly, "The Yakkhiṇī has taken my son!" Men armed with weapons came and, following the sign given by the queen, pursued the Yakkhiṇī.
23:
That ogress, unable to find food, fled and entered a water pipe. The child, thinking she was his mother, nursed from her. The ogress developed a motherly love for him, took him to a cemetery, and raised him in a cave. As the boy grew up, she brought him human flesh. Both of them lived there eating human flesh.

The boy did not know his human nature. He perceived himself as the son of an ogress. He was unable to vanish by discarding his physical form. Then, she gave him a root to enable him to vanish. By the power of that root, he wandered about eating human flesh while invisible. The ogress went to perform service for the Great King Vessavaṇa and died there.

The Queen gave birth to another son for the fourth time. Because he was freed from the ogress, he was healthy. They named him Prince Jayaddisa because he was born after conquering the enemy ogress. When he reached maturity, he attained mastery in all arts, raised the white parasol, and ruled the kingdom.

At that time, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the Chief Queen of that king. They named him Prince Alīnasattu. When he reached maturity, having learned all arts, he became the crown prince.

Later, the son of the ogress lost that root through negligence and, being unable to vanish, ate human flesh in the cemetery in visible form. People saw him, became frightened, and went to report to the king:

"Your Majesty, an ogre is eating human flesh in the cemetery in visible form. He will eventually enter the city, kill people, and eat them. It is proper to have him captured."

The king agreed, saying, "Very well," and ordered, "Capture him!" The army went and surrounded the cemetery. The son of the ogress, naked and terrified, fearing death, fled through the crowd wailing. The people, fearing death and crying "An ogre!", split into two groups.

The son of the ogress fled from that cemetery and entered the forest. He never returned to the human path again. Dwelling near a great forest called Mahāvaṭṭanī, he would capture people one by one as they traveled the road, take them into the forest, kill and eat them, making his home at the foot of a banyan tree.

Then, a brahmin merchant leader, having given a thousand pieces of money to the forest guards, set out on that road with five hundred carts.

Me, for me. Manasāpi, even in my heart. Appiyo, hatred. Na ca asi, has never occurred. Tasmā, therefore. Etena saccena, by this truth. Devā, may the deities. Sarantu, remember. Sāmi, dear husband and heir apparent. Anuññāto, being released by the man-eater Porisāda. Sotthi, safely. Tvaṃ, you, dear husband and heir apparent. Paccehi, may you be released and return.

The son, Prince Alīnasattu, also traveled towards the dwelling of the ogre Porisāda in the manner instructed by his father. The ogre thought: "Those known as kings possess much cunning; who can know what will happen?" Having thought thus, he climbed a tree and sat watching for the king's arrival.

"I am the son of Jayaddisa. Eat me today for the release of my father." He spoke this verse.

Thinking, "I will make him run away by some means," and wishing him to flee—

Therefore, Sakka, having squeezed the essence of the mountain, made the sign of the hare on the moon's disc. Because of that very sign of the hare, the moon-god is now known as 'Sasi' (the one with the hare), and he shines while fulfilling the desires and increasing the love of all people.

That prince had no fear of death. The Yakkha, thinking, "I have never before seen anyone so endowed with such courage in all this time," sat looking at the prince repeatedly with his hair standing on end in awe.

Having heard those words, the Porisāda Yakkha, wishing to release the prince, said:

94. O prince of great power! Just as the moon or the sun shines beautifully when released from the mouth of Rāhu on the fifteenth day, so may you, being released from me, the man-eater, shine in the kingdom of Kappila. "The eyes of Yakkhas are red and do not blink; they have no shadow and are fearless. This Porisāda is not a real Yakkha; he is truly a human. It is said that an ogress took my father's three elder brothers. Among those three, she must have eaten two, but one she must have raised with the love of a son. This Porisāda must be that very person. I shall take this Porisāda, inform my father the king, and establish him in kingship."

Thinking thus, he said, "Friend Porisāda, come! You are not a real Yakkha; you are my father's eldest brother. Come, go with me and wear the white umbrella of kingship, which is the property of our family." When the Porisāda replied, "I am not a human," the prince asked, "If you do not believe my words, is there anyone whom you do believe?" When the Porisāda said, "In such and such a place, there is a hermit with divine vision (Dibbacakkhu)," the prince took the Porisāda and went to the hermit.

As soon as the hermit with divine vision saw the two of them, he said, "For what purpose are you two, uncle and nephew, wandering in the forest?" and spoke of their kinship.

The Porisāda Yakkha believed the words of the hermit and said, "Dear son, you go on. In this single life, I have had two different natures. I have no desire for kingship. I shall become a monk." He then ordained as a monk in the presence of the hermit. Then, the crown prince Alīnasattu paid respects to his uncle Porisāda and returned to the royal city.

96. Monks, all the townspeople, the countryfolk, the elephant riders, the charioteers, and the infantry, saluting and with hands joined in reverence, approached Prince Alīnasatta, saying: "Homage to you! You have performed a deed that is extremely difficult to do."

Desiring to make this matter clear, the All-Knowing Buddha preached this verse. After preaching this, the All-Knowing Buddha, wishing to show the actions performed by the townspeople and others for Prince Alīnasatta upon his return to the royal city, said:

When the father, King Jayaddisa, heard that "the prince has arrived," he went out to welcome him. The son, Prince Alīnasatta, arrived surrounded by a great multitude and paid homage to his father. When he thus paid homage, King Jayaddisa asked his son, "Dear son, for what reason were you released from the hands of such a cruel man-eater (Porisāda)?"

"Noble Father, this Porisāda is not a yakkha; he is your elder brother. This Porisāda is my paternal uncle," he reported, explaining the whole situation, and added, "It is proper for you, Father, to see my uncle."

King Jayaddisa immediately had the drums beaten and went to the presence of the ascetics with a large retinue. The great ascetic (Dibbacakkhu) explained in detail everything: how the ogress had carried the Porisāda away and raised him without eating him, the reason for his behaving like a yakkha, and the fact that the Porisāda and King Jayaddisa were brothers.

King Jayaddisa said, "Elder brother, please come and rule the kingdom." "It is not proper, Great King," he refused. "If that is so, please come and stay in my royal garden; I will support you with the four requisites," the King said. "I will not come, Great King," he replied.
37:
When he said, "Great King, I will not follow," King Jayaddisa had a dam built across a mountain valley not far from the ascetics' hermitage, created a large reservoir, prepared fields, brought a thousand noble families to settle there, established a large village, and arranged for the regular offering of alms-food to the ascetics.

That village became known as "Cūḷakammāsadamma." The place where the Bodhisatta named Sutasoma tamed the Porisāda should be known as "Mahākammāsadamma."

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the All-Knowing Buddha proclaimed the Truths and identified the birth (Jātaka). At the conclusion of the Truths, the elder who supported his parents was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). He identified the birth as follows: "The mother and father of that time have now become the Great Royal Family; the ascetic was Sāriputta; the Porisāda was Angulimāla; the younger sister was Uppalavaṇṇā; the Chief Queen was Rāhulamātā; and Prince Alīnasatta was I myself."

## To support one's parents is a noble blessing.
The Jayaddisa Jātaka ends.

## 4. Chaddanta Jātaka
## On bearing a grudge due to misunderstanding one's husband

While residing at the Jetavana monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, preached this Chaddanta Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Kiṃ nu socasi nuccangi," concerning a certain young nun.

That young nun was a daughter of a good family in the city of Sāvatthī. Seeing the faults of household life, she ordained. One day, she went with other nuns to hear the Dhamma and, sitting before the decorated preaching throne, she looked upon the physical form of the All-Knowing Buddha, which was endowed with the perfection of noble appearance born from immeasurable merit and power. She thought, "While wandering in Saṃsāra, was I ever the wife of this Great Man?"

At that very moment, the knowledge of past lives (Jātissara-ñāṇa) arose in that young nun. "When he was the Chaddanta elephant king, I was the wife of this Great Man," the knowledge arose. Then, as she remembered this through her knowledge of past lives, great joy and rapture arose in her. Through the force of that rapture, she laughed loudly and then thought again:

"As for wives, those who desire the welfare of their husbands are very few; those who do not desire their welfare are very many. Did I desire the welfare of this Great Man, or did I desire his ruin?" As she reflected, she realized, "It was only that I did not desire his welfare."
38:
When that young woman recollected her past in order, she saw: "Holding a grudge in my heart for a slight offense, I targeted the Chaddanta elephant king, who was one hundred and twenty cubits long, and sent a hunter named Sonuttara to shoot him with a poisoned arrow, causing his death."

Upon seeing this, grief arose in the young nun. Her heart burned. Being unable to contain her sorrow, she breathed heavily and wept loudly.

Seeing the young nun, the All-knowing Buddha smiled. When the assembly of monks asked, "Venerable Sir, what is the cause for your smile?", the Buddha replied, "Monks, this young nun is weeping because she remembers a wrong she committed against me in a past life." Having said this, he related the story of the past.

The Story of the Past: Monks, in the past, in the Himalayan region, eight thousand elephants of the Chaddanta breed lived near Lake Chaddanta. Those elephants possessed great power and could fly through the air. At that time, the Bodhisatta was born as the son of the chief of those elephants.

The Bodhisatta was entirely white with red feet and a red face. When he reached maturity, he was eighty-eight cubits high and one hundred and twenty cubits long. He possessed a trunk fifty-eight cubits long, resembling a silver garland. His tusks were fifteen cubits in circumference and thirty cubits in length, endowed with six-colored rays. He was the leader of the eight thousand elephants and honored five hundred Paccekabuddhas. The Bodhisatta elephant king had two chief queens: Cullasubhaddā and Mahāsubhaddā. The Chaddanta elephant king lived in a Golden Cave, surrounded by the eight thousand elephants.

Lake Chaddanta was fifty leagues in length and fifty leagues in breadth. In the center of the lake, in an area twelve leagues in extent, there was no scum or moss; only water clear as emerald remained. Immediately surrounding that emerald-colored water was a forest of pure white lilies (Kallahāra) one league wide. Beyond the white lilies was a forest of pure blue lotuses (Nīluppala) one league wide. Then, forests of red lotuses (Rattuppala), white lotuses (Puṇḍarīka), red paduma lotuses, white paduma lotuses, and kumuda lotuses, each one league wide, stood surrounding the preceding ones.

Beyond these seven types of lotus forests, there was a mixed forest of all those lilies and lotuses, one league wide, surrounding the seven layers. Beyond the mixed forest, in water the depth of an elephant's waist, stood a forest of red rice (Rattasāli) one league wide. Beyond the red rice, at the edge of the water, was a forest of small shrubs one league wide, filled with fragrant and delicate flowers of blue, yellow, red, and white. These ten layers of forests were each one league wide.
39:
Beyond the forest of small shrubs stood forests of small beans, large beans, and green gram. Beyond those were forests of cucumbers, gourds, and pumpkins. Beyond the cucumbers, gourds, and pumpkins was a forest of sugarcane as tall as areca trees. Beyond the sugarcane was a forest of bananas with fruits as large as elephant tusks. Beyond the banana forest was a Sāla forest.

Beyond the Sāla forest was a jackfruit forest with fruits as large as water jars. Beyond the jackfruit forest was a tamarind forest with sweet fruits. Beyond the tamarind forest was a mango forest with sweet fruits. Beyond the mango forest was a wood-apple (Kapiṭṭha) forest. Beyond the wood-apple forest was a great mixed forest. Beyond the great forest was a bamboo forest.

(All these descriptions refer to the prosperity of the Chaddanta elephant king during his time. The Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya, however, describes the prosperity as it exists now.)

The bamboo forest was surrounded by seven mountains. Starting from the outermost of these seven mountains, the first was named Cūḷakāḷa, the second Mahākāḷa, the third Udaka. Inward from Udaka was Candapassa, inward from that was Suriyapassa, inward from that was Maṇipassa, and the seventh was Suvaṇṇapassa.

Mount Suvaṇṇapassa was seven leagues high. It surrounded Lake Chaddanta like the rim of an alms bowl. The inner side of Mount Suvaṇṇapassa was golden in color. With the light reflecting from the mountain's side, Lake Chaddanta appeared like the newly risen sun.

Among the six mountain ranges outside Mount Suvaṇṇapassa, one was six leagues high, one five, one four, one three, one two, and one was one league high.

In the northeast corner of Lake Chaddanta, in a place struck by the wind rising from the water, stood a great Banyan tree (Nigrodha). The trunk of that Banyan tree was five leagues in circumference and seven leagues high. In the four directions, the four main branches were each six leagues long. The branch that grew upwards was also six leagues high.

Thus, from its roots, the tree was thirteen leagues in height. From the tip of one branch to the tip of the opposite branch, it was twelve leagues. It was adorned with eight thousand aerial roots. It stood beautifully like a shaven emerald mountain.

On the Golden Mountain in the western direction of Lake Chaddanta, there was a Golden Cave twelve leagues long. The Chaddanta elephant king lived in the Golden Cave during the rainy and cold seasons, surrounded by eight thousand elephants. In the summer, he stayed among the aerial roots at the foot of the great Banyan tree, enjoying the cool breeze from the water.

Then one day, young elephants came and reported, "The great Sāla forest is in bloom." Accompanied by his retinue, he went to the Sāla forest, saying, "I shall play the Sāla game," and struck a Sāla tree in full bloom with his forehead. At that time, Cullasubhaddā stood on the upwind side; dry twigs mixed with old leaves and red ants fell upon her body. Mahāsubhaddā stood on the downwind side; flower pollen and petals fell upon her body. Cullasubhaddā thought, "This elephant king dropped flower pollen and petals upon his favorite wife..."
40:
Then, one day, the young attendant elephants came and reported to the Chaddanta elephant king, "The great Sal forest is in full bloom." The Chaddanta elephant king, thinking, "I shall enjoy the festival of the Sal forest with my retinue," went to the Sal forest and struck a certain fully blooming Sal tree with his forehead.

At that time, the queen named Cūḷasubhaddā was standing on the windward side. Dry branches and withered leaves mixed with red ants fell upon her body. The queen Mahāsubhaddā was standing on the leeward side. Upon her body fell flower dust, pollen, and petals.

Cūḷasubhaddā, thinking, "He caused flower dust, pollen, and petals to fall upon his beloved wife, but upon me, he caused withered leaves mixed with dry branches and red ants to fall. So be it, I shall know what to do," harbored a grudge against the Bodhisatta.

On another day, the Chaddanta elephant king went down to Lake Chaddanta with his retinue to bathe. Then, two young elephants, holding bundles of kusa grass with their trunks, bathed him as if cleaning the peak of a silver mountain. After the Chaddanta elephant king had finished bathing and come out, they bathed the two queens, Cūḷasubhaddā and Mahāsubhaddā. Those elephant queens also finished bathing, came out, and stood near the Bodhisatta. Afterward, eight thousand elephants went down into Lake Chaddanta, played in the water, brought various flowers from the lake, and adorned the Bodhisatta as if decorating a silver stupa. Then they adorned the two queens, Cūḷasubhaddā and Mahāsubhaddā.

At that time, while one elephant was wandering in Lake Chaddanta, he found a large Paduma lotus named Sattuddaya with seven layers of petals, brought it, and offered it to the Bodhisatta. The Chaddanta elephant king took that lotus with his trunk, scattered the pollen and dust on his forehead, and gave it to the chief queen, Mahāsubhaddā.

Seeing this, Cūḷasubhaddā thought, "He gave this great seven-layered Paduma lotus only to his beloved wife, not to me," and she harbored a grudge against the Bodhisatta once again.

Then one day, while the Bodhisatta was serving five hundred Paccekabuddhas with sweet fruits and lotus stalks mixed with honey, Cūḷasubhaddā offered the various fruits she had obtained to the venerable Paccekabuddhas and made a wish:

"Venerable sirs, when I pass away from this life, may I be reborn in the royal family of Madda as a princess named Subhaddā. When I reach the age of maturity, may I become the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī and be his beloved and pleasing queen, able to influence him according to my will. Having informed the King of Bārāṇasī, may I be able to send a hunter to shoot this elephant king with a poisoned arrow, causing his death, and may I be able to have his pair of tusks, which emit six-colored rays, brought to me."

From the time she made that wish, she refused to take food, became emaciated, and died before long. She was reborn in the womb of the chief queen of the King of Madda in the kingdom of Madda. They named the princess Subhaddā. When she reached maturity, they gave the princess Subhaddā to the King of Bārāṇasī. The King of Bārāṇasī loved her very much. She became the head of sixteen thousand women and also attained the knowledge of recollecting past lives (jātissara-ñāṇa).

Hearing those words, the King, wishing to grant the Queen's craving—

Hearing the King's words, Queen Subhaddā, wishing to show, "O Great King, my craving is very difficult to obtain. I will not speak of that craving now. However, let all the hunters that are within your majesty's kingdom be assembled. I shall speak in the midst of those hunters"—

100. "Let the hunters assemble, O King, whoever are in your realm.

100. O King, let all the hunters who are in your majesty's realm come together. To those hunters, I shall tell what kind of craving I have.

Before long, the hunters living in the kingdom of Kāsi came, bringing gifts according to their means, and reported their arrival to the King.

102. "O hunters, listen, as many as are gathered here. I saw in a dream a white elephant with six-colored tusks. I have need of its tusks; if I do not get them, I shall not live."

102. O hunters! As many of you as have gathered here in unison, listen to my words. In a dream, I saw an elephant king, entirely white, possessing tusks endowed with six colors. I desire the tusks of that elephant king. If I do not obtain them, my life shall be no more.

103. O Princess! Such an elephant as you saw in your dream, a six-tusked elephant endowed with six colors, has never been seen or heard of by our fathers or our grandfathers. Tell us of such an elephant-king as you have seen.

All those hunters were sixty thousand in number. The king, knowing that the hunters had arrived, stood at the window, stretched out his hand, and spoke to the queen, informing her of their arrival:

101. O Queen! These hunters are well-trained and skilled in piercing and killing. They are very brave and free from fear. They know the forests and they know the deer. All these hunters have sacrificed their lives for my benefit.

Hearing the king's words, Queen Subhaddā had the hunters summoned, wishing to inform them of her craving.

Hearing the queen's words, the hunters, wishing to ask her about the matter, spoke this verse:

103. "Neither by our fathers nor by our grandfathers..."

Having asked with this verse, they wished to ask again about the place where that elephant resided.
