104. "Four directions, four intermediate directions, above and below—these are the ten directions. In which direction does the elephant-king stay, the six-tusked one you saw in your dream?"

104. O Queen! There are these ten directions: the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, above, and below. In which of these ten directions does that elephant-king stay, the six-tusked one endowed with six colors that you saw in your dream?

When the hunters asked thus, Queen Subhaddā looked at all the hunters and saw among them a hunter named Sonuttara, who had large feet, calves like bundles of rice, large knees, large ribs, a thick and reddish beard, piercing yellow eyes, an ugly and terrifying appearance, and who stood out above all the other hunters. He had been an enemy of the Great Being in a previous life.

Thinking, "This hunter will be able to carry out my word," she obtained the king's permission, took Sonuttara to the top floor of the seven-storied palace, opened the northern lion-window, and stretching out her hand towards the northern Himavanta, she spoke these four verses to point out the place where the elephant-king stayed:

105. "Go straight from here in the northern direction, crossing the seven great mountains. There is a magnificent mountain named Suvaṇṇapassa, well-flowered and frequented by Kinnaras.

106. Having climbed that mountain, the abode of Kinnaras, look down at the foot of the mountain. Then you will see a kingly Banyan tree, the color of a dark cloud, with eight thousand trunks.

107. There stays the six-tusked elephant, entirely white, difficult for others to overcome. Eight thousand elephants guard him, with tusks like plow-poles, who strike with the speed of the wind.

108. They stand there, breathing fiercely; they are provoked even by the rustling of the wind. If they see a human being there, they would turn him to ashes; not even his dust would remain."

105. O hunter! Go straight from here towards the northern direction. After crossing the seven great mountain ranges, there is a mountain named Suvaṇṇapassa. That mountain is higher than the other six mountains; it is a forest full of well-bloomed flowers and is the constant haunt of Kinnaras.

106. Having climbed to the top of Suvaṇṇapassa, the abode of Kinnaras, look down at the foot of the mountain. Upon looking, you will see a kingly Banyan tree (Nigrodha) with eight thousand trunks, having the color of a dark cloud.

107. At the foot of that Banyan tree, the six-tusked elephant stays, entirely white and difficult for others to overcome. In the summer, he stays there receiving the breeze from the water. Eight thousand elephants guard him. Those elephants have tusks like pairs of plow-poles and are of such a nature that they pursue and kill enemies with the speed of the wind.

108. Those elephants stand there, emitting breaths that follow a terrifying and loud sound. They are angered even by the rustling of grass or leaves moved by the wind. If they see a human being who has arrived there, they would turn him to ashes. Not even the dust of that person, destroyed by the wind from their trunks, would remain in that place.
44:
109. "O Queen, there are many ornaments of gold in the royal palace. There are ornaments made of pearls, gems, and lapis lazuli. What will you do with ornaments of ivory? Do you wish to kill the elephant with six tusks, or will you have the hunters killed [under the pretext of the ornament]?" He spoke this verse.

109. O Queen. Because there are many ornaments of gold and silver in the royal palace, as well as ornaments made of pearls, gems, and lapis lazuli. All these jewel ornaments exist. Therefore, what will you do with ornaments of ivory? Do you wish to kill the elephant king who possesses tusks that emit six-colored rays? Or else, do you wish to have the hunters killed by using the ornament as a pretext?

Upon hearing the Queen's words, the hunter Sonuttara, being afraid of the danger of death, wished to reply to the Queen—

Thereafter, Queen Subhaddā, wishing to urge the hunter Sonuttara again by expressing her desire, spoke this verse:

110. "O hunter, I am jealous and distressed. I wither away, being distracted as I remember [the grudge]. O hunter, do this for me; I will give you five choice villages."

110. O hunter. I am both jealous and oppressed by mental distress. I, who repeatedly remember the enmity caused by that elephant king, am withered and distracted by the power of jealousy. O hunter, perform this task for my benefit. I shall give you five choice villages, each yielding a revenue of one hundred thousand per year.
45:
111. "O Queen, where does the elephant king dwell? Where does he take his stand? What is his path when he goes to bathe? How does that elephant king bathe? How shall we know the movements of the elephant?" He spoke this verse.

111. O Queen. In what place does the elephant king dwell? To what place of standing does he go? What is the path of that elephant king when he goes to bathe? How does that elephant king bathe? How shall we know the way the elephant goes to bathe?

Having spoken these words, she comforted the hunter, saying: "Friend hunter, I previously gave gifts to Paccekabuddhas and made an aspiration, saying, 'May I be able to have this Chaddanta elephant killed and bring his pair of tusks.' It is not something I merely saw in a dream; the aspiration I have made will be fulfilled. Go, do not fear." The hunter Sonuttara accepted her words, saying, "Very well, my lady," and then asked: "If that is so, please describe clearly and tell me the dwelling place of that elephant king."

Thereafter, Queen Subhaddā, wishing to tell the hunter the place she had seen through the power of her knowledge of past lives (jātissara-ñāṇa), spoke these two verses:

112. "O hunter, right there, not far from the elephant's dwelling, is that lotus pond. It is delightful, with good landing places and much water. It is in full bloom and frequented by swarms of bees. There, indeed, the elephant king bathes."
46:
113. "Having bathed his head, wearing a garland of lotuses, entirely white with limbs like a white lotus, he goes to his dwelling joyfully, preceded by his chief queen, Sabbabhaddā."

She spoke these two verses.

112. O hunter. Right there, near the elephant's dwelling, is that Chaddanta Lake. It is delightful, with pleasant landing places and much water. It is in full bloom all around with five kinds of lotuses. Swarms of bees and beetles constantly frequent it. There, in this Chaddanta Lake, the elephant king bathes.

113. Having bathed including his head, and wearing a garland of lotuses and other aquatic and terrestrial flowers, the Chaddanta elephant king, whose body is entirely white and endowed with white limbs like the petals of a white lotus, goes to his own dwelling joyfully, placing his chief queen named Sabbabhaddā in front.

Upon hearing this, the hunter Sonuttara agreed, saying, "Very well, my lady, I shall kill that elephant and bring his tusks." Then, the Queen, being greatly pleased, gave him a thousand pieces of money and dismissed him, saying, "Go home for now; after seven days from today, you shall depart for that Chaddanta Lake."

She then summoned the smiths and ordered: "Friends, we have need of adzes, axes, hoes, chisels, mallets, knives for cutting bamboo thickets, sickles, iron bolts, saws, iron shovels, and iron spikes. Make all these quickly and bring them." She also summoned the leather-workers and ordered: "Friends, it is necessary to make a leather bag capable of carrying a load of one kumbha. We also have need of large leather ropes, small leather straps, elephant-foot shoes, and leather umbrellas. Make all these quickly and bring them."

Both the smiths and the leather-workers quickly made all those implements and presented them. Queen Subhaddā prepared provisions for the hunter, placing all the equipment, starting with the fire-making kit, and all the provisions, starting with parched grain balls, into the leather bag. The total weight was one kumbha. (A kumbha is said to be twenty-seven bushels and two pecks.)
47:
Sonuttara the hunter also prepared his travel equipment and, arriving on the seventh day, stood after paying homage to the Queen. Then Queen Subhaddā said to the hunter, "Friend hunter, all your equipment is ready; take this leather bag." Now, this hunter Sonuttara possessed great strength, equal to the strength of five bull elephants. Therefore, he picked up the bag as if it were a small bundle of betel leaves, placed it under his arm, and appeared as if his hands were empty. Queen Subhaddā provided provisions for the hunter's wife and children, informed the King, and then sent Sonuttara on his way.

Sonuttara the hunter paid homage to both the King and the Queen, descended from the palace, and departed from the city in a chariot with a large retinue. Passing through a succession of villages and market towns, he reached the border regions. There, he sent back the people of the countryside and entered the forest with the border inhabitants. Having passed beyond the paths of men, he sent back the border inhabitants as well and proceeded alone. Upon reaching a distance of thirty yojanas—

He arrived in succession at eighteen types of thickets: first, the six thickets consisting of Dabba grass, Kāsa grass, ordinary grass, Tulasi thickets, Sara reeds, and the grass thicket known as Tirivacchaka; then thorny bamboo thickets, rattan thickets, mixed thickets, reed thickets, a grass thicket similar to Sara reeds which even a snake could hardly penetrate, a dense forest thicket, a forest of trees, a bamboo forest, a bamboo grove, a mud thicket, a water thicket, and the thicket of the seven mountains. Having reached these—
48:
114. There, having grasped her words,
Taking his quiver and bow, the hunter
Traversed seven great mountains
To the noble mountain named Suvaṇṇapassa.

115. Having ascended the rock, the abode of Kinnaras,
He looked down at the foot of the mountain.
There he saw the king of Banyan trees,
Resembling a dark cloud, with eight thousand trunks.

116. There he saw the elephant with six tusks,
Entirely white, difficult for others to overcome.
Eight thousand elephants protect him,
With tusks like chariot poles, swift as the wind.

117. There he saw a lotus pond nearby,
Delightful, with good landing places and abundant water,
Fully blooming and frequented by swarms of bees,
Where that elephant king bathes.

118. Having seen the elephant's gait and standing place,
And the path he takes for bathing,
The one of ignoble form approached to prepare a pit,
Sent by her who follows the will of her heart.

The Teacher spoke these five verses.

114. Monks, that hunter Sonuttara, taking the words of Queen Subhaddā who stood on the seventh floor of the palace, took his quiver and his great bow (which requires the strength of a thousand to string), reached the mountain thicket, and while searching through the seven great mountain ranges, saw the high mountain named Suvaṇṇapassa.

115. Ascending the summit of Suvaṇṇapassa, the abode of Kinnaras, he looked down at the foot of the mountain. There he saw the king of Banyan trees, the color of a dark rain cloud, with eight thousand trunks.

116. Monks, there he saw the elephant king standing at the foot of that Banyan tree, possessing tusks emitting six-colored rays, entirely white. He is difficult for others to oppress. Eight thousand elephants, with tusks like chariot poles, who kill enemies by chasing them with the speed of the wind, guard him.

117. Monks, reaching the vicinity of the king of Banyan trees within that Suvaṇṇapassa mountain, he saw that Chaddanta lake where the elephant king bathes—delightful, with good landing places, much water, five kinds of lotuses in full bloom, and surrounded by swarms of bees.

118. Monks, having seen all—the gait and standing place of the Chaddanta elephant king, and the path he takes to bathe—the hunter, who is of ignoble nature because he does not feel shame or fear towards evil, being sent by Queen Subhaddā who follows the whims of her mind, prepared a pit.

He cut neja grass and the like with a sickle, cut bamboo and such with a bamboo-cutting knife, chopped trees with an axe, and carved through very large trees with a chisel to make a path. He set up ladders in the bamboo groves, climbed up, cut the bamboo, and let it fall onto other bamboo thickets to walk across the tops. In the swamps, he laid dry wood in succession to walk over them. Then he laid a plank, stepped on it, took the plank he had just stepped on, and laid it in front again to cross the swamp. In the watery areas, he hollowed out a log to make a trough and crossed the water with it.

Standing at the foot of the mountain, he tied an iron hook (saṅkaku) to a rope, threw it to the mountain top to catch it, pulled the rope to climb, carved the mountain with an iron chisel as sharp as a thunderbolt, drove in an iron stake, stood on it, pulled up the iron hook, threw it higher again, and while standing on that iron stake, pulled the leather rope, took it, descended to tie it to the lower stake, held the rope with his left hand, took a mallet with his right hand, struck the rope to pull out the iron stake, and climbed again.

In this manner, having climbed to the mountain top, when descending the other side, he used the same method for other iron stakes. First, he drove an iron stake into the mountain top, tied a rope to a leather bag, wound it around the stake, and he himself stayed inside the bag, descending by loosening the coil of rope in the manner of a spider letting out its thread.

(Some also say he took the wind with a leather umbrella and descended like a bird.)

Thus, the All-Enlightened Buddha, wishing to reveal how the hunter took the words of Queen Subhaddā, departed from the city, crossed seventeen thickets, reached the mountain thicket, and there too crossed six thickets to ascend the summit of Suvaṇṇapassa Mountain, said:
49:
## 119. Having dug a pit, he covered it with planks;
The hunter, having hidden himself and his bow,
Struck the elephant that came near with a broad-headed arrow,
He who does evil deeds.

## 120. And the elephant, being pierced, let out a terrible trumpeting;
And all the elephants trumpeted a terrible sound.
Trampling grass and wood,
They ran in all eight directions.

## 121. Thinking \"I will kill him,\" as he reached out,
He saw the yellow robe, the banner of the seers.
To him touched by suffering, the thought arose:
\"The banner of the Arahats is not to be killed by the virtuous.\"

He preached these three verses.

119. Bhikkhave, O monks. Dukkaṭakammakārī, he who is prone to doing evil deeds. Luddo, the hunter Sonuttara. Kāsuṃ, the pit. Khaṇitvāna, having dug. Dhanuñca, the bow, and sarañca, the arrow. Abbhantare, inside the pit. Katvā, having placed. Phalakehi, with planks. Chādayi, he covered. Attānaṃ, himself. Odhāya, having entered and hidden. Passāgataṃ, who came near his pit. Nāgaṃ, the elephant king. Puthusallena, with a large poisoned arrow. Samappayi, he shot.

120. Bhikkhave, O monks. Viddho, shot by the hunter Sonuttara. Nāgo ca, the elephant king also. Ghoraṃ, a terrible. Koñcaṃ, trumpeting sound. Tikkhattuṃ, three times. Anādi, roared. Sabbe, all. Nāgā ca, the eight thousand elephants also. Ghorarūpaṃ, of a terrifying nature. Ninnaduṃ, made an echoing sound. Te, those eight thousand elephants. Tiṇañca, the grass, and kaṭṭhañca, the branches and leaves. Raṇaṃ, into pieces. Karonto, making and trampling. Samantato, from all around. Aṭṭhadisā, to the eight directions. Dhāviṃsu, they ran.

121. Bhikkhave, O monks. So, that Chaddanta elephant king. Etaṃ, this hunter Sonuttara. Vadhissanti, thinking \"I will kill him.\" Parāmasanto, while reaching out. Isīnaṃ, of the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahats who seek the collection of virtues such as the aggregate of virtue. Dhajaṃ, the banner. Kāsāvaṃ, the saffron robe. Addakkhi, he saw. Atha, then upon seeing it. Dukkhena, by suffering. Phuṭṭhassa, to the Bodhisatta who was oppressed. Arahaddhajo, that which is called the banner of Arahatship. Sabbhi, by the wise and virtuous. Avajjharūpo, is of a nature that should not be killed. Aññadatthu, indeed. Sakkātabboyeva, it is only to be honored. Iti ayaṃ saññā, such a perception. Udapādi, clearly arose.

Regarding how the hunter Sonuttara prepared the pit, this is the sequential account. That hunter Sonuttara reached the dwelling place of the Bodhisatta Chaddanta elephant king in seven years, seven months, and seven days. Having marked the dwelling place of the Bodhisatta in the manner already described, he thought, \"I will dig a pit here, and staying in that pit, I will shoot the elephant king with a poisoned arrow and bring him to the end of his life.\" Having decided this, he entered the forest, cut down trees for pillars and other needs, and prepared the building materials. When the elephants had gone to bathe, he dug a square pit at the elephant king's dwelling place with a large hoe. He scattered the excavated earth into the water as if sowing seeds. He set pillars upon stone mortars, placed beams and rafters, and laid down planks. He made a hole just large enough for an arrow to pass through. He covered the top with dust and refuse. He made an entrance for himself on one side. When the pit was finished, at dawn, he put on a head-covering, donned saffron-dyed robes, took his bow along with the poisoned arrow, descended into the pit, and stayed there.

The All-Knowing Exalted Buddha, wishing to make that matter clear, said:

The arrow of that hunter Sonuttara pierced through the navel of the Bodhisatta Chaddanta elephant king, crushing the internal organs such as the spleen and cutting the intestines. It exited through the back as if split by an axe and flew into the sky. Blood flowed from the wound where the arrow struck, like dye flowing from a broken dye-pot. Intense painful feelings arose.

That Bodhisatta elephant king, being unable to endure the painful feelings and having reached a state of suffering, roared a sound like a loud trumpeting three times, making the entire mountain echo simultaneously.
50:
All the eight thousand attendant elephants, upon hearing the sound of the Bodhisatta elephant king, became afraid of death and made a terrifying sound echoing the Bodhisatta elephant king's roar. Coming because of that sound and seeing the Bodhisatta elephant king in a state of painful suffering, they thought, \"We will catch the enemy,\" and they ran, trampling grass, leaves, and branches into pieces.

When the eight thousand attendant elephants had run in various directions, the Chief Queen named Subhaddā stood by his side, assisting and comforting him. The Bodhisatta elephant king, enduring the painful feelings, noted the direction from which the arrow came and thought, \"If this arrow had come from the east or other directions, it would have entered through the head or other parts and exited through the rear body. But this arrow entered through the navel and went out into the sky. Therefore, the enemy must be stationed inside the ground.\" Wishing to investigate the place where the enemy was stationed, he thought, \"Who can know this? How will it be? It is proper for Subhaddā to flee,\" and he said this:

\"Subhaddā, the eight thousand attendant elephants have run to the various directions to search for my enemy. But you, what are you doing near me?\" he asked.
51:
122. He who is not free from defilements, yet would don the yellow robe, being devoid of self-control and truth, he is not worthy of the yellow robe.

123. But he who has cast out defilements, is well-established in the virtues, and is endowed with self-control and truth, he indeed is worthy of the yellow robe.

This is the collection of these two verses.

122. Friend hunter, he who is not free from the stains of passion and defilements, and is devoid of the truth of self-restraint over the senses such as the eyes, yet wears the yellow-dyed cloth, that person is not worthy of that robe.

123. Friend hunter, but he who has vomited out the stains of defilements, who is well-established and perfected in the fourfold purity of virtue (catupārisuddhi-sīla), and who is endowed with the truth of self-restraint over the senses, that person who has discarded defilements is indeed worthy of the robe.

That Queen Subhaddā begged for forgiveness, saying, "O King, I stay to support and comfort you; please forgive me." After circumambulating him three times to the right and bowing to the four directions, as Queen Subhaddā flew into the sky, the Bodhisatta elephant king scratched the ground with his toenail and removed the plank covering the pit.

As the Bodhisatta looked through the opening where the plank was removed, he saw the hunter Sonuttara. He formed the thought, "I will kill that hunter," and as he extended his trunk—which was colored like a silver tassel—to seize him, he saw the yellow robe, which is the banner of the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahants. The hunter then placed the yellow robe in the Bodhisatta's trunk.

The Bodhisatta lifted the robe and placed it before him. At that time, even though the Bodhisatta was afflicted by such great pain, the right mindfulness arose in him: "The yellow robe, which is the banner of the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahants, is of a nature that should not be harmed by the wise; rather, it should be treated with utmost respect, honor, and devotion." Having reflected thus, the Bodhisatta wished to speak with the hunter.

After saying this, the Bodhisatta calmed his anger toward the hunter and asked: "Friend hunter, for what purpose do you shoot me? Is it for your own benefit, or were you incited by another?"

To clarify this matter, the Omniscient Buddha said—

When the Bodhisatta elephant king asked thus, the hunter Sonuttara, wishing to tell the reason for his killing to the Bodhisatta elephant king, said—
52:
124. The elephant, pierced by a great arrow, spoke to the hunter with a heart free from malice: "For what purpose, or for what reason, friend, did you kill me? Whose instigation is this?"

The Buddha taught this verse:

124. Monks, the elephant king, though pierced by a great arrow shot by the hunter, spoke thus to the hunter with a heart free from malice: "Friend hunter, for what purpose do you kill me? For what reason do you kill me? Whose instigation is this act?"

125. The chief queen of the King of Kāsi, named Subhaddā, who is honored in the royal house, saw you and told me, "I have need of his tusks."

126. There are many great pairs of tusks belonging to my fathers and grandfathers, which are well-collected and kept in the golden cave. That wrathful princess knows this; seeking my death, that foolish woman has harbored a grudge.

127. Rise, hunter, take your saw and cut these tusks of mine before I die. Tell that wrathful princess: "The elephant is slain; here are his tusks."

This is the collection of these two verses.

126. Friend hunter, there are many noble pairs of tusks belonging to my fathers and grandfathers that are well-stored in the golden cave. That princess Subhaddā, who follows the power of her anger, knows this well. Seeking my death, that foolish woman has harbored a grudge.

127. Friend hunter, rise up. Take the saw and cut these tusks of mine before I die. You should tell that wrathful princess Subhaddā: "I have killed the elephant king. Now, these are the tusks of that elephant king." Tell her that I have sent this message.

125. Lord elephant king, the chief queen of the King of Kāsi is named Subhaddā. That chief queen Subhaddā is honored in the royal palace. She saw you, the elephant king, in a dream. That chief queen Subhaddā herself told me, "I have need of the tusks endowed with six-colored rays." Thus she spoke to me.

Hearing the hunter's words, the Bodhisatta realized, "This is the work of Cūḷasubhaddā." Enduring the intense pain, he wished to tell the hunter: "That Subhaddā does not need my tusks; she sent you because she truly wants to kill me."

When the hunter Sonuttara heard the Bodhisatta's words, he rose from his place, took the saw, and approached him thinking, "I will cut the tusks." However, the Bodhisatta elephant king was eighty-eight cubits in height. Standing like a great silver mountain, he was unreachable, and the hunter Sonuttara could not reach the tusks.
53:
Because he could not reach, the Bodhisatta elephant king bent his body and lay prostrate. Then the hunter Sonuttara, treading on the Bodhisatta's trunk which was like a silver chain, climbed up and stood upon the elephant's frontal globes (kumbha) as if standing on the peak of Mount Kelāsa. He kicked the edge of the mouth with his knee, forced it open, and after descending from the head, inserted the saw into the mouth. Intense pain arose in the Bodhisatta. The mouth was filled with blood. As the hunter moved the saw back and forth, he was unable to cut them.

Then the Bodhisatta, spitting out the blood from his mouth and enduring the painful sensation, asked the hunter, "Friend hunter, why is it? Are you unable to cut them?" When he replied, "Lord, I am unable," the Bodhisatta, establishing mindfulness, said, "Friend hunter, if that is so, lift my trunk and let me hold the end of the saw. I no longer have the strength to lift the trunk myself." The hunter did as the Bodhisatta said. The Bodhisatta took the saw with his trunk and moved it to and fro. The tusks were cut like tender roots.

Then, having the hunter bring those tusks, he held them with his trunk and said, "Friend hunter, in giving these tusks to you, I do not give them thinking 'these are tusks I do not love or cherish.' I do not give them longing for the prosperity of Sakka, nor for the prosperity of Māra, nor for the prosperity of Brahmā. Indeed, I love the tusks of omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and a hundred-thousandfold more than these tusks. May this merit of mine be a condition for the penetration of omniscience."

Having given the tusks, he asked, "Friend hunter, how long did it take you to come to this place?" When the hunter replied, "It took seven years, seven months, and seven days," the Bodhisatta said, "Go then. By the power of these tusks, you shall reach Bārāṇasī within only seven days." He then performed a protection (paritta) for the hunter and sent him away. After he had sent him away, before the eight thousand attendant elephants and the Chief Queen Mahāsubhaddā arrived, he passed away.

The Omniscient Buddha, wishing to make this matter clear, said:
54:
128. That hunter, having risen and taken the saw,
Having cut the tusks of the noble elephant,
Taking the beautiful, peerless, and excellent tusks on earth,
Quickly departed from there.

The Buddha preached this verse:

128. Monks, that hunter Sonuttara, having risen, took the saw and cut the tusks of the noble elephant. Taking those tusks—which were endowed with grace, beautiful, and peerless among any other tusks on this earth—he quickly departed from that place called Visālamālaka.

129. Afflicted by fear due to the killing of the elephant,
Those elephants fled in the eight directions.
Not seeing the person who was the elephant's enemy,
They returned to where the elephant king was.

The Buddha preached this verse:

129. Monks, those eight thousand elephants, who were oppressed by the fear of death from the elephant-killer and reached suffering, fled in the eight directions. Those eight thousand elephants, not seeing the man who was the enemy of the elephant king, returned to the place called Visālamālaka where that elephant king was.

When that hunter Sonuttara had gone, those eight thousand elephants returned, not having seen the enemy. The Omniscient Buddha, wishing to make this matter clear, said—

Along with those eight thousand elephants, the Chief Queen Mahāsubhaddā also arrived. All those elephants wept and lamented at that place, Visālamālaka. They went to the presence of the Paccekabuddhas who were the teachers of the Bodhisatta elephant king and said, "Venerable sirs, the elephant king who was your supporter of the four requisites has been shot with a poisoned arrow and has died. Please come to perform the funeral rites at his cemetery."

Five hundred Paccekabuddhas came through the air and descended at Visālamālaka. At that moment, two young elephants lifted the body of the elephant king with their tusks, made it pay respects to the Paccekabuddhas, placed it upon a pyre, and cremated it. The Paccekabuddhas performed the recitation of the Dhamma throughout the three watches of the night at the elephant king's cemetery.
55:
130. Those elephants, wailing and weeping there,
Scattering funeral ashes on their own heads,
They all went to their own abode,
Placing the Great Queen, the all-auspicious one, at their head.

The Teacher spoke this verse:

130. "O Bhikkhus, those elephants, wailing and weeping there at the Visālamālaka, scattering funeral ashes on their own heads, all those eight thousand elephants, having surrounded the Great Queen named Sabbabhaddā, went to their own dwelling place."

131. Taking the tusks of the noble elephant,
Beautiful, auspicious, and incomparable on earth,
Shining all around with golden streaks,
That hunter approached the city of Kāsi.
He presented the tusks to the royal daughter,
Saying, 'The elephant is killed; behold, these are his tusks.'

The Teacher spoke this verse:

131. "O Bhikkhus, that hunter, taking the tusks of the noble elephant—tusks that were full of grace and beauty, incomparable to any other tusks on earth, and shining all around with rays from golden streaks, making the entire forest grove appear golden in color—arrived at the city of Bārāṇasī. That hunter Sonuttara said, 'O Queen, I have killed the Chaddanta elephant king. Now, these are his tusks,' and presented them to the royal daughter, Queen Subhaddā."

The eight thousand elephants, having extinguished the funeral fire, paid their respects, bathed, and then returned to their own place, with the Great Queen Mahāsubhaddā at their head.

To clarify this matter, the Omniscient Buddha spoke:

Sonuttara the hunter, taking the tusks of the elephant king, reached the city of Bārāṇasī before seven days had passed. To clarify this matter, the Omniscient Buddha spoke:
56:
132. Seeing the tusks of the noble elephant,
Her beloved husband in a previous birth,
Right there her heart broke;
Because of that, she, the foolish one, died.

The Teacher spoke this verse:

132. "O Bhikkhus, seeing the tusks of the noble elephant who was her beloved husband in a previous life, right there the heart of Queen Subhaddā broke. Because of that broken heart, that foolish woman died."

133. The young maiden you see now,
Wearing saffron robes and living the homeless life,
She was then the royal daughter Subhaddā,
I was then the elephant king.

134. Taking the tusks of the noble elephant,
Beautiful, auspicious, and incomparable on earth,
The hunter who approached the city of Kāsi,
He was then Devadatta.

135. This ancient conduct, practiced for a long time,
High and low, through many lives,
The Buddha, free from distress, sorrow, and arrows,
Having known it himself, spoke.

136. I was there at that time, O monks,
I was then the elephant king;
Thus remember the Jātaka.

The Teacher spoke these four verses:

133. "O Bhikkhus, do you see this young nun who has now reached maturity, wearing saffron-dyed robes, who has entered the homeless life and practices my teachings? At that time, she was the royal daughter Subhaddā. And now, I, the Buddha, was at that time the Chaddanta elephant king."

134. "O Bhikkhus, the hunter Sonuttara who took the beautiful, auspicious tus of the noble elephant—tusks incomparable to any others on earth—and went to the city of Bārāṇasī, that hunter was at that time Devadatta."

135. "O Bhikkhus, just as one can remember what was done in the morning before sunset, I, your teacher the Buddha—who is called 'Vītaddara' due to the absence of the heat of passions like lust, 'Vītasoka' due to the absence of sorrow over relatives or wealth, and 'Vītasalla' due to the absence of the arrows of lust—having known for myself this ancient conduct, which is high due to my own practice and low due to the conduct of Queen Subhaddā and the hunter Sonuttara, have preached it."

136. "O Bhikkhus, at that time, I was at that Chaddanta lake. Though I was there, I was not just any ordinary elephant; indeed, I was the elephant king. O monks, you should thus remember this connection of the Jātaka."

That Queen Subhaddā, receiving the tusks of the Bodhisatta elephant king—which were adorned with six-colored rays—upon a jeweled fan and placing them on her lap, looked at the tusks of her beloved husband from a previous life. Thinking, "The hunter Sonuttara has come after killing my beloved husband, who possessed such a mass of beauty, with a poisoned arrow and cutting off these tusks," she brooded in grief. Remembering the Bodhisatta, she was overcome with sorrow and, unable to bear it, her heart broke right there, and she died that very day.

To clarify this matter, the Omniscient Buddha spoke:
57:
These verses were established by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma, praising the virtues of the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala).

The Omniscient Buddha, who had attained Supreme Enlightenment and possessed great power, smiled in the midst of the fourfold assembly. Thinking, "Buddhas do not smile without a reason," the great Arahants, whose minds were fully liberated from defilements, asked for the reason. Thereupon, the Buddha related this Chaddanta Jātaka Dhamma teaching. Many who heard this teaching attained the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpanna) and so forth. As for that young nun, she later developed insight and attained Arahatship.

Having related this Dhamma teaching and wishing to conclude the Jātaka, the Omniscient Buddha identified the birth:

## Patience leads to Nibbāna, a true blessing.

The Chaddanta Jātaka is finished.

## 5. Sambhava Jātaka
## Regarding the Question of the Dhamma-yāga

The Present Story: While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened Buddha, who instructs the world including the devas, told this Sambhava Jātaka, adorned with the verses beginning with 'Rajjañca paṭipannāsma', concerning the Perfection of Wisdom.

The Present Story will be clearly revealed in the Mahāummagga Jātaka.

The Past Story: Long ago, in the city of Indapatta in the Kuru kingdom, a king named Dhanañjaya Koravya reigned. For this King Dhanañjaya Koravya, a brahmin named Sucirata was the chaplain and advisor on welfare and Dhamma. King Dhanañjaya Koravya, performing meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna), governed the country in accordance with the Ten Royal Virtues.

One day, King Dhanañjaya Koravya, having formulated a question called the Dhamma-yāga, seated his chaplain, the teacher Sucirata, on a seat and paid him honor and respect. Wishing to ask the question—

This Dhamma-yāga question is extremely profound. It is the domain of the Fully Enlightened Buddhas.
59:
141. O King, no one other than Vidhura is worthy of explaining this—the benefit and the Dhamma that you, O Khattiya, desire to practice.

142. O Teacher Sucirata, come. As my messenger, go to the presence of the wise Vidhura. Go, O Sucirata, taking this thousand nikkhas of gold. Give this gift for instruction in the benefit and the Dhamma.

141. O Great King, whatever benefit and whatever cause you desire to undertake and practice, O King, ruler of the land, no one other than the brahmin named Vidhura is worthy of answering that.
142. O Teacher Sucirata, come. As my messenger, go to the presence of the wise Vidhura. Go, taking this thousand nikkhas of gold. Give this gift so that he may instruct us in the benefit and the Dhamma.

It is appropriate to ask only the Fully Enlightened Buddha. In the absence of the Fully Enlightened Buddha, it is appropriate to ask a Bodhisatta who seeks Omniscience. The brahmin Sucirata, because he was not a Bodhisatta, was unable to answer that question. Although he could not, without pride in being a wise man, he wished to inform the king of his inability—

King Koravya, hearing the words of the chaplain Sucirata, said, "Teacher, if that is so, go quickly to the presence of Vidhura." Wishing to send the chaplain Sucirata, he gave him gifts—

In this verse, the method of defining a nikkha should be understood as follows: Four grains of barley are one chiñ-yway. Two chiñ-yway are one pè. Ten pè are one akkha. Eight akkha are one dharaṇa. Five dharaṇa are one suvaṇṇa. Five suvaṇṇa are one nikkha. Thus it is defined in the dictionary. In this Jātaka commentary, however, it is said that fifteen suvaṇṇa make one nikkha.

Having said this, he gave a gold plate worth a hundred thousand to record the answer, a vehicle for the journey, an army for an escort, and the gifts, and sent him off at that very moment.

The brahmin Sucirata, having departed from the city of Indapatta, did not go directly to the city of Bārāṇasī, but went to wherever wise men resided.

Having approached all various places and not finding the means to solve the problem in the whole of Jambudīpa, he eventually reached the city of Vārāṇasī. The All-Knowing Buddha, wishing to make this matter clear, said:

Vidhura had been a friend of the Brahmin Sucirata since childhood. They were fellow students under the same teacher. At that time, the Brahmin Vidhura was judging cases as if blocking the Ganges River, thinking, 'I will win the hearts of the people.' There was no opportunity to answer that question. Vidhura, wishing to inform the Brahmin Sucirata of that reason, said:

152. Youth Sañjaya, I am a messenger sent by the King named Koravya, who has a large retinue. Our lord King Koravya, of the Yudhiṭṭhila clan, says, 'You ask about the meaning and the law.' Being asked, you please explain that meaning and that law.
When he said this, the youth Bhadrakāra said to the priest Sucīrata: "Father, these days my heart is set on committing misconduct with another's wife, and my mind is troubled. Therefore, father, I am unable to answer you. My younger brother named Sañjaya is much more exceptionally wise than I. Ask that youth Sañjaya; he will answer your question." Thus, wishing to send him to the presence of the youth Sañjaya—
At that moment, the priest Sucīrata went to the presence of the youth Sañjaya, and when asked the reason for his coming after being offered hospitality by Sañjaya, he explained the reason for his arrival. The All-Knowing Buddha, wishing to make that matter clear, said:
At that time, the youth Sañjaya was also consorting with another's wife. Because of such consorting, the youth Sañjaya said to the priest Sucīrata: "Father, I am consorting with another's wife. While consorting, I cross the Ganges River to the other bank. Death is said to swallow me, who crosses the river both evening and morning. Therefore, my mind is troubled. I will not be able to answer you, father. There is my younger brother, the youth Sambhava, who is only seven years old from birth. He possesses wisdom that is a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and a hundred-thousandfold greater than mine."

154. Sambhava is my brother, my younger brother, O Sucīrata. Go and ask him, O Brahmin, about the meaning and the law.

154. Sucīrata, teacher Sucīrata. There is my younger brother, the brother named Sambhava. Brahmin, you go and ask my brother Sambhava about the meaning and the law.
155. O sirs, this matter is indeed wonderful! This does not please us. Three people—father and sons—among them, they do not know through wisdom.

He spoke these two verses.
155. O sirs, this problem is indeed something that has never happened among men. We cannot be pleased with this boy. The father, the wise Vidhura, and the sons, Bhadrakāra and Sañjaya—even these three, father and sons, do not know this problem through wisdom.

Desiring to make that matter clear, the Omniscient Buddha said:

The Bodhisatta, the youth Sambhava, seeing the Brahmin Sujīrata arrive and stand before him, asked, "Father, for what reason have you come?" When Sujīrata replied, "Dear son Sambhava, though I have wandered across the surface of Jambudīpa, I have not found anyone capable of answering the question I asked, and thus I have come to you," Sambhava thought, "It is said that a question undecided in the whole of Jambudīpa has come to me; I am indeed great in wisdom." Having gained a sense of shame and fear (hiri-ottappa), he discarded the dust in his hands, took the cloth from his shoulder and dressed himself, saying, "Father Sujīrata, please ask; I shall answer your question with the grace of a Buddha," thus making the declaration of omniscience.

Thereafter, the Brahmin Sujīrata asked the question with this verse:

170. "I am a messenger sent by the King, the renowned Koravya. Yudhiṭṭhila said, 'Ask about the Meaning and the Dhamma.' Being asked, O Sambhava, explain that Meaning and the Dhamma."

170. Kumāra, youth Sambhava. Ahaṃ, I. Yasassino, of the one with a great retinue. Koravyassa, named Koravya. Rañño, of the sovereign King. Pahito, sent. Dūto, am a messenger. Yudhiṭṭhilo, our lord King Koravya of the Yudhiṭṭhila lineage. Atthañca, the benefit. Dhammañca, and the cause. Pucchesi, you should ask. Iti, thus. Abravi, he said. Sambhava, friend Sambhava. Pucchito, being asked by me. Tvaṃ, you. Taṃ atthañca, that benefit. Taṃ dhammañca, and that cause. Akkhāhi, please explain.

Then, saying to the Brahmin Sujīrata, "Father, if that is so, then listen," he desired to answer the question on the sacrifice of Dhamma (Dhamma-yāga).

Standing in the middle of the main road, the voice of the Bodhisatta preaching the Dhamma with a sweet tone pervaded the entire city of Bārāṇasī, which was twelve yojanas in extent.
67:
172. "If asked by the King, 'Shall we do it today or tomorrow?', O Sujīrata, one should say so. Let the King Yudhiṭṭhila not live in negligence when a benefit has arisen.

173. "One should explain only the internal, O Sujīrata, when asked by the King. Let him not enter the wrong path, like a deluded and mindless person.

174. "One should not overstep oneself; one should not practice unrighteousness. One should not descend into a non-ford; one should not be joined with what is useless.

175. "The Khattiya who knows how to perform these things, that King always grows like the moon in the waxing phase.

176. "He becomes dear to his kinsmen and shines among his friends. With the breaking of the body, that wise one arises in heaven."

172. Tāta Sujīrata, father Brahmin Sujīrata. Raññā, if by your lord King. Ajja, today. Kusalaṃ, merit. Karissāma, shall we perform? Iti, thus. Puṭṭho, being asked. 173. Sujīrata, father Brahmin Sujīrata. Rājā, the King who asks you, father. Puṭṭho, being asked. Ajjhattanyeva, only the collection of the five aggregates. Saṃseyya, preach as impermanent. Mūḷho, a deluded one. Acetaso, a foolish worldling who lacks a mind associated with right view. Kummaggaṃ, the wrong path known as the sixty-two types of wrong view. Sevati yathā, just as he resorts to. Evaṃ, in this same way. Rājā, your lord King. Kummaggaṃ, the wrong path known as the sixty-two types of wrong view. Na niveseyya, should not resort to.

174. Brāhmaṇa, father Brahmin Sujīrata. Attānaṃ, oneself who is established in a happy state. Nātivatteyya, should not perform actions that lead to the four woeful states, overstepping human and divine bliss. Adhammaṃ, the evil practice known as the three types of misconduct. Na samācare, should not practice. Atitthe, in the non-ford known as the sixty-two types of wrong view. Nappatāreyya, should not descend. Anatthe, in what is useless. Yuto, joined. Na siyā, should not be.

175. Brāhmaṇa, father Brahmin Sujīrata. Yo khattiyo, whichever King. Etāni ṭhānāni, these matters I have preached. Kattuṃ, to perform. Jānāti, knows. So khattiyo, that King. Sukkapakkhe, in the waxing phase of the moon. Candimāva, like the moon. Sadā, at all times. Vaḍḍhate, shall increase in retinue and wealth.

176. Ñātīnañca, to kinsmen also. Piyo, dear. Hoti, he becomes. Mittesu ca, and among friends. Virocati, he shines. Kāyassa bhedā, after the breaking of the body of the karma-born form. Paraṃ, after. Sappañño, the wise one. So rājā, that King. Saggaṃ, to heaven. Upapajjati, reaches.

At that time, the King, the crown prince, and all the people assembled. The Bodhisatta brought forth the Dhamma teaching in the midst of the multitude.

Having thus acknowledged the answering of the question with this verse, now desiring to answer the question on the sacrifice of Dhamma:
68: When the youth Sambhava answered the Brahmin Sucirata's question with the grace of the All-Knowing Buddha, as if making the moon rise in the sky, the people shouted, clapped their hands, and gave a thousand cheers. They threw clothes and snapped their fingers. They also threw bracelets, armlets, rings, and so on. The wealth thus thrown amounted to one crore.
69:
The King of Bārāṇasī was also greatly pleased with the youth Sambhava and bestowed upon him much wealth and many attendants. The brahmin Sucīrata also honored him with a thousand gold nikkhas, wrote the answer to the question on a gold plate with genuine cinnabar, and then went to the city of Indapattha to answer the question called Dhamma-yāga for his lord, King Koravya. King Koravya, having practiced according to that Dhamma-yāga, filled the heavenly realm.

Identifying the Jātaka, the All-Knowing Buddha brought forth this Dhamma teaching and said, "Monks, not only now is your teacher of great wisdom; in the past also, he was indeed of great wisdom," and then he identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Ānanda was King Dhanañjaya Koravya, Anuruddha was the brahmin Sucīrata, Mahākassapa was the wise Vidhura, Moggallāna was the youth Bhadrakāra, Sāriputta was the youth Sañjaya, and I myself was the wise Sambhava."

## Brave in wisdom, prominent in the assembly, exalted in glory.

The Sambhava Jātaka ends.

## 6. Mahākapi Jātaka

## On becoming a human-peta for offending a benefactor

The Teacher, the All-Knowing One who disciplines the world including the devas, while residing at Veluvana Monastery, told this Mahākapi Jātaka, adorned with verses beginning with "Bārāṇasyaṃ ahū rājā," concerning Devadatta's attempt to roll a stone [at him].

That story is true. After Devadatta had dispatched archers, he later made an effort to kill the Buddha by rolling a stone. When the monks were speaking words of blame regarding Devadatta's lack of gratitude, the All-Knowing Buddha said, "Monks, not only now has Devadatta rolled a stone at me; in the past also, he did roll one down," and he brought forth the past.
70:
In the past, monks, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, a certain brahmin farmer living in a Kāsī village, after plowing his field, released his oxen and began to work with a hoe. The oxen, while eating leaves in a thicket, gradually entered the forest and ran away. The farmer, noting the time, put down his hoe and looked for the oxen, but not seeing them, he became distressed. While searching for the oxen and wandering inside the forest, he entered the Himalayas.

That brahmin searching for his oxen lost his way in the Himalayan forest and, having traveled for seven days without food, saw a Tinduka tree. He climbed the tree and, while eating the Tinduka fruits, slipped from the tree and fell into a sixty-cubit deep abyss. Then, ten days passed for that brahmin who had fallen into the abyss.

At that time, the Bodhisatta was born in the monkey species. While eating various fruits, he saw the man. He practiced with stones [to test his strength], rescued the man from the abyss, and placed him on a small rock plateau. The Bodhisatta said, "O brahmin, I am very exhausted; I will sleep for a moment, please watch over me."

While the Bodhisatta was sleeping, that brahmin split the Bodhisatta's head with a stone. The Great Being, knowing his deed, jumped up and sat on a branch, saying, "O man, you go by the ground; I will go along the treetops showing you the way." Having led the man out of the forest and placed him on the road, he returned to the foot of the mountain. That man, having offended the Great Being, became a leper and was a human-peta in this very life.

Wandering for seven years oppressed by suffering, he entered the garden named Migājina in Bārāṇasī, spread a banana leaf between the walls, and lay down in pain. At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī went to the garden and, while wandering there, saw him and asked, "Who are you? What have you done to reach this suffering?" The man told him everything in detail. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:

177. There was a king in Bārāṇasī, the prosperer of the Kāsī realm. Surrounded by friends and ministers, he went to the Migājina garden.

178. There he saw a brahmin, white and speckled with leprosy, like a withered Koviḷāra tree, thin and covered with veins.

179. Seeing the man who had reached extreme misery and fallen into distress, the King, being frightened, said, "Which of the yakkhas are you?"

180. "Your hands and feet are white, and your head is even whiter than them. Your body is of a mottled color, and you are full of scabs."

181. "Your back is uneven, resembling a string of beads. Your limbs are like black knotted vines; I have never seen another like this."

182. "Your feet are covered in dust, you are terrified, thin, and covered with veins. You are hungry and parched; from where have you come? Where are you going?"

183. "Friend, you are ill-looking, of bad form, of ugly complexion, and of fearsome appearance. Even your own mother who gave birth to you would not wish to see you."

184. "What deed did you do in the past? Whom that should not be killed did you slay? Having committed what crime have you come to this suffering?"

The Teacher spoke these eight verses.
71:
The Bodhisatta, knowing the Brahmin's intention, leaped up and stayed on a tree branch. He said, "O man, you travel by the ground; I shall go by the tips of the branches, guiding you on the way." Having led the man out of the forest and left him on the path of humans, he entered the foot of the mountain.

Because that Brahmin had offended the Bodhisatta, he became a leper and turned into a human-peta in this very life. For seven years, oppressed by suffering, he wandered until he entered the Migāzina Garden in the city of Bārāṇasī. There, he lay down on banana leaves spread between the walls, experiencing intense pain.

At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī went to the garden. While wandering there, he saw the human-peta and asked, "Who are you? What action did you perform to fall into such misery?" The human-peta then related the whole story in detail to the King of Bārāṇasī.

The Omniscient Buddha, wishing to clarify this matter, said:

Then the Brahmin, who had become a human-peta, wishing to inform the King of Bārāṇasī who had questioned him:
72:
185. "Indeed, I will tell you, just as it happened. For the wise in this world praise one who speaks the truth."

... [etc.]
74:
He spoke these thirty-seven verses, beginning with: "I tell you this, sirs, as many as are gathered here. Do not betray your friends, for a betrayer of friends is evil."

185. "Great King, I will tell you truly, just as a wise man speaks. Indeed, the wise in this world praise one who speaks the truth."

186-7. "Great King, while I was wandering alone searching for my cattle, I lost my way in the forest and, passing beyond the paths of men, reached the Himālaya. I was lost in a desolate, dry, and difficult wilderness, a forest frequented by various elephants and wild beasts. There, I wandered for seven days, oppressed by hunger and thirst."

188. "There, in the Himālaya, I saw a Tinduka tree standing on uneven ground, hanging over a precipice, and bearing ripe, sweet fruit. I was oppressed by intense hunger."

189. "I ate the Tinduka fruits that had fallen, blown by the wind. They pleased me greatly. Not being satisfied, I thought, 'I will climb the tree and eat my fill,' and so I climbed the tree."

190. "Great King, I had eaten one fruit and was longing for a second. As I stretched out my hand for that desired fruit, the branch I had climbed broke, as if cut by an axe."

191. "Great King, I fell together with the branches, feet up and head down, into a mountain abyss that had no foothold or anything to cling to."

192. "Because the water was sixty cubits deep, I could not reach level ground. There, devoid of joy, I lay for ten full nights."

193. "Great King, then a monkey king, a dweller of the cliffs with a black muzzle, came to that place, moving from branch to branch and eating forest fruits."

194. "Great King, that monkey king, seeing me thin and pale, felt compassion for me. He asked, 'O man, who are you? You are oppressed by suffering here.'"

195. "'Are you a human or a non-human? Tell me about yourself.' Thus he asked. I raised my joined palms to him and spoke these words:"

196. "'O King of Monkeys, I am a human who has met with ruin. I have no other way out from here. Therefore, I say to you, may you be well. Please be my refuge.'"

197. "Great King, the monkey, having moved about the mountain, took a heavy stone and practiced lifting it. Then that noble being spoke these words:"

198. "'Come, man, climb onto my back and clasp my neck with both arms. I will lift you out of this mountain abyss with speed.'"

199. "Great King, hearing his words, I climbed onto the back of that glorious and wise monkey king and clasped his neck with both arms."

200. "Great King, that powerful and mighty monkey, though struggling with the effort, rescued me from that mountain abyss with speed."

201. "Great King, after rescuing me, that wise and noble being spoke these words: 'Friend, I urge you, watch over me for a moment while I sleep.'"

202. "'There are lions, tigers, leopards, bears, and hyenas. They might harm me while I am heedless. If you see them, ward them off.'"

203. "Great King, thus that monkey, having placed himself under my protection, slept for a moment. Then, I conceived a wicked and improper thought:"

204. "'Just as other beasts in the forest are food for humans, so is this monkey fit to be eaten. I am hungry. What if I kill and eat this monkey?'"

205. "'After eating my fill, I will take the monkey meat as provisions and go. I will escape this difficult journey. It will be my travel ration.' Thus I thought."

206. "Great King, after thinking thus, I took a stone and struck him on the head. But because my body was exhausted, my blow was weak."

207. "Great King, that monkey quickly sprang up, smeared with blood, and looked at me, weeping with eyes full of tears."

208. "'Sir, may you be well. Do not do such a thing to me. Though I rescued you from the abyss, you have done such a cruel deed. Long-lived one, a person like you should indeed ward off other enemies.'"

209. "'O man, doer of evil deeds! Oh, how strange! I lifted you from such an uneven, difficult precipice.'"

210. "'O man, I brought you back as if from the next world. Yet you, being wicked, thought of that evil. You thought to betray me with such a wicked act.'"

211. "'O unrighteous one, even though you have acted thus, may you not meet with such bitter pain as I have felt. May that evil deed not destroy you, just as the fruit of the bamboo destroys the bamboo plant.'"

212. "'O wicked and unrestrained one, I have no trust in you. Come, follow behind me, keeping yourself in my sight.'"

213. "'O unrighteous one, you are now free from the hands of wild beasts and have reached a place near humans. This is your path; go as you please.'"

214. "Great King, having said this, the mountain-dwelling monkey washed his blood-stained head in a lake, wiped away his tears, and then returned, climbing back up the mountain."

215. "Great King, I was cursed by that monkey with those words. Therefore, oppressed by a body burning with the fire of painful feelings, I approached a lake to drink water."

216. "Great King, the entire lake appeared to me as if it were burning with fire, smeared with blood, and looking like pus and gore."

217. "Great King, as many drops of water as fell on my body, that many boils, the size of half a bael fruit, arose."

218-9. "Great King, those boils burst and foul-smelling pus and blood flowed out. Wherever I go, in villages or towns, men and women with sticks in their hands ward me off, saying, 'Evil creature, surrounded by a foul stench, do not come near us!'"

220. "Great King, I have been experiencing this suffering for seven years now. I am undergoing the results of my own evil deeds committed in the past."

221. "Great King, therefore I tell you all who are gathered here: may you be well. Do not betray your friends. Truly, a betrayer of friends is very evil."

222. "He who betrays friends in this world becomes a leper or is afflicted with white leprosy. After the breakup of the body, the betrayer of friends is reborn in hell."

To show the danger of betraying friends, the All-Enlightened Buddha, after attaining Buddhahood, spoke this verse:
75: Even as that wretched man was speaking with the King of Bārāṇasī, the earth opened up. At the very moment the earth opened, he passed away and was reborn in the Avīci Hell. When the man was swallowed by the earth, the King of Bārāṇasī left the Migādāya and entered the city.
76: Having delivered this Dhamma teaching of the Mahākapi Jātaka, the Omniscient Buddha identified the birth-story: "Monks, not only now has Devadatta rolled a stone at me; in the past, he also rolled a stone at me." He said, "At that time, Devadatta was the wretched man who betrayed his friend."
77:
"And I myself was the Monkey King at that time." Thus he identified the birth-story.

## For the one who is ungrateful to a benefactor, that person is ruined.

The Mahākapi Jātaka is finished.

## 8. Paṇḍaranāgarāja Jātaka

## Being Swallowed by the Earth Due to Lying

The Present Story: While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Paṇḍaranāgarāja Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Vikiṇṇavācaṃ," concerning Devadatta being swallowed by the earth because of telling lies.

This is the truth. At that time, when the monks were speaking about the lack of virtue and the blame of Devadatta, the Omniscient Buddha said, "Monks, not only now has Devadatta been swallowed by the earth for telling lies; in the past, he was also swallowed by the earth for telling lies." Having said this, he brought forth the past.
79:
Story of the Past: Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, five hundred merchants went to sea by ship. On the seventh day, not seeing the shore, the ship was wrecked in the middle of the ocean. Except for one man, the rest of the crew became food for fish and turtles. That man, driven by the force of the wind, reached the port named Karampiya.

Emerging from the sea, he adopted the guise of a naked ascetic and went into that port to seek food. People praised him, saying, "This monk has few desires and is easily contented," and they paid him honor and offerings.

Thinking, "I have found a means of livelihood," he did not desire the clothes offered by the people. The people, thinking, "There is no monk more wanting in desires than this one," were greatly inspired with faith. They built a monastery for him and let him reside there. He became famous as the "Karampiya Acelaka." This ascetic living at the Karampiya port received great offerings and honors.

At that time, both a Naga king and a Garuda king came to wait upon that ascetic. Between the two, the Naga king was named Paṇḍaraka. Then one day, the Garuda king went to the ascetic, paid homage, and sitting in a suitable place, spoke thus: "Venerable Sir, when our kinsmen capture Nagas, many Garudas perish."
80:
He spoke these eight verses:

223. One who speaks scatteredly, whose counsel is not hidden,
Who is unrestrained and does not investigate [the listener].
Fear follows such an ignorant person,
Just as the Supaṇṇa follows the Naga Paṇḍaraka.

224. A man who, out of delusion, joyfully reveals
A secret counsel that should be protected.
Fear quickly follows that person of broken counsel,
Just as the Supaṇṇa follows the Naga Paṇḍaraka.

225. A false friend is not worthy to know a serious and secret matter.
Even a good friend who is unwise, or a wise one who acts against one's interest, is not worthy.

I placed my trust in that naked ascetic.
To him, I revealed my secret matter;
Now, having lost my purpose, I weep piteously.

227. O Great Being (Brahme), I was unable to restrain
This most secret word of mine to that ascetic.
Indeed, from his side, fear has come upon me;
Now, having lost my purpose, I weep piteously.

228. A man who, thinking someone is a true friend,
Reveals a secret matter to one of low birth.

229. One whose speech is indirect and uncovered, who enters among the wicked,
Who utters secret words in assemblies.
