"We do not know the method by which those Nagas are captured. Those Nagas must have a secret reason. Would you, venerable sir, be able to act as if you are close friends and ask them for that reason?" the Garuda asked. The ascetic agreed, saying, "Very well." When the Garuda King had paid respects and left, and the Naga King arrived, the ascetic, while receiving the Naga King's respects, questioned him.

"O Naga King, when the Garudas capture you, many Garudas perish. Why is it that the Garudas who try to capture you are unable to do so?" he asked. "Venerable sir, this matter is our secret. If I were to speak of this matter, it would bring about the destruction of all my kinsmen," the Naga replied. "O Naga King, do you think I would tell this to others? I will not tell this to anyone else. I ask only because I wish to know. You may speak without fear, trusting in me," the ascetic said. The Naga King said, "Venerable sir, I will not speak," and after paying respects, he departed. The next day, the ascetic asked again. On that day too, the Naga did not tell the ascetic.

Then, on the third day, when the Naga King came, the ascetic asked, "O Naga King, it has been three days now that I have asked you. Why do you not speak?" "Venerable sir, I do not speak because I fear that you will tell others," the Naga replied. "I will not tell anyone else."
81:
"Speak without fear," the ascetic said. Then, the Naga King took a promise from him, saying, "Venerable sir, in that case, please do not tell anyone else."

"Venerable sir, we swallow large stones and, becoming heavy, we lie down. When the Garudas come, we open our mouths and show our teeth as if to bite. When those Garudas come and seize us by the head, they struggle to lift us because we are very heavy. While they try to pull us out of the water, the water overwhelms them. Those Garudas sink and die right there in the water. For this reason, many Garudas perish. What is the use of those foolish Garudas seizing us by the head? If they were to hold us by the tail, keeping our heads downward, and make us vomit the swallowed food so that we become light, they would be able to fly away with us." Thus, the Naga King Paṇḍaraka revealed their secret to that immoral naked ascetic.

When the Naga King left, the Garuda King came, paid respects to the ascetic Karampiya, and asked, "Venerable sir, have you asked the Naga King for the secret?" The ascetic replied, "I have asked," and told him everything exactly as the Naga King had described.
82:
231. Ko nīdha tiṇṇāṃ garahaṃ upeti.
Asmīdha loke pāṇabhū nāgarāja.
Samaṇo supaṇṇo athavā tvameva,

Hearing the words spoken by the ascetic, the Garuḷa King thought, "The Nāga King has spoken inappropriately; one should not reveal the cause of the destruction of one's kinsmen to others. Nevertheless, this very day, I should create a Garuḷa-wind and first seize that Nāga King." Having thought thus, the Garuḷa King created a Garuḷa-wind, seized the Nāga King Paṇḍaraka by the tail, turned him upside down, made him drop the food he had taken, and leaped up, flying into the sky.

Paṇḍaraka the Nāga King, hanging upside down in the sky, lamented, saying, "I alone have brought about my own suffering."

Thus, while Paṇḍaraka the Nāga King lamented with eight verses while hanging upside down in the sky, the Garuḷa King heard his voice and, desiring to reproach him, said, "O Nāga King, having told your secret to a naked ascetic, why do you cry now?" and spoke this verse:

Kiṃ kāraṇā paṇḍarakaggahito.

231. O Nāga King, in this world of living beings, who among the three of us here—the ascetic, the Garuḷa, or yourself—incurs reproach? Would the ascetic monk incur reproach? Or would the Garuḷa King incur reproach? Or is it you yourself who incurs reproach? O Paṇḍaraka the Nāga King, for what reason did the Garuḷa King seize me? Having thought thus, reproach only yourself.
83:
Hearing these words, Paṇḍaraka the Nāga King, wishing to explain his reasons to the Garuḷa King, spoke this verse:

232. Samaṇāti me sammattatto ahosi,
Piyo ca me manasā bhāvitatto.
Tassāhamakkhiṃ vivariṃ guyhamatthaṃ,
Atītamattho kapaṇaṃ rudāmi.

232. O Garuḷa King, I regarded that ascetic monk as a virtuous person. He was dear to me, and I considered him to be noble-minded. Thinking thus, I spoke and revealed my secret to that ascetic. Now, with my welfare gone, I cry in my desolation.

Thereafter, the Garuḷa King, showing that one should not fear death, said, "Do not reproach the blameless naked ascetic; reproach only yourself." Desiring to preach the Dhamma to Paṇḍaraka the Nāga King, he spoke these four verses:

233. Na catthi satto amaro pathabyā,
Pajñāvimā natthi na ninditabbā.
Saccena dhammena dhitiyā damena,
Alabbhamabyāharatī naro idha.

234. Mātā pitā paramā bandhavānaṃ,
Nāssa tatiyo anukampakatthi.
Tesampi guyhaṃ paramaṃ na saṃse,
Mantassa bhedaṃ parisaṅkamāno.

235. Mātā pitā bhaginī bhātaro ca,
Sahāyā vā yassa honti sapakkhā.
Tesampi guyhaṃ paramaṃ na saṃse,
Mantassa bhedaṃ parisaṅkamāno.

236. Bhariyā ce purisaṃ vajjā, komārī piyabhāṇinī.
Puttarūpayasūpetā, ñātisaṅghapurakkhatā.
Tassāpi guyhaṃ paramaṃ na saṃse, mantassa bhedaṃ parisaṅkamāno.

233. O Nāga King, there is no being on this earth who is immortal. There is no quality like wisdom that is beyond reproach. O Nāga King, in this world, a person achieves the unattainable—the eight attainments, the Paths, Fruits, and Nibbāna—through truth, righteousness, fortitude, and restraint. Therefore, reproach only yourself.

234. O Nāga King, among kinsmen, mother and father are the supreme. There is no third being as compassionate to their child as they are. Yet, a wise person, fearing the disclosure of a secret, should not reveal a supreme secret even to them.

235. O Nāga King, even if one has mother, father, sister, brothers, friends, or relatives such as uncles and cousins, a wise person, fearing the disclosure of a secret, should not reveal a supreme secret even to them.

236. O Nāga King, even if a wife says, "Tell me," though she avoids other men, was wed in her youth, speaks endearingly, is endowed with children, beauty, and wealth, and is surrounded by a host of relatives—a wise person, fearing the disclosure of a secret, should not reveal a supreme secret even to her.

Having preached with these verses, he desired to preach again by giving further advice to the Nāga King.
84:
He spoke these seven verses:

237. One should not reveal a secret matter; one should guard it like a treasure. Indeed, the revealing of a secret matter is not praised by the wise.

238. A wise man should not tell a secret to a woman, nor to an enemy, nor to a person who can be led away by material gain, nor to a person who is a 'heart-thief' (a false friend).

239. If a person reveals a secret matter that should not be known, then out of fear that the secret counsel will be broken, he becomes like a slave and must endure [the other's whims].

240. As many people as know the secret counsel of a man, that many causes of anxiety he has; therefore, one should not release a secret.

241. One should speak of a secret in a secluded place by day; at night, one should not raise one's voice excessively. For eavesdroppers hear the counsel, and thus the secret quickly meets its destruction.

242. Just like a great iron city, without a gate, well-built, and surrounded by three moats—so do those who keep their secret counsel appear to me in this world.

243. Those who keep their secret counsel, whose speech is not scattered, and who are firm in their own interests—enemies keep away from them, just as those who wish to live keep away from a group of venomous snakes.

237. Nāgarāja, O King of Nagas. Guhyamatthaṃ, a secret matter. Nidhiṃ yathā, like a treasure. Rakkheyya, one should guard it. Na vivareyya, one should not reveal it. Hi-saccaṃ, it is true. Guhyo, secret. Attho, matter. Pātukato, making manifest. Pajānatā, by the wise. Na sādhu-nappasattho, is not praised.

238. Nāgarāja, O King of Nagas. Paṇḍito, a wise man. Thiyā, to a woman. Amittassa ca, and to an enemy. Guhyaṃ, a secret word. Na saṃseyya, should not be told. Yo ca, and whoever. Āmisena, by some material gain. Saṃhīro, is easily led away. Tassapi, to him also. Guhyaṃ, a secret word. Na saṃseyya, should not be told. Yo ca naro, and whatever man. Hadayattheno, is a 'heart-thief' who is a false friend, speaking one thing while thinking another. Tassapi, to him also. Guhyaṃ, a secret word. Na saṃse, should not be told.

239. Nāgarāja, O King of Nagas. Yo naro, whatever man. Asambuddhaṃ, that which should not be made known. Guhyaṃ, secret. Atthaṃ, matter. Sambodhayāti, if he should make it known. Mantabhedabhayā, one who fears the destruction of the counsel. Tassa, of that person who knows. Dāsabhūto, becoming like a slave. Titikkhati, must endure.

240. Nāgarāja, O King of Nagas. Mantinaṃ, among those who have been consulted. Yāvanto, as many as. Purisassa, of a man. Guhyaṃ, secret. Atthaṃ, matter. Jānanti, know. Tāvanto, that many. Tassa, to that person. Ubbeghā, cause anxiety. Tasmā, therefore. Guhyaṃ, a secret word. Na vissaje, one should not let others know.

241. Nāgarāja, O King of Nagas. Divā, by day. Vivicca, going to a secluded place. Rahassaṃ, a secret word. Bhāseyya, should be spoken. Rattiṃ, at night. Ativelaṃ, exceeding the limit, making a loud sound. Giraṃ, speech. Na pamuñce, one should not release. Hi-yasmā, for. Upassutikā, eavesdroppers who approach the place of counsel and stand outside the walls. Mantaṃ, the counsel. Suṇanti, hear. Tasmā, therefore. Manto, the counsel. Khippaṃ, quickly. Bhedaṃ, to destruction. Upeti, reaches.

242. Dujivha, O King of Nagas. Advārakaṃ, having no gate. Ayasā kataṃ, made of iron. Bhaddasālaṃ, endowed with beautiful halls, pavilions, houses, and markets. Samantakhātā, dug all around. Parikhā, endowed with three moats. Mahantaṃ, great. ayanagaraṃ yathā, like an iron city. Evampi, even so like this iron city. Idha, in this world. Guhyamantā, those who have secret counsel. Ye narā, which persons. Santi, there are. Te narā, those persons. Me, to me. Khāyanti, appear.

243. Dujivha, O King of Nagas. Guhyamantā, those who have secret counsel. Sadatthesu, in their own interests. Daḷhā, those who are firm. Ārā, from afar. Vyavajanti iva, as if they avoid. Avikiṇṇavācā, having speech that is guarded and not scattered. Āsīvisā, called swift-venomed snakes. Sattusaṅghā, from a host of enemies. Jīvitukāmā, those who wish to live. Ārā, from afar. Vyavajanti iva, as if they avoid. Evaṃ, in this way. Tehi, from those who have secret counsel. Amittā, enemies. Ārā, from afar. Vyavajanti, avoid.

When the Garuḍa King preached the Dhamma in this way, the Naga King Paṇḍaraka, realizing that the ascetic was without virtue, said: "O Garuḍa King, I have come to ruin because I spoke a secret to that ascetic, thinking he was a virtuous monk. What kind of practice makes one a true monk who reaches the heavenly realm?" Desiring to ask the Garuḍa King about this matter, he said:

Atthā ca dhammā ca apaggatāmhā.
85:
How does one reach the heavenly place?

He spoke these two verses.
86:
244. Leaving home, the naked ascetic wanders for the sake of food, shaven-headed. To that naked, shaven-headed one, I revealed my secret. We have been deprived of our benefit and our cause.

245. O Garuḍa King, with what virtue, by undertaking what practice, and by abandoning the unwholesome attachments of 'mine', does a monk, while practicing, reach the heavenly realm, which is supreme with its sights and sounds?

244. Supaṇṇarāja, O King of Garuḍas. Gharaṃ, home. Hitvā, having abandoned. Pabbajito, having become a monk. Acelo, not wearing clothes. Naggo, naked. Muṇḍo, shaven-headed. Ghāsahetu, for the sake of seeking food. Carati, he wanders. Tamhi nukkho, to that naked, shaven-headed monk. Guhyaṃ, secret. Atthaṃ, matter. Vivariṃ, I revealed. Mayaṃ, we. Atthā ca, from benefit. Dhammā ca, and from the cause. Apaggatā, have been deprived. Amhā, we are.

245. Supaṇṇarāja, O King of Garuḍas. Kiṃ sīlo, endowed with what virtue. Kena vatena, by undertaking what practice. Vattaṃ-vattanto, practicing. Mamāyitāni, unwholesome states of craving that cling to things as 'mine'. Hitvā, having abandoned. Caraṃ-caranto, one who practices. Kathaṃkaro, acting in what way. Samaṇo, a monk. Saggaṃ, the heavenly realm, supreme with its forms and so on. Ṭhānaṃ, place. Upeti, does he reach?

To answer the question of the Naga King Paṇḍaraka, the Garuḍa King spoke this verse:

246. Endowed with shame (hiri), patience, and restraint, free from anger, having abandoned slander, and having given up attachments while practicing as a monk—acting thus, one reaches the heavenly realm.

246. Nāgarāja, O King of Nagas. Hiriyā, with shame arising from within (hiri) and dread arising from without (ottappa). Titikkhāya, with patience. Damena, with restraint of the senses. Upeto, endowed. Akkodhano, having the habit of not being angry. Pesuṇiyaṃ, slanderous speech.
87:
247. "Just as a mother, seeing her young son born of her own body, feels a thrill through all her limbs at his touch, so too, O King of Birds, have you appeared to me; look upon me with compassion as a mother looks upon her son."

247. O Dijiinda, King of Birds and King of Garudas. Just as a mother (mātā), knowing the pleasant touch of her young (taruṇaṃ) son (puttaṃ) born of her body (tanujjaṃ), fills her whole body (sabbagattaṃ) with the touch of her son; even so, you, O King of Garudas, have appeared (pāturahu) to me. Therefore, look (passa) upon me (maṃ) with compassion, just as a mother (mātā) has compassion (anukampamāno) for her son.

248. "Come now, you are released from death, O double-tongued one! For there are three kinds of sons and no other: the resident pupil, the one given, and the one born of oneself. You have become one of these sons to me; rejoice!"

248. O Dujivha, King of Nāgas. Come (handa), I am very compassionate. Now (ajja), you (tvaṃ) are released (muñca) from death (vadhā). Because (hi-yasmā) there are only three (tayo hi) kinds of sons (puttā): the resident pupil (antevāsī), the one given by others (dinnako) to be a son, and the one born of oneself (atrajo). There is no (na atthi) fourth son other (añño) than these three. Therefore, you (tvaṃ), O King of Nāgas, have become (ahosi) one (aññataro) of my sons (putto). Rejoice (rajjassu)!

By abandoning (pahāya) and giving up (hitvā) the cravings (mamāyitāni) that cause attachment, one who practices (caranto) is called a Samana. Only a monk who acts (karo) thus (evaṃ) reaches (upeti) the heavenly (saggaṃ) realm (ṭhānaṃ), which is noble with forms and so on.

Hearing this Dhamma talk from the King of Garudas, the Nāga King Paṇḍaraka, wishing to beg for his life—

When the Nāga King pleaded thus, the King of Garudas, wishing to grant the Nāga King his life—

Having spoken these words, he descended from the sky and placed the Nāga King on the ground. Wishing to make this matter clear, the All-Knowing Blessed One spoke these verses:
88:
251. "Having made a pact with an enemy, O womb-born one, with one born of an egg, why do you lie there with fangs bared? From where has fear come to you?"

251. O Jalābuja, Nāga King born from a womb. Having made (katvā) a friendly agreement (sandhiṃ) with the Aṇḍaja, the egg-born King of Garudas, you lie (sesi) with your fangs (dāṭhaṃ) bared (vivariya). From where (kuto) has fear (bhayaṃ) come (āgataṃ) to you (taṃ)?

252. "One should suspect an enemy, and even a friend one should not trust. Fear arising from a place of safety cuts even the roots."

253. "How can I trust you, with whom I have had a quarrel? One must remain cautious; he does not delight in enemies."

249. "Having spoken these words, the Garuda released the double-tongued one. Standing on the ground, the bird comforted the double-tongued one: 'You are now released and have transcended all fears; be protected by me on land and in water.'"

250. "As a skilled physician is to the sick, as a cool lake is to the thirsty, as a house is to those afflicted by the cold of snow, so do I become your refuge."

249. O Monks (bhikkhave). Having spoken (vatvā) these words (icceva vākyaṃ), the King of Garudas (supaṇṇo) released (vissajji) the Nāga King (dujivhaṃ). The bird (dijo), the King of Garudas, standing (patiṭṭhāya) on the ground (bhūmyaṃ), comforting (samassāsento) the Nāga King (dujivhaṃ), said: "Now (ajja), I release you (tvaṃ), O Nāga King. You have transcended (ativatto) all fears (sabbabhayā). Be (hohi) protected (abhigutto) by me (mayā) on land (thale) and in water (udake)."

250. O Nāga King (nāgarāja). Just as a skilled (kusalo) physician (bhisakko) is a refuge (saraṇaṃ) for the sick (ātaṅkinaṃ), and just as a cool (sīto) lake (rahado) is a refuge for the thirsty (pipāsitānaṃ), and just as a house (vesmaṃ) is a refuge for those oppressed (aṭṭitānaṃ) by the cold of snow (himasīta), even so (evampi), I (ahaṃ) become (bhavāmi) your (te) refuge (saraṇaṃ).

That Nāga King Paṇḍaraka went to the Nāga realm. The King of Garudas went to the Garuda realm and thought, "I have released the Nāga King Paṇḍaraka after making him swear an oath and trust me. I wonder what the state of that Nāga King's heart is toward me? I shall test him." He went to the Nāga realm and created the force of a Garuda-wind. Seeing the King of Garudas acting thus, the Nāga King thought, "He must have come to capture me." He manifested a body a thousand fathoms long, swallowed stones and sand to make himself heavy, placed his tail downwards, spread his hood over his coils, and lay there as if to bite and kill the King of Garudas.

Seeing the Nāga King in that state, the King of Garudas, wishing to ask the reason—

Hearing the words of the King of Garudas, the Nāga King Paṇḍaraka, wishing to inform the King of Garudas of his reason—
89:
255. He preached this verse:

255. Monks, those of divine complexion and delicate form, both equal, pure, and like a mass of merit. Those two noble beings, having formed a friendship and reached a state of physical intimacy, approached the naked ascetic named Karampiya, like two horses yoked to the front of a chariot.

254. He spoke these three verses:

252. O Garuda King (Suvaṇṇarāja), one should not trust an enemy, nor even a friend, even after making an appointment. From a friend who is thought to be safe, fear may arise. That fear indeed cuts off the very roots of life.

253. How can one trust someone with whom one has had a quarrel? One should remain steadfast with constant effort. He who stands firm with constant effort is not tainted by intimacy with enemies.

254. If someone trusts you, do not trust them in return. If someone is unsuspicious of you, you should still be suspicious of them. A wise man should exert effort in such a way that others do not know his true nature.

Having conversed thus with one another, being in harmony and rejoicing, both the Garuda king and the Naga king went to the hermitage of the naked ascetic.
90:
256. He preached this subsequent verse:

256. Monks, at that time, the Naga king Paṇḍaraka approached the naked ascetic by himself and said this: "O immoral ascetic, now I am released and have transcended all fears. Surely, we are not dear to your heart."

257. He spoke this verse:

257. Naga king, because the Garuda king was undoubtedly dearer to me than the Naga king Paṇḍaraka. That is the truth. Therefore, being stained by affection for that Garuda, I committed this evil deed knowingly, not out of delusion.

258. He spoke these two verses:

258. O naked one, for a monk who clearly sees this world and the next, there is no such thing as 'dear' or 'not dear.' But you, with the appearance of those well-restrained, wander about deceiving this world while being unrestrained in body, speech, and mind.

259. O immoral one, you are a pretender of the noble ones while not being noble yourself. Though unrestrained, you appear restrained. You are of a dark nature, born of unwholesome states, and possess the character of the ignoble. You have practiced much evil and misconduct.

Wishing to make this matter clear, the All-Enlightened Buddha said:

Having reached the ascetic's hermitage, the Garuda king thought: "This Naga king will not give his life to the ascetic; I will not pay homage to that immoral ascetic." Having thought so, the Garuda king stood outside and sent only the Naga king to the ascetic.

Wishing to make clear the fact of that sending, the All-Enlightened Buddha said:

Thereafter, the naked ascetic, wishing to inform the Naga king of his own actions—
91:
261. Therefore, one should not betray friends;
There is no other evil more wicked than betraying a friend.
Struck by the poison of his own deed, he is struck down into the earth;
For by the word of the Indra [Naga King], the one who feigned restraint was destroyed.

He spoke this concluding verse:

261. Bhikkhus, monks. One should not betray friends. Why? Because there is no other evil more particularly wicked than the misdeed of betraying a friend. Therefore, having reached the end of the poison which is the kamma of betraying the friend he himself had partaken in, he is buried in the earth. This word is true. By the truthful word of the Indra, the Naga King Pandaraka, the ascetic Karampiya—who, though not restrained, claimed to be so—was destroyed.

Hearing those words, the Naga King Pandaraka, wishing to revile that ascetic—

Having thus reviled the ascetic, the Naga King, now wishing to curse him, spoke this verse:

260. You have betrayed the innocent, you are a betrayer and a slanderer.
By this word of truth, may your head split into seven pieces.

260. O betrayer of friends! You have betrayed an innocent friend. You are a slanderer. By this truthful word of such a nature, may your head split into seven pieces.

While the Naga King Pandaraka was thus cursing him, the head of the ascetic named Karampiya split into seven pieces. Right where he was sitting, the earth opened up. That ascetic entered the earth and was reborn in the Avīci hell. The Naga King and the Garuda King also returned to their respective abodes.

The Perfectly Enlightened One, wishing to make manifest the fact of that ascetic being swallowed by the earth—

[The Conclusion of the Jātaka:] The Perfectly Enlightened One, having brought forth this Pandara Nāgarāja Jātaka Dhamma teaching, said, "Bhikkhus, not only now has Devadatta told a lie and been swallowed by the earth; in the past also, he was swallowed by the earth for telling a lie." He then identified the birth: "At that time, the ascetic was Devadatta, the Naga King was Sāriputta, and the Garuda King was I myself."

## If one reveals a secret, that person shall perish.

The Pandara Nāgarāja Jātaka is concluded.
92:
## 9. Sambulā Jātaka
## On the conduct of a noble daughter and honoring her husband like a deity

The Present Story: While the Fully Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, was residing at Jetavana Monastery, he told this Sambulā Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Kā vedhamānā," concerning Queen Mallikā. The present story is detailed in the Kummāsapiṇḍa Jātaka.

In particular, that Queen Mallikā, through the power of her gift of three handfuls of barley gruel to the Buddha, became the chief consort of King Kosala on that very day. She was endowed with the five good qualities, such as rising before her husband. She was wise, a servitor of the Buddha, and one who honored her husband like a deity.

The fact that Queen Mallikā honored her husband like a deity became famous throughout the city of Sāvatthī. Then one day, in the Dhamma Hall, the monks raised a discussion: "Friends, it is said that Queen Mallikā is endowed with good conduct and honors her husband like a deity."

The Fully Enlightened Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such and such a discussion," he said, "Monks, not only now is Mallikā endowed with good conduct and honors her husband like a deity; in the past also, she honored her husband like a deity." He then brought forth the past story.

The Past Story: Monks, in the past, King Brahmadatta of Bārāṇasī had a son named Sotthisena. When he came of age, King Brahmadatta appointed Prince Sotthisena as the viceroy. The chief consort of that viceroy was named Sambulā. She possessed supreme beauty and was endowed with a radiant complexion. She appeared like the flame of a lamp burning in a windless place.

Later, leprosy broke out on the body of King Sotthisena. The physicians were unable to cure it. When the leprosy sores broke open, Prince Sotthisena became disgusted and fell into despair, thinking, "What use is kingship to me? I shall die a helpless death in the forest." He informed his father, King Brahmadatta, and leaving the delightful golden palace, he departed from the city. Although Queen Sambulā was urged to turn back by many means, she did not return and said, "I will care for my lord the prince in the forest," and departed from the city together with the prince.
93:
262. Who are you, trembling by the mountain cleft, standing alone, O one with shapely thighs? You are questioned by me, whose hand could measure your waist; tell me your name and your kin.

263. Illuminating the lovely forest, frequented by lions and tigers. Who are you, O beautiful one? Whose daughter are you, O one with a slender waist? I salute you, O blessed one; I, a Dānava, pay homage to you.

He spoke these two verses.

262. *Saṃhitūru*: a woman with noble and well-formed thighs. *Girikandarāyaṃ*: by the mountain cleft. *Vedhamānā*: trembling due to the cold. *Kā*: who are you? *Tuvaṃ*: you. *Ekā*: alone. *Tiṭṭhasi*: you stand. *Pāṇippameyya majjhe*: a woman with a waist that can be measured by a hand. *Me*: by me. *Puṭṭhā*: questioned. *Asi*: you are. *Me*: to me. *Nāmañca*: your name. *Bandhave ca*: and your kin. *Akkhāhi*: tell.

263. *Kalyāṇi*: a woman endowed with the five beauties. *Sīhabyagghanisevitaṃ*: a place frequented by lions and tigers. *Rammaṃ*: delightful. *Vanaṃ*: the whole forest. *Obhāsayaṃ*: you illuminate with the radiance of your body. *Tuṃ*: you. *Kā vā*: who are you? *Asi*: are you? *Sumajjhime*: a woman with a slender waist and broad hips. *Tuṃ*: you. *Kassa vā*: whose daughter are you? *Bhadda*: O blessed one. *Dānavā*: named Dānava. *Ahaṃ*: I. *Taṃ*: you. *Abhivādemi*: I salute. *Te*: to you. *Namo*: homage. *Atthu*: let there be.

Prince Sotthisena entered the forest and, in a place endowed with shade and water and easy-to-find fruits of various sizes, built a leaf-hut and dwelt there. Princess Sambulā served the prince. In what manner did she serve him?

Princess Sambulā would rise early in the morning, sweep the leaf-hut, prepare drinking and washing water, and offer a tooth-stick and face-washing water. After he had rinsed his mouth, she would grind various medicines and apply them to the prince's leprosy sores. She would feed him various sweet fruits, rinse his mouth, and after washing her hands well, she would say, "My lord, be not heedless," and salute him. Then, taking a basket, a spade, a hook, and a pole, she would enter the forest to gather fruits. Having brought back the fruits and placed them in a suitable spot, she would fetch water in a pot and bathe Prince Sotthisena with various medicinal powders and fine clay, and again offer him sweet fruits.

At the end of the meal, she would offer water scented with perfume. She herself would then eat the fruits. Having prepared a wooden bed, when the prince lay down upon it, she would wash his feet, massage his head, back, and limbs, and then lie down beside the bed. In this manner, she cared for her husband.

One day, while gathering fruits in the forest, Princess Sambulā saw a small stream. Setting down the basket from her head by the stream, she thought, "I will bathe," and entered the water. She rubbed her body with turmeric powder and bathed. Having washed her body well, she came out of the water, dressed in bark garments, and stood by the stream. At that moment, the whole forest was illuminated at once by the radiance of Princess Sambulā's body.

At that instant, a Dānava ogre, wandering in search of food, saw Princess Sambulā. His heart was filled with passion, and wishing to ask about her, he spoke.

Princess Sambulā, hearing the words of the Dānava and wishing to inform him of her situation, spoke these three verses:

264. The son of the King of Kāsi is known as Sotthisena. I am Sambulā, his wife; know this, O Dānava.

265. I salute you, sir; I, Sambulā, pay homage to you. The son of Videha, O blessed one, lives in the forest, afflicted with illness.

266. Oppressed by disease, he is alone; I, alone, attend to him. Searching the forest for honey and meat left by lions and tigers, whatever I bring is his food. Surely today his body will be in distress.

264. *Dānava*: O Dānava ogre. *Kāsirājassa*: of the King of Kāsi. *Yo putto*: which son. *Atthi*: there is. *Taṃ puttaṃ*: that son. *Sotthisenoti*: as Sotthisena. *Vidū*: everyone knows. *Ahaṃ*: I. *Tassa*: of that Prince Sotthisena. *Sambulā*: named Sambulā. *Bhariyā*: am the wife. *Evaṃ*: thus. *Jānāhi*: know.

265. *Bhante*: O Lord Dānava. *Sambulā*: named Sambulā. *Ahaṃ*: I. *Taṃ*: you. *Abhivādemi*: salute. *Te*: to you. *Namo*: homage. *Atthu*: let there be. *Bhaddante*: O Lord Dānava. *Vedehaputto*: the son of the King of Videha, Prince Sotthisena. *Āturo*: being ill. *Vane*: in the forest. *Vasati*: dwells.

266. *Rogasammataṃ*: oppressed by disease. *Ekaṃ*: who is alone. *Taṃ*: that prince. *Ekā*: alone. *Ahaṃ*: I. *Upaṭṭhahaṃ*: attend to. *Ahañca*: as for me. *Vanaṃ*: in the forest. *Migābilaṃ*: the remains of the prey of lions and tigers. *Madhu-maṃsaṃ*: honey and meat. *Uñchāya*: searching for. *Yaṃ*: whatever food. *Ahaṃ*: I. *Āharāmi*: bring. *Taṃ*: that. *Bakkho*: he eats. *Ajja*: today. *Tassa*: of that husband prince. *Sarīraṃ*: the body. *Nādhati nūna*: will surely be in distress.
94:
267. He spoke this verse:
267. "O Sambulā, what will you do in the forest with a prince who is afflicted by disease? I shall be your husband."

268. She spoke this verse:
268. "O Lord Dānava, oppressed by sorrow and with a body fallen into misery and loneliness, what beauty do I possess? O Lord Dānava, seek another woman more beautiful than I."

269. He spoke these three verses:
269. "O Sambulā, come, climb this mountain. I have four hundred wives. Among them, you shall be the chief, with all your desires fulfilled."
270. "O Sambulā, who has a complexion like the light of the stars, whatever things you desire in your heart, I truly have them in abundance. Rejoice with me today."
271. "O Sambulā of tender frame, if you do not become my chief queen, you shall suffice for my morning meal; in the morning, you shall be my food."

272. The Blessed One spoke these two verses:
272. "Monks, that fierce ogre with seven matted locks and protruding tusks, a man-eater, seized Princess Sambulā by the arm in the forest, she who saw no protector."
273. "Monks, oppressed by the ogre who looks with eyes of lust, having fallen into the power of the enemy, she grieves only for her husband."

Thereafter, the Dānava ogre, wishing to seduce the princess—

Wishing to reject the words of the Dānava ogre who spoke such seductions, Princess Sambulā—

When Princess Sambulā rejected him thus, the Dānava ogre, wishing to seduce her again by threatening her—

Having spoken such seductions and seizing Princess Sambulā by the hand, she fell into great grief. The All-Enlightened One, wishing to make this clear—

Princess Sambulā, being greatly oppressed by grief and terror, while weeping and lamenting, wished to appeal to the deities—

"Surely there are no world-protectors here."
95:
274. She spoke these two verses:
274. "O noble deities, the pain of this ogre eating me is not so great as the thought of how my husband's mind might turn otherwise. This change in my lord's mind is a greater suffering for me."
275. "Surely there are no gods; surely they have gone away. Surely there are no world-protectors in this world. Surely there are no restrainers of those who are unrestrained and act with violence."

At that moment of lamentation, by the power of Princess Sambulā's virtue, the abode of Sakka, King of Gods, trembled. The Pandukambala stone throne showed signs of heat. Sakka, upon reflecting, understood the cause, took his thunderbolt weapon, and arriving swiftly, stood above the ogre's head, wishing to threaten the Dānava ogre—
96:
277. She reached the hermitage, released from the man-eater, like a bird returning to its nest after flying away, or like a cow returning to its stall seeking its calf.

278. There, the renowned Princess Sambulā lamented, her eyes dimmed by the heat of grief, not seeing her protector in the forest.

## 10. Gandhatinduka Jātaka
## The Reason Why Sovereign Kings Should Not Follow the Four Wrong Paths

**The Present Story**
The All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, told this Gandhatinduka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Appamādo amataṃ padaṃ," concerning the instruction given to King Pasenadi of Kosala.

The details of the instruction to that king have been explained previously.

**The Past Story**
In the past, in the city of Uttarapañcāla in the kingdom of Kapila, a king named Pañcāla ruled unrighteously and heedlessly, established in the four wrong paths (agati). At that time, all his ministers and others also became unrighteous.

The inhabitants of the country, oppressed by taxes, took their wives and children and fled to the forest like deer. In the places where villages once stood, there were no longer villages. Because the people feared the king's messengers, they were unable to stay in their houses during the day. They surrounded their houses with thorn branches, stayed there at night, and fled into the forest as soon as dawn broke. During the day, the king's messengers looted, and at night, thieves did.
104:

He spoke these eleven verses:

297. "Great King, heedfulness is the path to the Deathless Nibbāna. Heedlessness is the path to repeated death. Those who are heedful do not die. Those who are heedless are as if already dead."

298. "Great King, from intoxication—due to health, youth, or long life—heedlessness arises. From heedlessness, the destruction of lineage, wealth, and life arises. From the destruction of wealth and attendants, faults arise. O noble King Bharata, therefore, do not be heedless."

300. "O Great King, promoter of the kingdom's welfare, in the realm of a heedless king, all wealth perishes. That heedlessness is called the cause of the king's suffering."

301. "Great King, you are excessively heedless. This heedlessness is not the practice of ancient kings. Thieves are destroying your prosperous country, which is full of food and drink, gold and silver."

302. "Great King, your sons will not be able to maintain the lineage. There will be no treasuries of gold, nor stores of grain. When the kingdom is being looted, you will lose all your wealth."

306. "Great King, for kings who do not perform evil, who strive at the proper time, and who are diligent, all wealth increases, just as a herd of cows increases when accompanied by a bull."

307. "Great King, go and wander through the kingdom and the countryside, listening closely to the people. Having seen and heard there, you shall then act accordingly."

At night, thieves loot.

At that time, the Bodhisatta was a tree-deity in a Gandhatinduka tree outside the city. Every year, he received an offering worth a thousand from the king. The Bodhisatta tree-deity thought:

"This king rules heedlessly; he is destroying the entire kingdom. Except for me, there is no one else capable of establishing the king in proper conduct. He has also been helpful to me, honoring me with an offering worth a thousand every year. I will advise him."

Having thought thus, the tree-deity entered the king's magnificent bedchamber at night, stood by the side of the head of the bed, emitted a radiance, and remained in the air.

The king, seeing the Bodhisatta shining like the young sun, asked: "Who are you, and for what reason have you come here?"
105:
Hearing the King's words, the Bodhisatta said, "Great King, I am the deity guarding the Tindi tree. I have come with the intention of giving counsel to Your Majesty." When asked, "What kind of counsel will you give me?", he replied: "Great King, Your Majesty rules with heedlessness. Therefore, your entire country is being plundered and ruined. A ruler who governs with heedlessness cannot remain the lord of the whole land; he meets with ruin in this present life and is reborn in the great hell in the life hereafter. When such rulers are heedful, the people living both within and outside the kingdom become heedful as well. Therefore, a ruler should be exceedingly heedful." Wishing to teach the Dhamma, he spoke these verses:

297. Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless; heedlessness is the path to death. The heedful do not die; the heedless are as if already dead.
...
In this manner, the Bodhisatta admonished the King with eleven verses, saying, "O King, go now. Do not delay, but investigate. Do not destroy the country," and then returned to his own abode.

Upon hearing the Bodhisatta's words, the King was struck with emotion (saṃvega). The next day, he entrusted the kingdom to his ministers and, together with the chaplain, left the city through the eastern gate early in the morning and traveled for one league.

In a certain village there, an old man brought thorn branches from the forest, fenced and closed his house gate, took his wife and children, and entered the forest. In the evening, when the king's men had departed, he returned to his house. Pricked by a thorn at his house gate, he sat squatting, and while pulling out the thorn, he wished to curse the king.

That old man's reviling occurred through the power of the Bodhisatta. (It should be understood that the old man reviled because the Bodhisatta, the deity of the Tindi tree, had possessed him.)

The Bodhisatta, the deity of the Tindi tree, possessed the chaplain's body and said: "Great King, let us go further and investigate first." As the King and the chaplain went from that village to another, they heard the voice of an old woman on the way.

That poor old woman was looking after two grown-up daughters. She did not let them go to the forest, but she herself brought firewood and vegetables from the forest to support them.
108:
313. When will this King Brahmadatta die? In whose kingdom maidens grow old without husbands.

313. In the kingdom of which King Brahmadatta, maidens remain without husbands and grow old. If those two daughters of mine had husbands, they would support me. At what time will this king named Brahmadatta die?

314. You have spoken poorly, you wretched woman, unskilled in the meaning of things. Where does a king search for a husband for maidens?

314. O wretched woman, skilled in what is not the cause, you have spoken bad words. Indeed, it is true. In what place must a king search for and provide a husband for maidens?

315. I have not spoken poorly, O Brahmin; I am skilled in the meaning of things. The subjects are unprotected, oppressed by unrighteous taxes.

316. For thieves devour by night, and tax collectors devour by day. In the kingdom of a deceitful king, there are many unrighteous people. When it is hard to live and hard to support a family, where will maidens find husbands?

315. O Brahmin, I have not spoken bad words. I am skilled in the causes of things. That king does not protect the villages and provinces. He oppresses them with unrighteous taxes.

316. Indeed, it is true. At night, thieves plunder and destroy. By day, the king's officials who collect taxes plunder and destroy. In the kingdom of a deceitful and wicked king, unrighteous people are many. In a kingdom where it is difficult to make a living, and when it is hard to support a wife and children, from where will maidens obtain husbands?

On that day, while that old woman was climbing a thicket to gather vegetables, she slipped and fell to the ground. Desiring to curse the king with death, she spoke these verses.

Through the power of the Bodhisatta, that old woman cursed in this manner. When she cursed thus, the Chaplain, desiring to restrain her, spoke this verse.

Hearing those words, the old woman, desiring to inform the Brahmin Chaplain of the reason, spoke these two verses.

When the king and the Brahmin heard the old woman's words, they said, "She speaks what is fitting." As they proceeded from that place to another, they heard the voice of a man plowing.

It is said that while he was plowing, his great ox named Sāliya was struck by the plowshare and fell down. That plowman, desiring to curse the king, spoke this verse.
109:
317. May the Pañcāla king lie thus, struck by a spear in battle, just as this poor Sāliya lies, struck by the plowshare.

317. Just as the ox named Sāliya lies miserably, having been struck by the plowshare, in the same way, may the Pañcāla king lie in the battlefield, having been pierced by a spear.

318. You are unrighteous, you wretch, to be angry with Brahmadatta. You who curse the king, though he has done you no wrong.

318. You wretch, you who curse the king even though he has not wronged you, you are angry with King Brahmadatta without cause.

319. I am angry with Brahmadatta with cause, O Brahmin. The subjects are unprotected, oppressed by unrighteous taxes.

320. For thieves devour by night, and tax collectors devour by day. In the kingdom of a deceitful king, there are many unrighteous people.

321. Hey! That woman who brings the meal must have had to cook again. She brought the meal at the wrong time. While looking out for the meal-bringer, Sāliya was struck by the plowshare.

319. O Brahmin, I am angry with King Brahmadatta with a rightful cause. That king does not protect the villages and provinces. He oppresses them with unrighteous taxes.

320. Indeed, the statement that the king does not observe the Dhamma is true. At night, thieves plunder and destroy. By day, the king's officials who collect taxes plunder and destroy. In the kingdom of a wicked king, unrighteous people are many.

321. Hey, Brahmin! That woman who delivers the meal must have had to cook the rice again. She brought the meal at an improper time. Because I had to wait and look out for the one bringing the meal, my ox Sāliya was struck by the plowshare.

When he cursed thus, the Chaplain, desiring to restrain the plowman, spoke this verse.

Hearing the Chaplain's words, the plowman, desiring to show the king's fault to the Chaplain, spoke these three verses.

When the king and the Chaplain heard the plowman's words, they said, "He speaks what is fitting," and they went forward and stayed in a certain village. Early the next morning, a certain deceitful cow kicked the milker with her leg and caused him to fall along with the pot of milk.

That milker, desiring to curse King Brahmadatta, spoke a verse.

Hearing those words, the Chaplain, desiring to restrain the milker's words, spoke a verse.

When the Brahmin Chaplain spoke with that verse, the milker, desiring to show the king's fault to the Brahmin, spoke a verse.

The king and the Chaplain said, "This milker speaks only what is fitting," and after leaving that village, they entered the road and headed toward the city. In a certain village, the king's messengers, for the sake of a sword scabbard, killed a young bull with brindled fur and took its hide. The mother cow, out of grief for her offspring, would neither eat grass nor drink water.
110:
322. May the Pañcāla king be thus slain, struck by a sword in battle, just as I am struck today and my milk is spilled.

322. Today, just as I am struck by the cow, and just as my pot of milk is spilled, in this same way, may the Pañcāla king be slain, being cut down by a sword on the battlefield.

323. When a beast spills milk or harms the herdsman, what fault is there in Brahmadatta that you blame him?

323. O man, when a beast spills milk or when it kicks the herdsman, what fault is there in King Brahmadatta in that spilling of milk or kicking? Your blaming him in such a way is not proper.

324. O Brahmin, the Pañcāla king is blameworthy, this king named Brahmadatta. The country folk are not protected; they are oppressed by unlawful taxes.

325. Indeed, thieves plunder by night, and tax collectors plunder by day. In the realm of a crooked king, there are many unrighteous people.

326. The cows were fierce and prone to running away, so that we did not milk them before. But now we milk them, being oppressed by those who desire milk.

324. O Brahmin, the Pañcāla king should be blamed. This king named Brahmadatta does not protect the provinces and villages. They are oppressed by unrighteous taxes.

325. Truly, thieves plunder and destroy at night. By day, the king's men who collect taxes plunder and destroy. In the kingdom of a corrupt king, unrighteous people are many.

326. Those cows that are fierce and have the habit of running away, we did not milk them in the past. But now, being oppressed by the king's men who demand milk, we must milk them.

327. May the Pañcāla king thus lament; may he wither away, bereft of his son, just as this poor cow runs about, bereft of her calf.

327. Just as this poor cow, being separated from her young calf, runs here and there lamenting, in this same way, may the Pañcāla king, being separated from his son, have to weep. May he wither away while bereft of his son.

She wanders about, lamenting.

Seeing that cow, the village children, wishing to curse the king, spoke this verse.

Thereafter, the chaplain, wishing to ask the reason for the children's curse, spoke.

Thereafter, the village children, wishing to show the king's fault to the Brahmin, spoke.

The king and the chaplain said, "You speak the truth regarding the cause," and they departed. As they went, they saw crows pecking with their beaks and eating frogs in a certain dried-up pond along the way.

The Bodhisatta, the deity of a Tinduka tree, when the king and the chaplain reached that place, by his own power, made the frog—
111:
328. When a beast runs or cries out even while the herdsman is guarding it, what fault is there here, O friends, in King Brahmadatta?

328. O friends, while the herdsman is even now guarding it, if a beast runs away or if it laments, what fault would there be in the Pañcāla king named Brahmadatta in such running or lamenting of the cow?

329. O Great Brahmin, the fault of King Brahmadatta is great. The country folk are not protected; they are oppressed by unlawful taxes.

330. Indeed, thieves plunder by night, and tax collectors plunder by day. In the realm of a crooked king, there are many unrighteous people. Why is the milk-drinking calf killed for the sake of a scabbard?

329. O Great Brahmin, the fault of King Brahmadatta is great. The king does not protect the villages and provinces. They are oppressed and tormented by taxes that are false and unrighteous.

330. Truly, our words that the king does not observe the Dhamma are true. Thieves plunder and destroy at night. By day, the king's men who collect taxes plunder and destroy. In the country of a deceitful and corrupt king, unrighteous people are many. Why is the young milk-drinking calf killed by the king's men, who follow the practices of the base, for the sake of a sword-scabbard?

331. May the Pañcāla king be thus eaten, slain in battle along with his son, just as I, a forest-dweller, am eaten today by village crows.

331. Just as I, born in the forest, am now being eaten by the crows that live in the village, in this same way, may the Pañcāla king, together with his son, be eaten by crows and vultures after being slain in battle.

Hearing the frog's curse, the chaplain wished to speak with the frog.

Hearing the chaplain's words, the frog wished to explain the reason to the chaplain.
112:
332. "Kings do not provide protection for all beings, O frog, in the world of men. A king is not considered unrighteous just because crows might eat a living being like you."

332. "O frog! Kings in the world of men do not provide protection for all beings. Crows might eat a being like you even while you are alive. Just because crows eat a frog like you, one cannot say that the king does not practice the Dhamma."

333. "O Brahmin who practices the holy life, you speak endearing words to a wicked king. You appear unrighteous indeed. You praise a king who is utterly negligent while his many subjects are being plundered and destroyed."

334. "O Brahmin, if this were a well-governed kingdom, prosperous, happy, and peaceful, and if the crows had eaten the choice portions of the food offerings, they would not be eating a living being like me."

333. "O Brahmin of noble practice! You speak endearing words to a wicked king. You truly seem unrighteous. You praise a king who is extremely negligent while many beings are being plundered and destroyed."

334. "O Brahmin! If this country were a prosperous and pleasant land, if this kingdom were flourishing, joyful, and very peaceful, then the crows, who make unpleasant sounds, would have eaten the choice portions of the food offerings and would not eat a living being like me."

This cursing in these six places occurred only through the power of the Bodhisatta.
113:
Hearing the words of the frog, the king and the chaplain said, "Starting from the frog, a mere animal living in the forest, everyone is cursing only us." They returned from that place to the city and palace, and ruling righteously, they established themselves in the Bodhisatta's admonition and performed meritorious deeds such as almsgiving.

Concluding the birth story, the All-Enlightened Buddha brought forth this Dhamma teaching to King Kosala and said, "Great King, those who are lords of the land should abandon following the four wrong paths and rule righteously." He then identified the birth: "Great King, at that time, I myself was the deity guarding the Tinduka tree."

## In a land where corruption rules, that kingdom shall fall.

The Gandhatinduka Jātaka ends.
114:
## 1. Tesakuṇa Jātaka

## The Three Noble Birds who Preached the King's Duty

The All-Enlightened Buddha, who is capable of admonishing the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Tesakuṇa Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Vessantaraṃ taṃ pucchāmi," by way of admonishing King Kosala.

That is true. The All-Enlightened Buddha called King Kosala, who had come to Jetavana Monastery to hear the Dhamma, and said, "Great King, a king should rule righteously. This is true. When kings are unrighteous, their sons and daughters also become unrighteous." Admonishing him in this manner as found in the Catukka Nipāta, He explained the disadvantages of falling into the four wrong paths and the benefits of not doing so. He elaborated on the faults of sensual pleasures, saying they are like dreams.

"Great King, because for these beings, there is no appointment with Death, no taking of bribes, no fighting of battles, and no victory over Death. All beings must go to the realm of Death. Therefore, for those beings who must pass on to another life, there is no other refuge except for the good deeds they have performed themselves."
115:
In the manner already described, since one cannot take wealth, possessions, and attendants to the next life—as they are met only for a brief moment and must certainly be abandoned—it is not proper to be negligent by relying on wealth, property, and the retinue of ministers and soldiers. One should rule righteously with mindfulness.

This is true; even before the Buddha's appearance, ancient kings, established in the advice of the wise, ruled righteously and filled the heavenly realms." Thus, being requested by King Kosala, He brought forth the past.
116:
The king's actions, even towards animals, were such that he went about saying, "My son, my daughter."

Hearing this, the ministers thought, "These ministers do not know the wisdom of my sons; I will make it clear to them." Then, the king sent a minister to Vessantara, saying, "Your father wishes to ask a question; when should he come to ask?" That minister went, paid respects to Vessantara, and informed him of the message. Hearing this, Vessantara called his attendant minister and asked, "My father wishes to ask me a question; it is proper to honor him when he comes here. When should he come?" The minister said, "Let your father come on the seventh day from now." Hearing this, Vessantara sent word back, saying, "Let my father come on the seventh day from now."

The minister returned and informed the king. On the seventh day, the king had drums beaten throughout the city and went to his son's dwelling. Vessantara had great honors prepared for the king, extending even to the servants and laborers. The king ate at the house of the Vessantara bird, enjoyed great glory, and returned to his own dwelling. He then had a great pavilion built in the palace courtyard, had drums beaten throughout the city, and sat in the middle of the decorated pavilion surrounded by a great crowd. He sent a message to the minister, saying, "Bring Vessantara."

The minister brought Vessantara, seating him on a golden throne. The Vessantara bird sat on his father's lap, played with his father, and then went to sit on that same golden throne. Then the king, questioning him on the duties of a king (rājadhamma) in the midst of the great crowd, spoke this first verse:

1. "Vessantaraṃ taṃ pucchāmi, sakuṇa bhaddamatthu te,
Rajjaṃ kāretukāmena, kiṃ su kiccaṃ kataṃ vara"nti.

1. *Sakuṇa*, O beautiful bird named Vessantara. *Te*, to you, dear son. *Bhaddaṃ*, may there be most excellent auspiciousness. *Atthu*, may it be so. *Vessantaraṃ*, you who are named Vessantara because you are covered with variegated and beautiful colors. *Taṃ*, you, dear son. *Pucchāmi*, I shall ask. *Rajjaṃ*, the kingship. *Kāretukāmena*, by one who wishes to exercise. *Kiṃsu kiccaṃ*, what deed. *Kataṃ*, having been done. *Varaṃ*, is noble? *Tāta*, dear son Vessantara. *Tvaṃ*, you, dear son. *Kathehi*, please answer.

Then Vessantara, without yet answering the question, first spoke the second verse, reminding the king of his heedlessness:

2. "Cirassaṃ vata maṃ tāto, kaṃso bārāṇasiggaho,
Pamatto appamattaṃ maṃ, pitā puttaṃ acodayī"ti.

2. *Bārāṇasiggaho*, he who favors the people of Bārāṇasī with the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu). *Kaṃso*, the king named Kaṃsa. *Tāto*, my noble father. *Vata*, indeed. *Maṃ*, me. *Cirassaṃ*, for a long time. *Pamatto*, being heedless. *Appamattaṃ*, who is diligent. *Puttaṃ*, the son. *Maṃ*, me. *Pitā*, my father who raised me. *Ajja*, only now. *Acodayi*, does he question.

Story of the Past: Great King... In the past, when King Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, he had no children and did not obtain any despite his prayers. One day, King Brahmadatta went to the royal garden with a large retinue, played in the garden for the whole day, had a seat prepared near a sacred Sal tree, and took his rest upon that seat.
117:
3. First of all, one should restrain falsehood, anger, and frivolity. Then one should perform one's duties; that, indeed, they call the vow of a Khattiya.
4. Dear father, whatever deed you might do while being lustful or angry, which you would surely regret later, do not do that again.
5. For a negligent Khattiya, O increaser of the realm, all wealth perishes; that is called the king's misery.
6. Dear father, Siri and Alakkhī, when asked, said this: 'I delight in the man who is energetic, striving, and unenvious.'
7. In the envious, the ill-hearted, the man who spoils deeds, O Great King, Kāḷakaṇṇī delights, she who breaks the wheel of fortune.
8. So you, be kind-hearted to all, be a protector of all; drive away Alakkhī, O Great King, and be the dwelling place of Lakkhī.
9. The man endowed with Lakkhī and firmness is great; O Lord of Kāsi, he cuts the root and the top of enemies.
10. Even Sakka, the Lord of Beings, is not negligent in exertion; he, having established firmness in what is good, applies his mind to exertion.
11. Gandhabbas, ancestors, and Devas share the life of such a one. Deities stand by the one who exerts and is not negligent.
12. So, being non-negligent and free from anger, dear father, perform your duties. Strive in your tasks; the lazy one finds no happiness.
13. Therein are your steps of conduct; this is the instruction. It is enough to make friends happy and to cause suffering to enemies.

He spoke these verses:

3. Dear father, King Brahmadatta. A king, first of all, should avoid speaking falsehood, getting angry, and being frivolous. Then, he should decide the affairs and duties of the citizens. O Khattiya, father, I have spoken these words: that one should avoid falsehood, anger, and frivolity and manage the state. Ancient sages have called this conduct the 'King's Vow'.

4. Dear father, if you, being lustful or angry, perform a deed that you would undoubtedly regret later, do not do such a deed again after having done it before.

5. O Great King, father, who increases the population of the realm. In the kingdom of a negligent Khattiya, all wealth perishes. Ancient sages call this loss of wealth the king's misery. Therefore, dear father, do not be negligent.

6. Dear father, lord of the land. Both the goddess Siri and the goddess Alakkhī, when asked by the merchant Suciparivāra in the city of Bārāṇasī, spoke these words. Dear father, among those two goddesses, Siri first said: 'O Great Merchant Suciparivāra, I delight in the man who is active, energetic, and not envious of others' wealth.'

7. Dear father, Alakkhī said: 'O Great Merchant Suciparivāra, I delight in the man who is envious, ill-hearted, and a destroyer of merit.' O Great King, in this way, Kāḷakaṇṇī, who destroys the wheel of merit, delights in the base man who is envious, ill-hearted, and a destroyer of merit.

8. O Great King, Lord of Kāsi, father. You, the ruler of the land, having a good heart toward all the people of the realm, be a protector and supporter of all. Drive away Alakkhī. Be the dwelling place of Lakkhī.

9. O Lord of Kāsi, father. That man who is endowed with fortune and firmness, and has noble aspirations, cuts the root and the top of his enemies.

10. O Lord of the people of Kāsi, father. Strive for me. A man endowed with effort cuts the root and sprout of enemies. Thus, you, the wise bird Vessantara, gave instruction. If you should say, 'Am I not the king, the ruler of the land, who cuts the root and sprout of enemies? How is your word of instruction appropriate, my dear wise bird Vessantara?'—the word of instruction I spoke is indeed appropriate. Even Sakka, the King of Devas, is not negligent in effort. That Sakka, having made an effort only in good deeds, still applies his mind to exertion. Therefore, it is appropriate.

11. Gandhabbas, Brahmas, and the Devas of the six sensual heavens share the life of such a person who exerts in good deeds and is not negligent. Therefore, the deities protect such a person.

12. Dear father, King of the realm. You, being non-negligent and without anger, manage and command the affairs of the state yourself. Strive. A person who is lazy in his duties cannot find happiness.

13. Dear father, King Brahmadatta. In your question, 'What deed done is best?', these verses starting with 'First of all, falsehood...' are the sets of kingly conduct. Practice these kingly conducts. This is the instruction I give to you. A king who practices according to my instruction is able to make his loved ones—the queen, sons, daughters, and others—happy, and to cause suffering to his enemies.

## Finding the Bird's Nest
After sleeping for a while and waking up, the king looked at the Sal tree and saw a bird's nest at the top. As soon as he saw it, King Brahmadatta felt love for the birds. The king called a servant and said, 'Climb the Sal tree and find out whether there is anything in that bird's nest or not.'
118: That courtier said, "Very well, your Majesty," and climbed up. Seeing three eggs in that nest, he reported to King Brahmadatta. The King said, "In that case, do not let your breath fall upon those eggs." He further instructed, "Spread a layer of cotton in a flower basket, place all three eggs upon that cotton, and descend gently." After he had descended, the King held the flower basket in his hands and asked the ministers, "O ministers, what kind of eggs are these?" When King Brahmadatta asked this, the ministers replied, "Your Majesty, we do not know; the hunters will surely know."
119:
## The Ministers and the Bird Eggs
King Brahmadatta had the hunters summoned and questioned them. The hunters reported, "Great King, among these three eggs, one is an owl egg, one is a myna egg, and one is a parrot egg." When asked, "Friends, can the eggs of three different birds be in a single nest?" they replied, "Your Majesty, it can happen; if there is no danger and they are well-placed, the eggs do not perish." King Brahmadatta was pleased and, thinking, "These eggs shall be my children," he entrusted the three eggs to three ministers, saying, "These eggs shall be my children. You must guard them well and report to me when they hatch from their shells." Those ministers took great care of the eggs.
120:
## The Naming of Vessantara
Among those three eggs, the owl egg hatched first. The minister in charge of the egg summoned a hunter and said, "Find out whether it is female or male." When the hunter investigated and said, "It is male," the minister approached King Brahmadatta and reported, "Your Majesty, your son has been born."

King Brahmadatta was delighted, gave much wealth to that minister, and said, "Rear my young son well, and give him the name 'Vessantara'." He then dismissed him. That minister did exactly as King Brahmadatta had commanded.

## The Naming of Kuṇḍalinī
Thereafter, after a day or two had passed, the myna egg hatched.
121:
14. Can you, O Kuṇḍalinī, sister of the warrior, tell me?
What is the best course of action for one who desires to rule a kingdom?

He spoke this verse:

14. O Khattabandhuni, sister of the commander-in-chief; O Kuṇḍalinī, so named because of the two glowing, earring-like marks on your two ears; will you be able to answer? Do you understand the meaning of the question I ask? If you are able to answer, I shall ask you. For one who wishes to exercise sovereignty, what practice is the most excellent?

The minister in charge of the myna egg also had a hunter investigate the newly hatched young myna. Upon hearing, "It is female," he went to King Brahmadatta and reported, "Your Majesty, your daughter has been born."

King Brahmadatta was pleased and gave much wealth to that minister as well, saying, "Rear my daughter well, and give her the name 'Kuṇḍalinī'." He then dismissed him. That minister also did exactly as King Brahmadatta had commanded.

## Jambuka
Again, after a day or two had passed, the parrot egg hatched. The minister in charge of the parrot egg also had a hunter investigate the newly hatched young parrot. When the hunter said, "It is male," he went to King Brahmadatta and reported, "Your Majesty, your son has been born."
122:
When the King asked about the duties of a king (Rājadhamma), she said, “Dear father, you likely think, ‘What will a mere female say?’ to test me. I shall explain the entire Rājadhamma to you by condensing it into just two principles,” and she spoke these eleven verses:

15. “Dear father, there are only two foundations upon which everything is established: the acquisition of what has not been obtained and the protection of what has been obtained.

16. Dear father, seek out ministers who are wise and skilled in affairs; those who are not gamblers or cheats, not drunkards, and not destroyers of wealth.

17. Dear father, just as a charioteer controls his chariot, the minister who protects your wealth should be the one to manage your affairs. Having honored such a person, appoint him to the office of treasurer.

18. O Protector of the World, having treated your subordinates well, personally oversee your wealth. Perform the burying of treasures and the giving of loans with your own eyes; do not do so by relying on others.

19. Dear father, you should personally know the income and the expenditure. You should personally know who has performed their service and who has not. Punish those who deserve punishment and reward those who deserve reward.

20. O Chief of Charioteers, personally administer the affairs of the countryside. Do not let unrighteous officials destroy your wealth and the kingdom.

21. Do not perform or order tasks in haste. For a deed done in haste brings regret to the foolish later on. Act with deliberation and calmness.

22. Dear father, do not let your heart be overcome by intense anger toward the misdeeds of others. For many prosperous families have been brought to ruin through anger.

23. Dear father, do not be led astray into harmful ways by thinking ‘I am the sovereign.’ Let there be no suffering for the men and women in your realm.

24. For a king who follows his desires and is devoid of dread for consequences, all his wealth perishes; that is called the king’s misery.

25. These are the sets of duties, the very instruction for your question. Now, be diligent, a doer of merit, not a drunkard, and not a destroyer of wealth. O Great King, be virtuous; the immoral fall into states of ruin (vinipātika).”

King Brahmadatta was pleased and gave much wealth to that minister, saying, “Take good care of my son; hold a festival for him with a large retinue and name him ‘Jambuka’.” The minister did exactly as the King commanded.

## The Answering of Questions by Vessantarā

Those three birds grew up in the houses of the three ministers under the protection of the princes. King Brahmadatta called them “my son” and “my daughter.”

At that time, the courtiers mocked the King among themselves. They mocked him saying, “Friends, look at our King’s behavior; he goes about calling even animals ‘my son’ and ‘my daughter’.”

Hearing these words, King Brahmadatta thought, “These ministers do not know the wisdom of my children. I will make it clear to them.” Having thought so, he sent a minister to Vessantarā with the message: “Noble Vessantarā, your father the King wishes to ask a question. Ask her at what time he should come to ask.”
123: The minister went and paid homage to Vessantara, reporting the message that had been sent. Upon hearing these words, Vessantara summoned his guardian minister and said, "Friend guardian, I hear that my royal father wishes to ask me a question. When he comes to our home, it is proper to perform honors and offerings to him. At what time should he be invited to come?" The guardian minister replied, "My Lord, let him come on the seventh day from today." Hearing the guardian minister's reply, Vessantara said, "Let my royal father come on the seventh day from today," and sent the messenger back.
124:
That minister arrived and reported to King Brahmadatta. On the seventh day, King Brahmadatta had the drum beaten throughout the city of Vārāṇasī and proceeded to the residence of his son Vessantara. Prince Vessantara had great honors and offerings prepared for his father, King Brahmadatta. He even had honors and offerings made for the lowliest of servants and workers.

King Brahmadatta took his meal at the residence of the owl named Vessantara and enjoyed great luxury. Then, returning to his own palace, he had a great pavilion built in the palace courtyard, had the drum beaten throughout Vārāṇasī, and sat in the midst of a multitude in the decorated pavilion. He then sent a minister, saying, "Bring Vessantara here."

The guardian minister brought Vessantara, seating him on a golden dais.
125:
The owl named Vessantara stayed in the lap of his father, King Brahmadatta, playing with him, and sat only on the golden dais. While he was there, King Brahmadatta wished to ask Prince Vessantara about the duties of a king (rājadhamma) in the midst of the people.

Hearing this, Vessantara did not answer the question immediately, but first wished to rebuke King Brahmadatta for his negligence.
126:
26. "We have asked Kosiyagotta, and likewise Kuṇḍalinī. Now you, Jambuka, tell us the supreme strength among strengths."

26. "Dear Jambuka, my son Jambuka. I have already asked your elder brother Vessantara, of the Kosiya lineage, and your sister, the female myna bird named Kuṇḍalinī, about the duties of a king. Now, dear son Jambuka, I shall ask you likewise. Tell me now, what is the supreme strength among strengths, and what are the duties of a king?"

Thus, Vessantara rebuked him with this verse, and wishing to preach the kingly duties, he said, "Great King, a king should rule righteously, established in the three principles."

## Vessantara is Appointed Commander-in-Chief

Thus, after the owl named Vessantara rebuked King Brahmadatta for his negligence with one verse and preached the kingly duties with eleven verses, the people, filled with wonder and amazement at how he answered the question with the grace of a Buddha, raised many shouts of "Sādhu!"

King Brahmadatta, being filled with joy, called his ministers and asked, "Ministers, who performs the duties described by my son Vessantara, who has preached the kingly duties in this way?"

## Kuṇḍalinī Preaching the Dhamma
Again, after a day or two, King Brahmadatta sent a messenger to Kuṇḍalinī as before. On the seventh day, he went to Kuṇḍalinī's dwelling, returned, and sat in the middle of the previous pavilion. He had Kuṇḍalinī brought to him, and as she sat on a golden pedestal, he wished to ask her about the duties of a king.
When King Brahmadatta asked about the duties of a king with the verse beginning with "Sakkhisi," Kuṇḍalinī said, "Dear Father, you seem to be testing me, thinking, 'How can a young female bird answer?' I shall preach all the duties of a king to you, father, by condensing them into only two factors."
128:
## Kuṇḍalinī Appointed as Treasurer
Thus, the female myna bird named Kuṇḍalinī also preached the duties of a king with eleven verses. King Brahmadatta was greatly pleased and summoned his ministers to ask: "O ministers, whose duties has my daughter Kuṇḍalinī, who preached the duties of a king in the manner described, performed?"
129:
"Your Majesty, the Treasurer has performed his duty," they reported. "In that case, I grant the position of Treasurer to my daughter Kuṇḍalinī," the King declared, and he appointed the myna bird named Kuṇḍalinī to the post of Treasurer. From that time on, the myna bird named Kuṇḍalinī remained in the position of Treasurer and managed her father's affairs.

The problem solved by the myna bird named Kuṇḍalinī is concluded.

The minister in charge of the royal birds brought the wise Jambuka, seating him on a golden seat and carrying that golden seat on his head. The wise Jambuka played in the lap of his father, King Brahmadatta, and then went to sit on the golden seat.
