133:
## 2. Sarabhaṅga Jātaka
## Wisdom alone is the mark of success in all things

**The Present Story**

The Master, the Teacher of the world including the devas, while staying at Veḷuvana Monastery, told this Sarabhaṅga Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Alankatā kuṇḍalino suvatthā," concerning the parinibbāna of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.

Indeed, the Venerable Sāriputta, having informed the Buddha who was staying at Jetavana Monastery of his impending parinibbāna, went to Nālaka village and passed away in the room where he was born. Hearing of the Venerable Sāriputta's parinibbāna, the Buddha went to Rājagaha and stayed at Veḷuvana Monastery.

## The Manner of Venerable Moggallāna’s Parinibbāna

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was staying at the Black Rock (Kāḷasilā) on the side of Mount Isigili. With his psychic power (iddhi) which had reached the pinnacle of majesty, he traveled to the celestial realms and to the Ussada hells.

Seeing the great prosperity and bliss of the Buddha's disciples in the celestial realms, and the great suffering of the heretics' disciples in the Ussada hells, he returned to the human world and preached to the people: "This lay follower, man or woman, has been reborn in such-and-such a heaven and enjoys great prosperity. Among the disciples of the heretics, this person or that person has been reborn in such-and-such a state of misery, such as hell."

People gained great faith in the Dispensation (Sāsana) and abandoned the heretics. Great honor and offerings accrued to the Buddha's disciples, while the gains and honor of the heretics declined.

The heretics, harboring a grudge against the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, thought: "If this monk Moggallāna lives, our supporters will be ruined and our gains will diminish. Let us kill him." They gave a thousand pieces of money to a bandit named Samaṇaguttika to kill the Elder.

The bandit Samaṇaguttika, thinking "I will kill the Elder Moggallāna," went to the Black Rock with a large following. When the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw the bandit coming, he flew away by psychic power. The bandit, not seeing the Elder that day, returned and came again the next day and the day after; thus he came for six days. The Elder likewise departed by psychic power. On the seventh day, the aparāpariyavedanīya kamma (kamma to be experienced in a future life) committed by the Elder in the past found its opportunity.

## The Result of Kamma

In a past life, the Elder, influenced by his wife's words and wishing to kill his parents, took them to the forest in a cart. He then made it appear as if bandits were attacking and beat his parents. Because of their failing eyesight, the parents could not see and did not realize it was their own son beating them. Thinking "These are surely bandits," they cried out for their son's sake: "Dear son, these bandits are beating us; you, dear son, must escape!"
134:
The young man thought: "These old people, even though I am beating and striking them, cry out only for my benefit. I have committed an improper act." Then, comforting his elderly parents and pretending that the bandits had fled, he massaged their hands and feet and said, "O mother and father, do not be afraid; the bandits have fled." He then took them back to his home.

## The Assault by the Bandits
That evil kamma, having found no opportunity for such a long time, remained like a heap of embers covered with ash, and then pursued and seized him in this final body. This is true. For example, when a hunter sees a deer and releases a dog, the dog pursues the deer and catches it wherever it reaches it; in the same way, kamma gives its result in whatever place it finds an opportunity. There is no one who is free from that kamma.

The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, knowing that the kamma he had committed was pulling him, did not flee. Due to the consequence of that evil kamma, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was unable to fly into the air. His psychic power, which was capable of taming the Nāga king Nandopananda and shaking the Vejayanta Palace, became weak due to the power of the unwholesome kamma of having beaten his parents.

The bandit Samanaguttika caught the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and, crushing the Elder's bones until they were the size of broken rice grains, he beat him and ground them to powder. Having made the body as flat as straw and thinking, "Now he is dead," he threw him onto a bush and departed with his followers.

## The Display of Psychic Powers
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna regained consciousness and thought, "I shall attain Parinibbāna after seeing the Teacher." He bound his body with the cord of Jhāna, made it firm, and flew into the air. Traveling through the sky, he went to the presence of the Teacher, paid homage to the Teacher, and said, "Venerable Sir, my life-force is relinquished; I shall now attain Parinibbāna."

When the Teacher asked, "Moggallāna, will you attain Parinibbāna?", he confirmed that he would. When asked, "Where will you go to attain Parinibbāna?", he replied, "I shall attain Parinibbāna on the Black Rock (Kāḷasilā) on the side of Mount Isigili." The Teacher said, "If that is so, Moggallāna, preach the Dhamma to me before you go; for there will be no more seeing such a disciple after this time." The Venerable Moggallāna replied, "I will do so, Venerable Sir." He paid homage to the Teacher, rose into the air, and performed various psychic miracles, just as the Venerable Sāriputta had done on the day of his Parinibbāna. After preaching the Dhamma and paying homage to the Teacher, he attained Parinibbāna on the Black Rock on the side of Mount Isigili.

## The Funeral Festival
At that very moment, the six deva worlds of the sense sphere were filled with a great uproar, saying, "It is said that our teacher, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, has attained Parinibbāna." They came bringing divine scents, flowers, incense, and various kinds of wood. A sandalwood pyre ninety-nine cubits high was built.

The All-Knowing Buddha stood near the Elder and had the body placed upon the sandalwood pyre. A rain of flowers fell over an area of one league around the cemetery. Humans were among the devas, and devas were among the humans.

In succession, Yakkhas stood among the devas, Gandhabbas stood among the Yakkhas, Nāgas stood among the Gandhabbas, Garuḍas (Venateyyas) stood among the Nāgas, and Kinnaras stood among the Garuḍas. Between the umbrellas, there were yak-tail whisks. Between those umbrellas and yak-tail whisks, there were banners. For seven days, they celebrated the festival of the virtuous (Sādhukīḷana).
135:
## A Stupa is Built
The All-Enlightened One had the relics of the Venerable Moggallāna taken and caused a stupa to be built at the entrance of the Veluvana Monastery.

At that time, a discussion arose in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, the Venerable Sāriputta did not attain parinibbāna in the presence of the Buddha, and thus did not receive great honors from the Buddha. However, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna attained parinibbāna in the presence of the Buddha and thus received great honors."

The All-Enlightened One arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such a discussion," He said, "Monks, not only now has Moggallāna received great honors in my presence; he received them in the past as well." Having said this, He brought forth the past.

In the past, monks, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta took conception in the womb of the chaplain's wife. After ten months, at dawn, the mother gave birth. At that moment, throughout the entire city of Bārāṇasī, which spanned twelve yojanas, all weapons blazed with light.

At the very moment of the son's birth, the chaplain went outside, looked at the sky, and seeing the conjunction of the stars, knew: "Because this boy is born under this constellation, he will become the foremost among all archers in the whole of Jambudīpa." Early in the morning, he went to the palace and inquired if King Brahmadatta had slept well. When the King said, "Teacher, how could I have slept well? Today, in the entire palace, all weapons blazed," the chaplain replied, "Great King, do not be afraid. It was not only in your palace that the weapons blazed, but in the entire city. Great King, this happened because a boy was born in our house today."

"Teacher, what will be the benefit for the boy born in this way?" the King asked. "Great King, a son born like this will not be one of little power. Indeed, that boy will become the foremost among all archers in the whole of Jambudīpa." When he said this, the King said, "Teacher, very well. If that is so, look after the boy and show him to us when he reaches maturity." He then gave a thousand coins for the nursing expenses.

The chaplain took the thousand coins, went home, gave them to his wife, and on the day of naming the son, because the weapons had blazed at the moment of birth, he named the boy "Jotipāla."

## Jotipāla Learns the Art of Archery
That youth Jotipāla grew up with a large retinue. At the age of sixteen, he possessed a magnificent appearance. Then, his father, the chaplain, seeing his son endowed with physical perfection, said, "Dear son, go to the city of Takkasilā and learn the art of archery in the presence of the world-renowned teacher." The youth Jotipāla agreed, saying, "Very well."

Taking a thousand coins for the teacher's fee, he paid respects to his parents and went to Takkasilā. Having given the thousand coins, he completed his studies in just seven days.

Then, the world-renowned teacher was greatly pleased with the youth Jotipāla and gave him his own precious sword, a bow made of joined ram's horns, a quiver with a strap, his own suit of armor, a tunic, and a turban. He said, "Dear Jotipāla, I am old. Now, you must teach these young students." He then entrusted five hundred young students to the youth Jotipāla.

## Jotipāla Receives a Thousand Daily
The Bodhisatta took all the equipment, paid respects to his teacher, and returned to Bārāṇasī. He paid respects to his parents and stayed there. Then, the father, the chaplain, seeing the youth Jotipāla standing after paying respects, asked, "Dear son, have you learned the art?" "Father, I have learned it," he replied.

When the chaplain heard the words of his son Jotipāla, he went to the palace and asked, "Great King, my son has learned the art and returned. What should he do?" "Teacher, let him serve us," the King replied. "Great King, please determine the allowance for the youth Jotipāla," he submitted.
136:
When the King said, "Let the youth Jotipāla receive a thousand coins daily," the chaplain agreed, saying, "Very well." He went home, summoned his son Jotipāla, and said, "Dear son, serve the Great King." From that time on, the youth Jotipāla received a thousand coins daily and served the King.

## The Archery Skill of Jotipāla
Those who served at the King's feet constantly grumbled: "We do not see any work done by the youth Jotipāla. He takes a thousand coins every day. We wish to see the skill of this youth Jotipāla." King Brahmadatta heard the words of those courtiers and spoke to the chaplain. The chaplain said, "Very well, Great King," and informed his son.

The youth Jotipāla said, "Father, very well. I will demonstrate on the seventh day from today. Let King Brahmadatta assemble the archers within his kingdom." The chaplain went and informed King Brahmadatta of this matter. King Brahmadatta had the drum beaten throughout the city of Bārāṇasī to assemble the archers. Sixty thousand archers gathered.

King Brahmadatta, knowing that the sixty thousand archers had assembled, had the drum beaten again, saying, "Let the city dwellers watch the skill of the youth Jotipāla." He had the palace courtyard prepared and, surrounded by a great multitude, sat on a noble throne. He summoned the archers and sent word, "Let the youth Jotipāla come."

The youth Jotipāla placed the ram's horn bow, the quiver, the armor, the tunic, the turban, and other items given by the world-renowned teacher inside his garments. He had his sword brought and went to the King in his ordinary attire, standing in a suitable place.

## Emerging Bravely
The sixty thousand archers made a pact: "The youth Jotipāla has come to demonstrate his archery skill. Since he has come without a bow, he must want to take a bow from our hands. Let us not give one to Jotipāla." King Brahmadatta summoned the youth Jotipāla and said, "Demonstrate your skill."

The youth Jotipāla had a curtain set up and, staying inside the curtain, removed his ordinary clothes and put on the armored tunic. He placed the turban on his head, fixed the bowstring, which was the color of coral, to the ram's horn bow, slung the quiver over his shoulder, and fastened the sword on his left side. He polished the arrow, which had a tip like a thunderbolt and was fitted with a shaft, with his fingernail. Then, opening the curtain, he emerged like a decorated young Naga coming out of the earth, and stood there showing a gesture of respect to the King.
137:
Upon seeing the youth Jotipāla, the multitude clapped their arms, shouted in acclaim, and cheered. King Brahmadatta said, "Friend Jotipāla, show your skill."

## Protection with a Single Arrow by Jotipāla
"Great King, among your sixty thousand archers, please summon the four archers who are target-hitters (akkhaṇavedhī), hair-splitters (vālavedhī), arrow-hitters (saravedhī), and sound-hitters (saddavedhī)." Upon this request, King Brahmadatta had them summoned.

The Bodhisatta constructed a pavilion within a square enclosure in the royal courtyard. He stationed the four archers at the four corners, providing each with thirty thousand arrows and an assistant to hand them the arrows. Standing in the center of the pavilion, holding a diamond-tipped arrow (vajiragga-nārāca), he said, "Great King, let these four archers shoot at me simultaneously. I shall ward off the arrows shot by these four archers with a single arrow."

King Brahmadatta commanded his champion archers, "Do as he says." The archers replied, "Great King, we are target-hitters, hair-splitters, arrow-hitters, and sound-hitters. Jotipāla is but a young lad. We shall not shoot at him." The Bodhisatta Jotipāla then said, "If you are able, shoot at me."

The four archers agreed, saying "Very well," and shot their arrows all at once. The Bodhisatta warded off those arrows with only his diamond-tipped arrow, letting them fall where he wished.

Indeed, as if surrounding a Bodhi-pavilion with lathed pillars, he shot so that arrow-head met arrow-head, fletching met fletching, shaft met shaft, and vane met vane, without any overlapping, thus creating a chamber of arrows (saragabbha). The archers' arrows were exhausted. Knowing that their arrows were spent, the youth Jotipāla, without destroying the arrow-chamber, leaped up and stood before King Brahmadatta.

The multitude shouted in acclaim, clapped their arms, cheered, and snapped their fingers in a great uproar, throwing their clothes and ornaments. The wealth thus collected amounted to eighteen crores.
138:
Then King Brahmadatta asked the youth Jotipāla, "Friend Jotipāla, what is this skill called?" "Great King, it is called the warding off of arrows (Sarapaṭibāhana)," he replied. "Is there anyone else who knows this?" the King asked. "Great King, in the whole of Jambudīpa, there is no one else besides me who knows this."

## The Archery Skill of the Circular Shot
"Friend Jotipāla, show another skill as well," the King commanded. "Great King, those four archers stationed at the four corners were unable to hit me. Now, I shall hit all four archers stationed at the four corners with a single arrow." However, the four archers did not dare to stand there.

The Bodhisatta then had four banana trees placed at the four corners. He tied a red silk thread to the nock of a diamond-tipped arrow and, aiming at one banana tree, he shot. The diamond-tipped arrow pierced that banana tree, then the second, then the third, and then the fourth. It then entered the very hole in the first banana tree and returned to the Bodhisatta's hand. The banana trees stood encircled by the red thread. The multitude raised thousands of cheers.

## Various Archery Skills Beyond Compare
King Brahmadatta asked, "Friend Jotipāla, what is this skill called?" "Great King, it is called the circular shot (Cakkaviddha)," he replied.

"Friend Jotipāla, show another archery skill as well," the King commanded. The Bodhisatta then demonstrated the skill of shooting arrows to appear like a creeper (Saralaṭṭhi), like a rope (Sararajju), piercing arrow with arrow (Saravedhī), appearing like a palace (Sarapāsāda), like a pavilion (Saramandapa), like a staircase (Sarasopāna), like a wall (Sarapākāra), and like a lotus pond (Sarapokkharaṇī). He made an arrow-lotus (Sarapaduma) bloom and caused an arrow-rain (Saravassa) to fall.

Having shown these twelve archery skills which are not shared by other archers, he then shot and broke seven great targets, also unshared by others.

He pierced a fig-wood plank eight finger-breadths thick, a padauk-wood plank four finger-breadths thick, a copper plate two finger-breadths thick, and an iron plate one finger-breadth thick. He pierced a hundred planks joined together. He shot an arrow through the front of a straw-cart, a sand-cart, and a wood-cart, making it exit through the back; and shot through the back to exit through the front. He sent arrows to a distance of four usabhas in water and eight usabhas on land. He hit a hair at a distance of one usabha, using a wild eggplant as a target. The Bodhisatta shot arrows to form palaces and such in the sky, and then, using a single arrow, he brought them down and dismantled them. Thus, he became known by the name "Sarabhaṅga" (Arrow-breaker). While he was demonstrating these many skills, the sun set.

Then the King, having promised him the position of Commander-in-Chief, said, "Jotipāla, it is late today. Tomorrow you shall receive the honors of the Commander-in-Chief's office. Come after having your hair and beard trimmed and bathing." He gave him a hundred thousand for his daily expenses.
139:
## Jotipāla Enters the Forest

While the young Jotipāla was demonstrating his archery skills to such an extent, the sun set. At that time, King Brahmadatta, wishing to appoint Jotipāla to the position of Commander-in-Chief, said, "Young Jotipāla, it is not yet the time today. Tomorrow you shall receive the honor of the Commander-in-Chief's post. Go, groom your hair and beard, bathe, and return." Having said this, the King gave him one hundred thousand in wealth for his provisions that day.

The Bodhisatta thought, "I have no need for this wealth." He gave his own wealth, amounting to one hundred and eighty million, back to its owners. Accompanied by a large retinue, he went to the river to bathe. After grooming his hair and beard and bathing, he adorned himself with all kinds of ornaments. With incomparable glory, he entered his house, ate various kinds of choice food, and ascended his magnificent bed. After sleeping for two watches of the night, he awoke in the last watch. He rose, sat cross-legged upon the bed, and reflected on the beginning, middle, and end of his art.

"In the beginning of my art, only the killing of others is apparent. In the middle, the indulgence in the objects of defilements is apparent. In the end, rebirth in the realms of misery and hell is apparent. The act of taking life, as well as the extreme negligence in wholesome deeds due to the indulgence in the objects of defilements, leads to rebirth in hell. King Brahmadatta has offered me the noble position of Commander-in-Chief. I shall have great wealth. I shall have many wives, sons, and daughters. Truly, the objects of defilements, when they reach abundance and expansion, are difficult to renounce. It is proper for me to leave the house this very moment, enter the forest alone, and ordain as an ascetic."

Thinking thus, he rose from his noble bed and, without letting anyone know, descended from the palace. He departed through the main gate and entered the forest alone, heading towards the Kapittha forest, which spanned three yojanas, by the banks of the Godhāvarī River.

## Jotipāla as an Ascetic

Knowing of Jotipāla's renunciation, Sakka, the King of Devas, called the celestial architect Vissakamma and said, "Dear Vissakamma, the young Jotipāla has gone forth in renunciation. There will be a great gathering of ascetics. Create a hermitage in the Kapittha forest by the banks of the Godhāvarī River and prepare the requisites for an ascetic." Vissakamma did exactly as Sakka had commanded.

When the Bodhisatta reached that place and saw a single-footpath, he thought, "This must be a dwelling place for renunciants." He followed the path to the hermitage. Seeing no one there, he entered the leaf-hut and saw the requisites of an ascetic. He thought, "Sakka, the King of Devas, must have known of my renunciation."

He discarded his lay clothes and put on the red bark garments. He placed a black antelope skin over one shoulder, tied his hair in a matted coil, slung a carrying pole with requisites over his shoulder, and took a staff used by the elderly. Leaving the leaf-hut, he stepped onto the walkway and paced back and forth a few times. Beautifying the forest with the glory of a monk, he performed the preliminary exercises for kasina meditation. On the seventh day after his ordination, he attained the eight meditative attainments and the five superknowledges. He lived alone, sustaining himself on forest roots and fruits gathered through the practice of seeking alms.

## Many People Ordain

The mother, father, dear friends, and relatives of Jotipāla, not seeing him, wandered about weeping and lamenting.

Then, a hunter entered the forest and, seeing the Bodhisatta Jotipāla living in the Kapittha hermitage, recognized him. He went and exchanged pleasantries with the Bodhisatta, then went to the city and informed Jotipāla's parents. The parents, in turn, informed King Brahmadatta.

King Brahmadatta said, "Come, let us go and see the young Jotipāla." Taking Jotipāla's parents and accompanied by a great multitude, he reached the Godhāvarī River by the path shown by the hunter. The Bodhisatta came to the riverbank and, sitting in mid-air, preached the Dhamma and led all of them to the hermitage. There also, while remaining seated in the air, he preached the Dhamma to them, explaining the perils of sensual pleasures.

Starting with King Brahmadatta, everyone ordained as ascetics under the Bodhisatta Jotipāla. The Bodhisatta remained in that Kapittha hermitage by the Godhāvarī River, surrounded by the assembly of monks.
140:
Then, the fact that the Bodhisatta Jotipāla was living in the Kapittha hermitage by the Godhāvarī River became famous throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa. Other kings also came with their subjects and ordained under the Bodhisatta Jotipāla. The gathering of ascetics was vast. Gradually, the assembly grew to hundreds of thousands. Among that assembly, whenever anyone entertained thoughts of sensual desire, ill-will, or cruelty, the Bodhisatta would go and sit in the air before that person to preach the Dhamma and instruct them in the preliminary exercises for kasina meditation.

## The Seven Famous Disciple Ascetics

Abiding by the instructions of the Bodhisatta Jotipāla, seven chief disciples attained the eight meditative attainments and reached the perfection of Jhāna. They were:
1. Sālissara the Ascetic
2. Meṇḍissara the Ascetic
3. Pabbata the Ascetic
4. Kāḷadevila the Ascetic
5. Kisavaccha the Ascetic
6. Anusissa the Ascetic
7. Nārada the Ascetic

Later, the Kapittha hermitage became full. There was not enough space for the multitude of ascetics. Then the Bodhisatta called the ascetic Sālissara and said, "Friend Sālissara, this hermitage is not enough for all these ascetics. Take this group of ascetics and live near the market town of Kalappacullaka in the territory of the King of Majjha."

Sālissara replied, "Very well," and accepting the words of his teacher Jotipāla, he took thousands of ascetics and went to live at the Kalappacullaka market town.

As more people came and ordained, the hermitage became full again. The Bodhisatta called the ascetic Meṇḍissara and sent him away, saying, "Friend Meṇḍissara, take this group of ascetics and live on the banks of the Sātodikā River on the borders of the Suraṭṭha country."

Again, the Kapittha hermitage became full. In this manner, for the third time, he called the ascetic Pabbata and sent him, saying, "Friend Pabbata, there is a mountain named Añjana in the great forest. Live in dependence on that Mount Añjana."

For the fourth time, he called the ascetic Kāḷadevila and sent him, saying, "Friend Kāḷadevila, there is a mountain named Ghanasela in the kingdom of Avanti in the Dakṣiṇāpatha. Live in dependence on that Mount Ghanasela."

Once more, the Kapittha hermitage became full. Thus, groups of thousands of ascetics were established in five locations.
141:
The ascetic Kisavaccha, having taken leave of the Bodhisatta, dwelt in a park near the city of Kumbhavatī in the kingdom of King Daṇḍakī. The ascetic Nārada dwelt in the midst of the mountain range called Anjanagiri in the Middle Country. The ascetic Anusissa remained in the presence of the Bodhisatta.

## King Daṇḍakī's Offense Against the Ascetic
At that time, King Daṇḍakī demoted a certain courtesan who had previously received honors. As she was wandering about according to her nature, she came to the park and, seeing the ascetic Kisavaccha, thought, "This man must be an ill omen. I will wash away my ill luck upon his body, bathe, and then depart." She chewed her tooth-stick and, before anyone else, spat phlegm upon the body of the ascetic Kisavaccha, spitting into his matted hair. She then placed the chewed tooth-stick on his head, washed her own head, and left.

King Daṇḍakī, remembering the courtesan, reinstated her to her former position. Being very foolish and deluded, she thought, "Because I cast my ill luck upon the body of that wretch, the King has restored my status; I have regained my fame."

Not long after, King Daṇḍakī demoted his chaplain (purohita). The chaplain went to the courtesan and asked, "For what reason have you regained your position?" She replied, "Teacher, I regained it because I cast my ill luck upon the body of a wretch in the royal park." The chaplain went and, just as the courtesan had said, cast his ill luck upon the body of the ascetic Kisavaccha. The King then reinstated the chaplain to his position.

Later, a rebellion broke out in the border region. King Daṇḍakī set out for war, surrounded by his fourfold army. Then the very foolish chaplain asked the King, "Great King, do you desire victory or defeat?" When the King replied, "I desire victory," the chaplain said, "If you desire victory, go and cast your ill luck upon the body of the wretch who dwells in the royal park before marching out."

Taking the chaplain's word, the King said, "Let those who march to war with me cast their ill luck upon the body of the wretch in the park." He entered the park, chewed a tooth-stick, and before all others, the King himself spat and threw his tooth-stick into the matted hair of the ascetic Kisavaccha, and then washed his head. The entire army did exactly as the King had done to the ascetic.

As the King was departing, the general (senāpati) arrived and, seeing the teacher Kisavaccha, removed the tooth-sticks and other filth, bathed him well, and asked, "Venerable sir, what will happen to the King?" The ascetic replied, "Lay disciple, I have no malice in my heart, but the deities are angry. On the seventh day from today, the entire kingdom will be destroyed. Take your wife and children, flee quickly, and go to another country."

The general, trembling with fear, went and informed the King. Even after hearing the general's words, King Daṇḍakī did not heed them. The general returned to his home, took his wife and children, and fled to another country.

When the teacher Sarabhaṅga learned of this matter, he sent two young ascetics, saying, "Bring the ascetic Kisavaccha here through the air on a couch-litter."
142:
## The Destruction of the Kingdom of Kumbhavatī
King Daṇḍakī fought the war, captured the rebels, and returned to the city. Upon his arrival, the deities first caused it to rain. When all the filth had been washed away by the flood of rain, they caused a rain of white sand to fall. Upon the white sand, a rain of celestial flowers fell. Upon the flowers, a rain of beans (māsaka) fell. Upon the beans, a rain of coins (kahāpaṇa) fell. Upon the coins, a rain of celestial ornaments fell.

The people, filled with joy, began to collect the ornaments made of wrought and unwrought gold. Then, a rain of various kinds of blazing weapons fell upon their bodies. The people were cut into pieces.

As they were being cut, great glowing coals fell upon them. Upon the coals, great blazing mountain peaks fell. Upon the mountain peaks, a rain of fine sand fell, filling the area to a height of sixty cubits. Thus, an area of sixty leagues (yojana) was destroyed. The destruction of that kingdom became famous throughout all of Jambudīpa.

## The Three Kings Visit the Hermitage
Then, the rulers of the neighboring kingdoms—King Kāliṅga, King Aṭṭhaka, and King Bhīmaratha—pondered. They thought: "In the past, it is heard that King Kalābu of Kāsi in Bārāṇasī offended the ascetic Khantivādī and was swallowed up by the earth. Likewise, King Nāḷikera had ascetics bitten by dogs and was swallowed up by the earth. King Ajjuna of the Thousand Arms offended the ascetic Aṅgīrasa and was swallowed up by the earth. Now, it is heard that King Daṇḍakī offended the ascetic Kisavaccha and has come to ruin along with his kingdom. We do not know the place where these four kings have been reborn. There is no one other than our teacher, the ascetic Sarabhaṅga, who is capable of explaining this. Let us approach the teacher Sarabhaṅga and ask these questions."

Having so pondered, the three kings set out with a large retinue to ask the questions. These three kings did not know that the others had also set out; each thought, "I alone am going." They met one another near the Godhāvarī River.
143:
50. Adorned, wearing earrings, well-clothed,
With swords bound with beryl and pearls.
O noble ones in the chariot, who are you?
How are you known in the world of men?

He spoke this first verse.

50. O noble ones, the most excellent among those who ride in chariots. Adorned with ornaments. Wearing jeweled earrings. Dressed in fine clothes. Carrying precious swords with hilts decorated with beryl, gems, and pearls. You, noble sirs, ride together in a single chariot. Who are you? How are you known in the world of men?

Those three kings dismounted from their chariots and, all three riding in a single chariot, reached the banks of the Godhāvarī River.

## Sakka Arrives Before the Hermit

At that moment, Sakka, the King of Devas, seated on the Paṇḍukambala stone throne, pondered seven questions. He thought, "Except for the Teacher Sarabhaṅga, there is no one in the world of devas and men capable of answering these questions. I shall ask these questions of the Teacher Sarabhaṅga. These three kings have also reached the Godhāvarī River to ask him questions. I myself will ask their questions too." Surrounded by deities from the two deva realms, he descended from the deva world.

## When the Hermit Kisavaccha Passed Away

On that very day, the hermit Kisavaccha passed away. To perform the funeral rites for the hermit Kisavaccha, thousands of ascetics came from five places and built pavilions. The host of thousands of ascetics prepared a sandalwood pyre for the hermit Kisavaccha and cremated his body. A rain of divine flowers fell for half a league around the cremation ground. The Great Being Sarabhaṅga, having seen to the disposal of the body, entered the hermitage and sat surrounded by the host of ascetics.

When those three kings reached the riverbank, there was the sound of a great army, vehicles, elephants, horses, and musical instruments. Hearing that sound, the Great Being called his disciple, the hermit named Anusissa, and said, "Dear Anusissa, go and find out first what this sound is."

## Anusissa Asks to Know the Matter

That hermit Anusissa took a water pot and went to that place. Seeing the three kings, wishing to ask, he spoke the first verse:
144:
51. I am Aṭṭhaka, and this is Bhīmaratha.
And this is the King of Kaliṅga, known as Uggata.
To see the well-restrained hermits,
We have come here to ask questions.

He spoke this second verse.

51. Venerable sir. I am King Aṭṭhaka. This king is King Bhīmaratha. This king is the King of Kaliṅga, who is famous and renowned like the sun and the moon. We have come to this place to see the hermits who are well-restrained in their physical gates and other faculties. Wishing to ask questions of the Teacher Sarabhaṅga, we have come.

52. You stand in the sky, in the firmament,
Like the moon on the fifteenth day in the middle of its path.
I ask you, O Yakkha of great power,
How are you known in the world of men?

He spoke this third verse.

52. O Yakkha of great power. You, O divine being, stand in the supportless sky, just like the moon that stands in the middle of the firmament on the fifteenth day of the full moon. I ask you, O divine being: How are you known in the world of men?

## Wishing to See the Venerable Hermit

Hearing the words of the hermit Anusissa, the three kings dismounted from the chariot, paid respects, and stood there. Among them, King Aṭṭhaka, wishing to converse with the hermit Anusissa, spoke the second verse.

Then the hermit Anusissa said to the three kings, "O Great Kings, it is well. You have come to the right place. I urge you: bathe, rest, enter the hermitage, pay respects to the host of ascetics, and ask your questions to the Teacher Sarabhaṅga." Having exchanged pleasantries with the kings, he shouldered the water pot and, while wiping away water droplets, looked up at the sky.

## Who Are You? Your Identity is Unclear

He saw Sakka, the King of Devas, surrounded by a host of deities, descending from the deva world while riding on the back of the noble elephant Erāvaṇa. Wishing to converse with Sakka, the hermit Anusissa spoke the third verse.

## Sakka, the Lord of Devas

Hearing those words, Sakka, the King of Devas, wishing to announce his name and the reason for his coming to the hermit Anusissa, spoke the fourth verse:

53. He whom the devas call 'Sujampati',
And whom they call 'Maghavā' in the world of men—
That King of Devas has arrived here today
To see the well-restrained hermits.

53. Venerable sir. The King of Devas whom they call 'Sujampati' (husband of Sujā) in the deva worlds, and whom they call 'Maghavā' in the world of men—I am that King of Devas. I have arrived at this place today to see the host of hermits who are well-restrained in their physical gates and other faculties.
145:
54. Sages gathered here, heard of from afar,
Possessed of great power and psychic virtues.
With a devoted heart, I pay homage to you, noble ones,
Who are the best of men in this world of living beings.

He spoke this fifth verse.

54. Bhante, O Venerable Ones. Samāgatā, who have gathered together. Mahiddhikā, who possess great power. Iddhiguṇūpappannā, who are endowed with the fivefold psychic virtues. Isayo, the noble sages. No amhehi, by us. Thitehi eva, who are indeed situated. Dūre, in the distant celestial realm. Sutā, have been heard of. Ye ayire, which noble ones. Manussaseṭṭhā, are the best among men. Attha, are. Jīvaloke, in the world of living beings. Te ayire, to those noble ones. Ahaṃ, I. Pasannacitto, with a devoted heart. Vandāmi, pay homage.

55. The scent of sages long-ordained,
Wafts from their bodies, carried by the wind.
Move away from here, O Thousand-eyed One,
The scent of sages is impure, O King of Gods.

He spoke this sixth verse.

55. Sahassanetta, the King of Gods, Sakka, who possesses the vision of a thousand eyes. Isīnaṃ, of the sages. Ciradikkhitānaṃ, who have long been ordained as monks. Gandho, the scent. Kāyā, from the body. Mālutena, by the wind. Cuto, being moved. Gacchati, wafts. Paṭikkamma, move away. Ito, from this downwind place. Devarāja, O King of Gods. Isīnaṃ, of the sages. Gandho, the scent. Asuci, is repulsive like impurity.

## Reporting Back to the Great Sage Sarabhaṅga
Then, the sage Anusissa said to the King of Gods, "O King of Gods, very well, you and the others should come later." Having said this, he took the water pot, entered the monastery, stored the water pot, and informed the Great Being, the teacher Sarabhaṅga, of the arrival of the three kings and the King of Gods for the purpose of asking questions. The Bodhisatta Sarabhaṅga sat in a noble, spacious, single-pinnacled pavilion, surrounded by a group of sages. The three kings arrived, paid homage to the group of sages, and sat in a suitable place.

## Sakka Must Pay Homage
Sakka also descended, approached the group of sages, stood with palms joined, and paid homage to the group of sages. Desiring to praise the group of sages—

## One Should Not Stay Downwind
Having thus praised the group of sages, Sakka sat in a suitable place, avoiding the six faults of sitting. Then, seeing Sakka sitting downwind of the sages, the sage Anusissa, wishing to forbid him, said—

## The Scent of the Virtuous is Fragrant
Hearing those words, the King of Gods, wishing to inform the sage Anusissa of his reason for not wanting to move from that downwind spot—

## Asking Permission to Inquire
Having spoken these words, he said, "Venerable Anusissa, I have come with great effort to ask a question; please grant me the opportunity."
146:
56. Let the scent of sages long-ordained,
Waft from their bodies, carried by the wind.
Like a fragrant garland of diverse flowers,
We desire this scent, O Venerable One.
For here, the gods do not perceive it as repulsive.

He spoke this verse.

56. Bhante, O Venerable Ones. Ciradikkhitānaṃ, who have long been ordained as monks. Isīnaṃ, of the noble sages. Gandho, the scent. Kāyā, from your bodies. Mālutena, by the wind. Cuto, being moved. Gacchatu, let it waft. Etaṃ gandhaṃ, this scent of the noble sages. Surabhiṃ mālaṃ iva, like a fragrant garland of flowers. Vicittapupphaṃ, with beautifully arranged blossoms. Pāṭikaṅkhāma, we desire. Hi saccaṃ, it is true. Ettha, in this scent of the virtuous. Devā, the gods. Paṭikkūlasaññino, having the perception of repulsiveness. Na honti, are not.

57. Purindada, Lord of Beings, Renowned,
Lord of Gods, Sakka, Maghavā, Husband of Sujā.

Hearing Sakka's words, the sage Anusissa rose from his seat and, wishing to have the group of sages grant permission, said—

That King of Gods, crusher of the Asura hosts,
Seeks the opportunity to ask a question.

58. Who among these wise ones here,
When asked, will explain the subtle questions
Of the three kings, the lords of men,
And of Vāsava, the Lord of Gods?

He spoke this pair of verses.

57. Bhonto, O Noble Ones. Purindado, who formerly gave gifts first. Bhūtapati, the leader of beings. Yasassī, who has a large retinue. Devānaṃ indo, the lord of the gods. Maghavā, of the lineage of Magha. Sujampati, the husband of Sujā. Asuragaṇaṃ pamaddano, who can crush the host of Asuras. Sakko devarāja, the King of Gods, Sakka. Pañhaṃ, a question. Pucchituṃ, to ask. Okāsaṃ, an opportunity. Ākaṅkhati, desires.

Tesaṃ paṇḍitānaṃ, among those wise sages. Puṭṭho, being asked. Ko neva (ko nu eva), which sage indeed. Byākarissati, will be able to answer?

59. This sage Sarabhaṅga is an ascetic,
Who, since birth, has abstained from sexual intercourse.
The son of a teacher, well-disciplined in character,
He will explain their questions.

He spoke this verse.

59. Bhante Anusissa, O Venerable Anusissa. Sarabhaṅgo, who can destroy arrow-pavilions and such created in the sky by striking them down with a single arrow. Tapassī, who practices austerities. Yato jāto, from the time he was born. Tato paṭṭhāya, from then on. Methunasmā virato, who has abstained from sexual intercourse. Āceraputto, the son of the royal chaplain teacher. Suvinītarūpo, who is well-disciplined in nature. Ayaṃ isi, this sage. Atthi, exists. So, that sage. Nesaṃ, of those four kings. Pañhāni, the questions. Viyākarissati, will explain.

60. O Koṇḍañña, please explain the questions;
The sages of good character entreat you.
O Koṇḍañña, this is the way among men:
This burden falls upon the one who is mature in wisdom.

He spoke this subsequent verse.

60. Koṇḍañña, O sage of the Koṇḍañña clan. Sādhurūpā isayo, the sages of good character. Taṃ, you. Yācanti, entreat. Pañhāni viyākarohi, please explain the questions. Koṇḍañña, O sage of the Koṇḍañña clan. Yaṃ yasmā, because. Vuddhaṃ, upon one who is great in wisdom. Esa eso bhāro, this burden of answering questions. Āgacchati, falls. Eso, this falling of the responsibility to answer questions. Manujesu, among men. Dhammo, is the natural way.

## Who Will Answer Sakka's Question?
Hearing those words, the group of sages said, "O Venerable Anusissa, our equal, you speak as if you are standing on the ground and yet do not see the ground. Apart from the teacher Sarabhaṅga, who else would be able to answer the questions of those four kings?" Thus, wishing to inform the sage Anusissa of this fact—

## Sarabhaṅga Will Answer
Having spoken these words, the group of sages said to the sage Anusissa, "O Venerable Anusissa, our equal, you yourself should pay homage to the teacher Sarabhaṅga and, on behalf of the group of sages, ask him to grant the opportunity to answer the questions asked by Sakka." The sage Anusissa accepted, saying "Very well," and then paid homage to the teacher Sarabhaṅga, seeking to obtain the opportunity—

## 3. Alambusā Jātaka

## Experiencing Great Sorrow due to Loss of Perception

The Story of the Present: The All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Alambusā Jātaka, adorned with verses beginning with "Atha bravī brahmā indo," concerning a monk tempted by his former wife.

The Story of the Present is detailed in the Indriya Jātaka.

## Loss of Jhāna because of a Woman

In particular, the All-Knowing Buddha asked that monk, "Monk, is it true that you are dissatisfied?" When the monk replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Buddha asked, "Who caused you to be dissatisfied?" The monk replied, "Bhante, my former wife caused it." The Buddha then said, "Monk, this woman has worked for your harm before. Depending on this woman, you lost your jhāna and lay deluded and unconscious for three years. When perception returned, you wept with great lamentation," and he brought forth the past.

The Story of the Past: Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family in the Kāsī kingdom. When he reached maturity, he attained mastery in all arts, became an ascetic, and lived in a forest hermitage, subsisting on forest roots and fruits.

## The Son of the Doe
At that time, a certain doe ate grass mixed with semen and drank water at the place where the hermit had urinated. By doing only this, she became possessed of a mind attached to the hermit and conceived. From that time on, she did not go elsewhere but ate grass only in that place, foraging near the hermit's leaf-hut.

Upon investigating, the Bodhisatta came to know of that matter. Later, the doe gave birth to a boy. The Bodhisatta raised the boy with the love of a son and gave him the name "Isisiṅga."

Later, when Isisiṅga reached the age of discretion, the Bodhisatta ordained him. In his old age, the Bodhisatta took the hermit Isisiṅga to a forest of climbing plants named Nāri (Woman-forest), so called because its flowers bloomed in the shape of women, and exhorted him: "Dear son, in this Himavanta forest, there are beings called women who resemble these flowers. They bring great destruction to those who fall under their influence. It is not proper to fall under the influence of such women." Having said this, he later passed away to the Brahma realm.

## The Virtue of the Hermit
The hermit Isisiṅga lived in the Himavanta region, delighting in the sport of jhāna. He possessed fierce penance and supreme restraint of the senses.

## Sakka is Afraid
At that time, due to the power of the hermit Isisiṅga's virtue, Sakka's throne became warm. When Sakka reflected, he knew the cause and thought, "This hermit might displace me from my position as Sakka."

Thinking, "I will send a celestial nymph to destroy the virtue of this Isisiṅga," he surveyed the entire celestial realm. Among his attendants numbering two hundred and fifty million, he set aside the celestial nymph named Alambusā. Seeing no other nymph capable of destroying the hermit Isisiṅga's virtue, he summoned Alambusā and commanded her to destroy his virtue.

## 4. Saṅkhapāla Jātaka
The Present Story: The Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Saṅkhapāla Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Ariyāvakāsosi," concerning the practice of the Uposatha.

To elaborate on this: At that time, the Omniscient Buddha, gladdening the lay devotees who were observing the Uposatha, said, "Wise men of old, having renounced great Naga splendor, used to observe the Uposatha," and being requested by those devotees, He brought forth the past.

The Past Story: Lay devotees, in the long past, a king named Magadha ruled in the city of Rājagaha. At that time, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of that King Magadha. They named the Bodhisatta "Duyyodhana." When he reached the age of maturity, the Bodhisatta, having learned all the arts in the city of Takkasilā, returned and saw his father. Then, his father, King Magadha, having consecrated the Bodhisatta in kingship, became an ascetic and lived in the royal garden.

## The Great Ascetic King Magadha
The Bodhisatta went to his father's presence three times a day. Great gain and honor arose for the ascetic. Because of that impediment, the ascetic was unable to perform even the preliminary work for the Kasina meditation and thought: "Gains and honors are many for me. Living in this garden, I am unable to cut this bond. Without informing my son, I shall go to another place."
173:
Having thought thus, that ascetic, without letting anyone know, departed from the garden, passed through the Magadha kingdom, and in the Mahisaka kingdom, at a bend of the river named Kaṇṇaveṇṇā which flows from the lake named Saṅkhapāla, he built a leaf-hut depending on Mount Candaka. Living there, he performed the preliminary work for the Kasina, attained the Jhanas and Supernormal Knowledges (Abhiññā), and maintained his life through the practice of alms-gathering.

## The Naga King Comes to Listen to Dhamma
A Naga King named Saṅkhapāla, departing from the Kaṇṇaveṇṇā River with a large retinue, would occasionally approach and serve that venerable ascetic. The venerable ascetic preached the Dhamma to that Naga King Saṅkhapāla.

At that time, the ascetic's son, the King, desiring to see his father and not knowing where he had gone, made inquiries and searches. Learning that "He lives in such a place," he went there with a large retinue to see his father. Having established an encampment in a suitable place and leaving his followers there, he proceeded toward his father's hermitage with two or three ministers.

At that moment, Saṅkhapāla the Naga King was sitting with a large retinue listening to the Dhamma. Seeing the King of Magadha approaching, Saṅkhapāla paid homage to the ascetic, rose from his seat, and departed. The King of Magadha also paid homage to his father, performed the customary greetings, sat down, and asked, "Venerable sir, what king is this who came to your presence?" When told, "Dear son, this is the Naga King named Saṅkhapāla," the King of Magadha, depending on the splendor of that Naga King Saṅkhapāla, developed a desire for the Naga realm. After staying for two or three days and arranging for a constant supply of alms-food for his father, he returned to his own city.

He had alms-halls built at the four gates and, causing the whole of Jambudīpa to be stirred, he gave alms, observed the precepts, and practiced the Uposatha. He made a wish for the Naga realm and, at the end of his life, he was reborn in the Naga realm and became the Naga King Saṅkhapāla.

As time passed, that Naga King Saṅkhapāla became dissatisfied and unhappy with that Naga splendor. From then on, aspiring for human birth, he observed the Uposatha. At that time, for the Naga King Saṅkhapāla living in the Naga realm, the observance of the Uposatha was not successful; he met with the destruction of his virtue. From then on, departing from the Naga realm, he coiled himself around a termite mound situated between the great road and a single-path track not far from the Kaṇṇaveṇṇā River. Having resolved upon the Uposatha and undertaken the precepts, he surrendered himself to charity, thinking, "Let those who have need of my skin, flesh, and so on, take my skin, flesh, and so on." Lying on top of the termite mound and performing the duties of a recluse, he would stay there on the fourteenth and fifteenth days, and on the first day of the lunar fortnight, he would return to the Naga realm.

## The Magadha Prince King Becomes a Naga
The King of Magadha also paid homage to his father, the venerable ascetic, and after performing the polite customary greetings, he sat down and asked, "Venerable sir, what king is this who came to your presence?" When told, "Dear son, this is the Naga King named Saṅkhapāla," that King of Magadha, relying on the splendor of that Naga King Saṅkhapāla, developed a desire for the Naga realm. After staying for two or three days and arranging for a constant supply of alms-food for his father, he went to his own city—

He had alms-halls built at the four gates and, causing the whole of Jambudīpa to be stirred, he gave alms, undertook the precepts, and practiced the Uposatha. Thus, he made a wish for the Naga realm and, at the end of his life, he was born in the Naga realm and became the Naga King Saṅkhapāla.

As time passed, that Naga King Saṅkhapāla became dissatisfied and unhappy with that Naga splendor and happiness. From then on, making a wish for human birth, he observed the Uposatha. At that time, for the Naga King Saṅkhapāla living in the Naga realm, the observance of the Uposatha was not complete. He reached the destruction of his virtue.

On one such day, while he was lying there having undertaken the precepts in this manner, sixteen men living in a border village, thinking "We shall bring back meat," were wandering in the forest with weapons in their hands. Having found nothing and about to leave, they saw him lying on top of the termite mound. They thought, "Today we did not even get a young monitor lizard; we shall kill and eat this Naga King." Thinking, "However, if he is caught, this great one might flee; we shall pierce him with stakes while he is lying there to weaken him and then take him," they approached with stakes.

The Bodhisatta's body was large, the size of a single-hulled boat, and he was exceedingly beautiful, looking like a wreath of jasmine flowers that had been rolled up, with eyes like *jinjuka* seeds and a head like a *jayasumana* flower. Hearing the sound of the footsteps of those sixteen men, he brought his head out from between his coils and opened his red eyes. Seeing them coming with stakes in their hands, he thought: "Today my heart's desire will reach its pinnacle. I have surrendered myself to charity and am lying here having resolved upon my energy. Even if these men pierce my body with spears and make it full of holes, I will not open my eyes and look at them with anger." Fearing the breaking of his virtue, he made a firm resolve, tucked his head back into his coils, and lay still. Then they approached, grabbed him by the tail, dragged him and dashed him against the ground. They pierced him in eight places with sharp stakes and, having inserted thorny black rattan sticks through the wounds, they carried him on poles in eight places and set out on the great road. From the moment he was pierced with the stakes, the Great Being did not open his eyes to look at them with anger even once. As he was being carried by the eight poles, his head hung down and struck the ground. Then, saying "His head is hanging down," they laid him on the great road, pierced his nostrils with a sharp stake, inserted a rope, lifted his head, and fastened it to the end of a pole, and then they lifted him again and proceeded on the road.

At that moment, a householder named Āḷāra, a resident of the city of Mithilā in the kingdom of Videha, was traveling with five hundred carts while sitting in a comfortable carriage. Seeing those hunters carrying the Bodhisatta in that manner, he gave to each of the sixteen men a pair of oxen, a handful of golden coins, and garments for themselves and their wives, and thus had him released. Then, he (the Naga) went to the Naga realm and, without delay there—

## The Torture by the Hunters

Then the hunters approached the Naga King Saṅkhapāla, grabbed him by the tail, dragged him, and beat him against the ground. They pierced him in eight places with sharp stakes and inserted dark-colored, thorny rattan through the holes. Then, carrying him on a pole by those eight places, they set out on the main road.

The Bodhisatta, from the moment he was pierced with a spear and at any other point, did not look at those hunters with the power of anger by opening his eyes. The head of the Saṅkhapāla Naga king, who was being carried by eight carrying-poles, hung down and struck the ground. At that time, saying, "The Naga king's head is hanging down," they laid the Saṅkhapāla Naga king on the main road, pierced his snout with a thin spit, inserted a small rope, lifted his head, hung it from the carrying-pole, and resumed their journey along the main road.

## Rescue by the Merchant Aḷāra
At that moment, a householder named Aḷāra, living in the city of Mithilā in the kingdom of Videha, was traveling with five hundred carts while riding in a comfortable carriage. Seeing the sons of the hunters who had captured the Bodhisatta in such a manner and were bringing him along, he gave to those sixteen hunters sixteen oxen from the carts, along with a handful of gold coins each. He also gave clothing and blankets to all the hunters, and garments and ornaments to their wives, and thus secured his release.

## Aḷāra Becomes an Ascetic
That Saṅkhapāla Naga king went to the Naga realm, but did not stay there long. He came out with a large retinue, approached the merchant Aḷāra, and after speaking of the virtues and glories of the Naga realm, took the merchant Aḷāra with him to the Naga realm. There, he gave the merchant Aḷāra great wealth along with three hundred Naga maidens, and satisfied him with divine sensual pleasures.

The merchant Aḷāra lived in the Naga realm for a full year, enjoying divine sensual pleasures. Then, saying to the Naga king, "Friend Naga king, I desire to become a monk," he took the requisites of an ascetic and went from the Naga realm to the Himalaya region. Having ordained there and lived in the Himalayas for a long time, he later traveled on a pilgrimage and arrived at the city of Vārāṇasī. Staying in the royal park, he entered the city for alms at dawn and went to the gate of the king's palace.

## Weariness of the World and Going Forth

195. O assembly! I make it known to the townspeople, to friends and ministers, and to the attendants. A grey hair has appeared on my head. Now, I delight in the state of a monk.

The Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, told this Cūḷasutasoma Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Āmantayāmi nigamaṃ," concerning the Perfection of Renunciation (Nekkhamma Pāramī).

The story of the present is just like the Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka.

In the past, the city of Vārāṇasī was a city named Sudassana. In that city of Sudassana, a king named Brahmadatta ruled. The Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of King Brahmadatta's chief queen. Because the Bodhisatta had a face as beautiful as the full moon, they named him "Prince Soma." When he reached the age of discretion, he loved learning and was fond of listening to good words. Therefore, they knew him as "Sutasoma."

When Prince Sutasoma reached adulthood, he studied all the arts in the city of Takkasilā. Upon his return, he received the white umbrella of his father and ruled righteously. His wealth and prosperity were great. King Sutasoma had sixteen thousand queens, led by Candādevī. Later, as his family grew with sons and daughters, he became dissatisfied with the household life and desired to enter the forest to become an ascetic.

## Desiring to Renounce upon Seeing a Grey Hair

One day, King Sutasoma called his barber and said, "Friend barber, when you see a grey hair on my head, please inform me." The barber agreed to the King's words. Later, when he saw a grey hair, he informed the King. The King said, "Friend barber, if that is so, pluck that grey hair and place it in my hand." The barber plucked it with golden tweezers and placed it in the King's hand.

Upon seeing that grey hair, the Bodhisatta King Sutasoma was struck with fear, thinking, "Old age has overcome my body." Taking that grey hair, he descended from the palace and sat upon the royal throne prepared in a place where the people could see him. He summoned eighty thousand ministers led by the Commander-in-Chief, sixty thousand Brahmins led by the Chaplain, and many other people from the country, the provinces, and the market towns. Wishing to inform them, he said, "A grey hair has appeared on my head; I am old. Know that I wish to become a monk."

The Queen Mother, having come in haste, said, "Dear son, is it true that you wish to go forth?" and wishing to lament while blaming her son, she spoke:

## The Father's Prohibition

Even though she lamented with these two verses, the Bodhisatta did not say anything at all to his mother. The mother, weeping and wailing, stayed in a suitable place on her own. Then, they informed the father of King Sutasoma. The father came and, wishing to question his son, spoke:

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta remained silent. Then the Great King, the father, said to his son, "Dear Sutasoma, even if you have no affection for your mother and father, your many sons and daughters are still young; they will not be able to live as human beings without you. You shall go forth when those sons and daughters reach maturity," and wishing to state the reason, he spoke this second verse:

201. "You have many children, young, who have not yet reached their prime. These sweet-voiced ones, not seeing you, will, I think, come to grief."

Nigacchanti manye: I think they will reach.

## Sutasoma Teaches the Dhamma

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta, wishing to preach the Dhamma to his father, spoke this verse:

202. "With these children of mine, young and not yet in their prime, with all of you, sweet-voiced ones, even after staying for a long time, there is the nature of separation."

Etehi puttehi ca: These children and. Tumhehi ca: With you, father, as well. Ciraṃ: For a long time. Ṭhatvāpi: Even after staying together. Me: For me. Vināsabhāvo: There is only the nature of destruction [separation].

203. "Is your heart broken, or do you have no compassion for us, that you go forth without regard for us while we are wailing, O Lord?"

Tena kāraṇena, for that reason. Taṃ, to you, O King. Mayaṃ, we. Vadāma, shall say. Amhesu, towards us. Tuyhaṃ, your. Hadayaṃ, heart associated with loving-kindness. Chinnaṃ nu, is it broken? Adu, or if not so. Karuṇā ca, and compassion. Te, for you. Natthi, is it altogether absent?

204. "My heart is not broken, and I do have compassion for you. But because I aspire for heaven, I shall go forth."

Karuṇāpi, compassion also. Atthi, exists. Yasmā, because. Saggañca, for heaven also. Patthayāno, I aspire. Assa, it is so. Tena, therefore. Ahaṃ, I. Pabbajissāmi, shall go forth.

## The Weeping of the Concubines
With these verses beginning with "Puttehi," the Bodhisatta preached the Dhamma to his father. When the father heard the words of his son's Dhamma talk, he remained silent. After that, the seven hundred queens of the Bodhisatta were informed. Those queens descended from the palace, went to the Bodhisatta, and holding his ankles, they wept.

## Sutasoma Preaches the Dhamma
The Bodhisatta, hearing the sound of the weeping of those queens who were rolling at his feet and crying, wished to comfort them with words of Dhamma.

## The Chief Queen's Obstruction
Thereafter, they informed the Chief Queen of the Bodhisatta. Even though she was heavy with child and her pregnancy was full-term, she came, paid homage to the Bodhisatta, and standing in a suitable place, she wished to prevent him by lamenting and wailing.

When the Chief Queen heard the words of the Bodhisatta, she was unable to restrain her grief and said, "O Lord, from this day forth, there is no such thing as glory for us," and clutching her breast with both hands, she let her tears flow and wept with a loud voice. When she wept thus, the Bodhisatta, wishing to comfort the Chief Queen, spoke. The Chief Queen, hearing the words of the Bodhisatta and being unable to remain there, ascended the golden palace and stayed there weeping.

At that time, the eldest son of the Bodhisatta saw the Chief Queen and, wishing to ask her, "Why is my mother, the Chief Queen, sitting and weeping?" he spoke this verse:

Thereafter, the Mother Queen, wishing to inform her son of the reason, spoke. 

## The Weeping of the Sons
When the eldest son heard the words of his mother, he said, "O Mother, what are you saying?"
195:
212. I who formerly went out to the park, fighting with rutting elephants; now that Sutasoma has gone forth, how shall I act?

212. "Mother! I who formerly, mounting a chariot yoked with four thoroughbred horses and adorned with all kinds of ornaments, went out to the park and engaged in combat with rutting elephants, and played other games such as horse-racing—now that King Sutasoma has gone forth, how shall I act?"

213. While my mother and my unwilling elder brother weep, I will even hold your hand; you shall not go against our will.

213. "Father! While my mother weeps and my elder brother is unwilling to be parted from you, you shall not go to renounce the world, leaving us who do not wish for this separation. I will hold your hand and keep you back."

214. Arise, nurse, and delight this prince elsewhere; let him not create an obstacle for me who aspires to heaven.

214. "Nurse, arise! Take this young prince and delight him elsewhere. Let my son not create an obstacle for me who aspires to heaven."

Saying, "If my father renounces the world, shall we not become truly helpless?", he wept.

Then the younger brother of that eldest son, who was only seven years old, seeing both his mother and brother weeping, approached his mother and asked, "Mother, why are you weeping?" Having heard the reason, he said, "If that is so, do not weep; I will not allow my father to renounce the world." After comforting both of them, he descended from the golden palace with his nurse, went to his father, and said, "Father, it is said that you are leaving us against our will to renounce the world; I will not allow you to renounce the world." He then firmly embraced his father's neck to prevent him.

The Bodhisatta thought, "This child is creating an obstacle for me. By what means can I make him leave?" Then, looking at the nurse, he said, "O nurse, take this jewel ornament; let this jewel be yours. Take my son away. Let him not create an hindrance for me." Being unable to push his son away with his own hands, he offered a bribe to the nurse to take him elsewhere, saying:
196:
215. Should I indeed take this light-maker? What use have I for this? When Sutasoma has gone forth, what shall I do with it?

215. "If I should take this jewel, which produces a brilliant light and is given as a gift—if King Sutasoma has gone forth, what benefit will I have from this jewel? What shall I do with it?"

216. Your treasury is vast, and your granary is full; the earth is conquered by you. Rejoice, O King, do not go forth.

216. "O King, your treasury of gold and silver is vast and complete. Your granaries are full. You have conquered and rule over all the people of the earth. O King, may you enjoy these; do not renounce the world."

217. My treasury is vast, and my granary is full; the earth is conquered by me. Renouncing that, I shall go forth.

217. "General Mahāsenagutta, my treasury of gold and silver is indeed vast and complete. My granaries are full. I have indeed conquered the many people of the earth. Renouncing that treasury and all else, I shall go forth."

That nurse, having taken the bribe and comforted the young prince, took him away to another place, weeping as she went.

## The General's Protest

Then the General thought, "This King likely thinks that the wealth in my palace is scarce. I shall inform him of the abundance of wealth and grain." Having thought so, the General rose from his seat, paid homage, and spoke.

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta, wishing to reject the plea, spoke.

## The Merchant's Protest

When the General had stepped aside after hearing those words, the merchant named Kulavaḍḍhana rose from his seat, paid homage, and pleaded.

The Bodhisatta, hearing the words spoken by the merchant Kulavaḍḍhana, wished to reject the plea.
197:
218. "O King, I have much wealth, so much that I cannot even count it. I give it all to you; please enjoy it and do not renounce, O King."

218. Deva, Your Majesty. I too have much wealth. I am not even able to count it. I offer all that wealth to you. Your Majesty, please delight in it. Do not renounce the world.

219. "I know you have much wealth, Kula-vaḍḍhana. I have been honored by you. But seeking the heavenly realm, I shall renounce."

219. Kula-vaḍḍhana, the Great Merchant. I know that you possess much wealth. I have been honored by you. I long for the heavenly realm. Therefore, I shall renounce.

221. "King Sutasoma, you delight in this state of renunciation. Now, renounce this very day. I too shall renounce; I cannot endure to remain without you."

221. King Sutasoma. You, my elder brother, delight in this state of a monk. Now, my elder brother, renounce this very day. I too shall renounce. I am not able to remain separated from you.

## Handing Over the Kingdom to the Younger Brother

Hearing those words, after the merchant Kula-vaḍḍhana had departed, the Bodhisatta called his younger brother named Somadatta and said, "Dear Somadatta, I am weary like a forest cock kept in a cage. Discontent with the household life overcomes me. I shall renounce this very day; you, dear brother, accept this kingship." Wishing to hand over the kingdom, he spoke this verse:

220. "I am greatly weary, Somadatta; discontent takes hold of me. Many are the dangers that appear to me; I shall renounce this very day."

220. Dear Somadatta. I am weary like a forest cock kept in a cage. Discontent with the household life severely oppresses me. Many dangers appear to me. I shall renounce this very day.

Hearing this, the younger brother Somadatta also wished to renounce and, wanting to make this clear to his elder brother the King, he spoke [Verse 221]. Then the Bodhisatta, wishing to refuse the words of his younger brother Somadatta, spoke this half-verse:

222. "It is not possible to renounce; for in the city and the country, no cooking is done."

222. Dear Somadatta. Having heard of my intention to renounce, in the city of Sudassana and throughout the countryside, no one lights a fire in the hearth to cook. Therefore, it is not proper for you to renounce.

## The People Wept

Hearing this, the multitude rolled at the feet of the Bodhisatta and, wishing to lament, spoke this half-verse:

"If Sutasoma renounces, what shall we do now?"

When King Sutasoma renounces, what shall we do now?
198:
223. "I think this life is being led away, like the little water in a laundry pot. In such a very short life, it is not the time to be negligent."

224. "I think this life is being led away, like the little water in a laundry pot. In such a very short life, blind fools are negligent."

225. "Bound by the bonds of craving, those fools increase hell, the animal realm, and the realm of ghosts. They increase the host of Asuras."

223. Friends. Just as the small amount of water placed in a laundry pot is quickly exhausted, so too is this life of beings easily exhausted. Thus I think. In such a very short life, there is no opportunity for beings with such brief lives to be negligent.

224. Friends. Just as the small amount of water placed in a laundry pot is quickly exhausted, so too is this life of beings easily exhausted. Thus I think. Even though life is so very short, fools are negligent.

225. Those fools, bound by the fetter called craving, increase the population of hell, the animal realm, and the realm of ghosts. They also increase the host of Kālakañjika Asuras.

## Sutasoma Preaches the Dhamma

Then the Bodhisatta, saying, "O people, do not grieve. Even if I were to stay for a long time, I would still eventually be separated from you. It is true that there is no such thing as a permanent conditioned state," and wishing to preach to the multitude, he spoke [the verses above].

## Cutting the Hair

Thus, after preaching to the people, the Bodhisatta ascended the palace named Pubbaka. Standing on the seventh floor, he cut his topknot with a sword and said, "I am no longer related to you in any way; take your own king," and he threw the topknot along with the turban into the midst of the people.

Taking that topknot, the people rolled on the ground and wept. In that place, a great cloud of dust arose. The people standing further back saw the rising dust and said, "The King must have cut his topknot and thrown it down with the turban. That is why this cloud of dust has arisen near the Pubbaka Palace." Wishing to lament, they spoke this verse:

227. "Dust rises not far away, near the Pubbaka Palace. I think the hair of our glorious King of Dhamma has been cut."

227. O assembled multitude. Not far from here, near the Pubbaka Palace, a cloud of dust rises. I think the hair of our glorious King of Dhamma has been cut.
199:
227. "This is his palace, strewn with golden flowers and garlands, where the king used to wander, surrounded by the women of the harem."

The Great Being sent an attendant to fetch the requisites of a monk. He had a barber shave his hair and beard, and laid his ornaments on the surface of the bed. He cut the fringes of red cloths and, wearing those saffron-dyed robes, hung an earthen bowl over his left shoulder. Taking a walking staff, he walked to and fro on the grand terrace, then descended from the palace and entered the main street. No one recognized him as he went.

Then, the seven hundred royal princesses of the Great Being went up to the palace. Not seeing the Great King Sutasoma but seeing only his ornaments, they descended and went to the remaining sixteen thousand women, crying out with a loud voice, "Our dear lord, the Great King Sutasoma, has renounced the world!" and they went outside lamenting.

At that moment, the multitude learned of the Great Being Sutasoma's renunciation. The whole city was thrown into an uproar, and they gathered at the palace gate, saying, "Our king has renounced the world, it is said." The people, thinking "The king will be here, or he will be there," went to the palace and other places used by the king. Not seeing the king, they wandered about and, wishing to lament, said:

Having lamented in various places in this manner, the people returned to the king's assembly hall and, wishing to lament further—
201:
243. "Your King Sutasoma has renounced the world, having abandoned this kingdom. Wearing saffron-colored robes, he wanders alone like a lone elephant."

243. Vo: your. Sutasomo: named Sutasoma. Rājā: the noble king. Imaṃ rajjaṃ: this kingship. Pahantvāna: having abandoned. Kāsāyavatthavasano: wearing saffron-dyed robes. Pabbajitā: having gone forth as a monk. Nāgova: like a great elephant. Ekako: alone. Carati: he wanders.

## The Great Renunciation of the People

After lamenting with this verse, they abandoned the wealth in their homes, took their sons and daughters by the hand, and left their houses to go to the Bodhisatta. The mother and father, the sons and daughters, the royal consorts, and the sixteen thousand dancing women also went in the same manner. Thus, the entire city became as if empty. The inhabitants of the countryside also followed behind the city dwellers. The Bodhisatta, taking a company of twelve yojanas, set out towards the Himalayas.

At that time, knowing the Bodhisatta's renunciation, Sakka, the king of gods, called Vissakamma and said, "Dear Vissakamma, King Sutasoma has set out on his renunciation. It is proper for him to have a place to stay. There will be a great gathering. Go and create a hermitage in the Himalayan region by the banks of the Ganges, thirty-six yojanas in length and fifteen yojanas in width." Vissakamma did as Sakka commanded, prepared the requisites for ascetics in the hermitage, created a single-footpath, and returned to the celestial realm.

The Bodhisatta traveled by that path, entered the hermitage, and first ordained himself, then ordained the others. Later, many people were ordained. The area of thirty-six yojanas was filled.

The manner in which Vissakamma created the hermitage, the manner in which many were ordained, and the manner in which the Bodhisatta arranged the hermitage should be understood as described in the Hatthipāla Jātaka.

In that hermitage, whenever a wrong thought such as a sensual thought arose in any of the ascetics, the Bodhisatta would approach them through the air, sit cross-legged in the sky, and give them counsel, speaking these two verses:
202:
244. "Do not remember the pastimes of pleasure and laughter of the past. Let not sensual desires destroy you; for the city of Sudassana is delightful."

245. "Cultivate a heart of loving-kindness, immeasurable, both by day and by night. You shall go to the city of gods, the abode of those of meritorious deeds."

He preached the combination of these two verses.

244. Bhonto sajjanā: O virtuous ones. Tumhe: you. Pubbe: in the past. Ratikīḷitāni ca: the pleasures that occurred through sensual enjoyment and through the power of physical and verbal play. Hasitāni ca: and the joys. Mā anussarittha: do not remember. Vo: you. Kāmā: sensual desires. Mā haniṃsu: let them not afflict you. Sudassanaṃ: named Sudassana. Rammaṃ hi: which is indeed delightful. Nagaraṃ: the royal city. Mā anussarittha: do not remember.

245. Bhonto sajjanā: O virtuous ones. Tumhe: you. Divā ca: by day. Ratto ca: and by night. Appamāṇaṃ: immeasurable. Mettacittañca: the heart associated with loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. Bhāvetha: cultivate. Atha: then. Tumhe: you. Puññakamminaṃ: of those with great merit. Āvāsaṃ: the abode. Devapuraṃ: to the Brahma realm. Agacchittha: you shall reach.

Wishing to give advice, he approached those various ascetics through the air and, sitting cross-legged in the sky, he gave them counsel.

That group of ascetics also stood in the Bodhisatta's advice and became destined for the Brahma realm. All such matters should be understood as described in the Hatthipāla Jātaka.

Identifying the Jātaka: The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, said, "Monks, not only now has the Tathāgata set out on the Great Renunciation; in the past also, he set out on the Great Renunciation." He then said, "Monks, those who were the mother and father then are now the royal family of the Sakyans, Siri Mahāmāyā and King Suddhodana. She who was Queen Candādevī then is now the mother of Rāhula. He who was the eldest son then is now Sāriputta. He who was the youngest son then is now Rāhula. She who was the nurse then is now Khujjuttarā. He who was the merchant Kulavaḍḍhana then is now Kassapa. He who was the general Mahāsenagutta then is now Moggallāna. He who was Prince Somadatta, the younger brother, then is now Ānanda. And I myself was King Sutasoma then."

## Turning Gray, Gaining Saṃvega, the Virtuous Renounce the World

The Cūḷasutasoma Jātaka is concluded.
203:
## 1. Nalinikā Jātaka
## The Destruction of Virtue through Sensual Desire
The Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, told this Nalinikā Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Uddahyate janapado,' concerning a monk tempted by his former wife.

The Omniscient Buddha asked that monk, 'Monk, who has caused you to be dissatisfied?' When the monk replied, 'Venerable Sir, my former wife has caused me to be dissatisfied,' the Buddha said, 'Monk, it is not only now that this woman has worked your harm; in the past also she worked your harm. Because of her, you fell away from the Jhanas and met with great ruin.' Having said this, He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Vārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a wealthy and renowned Brahmin family. Upon reaching maturity and completing his education, he embraced the life of an ascetic. Having attained the Jhanas and the higher knowledges (Abhiññā), he dwelt in the Himalayan region.

## The Young Ascetic Isisinga
In the manner described in the Alambusā Jātaka, a doe conceived a child by the Bodhisatta ascetic and gave birth to a boy. The boy was named 'Isisinga.' Later, when Isisinga reached maturity, his father, the Great Ascetic, ordained him as an ascetic and taught him the preliminary practices of the Kasiṇa. Before long, the young ascetic Isisinga attained the Jhanas and higher knowledges and delighted in the bliss of Jhana. He was an ascetic of fierce austerity and possessed supreme restraint of the senses.

## Sakka's Alarm
Due to the power of the young ascetic Isisinga's virtue, the throne of Sakka, King of Devas, trembled. Upon reflection, Sakka realized the cause and thought, 'I will destroy this ascetic's virtue by a stratagem.' He then prevented rain from falling throughout the entire kingdom of Kāsi for three years. The whole kingdom of Kāsi became as if scorched by fire. When the crops failed, the people, oppressed by famine, gathered and cried out in the palace courtyard.

At that time, King Brahmadatta, standing at the palace window, asked, 'What is the reason for this outcry?' The people replied, 'Great King, because it has not rained for three years, the entire country is parched. The people are suffering. O King, please make it rain.' Although the King took upon himself the five precepts and observed the Uposatha, he was unable to make it rain.
