## The Plan to Destroy the Ascetic's Virtue
'Great King, in the Himalayan region, there dwells an ascetic named Isisinga. He is of fierce austerity and supreme restraint of the senses. Whenever it rains, he becomes angry and looks up at the sky; therefore, it does not rain,' said Sakka. The King then asked, 'What should be done now regarding this young ascetic Isisinga?'

'If the virtue of that young ascetic Isisinga is destroyed, it will rain,' Sakka said. The King then asked, 'Who is capable of destroying the virtue of that ascetic Isisinga?' Sakka advised King Brahmadatta, 'Great King, your daughter Nalinikā is capable. Summon Nalinikā and send her, saying, "Go to such-and-such a place and destroy the virtue of the young ascetic Isisinga."' Having thus advised the King, Sakka returned to his own abode in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

On the following day, King Brahmadatta consulted with his ministers and summoned his daughter Nalinikā to send her on the mission.

## Regaining the Jhānas

Upon hearing the words of his father, the great hermit, the young hermit Isisiṅga became terrified, thinking, "That woman must be an ogress." He turned his mind back from the princess and said, "Father, I shall not leave this hermitage. Please forgive me," and paid his respects.
220:
The Great Hermit father comforted his son, the young hermit Isisinga, saying, "Come, dear boy, develop loving-kindness, develop compassion, develop appreciative joy, and develop equanimity," thus teaching him the meditation on the Brahmavihāras (Divine Abodes). The young hermit Isisinga practiced exactly as his father instructed. He once again attained the jhānas and higher knowledges (abhiññā).

Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching of the Nalinikā Jātaka and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher (the Buddha) identified the birth. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was dissatisfied and wished to disrobe was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). How did he identify the birth? — "The former wife of the monk who is now dissatisfied and wishes to disrobe was then the princess named Nalinikā; the monk who is now dissatisfied was then the young hermit Isisinga; and I myself was then the Great Hermit father." Thus he identified the birth.

## One who is biased and follows the side of folly will lose their wisdom.
The Nalinikā Jātaka is finished.

## 2. Ummādantī Jātaka
## The wise do not follow the dictates of defilements.
While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the All-Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Ummādantī Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Nivesanaṃ kassanudaṃ sunanda," concerning a dissatisfied monk.

## The Disease of Sensual Desire
One day, while that monk was walking for alms in the city of Sāvatthī, he saw a woman of supreme beauty, adorned with ornaments. His heart became bound to her, and being unable to turn his mind back from her, he returned to the monastery. From that time on, he was afflicted by passion like a deer struck by an arrow. He became thin, his veins stood out on his body, his complexion turned pale like a withered leaf, and he was unhappy, finding no mental peace in any posture. He neglected his duties to his teacher, and ceased his efforts in learning the Pali texts, the commentaries, and practicing meditation.

His friends and close monks asked him, "Friend, previously your faculties were calm and your face was bright. Now it is not so. What is the reason?" That dissatisfied monk replied, "Friends, I am dissatisfied (with the holy life)."
221:
## The Dangers of Sensual Pleasures
Then his friends and close monks said to him: "Friend, find delight (in the Sāsana). The arising of a Buddha is very rare; likewise, hearing the True Dhamma and obtaining a human birth are very rare. Having obtained a human birth and aspiring to make an end of the suffering of the round of rebirths, having left your weeping relatives and ordained out of faith, why do you follow the domain of defilements?

These defilements, starting from the lowliest creatures like earthworms, are common to all foolish people. Those five sensual pleasures which are the basis for these defilements are not truly delightful. In these five sensual pleasures, there is much suffering, much exhaustion, and many dangers.

Sensual pleasures are like bare bones; sensual pleasures are like a piece of meat; sensual pleasures are like a grass torch; sensual pleasures are like a pit of glowing coals; sensual pleasures are like a dream; sensual pleasures are like borrowed goods; sensual pleasures are like poisonous fruit; sensual pleasures are like a sword; sensual pleasures are like a stake; sensual pleasures are like the head of a cobra; sensual pleasures are like a great fire. Despite this, having ordained in such a Dispensation of the Buddha, will you follow the dictates of these defilements that bring only harm?" Thus they advised him.

Being unable to make him accept their words, they took him to the presence of the All-Enlightened Buddha in the Dhamma Hall. When asked, "Monks, why have you brought this monk who is unwilling?" they replied, "Venerable Sir, this monk is said to be dissatisfied."

The All-Enlightened Buddha asked, "Monk, is it true?" When he replied, "It is true, Venerable Sir," the Buddha said, "Monk, wise men of old, even while governing and advising a kingdom, did not follow the dictates of defilements when they arose, but restrained their minds and did not do what was improper." Then he brought forth the past.

The Story of the Past: Monks, in the past, in the city of Ariṭṭhapura in the kingdom of Sivi, a king named Sivi reigned. The Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of King Sivi's chief queen. They named him "Prince Sivi." The commander-in-chief also had a son born to him, whom they named "Abhipāraka." Both the king's son and the commander's son grew up as companions. When they were sixteen years old, they went to Takkasilā, learned the arts, and returned. The father, King Sivi, gave the kingship to his son. That son, King Sivi, appointed Abhipāraka to the position of commander-in-chief and ruled righteously.
222:
## Ummādantī
In that city of Ariṭṭhapura, a daughter was born to a merchant named Tiriṭivaccha, who possessed eighty crores. She possessed a noble complexion and had reached the pinnacle of loveliness. She was endowed with auspicious marks. On the day of her naming, they gave her the name "Ummādantī."

When Ummādantī reached the age of sixteen, she surpassed human beauty and was as beautiful as a celestial nymph. She was lovely to behold, pleasing, and endowed with supreme beauty of complexion. Whichever worldlings (puthujjanas) saw Ummādantī, they were unable to maintain their composure. Like those intoxicated by liquor, they became intoxicated with the intoxication of defilements and were unable to establish mindfulness.

## The Brahmins are Driven Out
Then, the merchant Tiriṭivaccha, the father of Ummādantī, approached King Sivi and said, "Great King, a jewel of a woman has been born in my house, worthy of a king. Please send brahmins who are readers of marks to examine this jewel of a woman and do as you please." King Sivi said, "Very well," and sent the brahmin priests.

Those brahmin priests went to the merchant Tiriṭivaccha's house, and having been received with great honor and hospitality, they ate milk-rice. At that moment, Ummādantī, adorned with all her ornaments, went into the presence of those brahmin priests. Upon seeing Ummādantī, the brahmins were unable to establish mindfulness; intoxicated with the intoxication of defilements, they did not even realize they had not finished eating. Some brahmins took a handful of rice and, thinking they were eating, placed it on their heads. Some dropped it under their armpits. Some struck the walls. All of them became like madmen.

Seeing those brahmins, Ummādantī thought, "These madmen are supposed to examine my marks!" and said, "Seize these brahmins by their necks and drive them out." Thus, she had them expelled.

## Reporting the Fault
Those brahmin priests, feeling humiliated, went to the King's palace and reported, "Great King, that woman named Ummādantī is a woman of ill-omen (kāḷakaṇṇī); she is not suitable for Your Majesty." King Sivi, thinking, "She is said to be a woman of ill-omen," did not have her brought to him.

## Bearing a Grudge Against the King
Ummādantī heard that news and said, "The King did not take me, saying I am a woman of ill-omen. Those who are truly of ill-omen are not like this." She then said, "Let it be; even if he did not take me because he thought I was a woman of ill-omen, if I ever see that King, I will make him know." Thus, she bore a grudge against King Sivi. Later, her father gave Ummādantī to the general Abhipāraka. Ummādantī became a wife who delighted the heart of General Abhipāraka.

## Ummādantī's Past Merit
By the fruit of what wholesome deed did Ummādantī become so beautiful? It was due to the result of the gift of cloth dyed with safflower.
223:
In the past, Ummādantī was born into a poor family in the city of Bārāṇasī. On a festival day, she saw women endowed with merit, adorned and playing while wearing safflower-dyed clothes. Desiring to wear such clothes and play, she informed her parents.

Her parents said, "Dear daughter, we are very poor; where would we get such clothes?" When her parents said this, she replied, "If that is so, please allow me to work for hire in a wealthy family. Those wealthy people will recognize my service and give them to me." When her parents gave permission, she approached a wealthy family and said, "I wish to work for hire for safflower-dyed cloth." Then, the wealthy people told her, "If you work for three years, we will recognize your service and give it to you." The young woman agreed, saying, "Very well," and undertook the work.

The wealthy people, recognizing her service even before the three years were completed, gave her a piece of thick safflower-dyed cloth along with another garment and sent her away, saying, "Go with your friends, bathe, and wear this." The young woman took her friends, went to the riverbank, placed the safflower-dyed cloth there, and bathed.

At that moment, a monk who was a disciple of Kassapa Buddha, whose robes had been stolen by thieves, arrived at that place wearing and wrapped in branches and leaves. Seeing the monk coming wrapped in leaves, the young woman thought, "This venerable one's robes must have been stolen by thieves." She reflected, "In the past, because I did not give, it has become difficult for me to obtain clothing." Thinking, "I will cut this safflower-dyed cloth into two pieces and offer one piece to the venerable one," she came up from the water, put on one of her garments, wrapped herself in another, and said, "Venerable sir, please stay." After prostrating to the elder, she cut the safflower-dyed cloth and offered one piece to the elder.

The elder stood in a suitable secluded place, discarded the branches and leaves he had worn, put on one end of the safflower-dyed robe, wrapped himself in the other, and came out. When he came out, due to the radiance of the safflower-dyed robe, his entire body emitted a solid red glow like the morning sun.

Seeing the elder, the young woman thought, "Previously, my venerable one was not so beautiful, but now he is as beautiful as the morning sun. I will offer this second piece of safflower-dyed cloth to that venerable one as well." She offered the second piece of safflower-dyed cloth and made an aspiration:

"Venerable sir, may I be endowed with supreme beauty in every life I wander. May no man who sees me be able to maintain his composure. May no other woman be more beautiful than I."

The elder also gave the blessing, "May your wish be fulfilled," and departed. That woman, after wandering in the celestial realms, was born at that time in the city of Ariṭṭhapura and became as she was.

## The Proclamation of the Festival
At that time, the Kattika festival was proclaimed in the city of Ariṭṭhapura. On the full moon day of Kattika, the city of Ariṭṭhapura was decorated and prepared.

## The General's Instruction
General Abhipāraka went to his house, which was a place of protection and security, and called Ummādantī, saying, "Lady Ummādantī, tonight is the night of the Kattika full moon festival. When the King makes a circumambulation of the city, he will first arrive at the gate of this house. Do not show yourself to the King. If the King sees you, he will not be able to maintain his mindfulness."

## The General Finds Out

## Making an Offering

When Abhipāraka heard his wife's words, he said, "Lady, you have ruined me." Early the next day, he ascended to the palace and stood at the door of the auspicious bedchamber. Hearing the voice of King Sivi lamenting out of longing for Ummadantī, he thought, "This King's mind is deeply attached to Ummadantī. If he does not get her, he will die. ## 3. Mahābodhi Jātaka

## Being Wise and Able to Refute the Doctrines of Others

The Present Story: While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Mahābodhi Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Kiṃ nu daṇḍaṃ kimajinaṃ," concerning the Perfection of Wisdom (Paññā-pāramī).

The present story will become clear in the Mahā-ummagga Jātaka. Specifically, at that time, the Omniscient Buddha said, "Monks, it is not only now that your teacher is wise and able to crush the doctrines of others; in the past also, your teacher was wise and able to crush the doctrines of others." Having said this, he related the past story.

## Bodhi the Wanderer

The Past Story: Monks, once upon a time, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of a wealthy Udicca Brahmin of eighty crores in the kingdom of Kāsi. They named him Bodhi-kumāra.

When Bodhi-kumāra reached maturity, he completed his education in Takkasilā and returned. After living as a householder for some time, he later renounced sensual pleasures, entered the Himālaya region, and was ordained as a wandering ascetic (paribbājaka). Living there for a long time, subsisting on forest roots and fruits, he descended from the Himālayas during the rainy season and, traveling by stages, reached Bārāṇasī. He stayed in the royal park and, on the following day, went for alms in the city in the becoming manner of a wandering ascetic, arriving at the palace gate.

## The King of Bārāṇasī's Devotion

King Brahmadatta, standing at a lion-window, saw Bodhi the Wanderer entering for alms. Impressed by the tranquility of his faculties, the King invited him into the palace, seated him on the royal throne, and after showing proper courtesy and listening to a brief Dhamma talk, offered him various choice foods of excellent flavor.
241:
The Bodhisatta, having accepted the food, thought: "This royal family has many faults and many enemies. Who will be able to deliver me from any danger that may arise?" Having thought thus, Bodhi the Wanderer saw a dog named Piṅgala, a royal favorite, standing nearby. He took a large lump of rice and showed an intention to give it to the dog. King Brahmadatta, understanding this, had a dog's bowl brought and had the rice given to the dog. The Bodhisatta gave it to the dog and finished his meal.

King Brahmadatta, having obtained the Bodhisatta's consent, had a leaf-hut built in the royal park within the city, offered the requisites of an ascetic, and had him reside there. Every day, he went two or three times to wait upon the Bodhisatta. At mealtime, the Bodhisatta always sat on the royal throne and ate the same food as the King. In this way, twelve years passed.

## The Five Wrong Views

King Brahmadatta had five ministers who advised him on matters of welfare and Dhamma. Among those five ministers, one held the doctrine of No-Cause (Ahetuka-vāda), one held the doctrine of Creation by a Supreme Being (Issarakata-vāda), one held the doctrine of Past Actions (Pubbekata-vāda), one held the doctrine of Annihilation (Uccheda-vāda), and one held the doctrine of Expediency (Khatta-vijjā-vāda).

Among them, the minister of the No-Cause doctrine taught the people: "These beings have no cause; they are purified through the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra)." The minister of the Creation doctrine taught: "This world was created by a Supreme Being like Brahmā or Viṣṇu." The minister of the Past Actions doctrine taught: "Whatever happiness or suffering arises for these beings is due solely to past actions." The minister of the Annihilation doctrine taught: "There is no such thing as going from this life to a future life; this world is annihilated at death." The minister of the Expediency doctrine taught: "If it is for one's own benefit, one should even kill one's parents and do as one pleases."

## The Ascetic Judge

These ministers, serving as judges for King Brahmadatta, were bribe-takers; they made the non-owner the owner and the owner the non-owner.

Then one day, a man who had lost a lawsuit to a fraudulent litigant saw the Bodhisatta entering the palace for alms. He paid homage and lamented: "Venerable sir, you eat your meals in the King's palace, but why do you ignore the ministers who act as judges and destroy the world by taking bribes? Just now, the five ministers took a bribe from a fraudulent litigant and, though I am the rightful owner, they made me the non-owner." He spoke thus and wept.

Out of compassion for that man who lost the case, the Bodhisatta went to the court and, judging according to the law, made the rightful owner the owner. The people gave a great shout of applause all at once.

When King Brahmadatta heard the sound, he asked, "What is this sound?" Upon hearing the reason, he approached the Bodhisatta, who had finished his meal, and asked, "Venerable sir, did you judge a case today?" When the Bodhisatta replied, "Yes, Great King," the King said, "Venerable sir, if you judge cases, it will be for the welfare and happiness of the people. From this day forward, please be the one to judge cases."
242:
“Great King, we are called ascetics; the task of judging cases is not suitable for us.” When he said this, the King replied, “Venerable sir, it is proper to judge out of compassion for the people. Venerable sirs, do not judge all day long. When you come from the park to this palace, please go to the court and decide four cases early in the morning. After having your meal, if you wish to return to the park, decide four more cases. In this way, the welfare and happiness of the people will be served.”

The Bodhisatta, being repeatedly entreated by King Brahmadatta, consented, saying, “Very well,” and from that day on, he judged cases as requested by the King. Those who used to win cases by bribery found no opportunity. Those ministers, unable to get bribes and becoming poor, plotted together.

## The Ministers Slander Him

“Since Bodhi the Wanderer began judging cases, we have received nothing. Now, let us denounce Bodhi the Wanderer as an enemy of the King, destroy the King's affection for him, and have him killed,” they planned.

Having plotted thus, the ministers approached King Brahmadatta and said, “Great King, Bodhi the Wanderer desires your harm.” When the King, disbelieving them, said, “This Bodhi the Wanderer is virtuous and endowed with wisdom; he would not do such a thing,” they replied, “Great King, please listen. He has brought all the city dwellers under his influence; indeed, he could not win over only the five of us. If you do not believe our words, observe his retinue when he comes to this palace.”

King Brahmadatta said, “Very well,” and while standing at the lion-window, he watched Bodhi the Wanderer approaching. Seeing him with a large following, and lacking personal understanding of the law, the King mistook the people coming for legal cases as the Wanderer's own retinue. His affection vanished, and he summoned the ministers, asking, “What shall we do?”

“Great King, have him arrested,” they replied. “How can I arrest him without seeing a serious offense?” the King asked. “In that case, Great King, reduce the customary honors and hospitality shown to him. Seeing the reduction of honors, the wise Bodhi the Wanderer will flee on his own without telling anyone,” they suggested. King Brahmadatta agreed, saying, “Very well,” and gradually reduced the honors shown to the Bodhisatta.

On the first day, they made him sit on a bare, empty couch. Seeing the empty couch, the Bodhisatta realized the King's affection had faded. Although he wished to leave for the park and depart that very day, he thought, “I will leave only after knowing for certain,” and so he remained.
243:
On the next day, they took the King's regular alms-food and other food, mixed them together, and gave the mixed food to Bodhi the Wanderer as he sat on the empty couch. On the third day, they did not allow him to enter the upper palace but placed the mixed food at the head of the stairs. The Bodhisatta took that mixed food, went to the park, and ate his meal. On the fourth day, they placed rice made of broken grains at the foot of the palace and gave it to him. The Bodhisatta took that rice as well, went to the park, and ate his meal.

King Brahmadatta asked the ministers, “Bodhi the Wanderer does not flee even though his honors have been reduced. What shall we do with him?” They replied, “Great King, he does not live for the sake of food; he lives for the sake of the throne. If he lived for the sake of food, he would have fled on the very first day.” “What shall we do now?” the King asked. “Great King, have him killed tomorrow,” they replied.

## Ordering the Killing of the Wanderer

King Brahmadatta said, “Very well,” and placing swords in the hands of those ministers, he said, “Tomorrow, stand between the main gate and the small gate. As he enters, cut off his head, chop him into pieces, and without letting anyone know, throw him into the cesspool. Then bathe and return.” The ministers agreed, saying, “Very well,” and after planning among themselves, “We will do this when he comes tomorrow,” they went to their respective homes.

King Brahmadatta, after eating his evening meal, lay on his royal bed and reflected on the virtues of the Bodhisatta. As he reflected, anxiety arose within him. Sweat poured from his body. Finding no peace on his bed, he tossed and turned.

At that time, the Chief Queen was sleeping near the King. The King did not even speak a word to her. Then the Queen asked him, “Great King, why do you not even speak to me? Have I committed some fault?”

“My Queen, there is no fault. However, it is said that Bodhi the Wanderer has become our enemy. Therefore, I have ordered five ministers to kill him tomorrow. Those five ministers, after killing him, will chop him into pieces and throw him into the cesspool. Yet, that Bodhi the Wanderer preached much Dhamma to us for twelve years. I have never personally seen any fault in him. But believing the words of others, I have ordered his death. For that reason, I am anxious.”

126. "But now he barks fiercely, showing his white fangs, having heard your words—you who are with your wife and have lost faith in me."

125. Great King. In your presence, O donor king. Those twelve years that I have lived depending on you. Throughout those twelve years, I have never known your dog named Piṅgala to bark fiercely at me.

126. Toward me. Of you, the Great King, who is with your queen and devoid of faith and devotion. Having heard your words. That dog Piṅgala. Showing his four white fangs. As if to warn me. He barks loudly at me.

When he spoke thus, the Chief Queen said to the King: "Great King, if he is indeed your enemy, even if you have this Bodhi the Wanderer killed, why do you worry? Even if an enemy were one's own son, one should kill him to ensure one's own happiness; do not worry." Thus she comforted him. King Brahmadatta, comforted by the Queen's words, fell asleep.

## The Dog's Rescue
At that moment, the dog named Piṅgala, raised in the palace, heard those words and thought, "Tomorrow, I should give life to this Bodhi the Wanderer by my own strength." Early the next morning, he descended from the palace, went to the great gate, rested his chin on the threshold, and lay waiting, watching the path by which the Great Being would come. The ministers also arrived early, holding swords, and stood between the great and small gates.

The Bodhisatta, noting the time, left the garden and went to the palace gate. Then, seeing the Bodhisatta, the dog named Piṅgala opened his mouth, showed his four fangs, and barked loudly: "Venerable Sir, do you not find alms elsewhere in the land of Jambudīpa? Our Great King has placed five ministers with swords between the two gates to kill you. Do not come bringing death upon your brow; depart quickly!"

The Bodhisatta, Bodhi the Wanderer, because he understood the sounds of all creatures, knew the reason. He turned back from that very spot, went to the garden, and took up his requisites to depart for another place.
245:
126. "But now he barks fiercely, showing his white fangs, having heard your words—you who are with your wife and have lost faith in me."

In that verse, 'abhibhūjitaṃ' means: I have never known such a great outcry to be made by this dog of yours. 'Ditto vā' means: as if warned. 'Sabhariyassa' means: having heard you speaking to your queen about the order given to the five ministers to kill me, saying, "Do you not find alms elsewhere? Your death has been ordered by the King; do not come here," he barks as if warned. 'Vītasaddhaṃ maṃ pati' means: he barks thus having heard your words, you who have lost faith in me.

Then the King, admitting his own fault and seeking forgiveness, spoke the fourth verse:

127. "This fault was committed just as you say, O Brahmin. Now I have even greater faith in you; stay, O Brahmin, do not go."

In that verse, 'bhiyyo' means: It is true that I gave such an order; that was my fault. But now I have even more faith in you than before. Stay right here; do not go elsewhere.

Hearing this, the Great Being said, "Great King, those called wise do not live with such people who are swayed by others and do not act with direct perception." To reveal the King's improper conduct, he said:

128. "At first it was all white, then it became mottled, and now it is all red; it is time for me to depart."

129. "At first it was inside, then in the middle, then outside; before it is cast out, I shall go by myself."

130. "One should not serve one who has lost faith, like a well without water; even if one digs it, the water smells of mud."

131. "One should serve only the faithful; one should avoid the unfaithful. One should associate with the faithful, like one desiring water associates with a lake."

132. "One should associate with a person who associates with him; one should not associate with one who does not. It is the way of the ignoble to not associate with one who associates with him."

## The King's Apology
King Brahmadatta, standing at the lion-window, saw the Bodhisatta coming and then turning back. He thought, "If this Bodhi the Wanderer were my enemy, he would go to the garden, gather forces, and prepare for war. If he is not my enemy, he will take his requisites and prepare to flee. I shall find out his intentions." He went to the garden and saw the Bodhisatta coming out of the leaf-hut, having taken his requisites to depart. Seeing him at the head of the walkway, the King paid respects and, standing in a suitable place, desired to question him.

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta thought, "This King thinks I do not know what he has done; I shall let him know." Desiring to let him know:

After that, King Brahmadatta, wishing to confess his fault and ask for pardon:

## Bodhi the Wanderer Asks Permission to Leave
Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta said, "Great King, those called wise do not live with those who believe the words of others and do not act with direct knowledge." Desiring to show the King's lack of respect:
246:
136. By staying too long, a loved one becomes unloved. I take my leave and go, before I become unloved by you.

He spoke these nine verses.

128. Great King, formerly the rice you gave me was all white. Then it became speckled. Now it has become all red. Now it is time for me to depart.

129. Great King, formerly the seat prepared for me was inside, on the royal throne under the white parasol. Then it was in the middle, at the head of the stairs. Then it was outside. Before the time comes when I am driven out by the neck, I shall go of my own accord.

130. Just as one should not resort to a waterless well, so, Great King, one should not resort to one who is devoid of faith. Even if one digs and scrapes at such a well, the water would smell of mud.

131. Great King, just as one desiring water reaches a deep lake and enjoys the clear water, so a wise man should associate only with one who has faith in him. He should avoid one who lacks faith.

132. Great King, one should associate with a man who associates with him and desires his welfare. One should not associate with an enemy who does not associate with him. He who does not associate with a friend who associates with him is one who follows the practice of the ignoble.

133. Great King, like a monkey dwelling among branches, he who does not associate with one who associates with him, nor resorts to one who resorts to him, is indeed the most wicked of men.

...

## Three Causes for the Ruin of Friendship

134. Great King, through too frequent contact, through lack of contact, and through asking for a beloved possession at an improper time—for these reasons, friends fall away.

135. Therefore, one should not visit constantly, nor should one stay away for too long. One should ask for what is to be asked at the proper time. In this way, friends do not fall away.

136. Great King, by staying too long, a loved one becomes unloved...
247:
...becomes unloved. Great King, we take our leave and go before we become unloved by you.

## Inviting the Great Being to Return

Upon hearing this, King Brahmadatta, wishing for him to return to his city, spoke this verse:

137. "Venerable Sir, if you do not recognize the salutation of us who thus entreat you, and do not heed the words of your hundred attendants, we entreat you thus: please make a turn to return here again."

The Bodhisatta, wishing to give his consent, spoke this verse:

138. "If no danger befalls us as we live thus apart, Great King, increaser of the realm, for you or for me, perhaps we may see each other again after the passing of days and nights."

Having spoken thus, the Great Being preached the Dhamma to the King, saying, "Great King, be diligent," and left the park. After collecting alms in a suitable place, he departed from Bārāṇasī and gradually reached the Himavanta region. After staying there for some time, he descended again and lived in the forest near a border village.

## The King Meets with Danger

From the time the Bodhisatta Mahābodhi the Wanderer left, those ministers again sat in judgment and committed plunder. They thought, "If the wanderer Mahābodhi comes back, our lives will be lost. What can we do to ensure he does not return?"
248:
Then those ministers had this thought: "These beings are unable to give up the place to which they are attached. What is the place of attachment for this Bodhi the Wanderer here in this city?" Upon investigating, they realized, "It is the King's Chief Queen." They thought, "It is possible that he might come back because of her. Let us have her killed beforehand." They said to King Brahmadatta: "Great King, a certain rumor is being heard in the city today."

"What rumor?" the King asked. "It is said, Great King, that Mahābodhi the Wanderer and the Queen are sending messages back and forth to each other."

"What are they saying?" When asked, they replied, "It is said that the Wanderer sent a message to the Queen asking, 'Is it possible to have the King killed by your power and give me the white parasol (sovereignty)?' And she sent a message back saying, 'Killing the King is my responsibility; let the Great Wanderer come quickly.'"

Believing the repeated words of those ministers, King Brahmadatta asked, "What should be done now?" When they replied, "Great King, it is proper to kill the Queen," he, without investigating or reflecting, said, "If so, you yourselves kill her, cut her into pieces, and throw her into the cesspool." They did as ordered.

The fact of the Queen's murder became well-known throughout the city. Then her four sons became enemies of the King, thinking, "This King has killed our innocent mother." The King fell into great fear.

## The Return of Bodhi the Wanderer
The Great Being, hearing the news through the grapevine, thought: "Except for me, there is no one else capable of pleasing those four princes and making them forgive their father, King Brahmadatta. I shall give life to the King and free the princes from evil."

Having so thought, the Great Being entered a border village the next morning, ate monkey meat given by the people, asked for the monkey skin, took it, dried it at his hermitage, made it odorless, and wore it, wrapped himself in it, and placed it on his shoulder. Why did he do this? He did it so he could say, "This monkey has been of great help to me."
249:
Taking the skin and eventually reaching Bārāṇasī, he approached the princes and advised them: "Princes, the evil deed of patricide has terrible consequences. You should not commit such an act. There is no being who is ageless or immortal. I have come only to bring harmony among you. Come when I send word to you." After advising the princes, he entered the royal garden within the city, spread the monkey skin, and sat on a stone slab.

Then the gardener saw the Great Being, went quickly, and informed King Brahmadatta. Upon hearing this, the King was filled with joy. He called his ministers, went to the garden, paid homage to the Great Being, and sat down, attempting to engage in pleasant conversation. The Great Being, without speaking to the King, only stroked the monkey skin. Then the King asked: "Venerable sir, you do not speak with me but only stroke the monkey skin. Is this monkey skin more helpful to you than I am?"

"Great King, indeed this monkey was of great help to me. I traveled sitting on its back. It brought me my water pot. It swept my living place. It performed the major and minor duties of conduct for me. But I, because of the weakness of my own mind, ate its meat, dried its skin, and now I sit and lie upon it. In these various ways, this monkey was once very helpful to me." The Great Being said this, attributing the designation of a 'monkey' to the monkey skin, with the intention of dismantling the ministers' doctrines through various metaphors.

This was the truth: because the Great Being used to sit on that monkey skin, he said, "I traveled sitting on its back." Because he used to carry the water pot while having the skin on his shoulder, he said, "It brought me my water pot." Because he used to sweep the ground with that skin, he said, "It swept my living place." Because his back touched the skin when lying down and his feet touched it when treading on it, he said, "It performed the major and minor duties for me." And because he had actually eaten the meat of that monkey when he was hungry, he said, "I, because of the weakness of my own mind, ate its meat."

Hearing this, the ministers, thinking, "This Bodhi the Wanderer has committed the act of killing," clapped their hands and mocked him, saying, "Look, sirs, at the deed of this monk! It is said he killed a monkey, ate its meat, and now wanders around with its skin."

## Refuting the Doctrine of Non-Causality
When the Great Being saw the ministers mocking him thus, he thought: "These ministers do not know that I have come with this monkey skin to dismantle their own doctrines. I shall make them understand." He first called the minister who held the doctrine of non-causality (Ahetukavāda) and asked: "Lay disciple, why do you mock me?"

139. If [you believe] that occurrences happen by chance, and follow [mere] existence,
Then whether one does what should not be done or what should be done without intention,
In such unintentional actions, how can one be tainted by sin?
250:
142. If a Supreme Lord of the whole world creates life,
Success and failure, and deeds good and bad,
Then man is merely an executor of orders, and the Lord is stained by that [deed].

When it was said, "Monk, you are mocked because you have committed the act of betraying a friend and taking life," the Bodhisatta then said, "Lay follower, if a person, believing in you and your doctrine, were to commit such acts of betraying a friend and taking life, whose deed would be evil, including that person's?" Desiring to destroy the doctrine of that Ahetukavāda (non-causality) minister, he spoke these three verses:

140. If that meaning and that doctrine are good and not evil,
And if your word is true, then the monkey was well-slain by me.

141. If you were to recognize the flaw in your own doctrine,
You would not blame me; for such is your doctrine.

139. Friend, lay follower. The world, by reaching one of the six classes (abhijāti) or by nature (bhāva), undergoes pleasure and pain. Unwillingly, one does what should not be done (evil) or what should be done (good). Thus you say. If this is your statement, then in this world, if one acts unwillingly, who indeed would be stained by evil?

140. Friend, lay follower. If that meaning of yours called Ahetukavāda and the words expressing it are good and not evil, and if your word—that beings experience pleasure and pain without cause—is true, then the monkey was well-slain by me.

141. Indeed, my statement that the monkey was well-slain is true. Friend, because your doctrine is of the same nature as my act. Therefore, when blaming me, if you were to know the fault in your own doctrine that deserves blame, you would not blame me.

★ The details of the six classes (abhijāti) mentioned in the first verse should be noted as follows:
Kaṇhābhijāti, Nīlābhijāti, Lohitābhijāti, Haliddābhijāti, Sukkābhijāti, and Paramasukkābhijāti—these are the six.
Among these, fishermen, hunters, thieves, executioners, and others who perform cruel deeds are called Kaṇhābhijāti (Black class).
Monks (Bhikkhus) are called Nīlābhijāti (Blue class).
Nigaṇṭhas (Jain ascetics) are called Lohitābhijāti (Red class).
Laypeople and Acelaka disciples are called Haliddābhijāti (Yellow class).
The lineage of Nanda, Vaccha, and Saṅkicca is called Sukkābhijāti (White class).
Ājīvakas are called Paramasukkābhijāti (Purest White class).
This is how they should be understood.

With these verses, the Bodhisatta rebuked the Ahetukavāda minister and made him speechless. That Ahetukavāda minister sat dejected with his head hanging down in the royal assembly.

## Refuting the Doctrine of Creationism (Issarakata-vāda)

After destroying the doctrine of the Ahetukavāda minister, the Bodhisatta addressed the minister who held the view that Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or a Supreme Lord created everything (Issarakata-vāda), saying: "Lay follower, if you truly believe in the doctrine of creation by a Supreme Lord, why do you mock me?" Desiring to destroy that doctrine, he said:
251:
145. If happiness and suffering are encountered only because of deeds done in the past, then this person is being released from the debt of the evil committed long ago. If this is a release from an old debt, who here is stained by sin?

143. If that meaning and that doctrine are good and not evil, and if your word is true, then the monkey was well-slain by me.

144. If you were to recognize the fault in your own doctrine, you would not blame me; for your doctrine is of such a nature.

He spoke these three verses.

142. Friend, lay devotee. If the Creator—Brahma, Vishnu, or a Lord—ordains the livelihood of all beings, their prosperity and ruin, and their good and evil deeds (wholesome and unwholesome kamma), then, if the Creator so ordains, a person is merely one who carries out instructions and is not stained by evil. Only the Creator would be stained by that evil.

143. Friend, lay devotee. If your proposition—that Brahma or Vishnu creates and ordains—is meaningful, and the words expressing it are excellent and not wicked, and if your statement is true, then it is well that I have killed the monkey.

144. Indeed, the statement 'it is well that the monkey was killed' is true. Friend, because your doctrine is of the same nature as my action, if you recognize the fault in your own doctrine when I am being reproached, you should not blame me.

## Refuting the Doctrine of Past Deeds (Pubbekata-vāda)

Thus, the Bodhisatta, like one taking a stick from a mango tree to knock down its fruit, destroyed the doctrine of creation by using that very doctrine. Then, addressing the minister who held the doctrine of past actions (Pubbekata-vādī), he said: "Lay devotee, if you believe the doctrine of past actions to be true, why do you mock me?" Desiring to destroy that doctrine as well, he spoke these three verses:

146. If that meaning and that doctrine are good and not evil, and if your word is true, then the monkey was well-slain by me.

147. If you were to recognize the fault in your own doctrine, you would not blame me; for your doctrine is of such a nature.

He spoke these three verses.

145. Friend, lay devotee. If a being encounters happiness and suffering only because of causes in a past life, then that being is now being freed from the debt of whatever evil was committed in the past. If there is such a release from an old debt, then for me too, there is a release from debt. Who in this world would be stained by evil?

146. Friend, lay devotee. If that meaning—that happiness and suffering occur only because of past deeds—and the words expressing it are true and excellent, and not wicked, and if your statement is true, then it is well that I have killed the monkey.

147. Indeed, the statement 'it is well that the monkey was killed' is true. Friend, because your doctrine is of the same nature as my action, if you recognize the fault in your own doctrine when I am being reproached, you should not blame me.

## Refuting the Doctrine of Annihilation (Uccheda-vāda)

In this way, the Bodhisatta destroyed the doctrine of that minister who held the view of past actions. Then, turning toward the minister who held the doctrine of annihilation (Uccheda-vādī), he said: "Lay devotee, you say there is no fruit of giving..."
252:
148. Depending on the four [elements] alone, form arises for living beings.
From where form arises, there it returns.
Here alone the soul lives; after death, it perishes.

149. This world is annihilated, both fools and the wise.
In a world being annihilated, who here is smeared by sin?

Having said these things, [the Bodhisatta thought,] "Thinking that beings are annihilated in this very life and that there is no such thing as going to the next world, why do you mock me?" Thus, wishing to destroy that minister's view as well, he threatened him and spoke these four verses:

150. If that purpose and that doctrine are beautiful and not evil,
And if your word is true, then the monkey was well-slain by me.

151. If you were to recognize the fault in your own doctrine,
You would not blame me; for your doctrine is such.

148. Friend, donor. The form (rūpakkhandha) of living beings arises depending only on the four great elements (mahābhūta) such as earth (pathavī). From whichever great elements the form arises, at the time of death, that form returns to and enters into that same group of elements. In this present world alone, the being lives. After death, the being that arose in another life does not come back to this present world, but perishes in that next world.

149. There are those who are fools and those who are wise. This world of people, being such as it is, is annihilated; it does not pass on to another life but is cut off in the present life. Thus you say. If, in the manner you have stated, the world of beings is annihilated, who in this world would be smeared by evil?

150. Friend, donor. If such a purpose (the meaning of annihilationism) and the doctrine (the words expressing that meaning) are good and not wicked, and if your word—that a being is annihilated after death—is true, then it is good that I have slain the monkey.

151. Truly, the statement that it is good to have slain the monkey is true. Friend, donor. Because your doctrine is of the same nature as the deed I have done, therefore, while you are blaming me, if you were to recognize the fault in your own doctrine, you would not blame me.

## Refuting the Doctrine of Khattavijjā
In this way, the Bodhisatta destroyed the view of the annihilationist minister. Then, calling the minister who held the doctrine of Khattavijjā (political science), he said, "Donor, you go about upholding this view that one should even kill one's parents to achieve one's own purpose. Why then do you mock me?" Thus, wishing to destroy that minister's doctrine as well, he said:
253:
153. Under whichever tree's shade one might sit or sleep,
One should not break its branch; for betraying a friend is evil.

154. But when a purpose arises, one should uproot it even with the roots.
Since I had a need for provisions, the monkey was well-slain by me.

152. In the world, there are those called 'Khattavida' (experts in statecraft), fools who think they are wise.
They say one should kill mother, father, and even an elder brother;
One should kill children and wife, if such a purpose should arise.

He spoke this verse:

152. Friend, donor. In the world, there are those who, though lacking wisdom, consider themselves wise and hold the view that the 'seed' of parents should be destroyed (Khattavida). They say that if a purpose arises where it is necessary to kill parents and others, then one should kill even one's mother and father. Furthermore, one should kill an elder brother, a younger brother, and even one's children and wife. You are one among those teachers of Khattavijjā.

With this verse, the Bodhisatta established that minister's view and then, wishing to declare his own view, he spoke:

155. If that purpose and that doctrine are beautiful and not evil,
And if your word is true, then the monkey was well-slain by me.

156. If you were to recognize the fault in your own doctrine,
You would not blame me; for your doctrine is such.

153. Friend, donor. Because one who betrays a friend is wicked, therefore, if one has sat or slept under the shade of a certain tree, one should not break the branches or leaves of that tree. Thus our teachers praise.

154. But you say that when a purpose arises, one should uproot even the roots. If it is right to do as you say, then since I had a need for provisions (sambala), it is good that I have slain the monkey.

155. Friend, donor. If such a purpose—the meaning that one should kill even one's parents if there is a need—and the doctrine are good and not wicked, and if your word is true, then it is good that I have slain the monkey.

156. Friend, donor. It is true. Because your doctrine is similar to the deed I have done, therefore, if you, while blaming me, were to recognize the fault in your own doctrine, you would not blame me.

## Preaching the Dhamma to the King
In this way, the Bodhisatta destroyed the view of that Khattavijjā-vādī minister as well. When those five ministers remained devoid of wisdom, he addressed the King: "Great King, you go about harboring these five great thieves who destroy the kingdom. How very foolish!"
254:
He spoke these two verses together:

157. The man who is a proponent of non-causality (Ahetukavāda), he who believes in the creation by a Lord (Issarakuttika), he who believes only in past actions (Pubbekata), he who is an annihilationist (Uccheda), and the man who follows the science of the kshatriyas (Khattavijjā).

158. These are unworthy men in the world, fools who think themselves wise. Such a person would commit evil and would also make others do so. Association with the unworthy ends in suffering and has a bitter result.

157. Great King, the man who holds the view that there is no cause (Ahetukavāda); the man who holds the view that a Lord such as Brahmā or Viṣṇu creates and ordains (Issarakuttika); the man who holds the view that happiness and suffering occur only because of deeds done in previous lives (Pubbekata); the man who holds the view that after death a being does not arise again but is annihilated (Uccheda); and the man who holds the view of Khattavijjā—these exist.

158. In the world, such unworthy men, though they lack wisdom, consider themselves wise. Such an ignoble person would commit evil himself. Furthermore, he would also cause others to do so. One who associates with such unworthy persons suffers a mass of misery and receives bitter and painful results.

Having said, "By associating with and following such people, individuals who are unwise may reach great suffering in the present life as well as great suffering in the life hereafter," and wishing to preach the Dhamma to the King:

Having preached thus, and now wishing to further the Dhamma teaching by way of an analogy, he spoke these twenty-five verses beginning with:

159. Formerly, a wolf in the form of a ram approached the flock of goats without suspicion... [and ending with] ...he makes his enemies tremble, like Indra, the lord of the Asuras.

159. Great King, in former times, a fierce wolf, in the guise of a ram and being free from suspicion, approached a flock of goats. Having killed a ewe (named uraṇī because she does not cry out even when beaten or oppressed), a she-goat, and a he-goat, and having terrified the flock, he fled to wherever he desired to go.

160. Great King, in that same way, some ascetics and brahmins who have a nature like that fierce wolf who kills and eats goats by pretending to be one, having made a disguise...
255:
...disguising themselves as monks, they deceive people. How do they disguise themselves? They pretend not to eat any food (Anāsaka). They pretend to sleep on the bare ground (Thaṇḍilaseyya). They carry dust and dirt (Rajojalla). They exert effort in a squatting posture (Ukkuṭikappadhāna). They pretend to eat by rotation, such as eating molasses once every seven or ten days (Pariyāyabhatta). They pretend not to drink water (Apānakatta). While their conduct is evil, they speak of themselves saying, 'We are Arahants.' In this way, they maintain a disguise.

161. Great King, in the world, these persons who are unwise yet consider themselves wise are unworthy and ignoble. Great King, such an ignoble person would commit evil himself. Furthermore, he would also cause others to do so. Great King, one who associates with the unworthy suffers a mass of misery and receives bitter, painful, and distressing results.

162. Great King, those beings who say, 'There is no result of effort (vīriya) associated with wisdom'; those beings who, relying on the view of non-causality, speak thus; and those beings who describe as empty and equal both the service rendered to others and the service rendered by others to oneself.

163. Great King, in the world, these beings who lack wisdom yet consider themselves wise are unworthy and ignoble. Great King, such an ignoble person would commit evil himself. Furthermore, he would also cause others to do so. Great King, one who associates with the unworthy suffers a mass of misery and receives results devoid of pleasure.

164. Indeed, Great King, if there were no result of physical and mental effort associated with wisdom, and if there were no result of good and evil deeds, then the King would not support craftsmen such as carpenters, nor would he have structures such as seven-storied palaces built.

165. Great King, because there is a result of effort and there is a result of good and evil deeds, therefore the King has structures such as seven-storied palaces built and supports craftsmen such as carpenters.

166. Great King, if the sky-god did not rain for a hundred years, and if snow did not fall, if it were so for a hundred years, this world would be cut off and this multitude of beings would perish.

167. Great King, because the sky-god rains and the snow falls after the rain, therefore the crops ripen and the people of the kingdom are protected for a long time.

168. Great King, among the cattle that are moving, if the leading bull goes crookedly, then all those following cattle go crookedly when the leader has gone crookedly.
256:
169. Great King, just so, among humans, he who is considered the chief—if he practices unrighteousness, how much more so the rest of the people? The whole realm dwells in suffering if the king is unrighteous.

170. Great King, among cattle that are crossing, if the lead bull goes straight, all the cows go straight, the leader having gone straight.

171. Great King, just so, among humans, he who is considered the chief—if he practices righteousness, how much more so the rest of the people? The whole realm dwells in happiness if the king is righteous.

172. Great King, whoever picks the unripe fruit of a great fruit-bearing tree does not know its flavor, and its seed is destroyed.

173. Great King, he who governs a kingdom—which is like a great tree—unrighteously, does not know its flavor, and his kingdom is destroyed.

174. Great King, whoever picks the ripe fruit of a great fruit-bearing tree knows its flavor, and its seed is not destroyed.

175. Great King, he who governs a kingdom—which is like a great tree—righteously, knows its flavor, and his kingdom is not destroyed.

176. Great King, that king who governs the countryside unrighteously, that Khattiya is at odds with all medicinal plants—roots, bark, leaves, flowers, fruits, ghee, oil, and so forth.

177. Great King, likewise, the king who harms the townspeople and those merchants engaged in buying and selling, who provide the essence of the realm through taxes such as one-sixth or one-tenth, he is at odds with the treasury.

178. Great King, the king who harms the archers who know the best ground for battle, and the famous ministers who are well-trained and experienced in warfare, he is at odds with the army.

179. Great King, just as an unrighteous Khattiya harms the townspeople and others, if he harms the sages who are restrained and live the holy life, seeking virtue, he is at odds with heaven.
257:
180. Great King, the unrighteous king who kills an innocent wife produces the evil cause for rebirth in a harsh hell and is at odds with his sons.

181. Great King, a king should practice righteousness toward the country folk, the townspeople, and the army. He should not harm sages and should act with fairness toward his wife and children.

182. Great King, just as Indra, the lord of the Asuras, makes his enemies tremble, so too does a lord of the earth, a protector of the realm who is free from anger and follows the ancient righteous kings, make his enemies tremble with his royal majesty.

Regarding 'Vakassūti': 'Vako assu', where 'assu' is a mere particle. This is what is meant: Great King, formerly there was a wolf in the form of a ram. Only its tail was long. It tucked its tail between its thighs and, appearing as a ram, approached a flock of goats without suspicion. There, having killed lambs and goats, it fled as it pleased. 

'Tathāvidheke': Similarly, some recluses and brahmins, using the marks of renunciation as a cover to hide themselves, appear as if they desire the welfare of others with sweet words, but they deceive the world. 'Anāsakā' etc. is said to show their 'cover'. Some deceive people saying, 'We are fasters, we eat nothing.' Others say, 'We sleep on the ground.' For others, dust and dirt is the cover. For others, the practice of squatting; even when moving, they jump and go in a squatting position. For others, the 'cover' is periodic eating, such as every seven or ten days. Others are 'non-drinkers', saying 'We do not drink water.' 

'Arahanto vadānā': Even though they act sinfully, they go about claiming 'We are Arahants.' 'Ete': Great King, whether it be these five types of people or others, as many as there are of those holding wrong views, all of them are bad men (asappurisa). 'Yamāhū': Those who say, those who speak.

'Sace hi vīriyaṃ nāssa': Great King, if there were no physical and mental effort associated with wisdom. 'Kမ္မံ': If there were also no kamma, whether good or bad. 'Na bhare': In that case, a king would not support carpenters or other workers. 'Napi yantāni': Nor would he have them build structures like seven-storied palaces. Why? Because of the absence of effort and kamma. 'Ucchijjeyyā': Great King, if for all this time it did not rain, nor did snow...
258:
## Making the Princes Pay Respects

Thus the Bodhisatta, having preached the Dhamma to King Brahmadatta, called the four princes and admonished them. Having revealed the king's affair, he said, "Pay respects to your royal father," and made them do so. Then he gave admonition to everyone, saying, "Great King, from this day forth, do not take the words of slanderers without reflection and perform such acts of oppression. Princes, you too must not offend your royal father."
259:
## The Ministers are Expelled

Then King Brahmadatta addressed the Bodhisatta: "Venerable Sir, I have offended you and the Queen; relying on these wicked men and taking their words, I committed this evil. I shall kill these five men."

"Great King, it is not proper to do so," he said. When he said this, the king said, "If that is so, I shall cut off the hands and feet of these wicked men."

"Great King, it is not proper to perform this cutting of hands and feet either," when he said this, King Brahmadatta agreed, saying "Very well." He then treated those five ministers like thieves who plunder everyone's property—making five top-knots on their heads, dragging them in baskets, and pouring cow dung over them—and thus dishonoring them, he expelled them from the kingdom.

The Bodhisatta stayed in the city of Bārāṇasī for two or three days, admonishing King Brahmadatta to "be heedful," and then departed for the Himālaya. There he attained the jhānas and higher knowledges (abhiññā), cultivated the Brahma-vihāras throughout his life, and was reborn in the Brahma realm.
260:
The All-Knowing Buddha, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, said: "Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata is wise and able to crush the doctrines of others; in the past also, the Tathāgata was wise and able to crush the doctrines of others." Then he identified the Jātaka: "Monks, those who are now Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Ajita Kesakambala, and Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta were then the five ministers of wrong view. Ānanda was then the king's dog named Piṅgala. I myself was then the wandering ascetic Mahābodhi."

The Mahābodhi Jātaka is finished.
261:
## 1. Soṇaka Jātaka
## On the Need to Listen to the Words of the Virtuous
The Story of the Present: While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Soṇaka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Kassa sutvā sataṃ dammi," concerning the Perfection of Renunciation (Nekkhamma Pāramī).
Indeed, while the All-Knowing Buddha was seated in the midst of the monks who were praising the Perfection of Renunciation in the Dhamma Hall, He said, "Monks, it is not only now that your Teacher has gone forth in the Great Renunciation; in the past, your Teacher also went forth in the Great Renunciation," and He brought forth the past.
The Story of the Past: Monks, in the past, a king named Magadha reigned in the city of Rājagaha. The Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of that King Magadha's chief queen. On the day of his naming, they gave him the name "Prince Arindama." On the very day Prince Arindama was born, a son was also born to the royal chaplain. They named that chaplain's son "Soṇaka."
Those two youths grew up together and, upon reaching maturity, possessed excellent appearances. Being indistinguishable in beauty, they went to Takkasilā to learn the arts. After completing their studies, they left Takkasilā, thinking, "We shall learn the beliefs and arts of all beings and the customs of the people." Traveling gradually, they reached Vārāṇasī, stayed in the royal park, and entered the city the following morning.
## Prince Arindama Becomes King
On that day, some people, thinking, "We shall perform a recitation of the Vedas for the brahmins," prepared thick milk-rice and arranged seats. Seeing the two youths approaching, they invited them into the house and had them sit on the prepared seats. In that house, a white cloth was spread over the Bodhisatta's seat, while a red rug was spread over Soṇaka's seat. Seeing this omen, Soṇaka knew, "Today, my dear friend Prince Arindama will become the King of Vārāṇasī, and he will give me the position of commander-in-chief."
After finishing their meal, both returned to the park. At that time, it was the seventh day since the King of Vārāṇasī had passed away, and the royal family was without an heir. The ministers and others, having bathed their heads early in the morning, assembled and, thinking, "We shall go to find one worthy of the kingdom," harnessed the Phussaratha (ceremonial chariot) and sent it forth. The Phussaratha left the city, went gradually to the royal park, and stopped at the park gate, prepared for someone to mount it.
The Bodhisatta was sleeping on the auspicious stone slab, covering himself including his head. The youth Soṇaka sat near the Bodhisatta. Hearing the sound of musical instruments, Soṇaka thought, "The Phussaratha has arrived for Prince Arindama. Today, this Prince Arindama will become king and will offer me the position of commander-in-chief. Even if he offers it, I have no desire for wealth and luxury. When Prince Arindama leaves, I shall go forth into the forest and become a monk." Thinking thus, he stayed in a suitable hiding place.
262:
The royal chaplain entered the park and, seeing the Great Being lying down, ordered the musical instruments to be played. The Great Being woke up, turned over, lay for a moment, then rose and sat cross-legged on the stone slab. Then the chaplain, raising his hands in salutation, said, "Great King, the kingship has come to you." "Is the royal family without an heir?" he asked. "Yes, Great King," he replied. "In that case, it is well," he said. Then they consecrated the Bodhisatta right there, placed him on the chariot, and entered the city with a great retinue. The Bodhisatta made a clockwise circumambulation of the city and ascended to the golden palace. Because of the greatness of his glory, the Bodhisatta did not remember the youth Soṇaka.
## The Youth Soṇaka Becomes a Paccekabuddha
As for the youth Soṇaka, after King Arindama had entered the city, he came and sat on the auspicious stone slab. At that moment, a withered leaf, detached from its stalk, fell from a Sal tree in front of Soṇaka. Seeing the withered leaf, Soṇaka thought, "Just as this withered leaf has fallen, so too my body will reach old age and fall." Developing insight (Vipassanā) through the realization of impermanence (Anicca) and so forth, he attained the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha. At that very moment, his lay appearance disappeared, and the appearance of a monk became manifest. That venerable Paccekabuddha, uttering an inspired word (Udāna), "Now there is no more rebirth for me," went to the Nandamūla Cave.
## The King Remembers His Friend
After forty years had passed, the Bodhisatta remembered and thought, "Where is my dear friend Soṇaka?" Although he repeatedly remembered Soṇaka, he could not find anyone who could say, "I have heard of him" or "I have seen him."
While sitting on the royal throne in the decorated great golden palace, surrounded by lute players, dancers, and singers, and enjoying royal luxury, he composed an inspired verse (Udāna) and, wishing to utter it in the form of a song, said: "If anyone hears from someone else and tells me, 'Friend Soṇaka lives in such a place,' I will give that person a hundred pieces of gold. If anyone sees him personally and tells me, I will give that person a thousand pieces of gold." He then spoke the first verse:
1. Kassa sutvā sataṃ dammi, sahassaṃ diṭṭha-soṇakaṃ;
Ko me soṇakam-akkhāti, sahāyaṃ paṃsukīḷitaṃ.
1. [Meaning:] Friends, who will tell me of my friend Soṇaka, my childhood playmate? To the one who hears of my friend Soṇaka's dwelling place and tells me, I shall give a hundred pieces of gold. To the one who tells me, "I have seen my friend Soṇaka," I shall give a thousand pieces of gold.
Then, a young dancing girl sang that inspired song as if taking the words right out of King Arindama's mouth. After that, other women of the court sang, "This song is our Great King's favorite song," and all the women of the harem sang it. Gradually, the city dwellers and the country folk also sang that song. King Arindama himself sang that song repeatedly.
## The Arrival of Venerable Soṇaka
After fifty years had passed, King Arindama had many children. The eldest son was named Prince Dီghāvu. At that time, the Venerable Soṇaka Paccekabuddha thought, "King Arindama wishes to see me. I shall go to King Arindama, speak of the faults of sensual pleasures and the benefits of renunciation, and I shall act in a way that leads him to become a monk." Having thought thus, he traveled through the air by psychic power and stayed in the royal park.

## The Wood-Gathering Boy Receives a Reward

At that time, a certain seven-year-old boy named Pañcacūḷaka, having been sent by his mother, went to gather wood in the forest near the royal park and sang that same song repeatedly. Then, the Venerable Paccekabuddha Soṇaka called the boy Pañcacūḷaka and asked, "Young boy, you sing only one song, not knowing any other. Do you not know any other song?" "Venerable sir, it is not that I do not know other songs; I do. However, our Great King loves only this song. Therefore, I sing this song repeatedly," he replied.

"Have you ever seen anyone who knows the response to that song?" he asked. "Venerable sir, I have never seen anyone," the boy replied. "I shall teach you the response to that song. Will you be able to go to King Arindama and sing the response?" he asked. "Venerable sir, I will be able to," the boy replied.

Then, the Venerable Paccekabuddha Soṇaka, wishing to let the boy Pañcacūḷaka hear the response song, spoke the words beginning with "Mayhaṃ sutvā." After teaching the response song, he sent Pañcacūḷaka away. "Young boy, go and sing this response song together with King Arindama. King Arindama will give you great wealth and happiness. What use do you have for wood? Go quickly!" he said.

The boy Pañcacūḷaka said, "Very well," and after learning the response song, he paid homage and said, "Venerable sir, please stay in this place for as long as it takes for me to bring the Great King." He then went quickly to his mother and said, "Mother, bathe and adorn me quickly. Today, I shall free you, mother, from poverty." After being bathed and adorned, he went to the palace gate and said, "Noble gatekeeper, please inform the King that a boy has arrived and stands at the gate, saying he will sing the song together with the Great King."

The gatekeeper went quickly and informed the King. King Arindama said, "Let him come," and after summoning him, said, "Dear boy, will you sing the response song together with me?" "Yes, Your Majesty, I will," he replied. When the King said, "If so, sing it," the boy replied, "Your Majesty, I shall not sing in this place. Rather, have the drum beaten throughout the city and assemble the people. I shall sing in the midst of the multitude."

King Arindama did as the boy requested. He sat on a throne in the midst of a decorated pavilion, gave the boy a suitable seat, and said, "Now, sing your song." "Your Majesty, please sing first, and afterwards, I shall sing the response," the boy replied. Then, King Arindama sang first:

## 2. Saṅkicca Jātaka
## Freedom from Sorrow through Hearing the Dhamma of the Virtuous

While staying in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove, the Teacher, the Fully Enlightened One, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Saṅkicca Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with “Disvā nisinnaṃ rājānaṃ,” concerning the parricide committed by King Ajātasattu.

This is the account: King Ajātasattu, depending on Devadatta and following his words, had his father, King Bimbisāra, killed. After the act of causing a schism in the Saṅgha, when Devadatta fell ill and was being carried on a litter to Sāvatthī to ask for the Buddha's forgiveness, he was swallowed by the earth near the gate of Jetavana Monastery. Hearing of this, Ajātasattu thought, “Venerable Devadatta became an enemy of the Buddha, was swallowed by the earth, and is bound for the Avīci hell. I, too, depending on him, killed my father, the righteous King. Will I also be swallowed by the earth?” Filled with fear, he found no delight in his royal splendor. Even when he tried to sleep for a moment, as soon as he drifted off, he would start up, crying out with a terrifying sound, feeling as if he were falling into an iron earth nine yojanas thick, being pierced by iron spikes, or being bitten and torn by dogs.

## Ajātasattu’s Visit to the Buddha

Then one day, on the full moon of the fourth month of the rainy season, the Komudī (Kattika) full moon, surrounded by his ministers, he looked at his own splendor and thought, “My father’s splendor was greater than this. Depending on Devadatta, I killed such a righteous King.” As he thought this, a burning sensation arose in Ajātasattu’s body, and his whole body became drenched in sweat.

Then he thought, “Who can dispel this fear of mine?” Realizing that “There is no one except the Fully Enlightened One, endowed with the Ten Powers,” he thought, “I have greatly offended the Blessed One. Who will lead me to him?” He concluded, “No one but Jīvaka can lead me.” To create an opportunity to go with Jīvaka, he uttered an exclamation: “How delightful, sirs, is this moonlit night!” and asked, “What ascetic or brahmin should we visit today?” When the ministers, who were disciples of Pūraṇa Kassapa and others, praised the virtues of teachers like Pūraṇa, he ignored their words and asked Jīvaka. Jīvaka spoke of the Buddha’s virtues and said, “Your Majesty, please visit the Blessed One.” He then had the elephant carriages prepared and set out for Jīvaka’s Mango Grove. After approaching and bowing to the Buddha, and being greeted by Him, he asked about the visible fruits of recluseship. Having heard the Buddha’s melodious discourse, the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, he declared his status as a lay follower at the end of the sermon, asked for the Buddha’s forgiveness, and departed.

## Attaining Peace of Mind

From then on, King Ajātasattu gave alms, kept the precepts, and associated with the Buddha. Hearing the melodious Dhamma and associating with a good friend (kalyāṇamitta), his fear vanished, his hair no longer stood on end, and having regained peace of mind, he lived happily in all four postures.

One day, a discussion arose in the Dhamma Hall: “Friends, King Ajātasattu was terrified after committing parricide. Depending on his royal splendor, he found no peace of mind and suffered in all postures. Now, however, through the Blessed One and by associating with a good friend, he is free from fear and enjoys the bliss of sovereignty.”

The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, what is the subject of your discussion as you sit here?” When they told him, he said, “Monks, it is not only now that this King Ajātasattu, having suffered due to killing his father, has found peaceful sleep through me. In the past, too, he killed his father and found peaceful sleep through me.” He then brought forth the past story.

The Story of the Past: Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, he had a son named Prince Brahmadatta. At that time, the Bodhisatta took conception in the house of the King’s chaplain. When he was born, they named him “Saṅkicca.” Both grew up together in the royal palace. Becoming friends, they went to Takkasilā upon reaching age, learned all the arts, and returned. Then the King appointed his son as viceroy. The Bodhisatta also remained with the viceroy. One day, the viceroy, seeing the great splendor of his father going to play in the park, became greedy for it. He thought, “My father is like a brother to me. If I wait for his death, I will only get the kingdom in my old age. What is the use of the kingdom then? I will kill my father and take the throne.” He told this to the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta restrained him, saying, “Friend, the act of parricide is grave; it is the path to hell. It is not possible to do this; do not do it.” Though he was restrained up to the third time, the prince consulted with his foot-servants. They also agreed...

He thought, "My father is like an elder brother to me. If I wait for his death, I will only obtain the kingship when I am old. What benefit is there in gaining the kingship at such an age? ## The Friend's Prohibition

The Bodhisatta forbade him, saying, "Prince, the act of parricide is extremely heavy; it is a cause for going to hell. It is not right to commit the murder of one's father; do not do it."

## Saṅkicca Departs for the Forest

When the viceroy spoke repeatedly and the Bodhisatta forbade him for the third time, the prince consulted with his attendants. Those attendants also agreed and investigated the means of King Brahmadatta's death. Knowing this, the Bodhisatta thought, "I will not be united with these people." Without asking permission from his parents, he left through the main gate, entered the Himalayas, and became an ascetic. Having developed the meditative absorptions and higher knowledges, he lived sustained by forest roots and fruits.

When the Bodhisatta had gone, the viceroy had his father, King Brahmadatta, killed and enjoyed the great royal wealth. Hearing that "the youth Saṅkicca has become an ascetic," many young men of good family left their homes and were ordained in his presence. The sage Saṅkicca lived there in the Himalayas, surrounded by a large company of sages. All those sages attained the meditative attainments.

The King, having killed his father, enjoyed the royal bliss for only a short time. From then on, he lived in fear and found no peace of mind, feeling as if he were suffering the tortures of hell.
282:
Upon reaching the garden gate, he thought: "Ascetics are worthy of great respect. It is inappropriate to approach the ascetic Saṅkicca in such an ostentatious manner." He then removed the five royal regalia: the fly-whisk with a handle of gold and jewels, the golden turban-band, the well-guarded auspicious sword, the white umbrella, and the golden sandals. Thus it is said, "He laid them aside." "Covering" means he set aside those royal regalia and handed them to the treasurer. "In Dāyapassa" refers to the garden of that name. "Then he knew the time" means he realized that now was the time to ask his questions. In the Pali, it appears as "yathākālaṃ," meaning he considered it the appropriate time to ask questions. "He proceeded" means he went forward. "Pecca" means having gone beyond, or it is a name for the next world; therefore, it means in the next world. He asks, "Venerable sir, I have practiced unrighteousness and committed the act of parricide. Tell me, where do parricides go? In which hell are they cooked?"

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta said, "In that case, Great King, listen," and first gave him an exhortation. The Teacher, explaining this matter, said:

## The King Remembers His Friend
The King remembered the Bodhisatta. He thought: "My friend, the youth Saṅkicca, warned me, 'The act of killing one's father is very heavy; do not do it.' Being unable to make me take his words, he fled to keep himself blameless. If Saṅkicca were here now, he would not have allowed me to commit parricide, and he would dispel this fear and terror of mine. Where does Saṅkicca live now? If I knew where he lived, I would have him summoned. Who will inform me of Saṅkicca's dwelling place?" Having thought thus, from that time on, King Brahmadatta spoke only of the Bodhisatta's virtues within the palace and at royal assemblies.

## The Ascetic Saṅkicca Arrives
Thus, after a long time had passed, the Bodhisatta thought: "King Brahmadatta remembers me. It is proper for me to go to King Brahmadatta's palace, preach the Dhamma to him, and free him from fear and terror." Having lived in the Himalayas for fifty years, he came through the air surrounded by five hundred ascetics, descended into the garden named Dāyapassa, and sat upon the auspicious stone slab surrounded by the assembly of ascetics.

The gardener, seeing the Bodhisatta, asked: "Venerable teacher of the group, what is your name?" Hearing "I am the wise Saṅkicca," the gardener recognized him and requested: "Venerable sir, please stay here while I go to inform the King. Our Great King wishes to see you." Having paid homage, he went quickly to the King's palace and reported the arrival of the ascetic Saṅkicca.

## The Eight Great Hells
83. O King. The Sañjīva hell, the Kāḷasutta hell, the Saṅghāta hell, and the two Roruvas (Jāla-roruva and Dhūma-roruva). Furthermore, the Mahā-Avīci hell, the Tapana hell, and the Mahātapana hell.

84. Thus, these eight great hells are proclaimed. They are difficult to escape and are crowded with hell-wardens who perform cruel deeds. For each great hell, there are sixteen Ussada hells.

## Hell for the Miserly
85. For those who are miserly and deceitful, these hells are the place of their suffering. They are terrible, fiery, of great danger, hair-raising in appearance, extremely terrifying, causing fear, and full of suffering.

86. They have four corners and four gates, divided and measured by the gate-ways. They are bounded by iron walls and covered with an iron lid of nine yojanas.

87. Great King. The ground of those hells is made of iron, joined with fire that blazes with brilliance. It stays always touching for a hundred yojanas all around.
