130. O Great King, those who are fraudulent, such as corrupt judges, are beaten day and night with glowing iron hammers. Then, those hell-beings with bodies difficult to move must always eat the vomit of others.

131. O Great King, hawks, jackals, vultures as large as carts, and flocks of crows, all with iron beaks, devour the evildoer who is writhing in pain.

132. Those who kill a deer with a deer, or a bird with a bird, those ignoble ones covered in the dust of passion, go to the Ussada hell.

81. O Great King, the Dhamma, the ten courses of wholesome action, is the noble path free from danger for those who do good. But the unrighteous path, the ten courses of unwholesome action, is a dangerous path for those who do evil. Unrighteousness leads to hell; righteousness leads to a happy destination.

82. O King, listen to me regarding the hells to which those beings go after death—those who practice evil and live unrighteously.

(Prose): The Great Being (Bodhisatta), though asked by the King about the hell for parricides, did not show it first. Instead, he spoke thus to show the eight great hells and sixteen Ussada hells. For what reason? If that specific hell were shown first, the King might die of a broken heart right there. But by seeing beings being cooked in these other hells, he would think, "There are many other evildoers like me; I will be cooked among them," and thus gaining support, he would remain healthy. To show those hells, the Great Being first split the earth by the power of his psychic potency and then revealed them.

The meaning of the names: Sañjīva is the hell where beings, cut into pieces by hell-wardens with various flaming weapons, come back to life again and again. The hell-wardens, shouting and leaping, take various flaming weapons and chase the beings on the glowing iron ground, striking them. When they fall on the blazing ground, they are marked with glowing black threads...
288:
## Hunters

132. Great King. 'Covered in dust' (rajasā channā) means being enveloped and covered by the dust of defilements. 'The unrighteous' (asanto) refers to those who are not virtuous. 'Those persons' (ye puggalā) refers to such individuals.
289: With a decoy deer (migena), they kill a multitude of deer (migaṃ). Or with a decoy bird (pakkhinā vā pana), they kill a multitude of birds (pakkhiṃ). Those persons (te puggalā) must go to the Ussada hell (nirayussadaṃ).
290:
## The Happiness of the Celestial Realm

In this way, the Bodhisatta, the ascetic Saṅkicca, having revealed and explained these hells to such an extent, now wished to reveal the celestial realm and show it to King Brahmadatta—
293: That King Brahmadatta, having heard the Dhamma discourse of the Bodhisatta, the ascetic Saṅkicca, found relief from that day forward.
294: The Bodhisatta, the ascetic Saṅkicca, stayed in that garden for a short while and then returned to his own dwelling in the Himavantā.
295:
He spoke these two verses:

133. The peaceful go upwards through deeds well-performed here.
Behold the fruit of well-performed deeds, the gods with Indra and Brahma.

134. Therefore I tell you, O Great King, O Lord of the Realm, practice the Dhamma.
O King, practice the Dhamma in such a way that you will not regret it later.

133. Mahārāja: Great King. Santo: those who are peaceful in body and so forth. Sa-indā: together with Indra, the king of gods. Sa-brahmakā: together with Brahma. Devā: the devas and brahmas. Idha: in this human world. Suciṇṇena kammunā: due to well-performed kamma. Uddhaṃ: to the celestial and Brahma realms. Gacchanti: they go. Suciṇṇassa phalaṃ passa: behold the fruit of well-performed practice.

134. Mahārāja: Great King. Taṃ-tasmā: therefore. Taṃ: to you, the king. Brūmi: I say. Raṭṭhapati: you who are the lord of the country. Rāja: Great King. Dhammaṃ: the Dhamma. Cara: practice. Yathā: in such a way. Yaṃ dhammaṃ: which Dhamma. Suciṇṇam: if well-practiced. Pacchā: in a later time. Nānutappeyya: one would not regret. Tathā: in that way. Taṃ dhammaṃ: that Dhamma. Carāhi: please practice.
296:
The All-Knowing Buddha, having brought this Dhamma teaching of the Saṅkicca Jātaka, said: "Monks, not only now have I comforted King Ajātasattu; in the past, when he was King Brahmadatta, I also comforted him." Then he identified the birth: "At that time, King Ajātasattu was King Brahmadatta, the Buddha’s assembly were the group of ascetics, and I myself was the wise ascetic Saṅkicca."

## Various Hells, Celestial Realms, Know Them All, Practice Well

The Saṅkicca Jātaka is concluded.
297:
## 1. Kusa Jātaka

## On Not Following the Sway of Defilements

The All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Kusa Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Idaṃ te raṭṭhaṃ", concerning a monk who was dissatisfied and wished to disrobe.

That monk, a son of a good family living in Sāvatthī, had ordained in the Sasana by dedicating his life. One day, while walking for alms in Sāvatthī, he saw a well-adorned woman. Looking at her with the perception that "all her limbs, such as hands, feet, and hair, are exceedingly beautiful," he was overcome by defilements and lived without delight in the Sasana. He had long hair and nails, dirty robes, a pale complexion like a withered leaf, and his veins were visible on his body.

## The Passing of Devas

For example, five omens appear to the sons of devas who are about to pass away from the celestial realm: "The flowers they wear wither; the clothes they wear become soiled; their complexion becomes dull; sweat comes out from both armpits; and they no longer delight in their celestial seats."

## The Disrobing of Monks

Similarly, five omens appear to monks who are dissatisfied and wish to fall away from the Sasana: The flowers of faith wither; the robes of virtue become soiled; their complexion becomes dull due to frowning and loss of aura; the sweat of defilements leaks out; and they no longer delight in forest dwellings, the roots of trees, or secluded places. These five omens appeared to that monk.

Then, the monks brought him to the presence of the All-Knowing Buddha and said, "Venerable Sir, this monk is dissatisfied." The All-Knowing Buddha asked, "Monk, is it true that you are dissatisfied?" When he replied, "It is true, Venerable Sir," the Buddha said, "Monk, you should not follow the sway of defilements. Women are exceedingly vile. Remove your attachment to that woman. Delight in my Sasana. It is true that because of attachment to women, even the wise men of old who possessed great power and majesty lost their aura and power and reached ruin and destruction." Having said this, he brought forth the past.

In the past, in the capital city of Kusāvatī in the Malla kingdom, a king named Okkāka ruled according to the ten kingly virtues. His chief queen, the head of sixteen thousand women, was named Sīlavatī. Queen Sīlavatī had no sons or daughters.

Then, the people living in the city and the people of the Malla kingdom gathered at the palace gate and cried out, "The Great King's country will perish!" King Okkāka opened the lion-balcony window and asked, "While I am ruling, there is no injustice. Why do you cry out?" They replied, "Great King, it is true that there is no injustice. However, you have no son to protect the lineage. Another king will take the country and destroy your kingdom. Therefore, pray for a son who is capable of ruling according to the Dhamma."

He asked, "If I pray for a son, what should I do?" They replied, "Great King, first, for one seven-day period, send out a young concubine as a 'Dhamma-observing woman'. If she obtains a son, it is well. If not, then send out a middle-aged concubine as a 'Dhamma-observing woman'. After that, send out the chief queen as a 'Dhamma-observing woman'. Among so many women, if any one of them has merit, you will surely obtain a son."
298:
## The Concubines Pray for a Son

Upon hearing their words, King Okkāka did as they requested. On the seventh day, after enjoying himself as he pleased, he asked the concubines who had come, "Ladies, how is it? Have you obtained a son?" All the concubines replied, "Great King, we have not." King Okkāka became displeased, thinking, "A son will not be born to me."

The citizens shouted again as before. King Okkāka asked, "Why do you shout? According to your words, I have sent out the concubines, yet not even one has obtained a son. What shall we do now?" They replied, "Great King, those concubines must be immoral and lacking in merit. They have no merit to obtain a son. Even if you do not obtain a son through them, do not be indifferent. Your Chief Queen, named Sīlavatī, is endowed with virtue. Please send her out; she will surely obtain a son."

King Okkāka agreed, saying, "Very well." He had the drums beaten to announce, "It is said that on the seventh day from now, King Okkāka will send out Queen Sīlavatī as a Dhamma-nāṭaka (righteous performer). Let all men assemble." On the seventh day, he had Queen Sīlavatī adorned, brought down from the palace, and sent her out.

## Sakka Grants the Boon of a Son

Due to the power of Queen Sīlavatī's virtue, Sakka's throne showed signs of heat. When Sakka reflected on the cause, he thought, "It is proper for me to grant the boon of a son to Queen Sīlavatī. Is there a suitable son for her in the celestial realm?" Upon searching, he saw the Bodhisatta. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having exhausted his lifespan in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, wished to be reborn in a higher celestial realm.

Sakka went to the door of that deity's mansion, summoned him, and said, "Friend, it is proper for you to go to the human world and take conception in the womb of King Okkāka's Chief Queen." Having secured his consent, he spoke to another deity, saying, "You too shall become a son of Queen Sīlavatī."

Thinking, "Indeed, let no one break the virtue of Queen Sīlavatī," he went to the gate of King Okkāka's palace in the guise of an old Brahmin. The people, having bathed and adorned themselves, gathered at the palace gate, saying, "I shall take the Queen! I shall take the Queen!" Seeing Sakka, they mocked him, asking, "Why have you come?" Sakka replied, "Why do you revile me? Though my body is old, my passion is not. I have come to take Queen Sīlavatī if I obtain her." By his own power, he stood at the very front of everyone.

No other person could stand in front of him due to Sakka's power. Thus, when the Queen, adorned with all ornaments, emerged from the palace, Sakka took her by the hand and led her away. Then, the people standing here and there reviled Sakka, saying, "O friends, look! An old Brahmin is taking away a Queen of such noble appearance. He does not know what is unsuitable for him."

The Queen, however, was neither distressed nor disgusted by the thought, "An old Brahmin is taking me away." King Okkāka, standing at the palace window, saw the old Brahmin and became displeased, wondering, "Who is taking the Queen away?"
299:
Sakka took the queen and left through the city gate. Near the gate, he created a house with an open door and a prepared wooden bed. Then Queen Sīlavatī asked Sakka, "Lord, is this your house?" Sakka replied, "Queen, yes. Previously I was alone, but now we are two. I shall go for alms to bring rice and such. Queen, sleep on this wooden bed." Saying this, Sakka touched the queen with his soft hand, suffusing her with a divine touch, and made her lie on that wooden bed. Due to the suffusion of the divine touch, the queen lost consciousness. Then, by his power, he took the queen to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and made her lie on a divine bed in a decorated mansion.

On the seventh day, the queen woke up and, seeing the fulfillment of such prosperity, realized, "That brahmin was not a human; he must be Sakka." At that time, Sakka was seated at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree, surrounded by a troupe of celestial dancers. Queen Sīlavatī rose from her bed, went to Sakka, paid homage, and stood in a suitable place.

Then Sakka said to Queen Sīlavatī, "Queen, I grant you a boon. Will you take it?" She replied, "Lord of Devas, if you wish to grant it, please give me the boon of a son." He said, "Queen, let alone one son, I shall give you two sons. Of those two sons, one will be wise but ugly, and the other will be very handsome but not wise. Of these two sons, which do you desire first?" She said, "Lord of Devas, I desire the wise son."

Sakka said, "Very well," and gave Queen Sīlavatī Kusa grass, divine cloth, divine sandalwood, a Pāricchattaka flower, and a lute named Kokanada. Then, taking Queen Sīlavatī, he entered King Okkāka's bedchamber, placed her on the same bed with the king, and touched the queen's navel with his thumb. At that moment, the Bodhisatta took conception in Queen Sīlavatī's womb. Sakka then returned to his own place in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Wise people knew that Queen Sīlavatī had become pregnant.

## The King Honored Her
Then, seeing Queen Sīlavatī wake up, King Okkāka asked, "Queen, who took you away?" She replied, "Great King, Sakka took me." The king said, "I saw with my own eyes an old brahmin taking you away. Why do you deceive me? I do not believe you." She replied, "Great King, please believe me. Sakka took me and brought me to the deva world." The king said, "Queen, I do not believe you."

Then the queen showed the king the Kusa grass and other things given by Sakka and said again, "Please believe me." King Okkāka said, "Queen, this Kusa grass can be obtained from any ordinary place. Therefore, I do not believe you." Then the queen showed the king the divine cloth and other items. Upon seeing the Kusa grass, divine cloth, and so on, King Okkāka believed her and asked, "Queen, even though Sakka took you, did you obtain a son?" She replied, "Great King, I have obtained one.
300:
I have conceived." Upon hearing this, King Okkāka was greatly pleased and provided the queen with pregnancy protection.

## Kusa and Jayampati
After ten months, Queen Sīlavatī gave birth to a son. They did not give him any other name but named him "Prince Kusa," based on the Kusa grass. When Prince Kusa was able to walk, another deva-son passed away from the deva world and took conception in Queen Sīlavatī's womb. They named that son "Jayampati."

The two royal brothers grew up with a great retinue. The elder brother, Prince Kusa, who was the Bodhisatta, was extremely wise. Without learning any art from a teacher, he reached perfection in all arts through his own wisdom alone.

Then, when Prince Kusa was sixteen years old, his father, King Okkāka, wishing to give him the kingship, called the Queen Mother and said:
"Queen, let us give the kingship to your son and have the harem attendants serve him. While we are still alive, let us see our son established in the kingship. Indeed, throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, whichever king's daughter our son desires, we shall bring that princess for our son and make her the chief queen. Find out the son's heart; which princess does our son like?"

## Questioning Prince Kusa
The Queen Mother Sīlavatī agreed, saying "Very well," and sent a female attendant, instructing her, "Go and inform the son of this matter and find out his heart." The female attendant went and reported the matter to the son.

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta thought: "I am not handsome. Even if beautiful princesses are brought, when they see me, they will flee, saying 'What shall I do with an ugly prince?' If they flee like this, it will be shameful for us. What use is household life to me? I will serve my mother and father while they are alive, and after they pass away, I will leave for the forest and ordain." Thus, the Bodhisatta Prince Kusa sent back the message: "I have no need for the kingship, nor for harem attendants. Indeed, after my mother and father pass away, I shall only ordain."
301:
That servant woman went and reported the words sent by the son to the Queen Mother. The Queen Mother also reported to the Great King Okkāka. When King Okkāka heard the words sent by his son, he was displeased; however, after two or three days had passed, he sent the message again. Prince Kusa refused yet again.

Having refused thus for the third time, on the fourth occasion he thought: "It is certainly not proper to be in constant opposition to my mother and father; I shall employ a certain stratagem." Having so reflected, Prince Kusa summoned the master goldsmith, gave him much gold, and commanded, "Make a statue of a woman." When the master goldsmith had departed, he took other gold and himself made a statue of a woman.

## I Will Marry Only One Who Resembles the Golden Statue

The intentions of Bodhisattas are always fulfilled. The golden statue made by the Bodhisatta was of such beauty that no living woman could match its splendor. Then the Bodhisatta had that golden statue dressed in linen cloth and placed in a royal chamber. When the Bodhisatta saw the golden statue brought by the master goldsmith, he disparaged it and said, "Friend, go and bring the golden statue placed in our royal chamber."

When the master goldsmith entered the royal chamber and saw that golden statue, he thought, "A goddess must have come to enjoy herself with the prince." Not daring to stretch out his hand, he came out and reported, "My Lord, there is a goddess alone in the royal chamber. I do not dare to approach her." The prince sent him again, saying, "Friend, go; this is but a golden statue; bring it." Only then did the master goldsmith bring it.

Prince Kusa placed the golden statue made by the master goldsmith in the treasury, and having had the statue he himself made adorned and placed upon a carriage, he sent it to the Queen Mother, saying, "If I obtain a princess of such a form, I shall marry her."

The Queen Mother summoned the ministers and said, "Friends, my son is of great merit, a son obtained through the gift of Sakka; he shall surely find a suitable princess. Friends, if you find a princess who resembles this golden statue, take her. Place this golden statue in a covered carriage and wander throughout the whole of Jambudīpa; in whichever king's presence you see a princess resembling this golden statue, give this statue to that king and say, 'Our Lord, King Okkāka, shall enter into a marriage alliance with you,' and having fixed the date, return."

## Searching with the Golden Statue

The ministers said, "Very well," and taking that golden statue, they departed with a large retinue. As they wandered, they arrived at a certain royal city. In that royal city, at the time of evening when many people gather, they adorned that golden statue with garments and ornaments, placed it upon a golden palanquin, and set it down on the path to the bathing ghat where the crowds gathered. The ministers themselves withdrew and stood to one side to listen to the talk of those who came and went.

The people looked at that golden statue and, not realizing it was a golden statue, praised it, saying, "Though this person is a human woman, she is as beautiful as a goddess; she is exceedingly lovely. Why has she come to stay in this place? From where has she come? In our city, there is no woman of such a form." Hearing these words, the ministers who were listening thought, "If there were a maiden of such a form in this city, [they would say] 'She is like such-and-such a princess...'"
302:
"They would say, 'She is like the daughter of such-and-such a minister.' Surely, there is no woman in this city who resembles this golden statue." Saying this, they took the golden statue and went to another city.

As the ministers traveled in this manner, they eventually reached the city of Sāgala in the kingdom of Madda. In that city of Sāgala, the King of Madda had eight daughters who possessed supreme beauty and were like celestial nymphs. Among those eight princesses, the eldest of all was named Pabhāvatī. From the body of Princess Pabhāvatī, rays of light radiated like the rising sun.

Because of that radiance, even in the darkness of a chamber measuring four cubits, there was no need to light a lamp. The entire chamber was filled with a single mass of light. The nurse of Princess Pabhāvatī was named Khujjā. After feeding Princess Pabhāvatī, this nurse Khujjā, intending to bathe the princess including her head, had eight beautiful maidservants carry eight water pots. As they went to fetch water in the evening, she saw the golden statue standing on the path to the landing place and, mistaking it for Princess Pabhāvatī, thought:

"This unruly girl sent us to fetch water so she could bathe her head, yet she came here before us and is waiting at the landing place." Becoming angry, she said, "Hey, you girl who brings shame to your family! Why have you come here before us and are waiting at the landing place? If the Great King, your father, should find out, we will be ruined!" She then struck the statue on the hip with her hand, and it felt as if her palm would break. Then, realizing it was a golden statue, she laughed and went to the beautiful maidservants, saying, "Friends, look at what I have done! Mistaking it for my daughter, I struck it. How can this golden statue compare to my daughter? I have only caused pain to my own hand."

## Pabhāvatī is Found

Then the messengers of King Okkāka took the nurse Khujjā by the hand and asked, "You said, 'My daughter is much more beautiful than this golden statue.' Whom are you talking about?" She replied, "I am talking about Pabhāvatī, the daughter of the King of Madda. This golden statue is not worth even a sixteenth part of Pabhāvatī."

The messengers of King Okkāka, with hearts full of joy, went to the palace gate and sent word, "The messengers of King Okkāka are standing at the gate." The King of Madda, rising from his seat and standing, commanded, "Call them in."

The messengers entered, paid homage to the King of Madda, and said, "O Great King, our lord King Okkāka inquires after your health." Having been received with due honor and hospitality, the King asked, "For what purpose have you come, sirs?" They replied, "Our lord King Okkāka has a son named Kusa, whose voice is like the roar of a lion king. His father, King Okkāka, wishes to hand over the kingdom to him and has sent us to your presence. We hear that you have a daughter named Pabhāvatī. Please give your daughter Pabhāvatī to our prince, King Kusa. And please accept this golden statue as a gift of offering." Saying this, they presented the golden statue to the King of Madda.

The King of Madda, with a joyful heart, thinking, "Such a marriage alliance with a Great King of this nature will be auspicious," gave his consent.
303:
Then the messengers of King Okkāka reported to King Madda: “Your Majesty, we cannot afford to delay. Having learned that the princess has been obtained, we shall report to our lord King Okkāka. Upon hearing this, our lord King Okkāka will come and take the princess away.” King Madda said, “Very well,” and after giving them gifts, he dismissed the messengers.

## Going to See the Daughter-in-law

Those messengers went and reported the matter to King Okkāka and Queen Sīlavatī. King Okkāka departed from the royal city of Kusāvatī with a large retinue and in due course arrived at the city of Sāgala.

King Madda went out to welcome him, brought King Okkāka into the city, and paid him great honor. Queen Sīlavatī, being wise, thought, “Who can know what will happen? How will it be?” After a day or two had passed, she said to King Madda, “Your Majesty, I wish to see my daughter-in-law.” King Madda agreed, saying, “Very well,” and had his daughter summoned. Princess Pabhāvatī, having adorned herself with all kinds of ornaments and surrounded by a retinue of nurses, came and paid respects to her mother-in-law, Queen Sīlavatī.

When Queen Sīlavatī saw Princess Pabhāvatī, she thought, “This young maiden is exceedingly beautiful, but my son is ugly. If she were to see him, she would not stay even for a single day but would flee. I must devise a scheme.”

Having so thought, Queen Sīlavatī invited King Madda and said, “Your Majesty, the daughter-in-law is suitable for my son. However, there is one thing to be said. There is a custom that has come down through our lineage; if this young maiden will observe that custom, I shall take her with me.” He asked, “What is your family custom?” She replied, “In our family, until there is a single conception, she is not permitted to see her husband during the day. If this young maiden will follow what I say, I shall take her.”

## Consecrated and Ascending the Throne

The father, King Madda, asked his daughter Pabhāvatī, “How is it, dear daughter? Will you be able to practice as Queen Sīlavatī says?” Princess Pabhāvatī replied, “Father, I shall be able to do so.” After Pabhāvatī had given her consent, King Okkāka gave much wealth and property to King Madda, took Princess Pabhāvatī, and returned to the great royal city of Kusāvatī. King Madda also sent Princess Pabhāvatī off with a large retinue.

King Okkāka went to Kusāvatī, had the city decorated, released all prisoners from their bonds, performed the royal consecration for his son, gave him the kingdom, made Princess Pabhāvatī the chief queen, and had the drum sounded throughout the city, proclaiming, “This is the command of King Kusa.” Among the kings across the surface of Jambudīpa, those who had daughters sent them to King Kusa. Those who had sons, desiring friendship with King Kusa, sent their sons to serve him. The retinue of the Bodhisatta’s performers became very large, and he ruled the kingdom with great glory.

## Desiring to See Pabhāvatī

King Kusa was not permitted to see Pabhāvatī during the day, and Princess Pabhāvatī was also not permitted to see King Kusa during the day. The two, king and queen, could only see each other at night. Among the two, Pabhāvatī’s bodily radiance was also indistinct and negligible [in the dark]. The Bodhisatta King Kusa would leave the auspicious royal chamber only at night.

After a day or two had passed, the king, desiring to see Pabhāvatī during the day, informed his mother. The Queen Mother refused, saying, “My son, do not desire to see Pabhāvatī during the day. Wait until you have at least one son.” But King Kusa pleaded and requested her again and again.
304:
## Throwing a Lump of Elephant Dung

When he pleaded thus again and again, the Queen Mother said to her son, “My son, if you wish to see her so much, go to the elephant stable and stay there in the guise of an elephant groom. I will bring Pabhāvatī to the elephant stable. When I bring her, look at her to your heart's content, but do not let her know that you are her husband.” King Kusa agreed, saying, “Very well,” and went ahead to the elephant stable.

The Queen Mother had the auspicious elephant stable decorated and said to Princess Pabhāvatī, “Dear daughter, come, let us look at your husband's elephants.” She took her to the elephant stable and showed them, saying, “This elephant is named so-and-so; this elephant is named so-and-so.”

When King Kusa saw Pabhāvatī following behind his mother in the elephant stable, in his guise as an elephant groom, he threw a lump of elephant dung at Pabhāvatī’s back. Pabhāvatī became angry and said, “I will report this to the King and have your hand cut off!” and she complained to Queen Sīlavatī. The Queen Mother calmed her daughter-in-law, saying, “Dear daughter, do not be angry,” and she stroked and massaged her back.

## Throwing a Lump of Horse Dung

Again, King Kusa desired to see her, and in the horse stable, in the guise of a horse groom, he saw Pabhāvatī and threw a lump of horse dung at her just as before. On that occasion too, the mother-in-law, Queen Sīlavatī, coaxed the angry Pabhāvatī and made her endure it.

## Showing the Younger Brother

Again one day, Pabhāvatī desired to see King Kusa and informed her mother-in-law, Queen Sīlavatī. The Queen Mother refused, saying, “Dear daughter, it is not proper; do not desire to see King Kusa.” Pabhāvatī also pleaded and requested again and again. Then the Queen Mother said to Pabhāvatī, “Dear daughter, if you wish to see him, tomorrow my son will circumambulate the city. Open the lion-window and look at King Kusa.”

Having said this, on the following day, she had the city decorated, had the younger brother, Prince Jayampati, take the appearance of the king, and had him mount the back of an elephant to circumambulate the city clockwise.
305:
The Queen Mother took Pabhavatī and, standing at the breezy palace gate supported by lions, said, "Dear daughter, look at the full glory and splendor of your husband." Princess Pabhavatī was very delighted, thinking, "I have obtained a husband who is handsome and suitable." On that day, King Kusa, in the guise of an elephant groom, sat in the rear seat behind his younger brother, Prince Jayampati. Looking at Pabhavatī as much as he desired, he mocked her according to his whim by making signs such as snapping his fingers.

When the elephant had passed, the Queen Mother asked Pabhavatī, "Dear daughter, did you see your husband?" "Mother, I saw him," she replied. "But the elephant groom sitting behind the King is very insolent. He made signs at me, such as snapping his fingers. Why do they allow such a shameless person to sit behind the King? Have that elephant groom driven away."

"Dear daughter," the Queen Mother said, "it is necessary to have guards behind the King."

## Pabhavatī's Investigation

Pabhavatī thought, "This elephant groom is extremely fearless; he does not even regard the King as a king. Could this man himself be King Kusa? It must be true; King Kusa must be extremely ugly, and that is why they do not show him to me." Thinking thus, Pabhavatī whispered into the ear of her hunchback nurse named Khujjā, "Mother, go and find out. Is the one sitting in the front seat the King, or is it the one in the rear seat? Go and find out."

"How shall I know?" the nurse asked. "Mother, what are you saying? If he is indeed the King, he will be the first to dismount from the elephant. Know it by this sign."

The nurse Khujjā went and stood in a suitable place and saw King Kusa dismount first, followed by his younger brother, Prince Jayampati. King Kusa, looking here and there, saw the nurse Khujjā and, realizing, "This Khujjā must have come for this reason," he had her called and strictly instructed her, "Do not tell Pabhavatī about this matter," and sent her away. The nurse Khujjā went back and reported, "Princess, the one sitting in the front seat dismounted first." Pabhavatī believed the words spoken by the nurse Khujjā.

## Grabbing the Golden Hand in the Pond

The Bodhisatta, wishing to see her again, pleaded with his mother. The Queen Mother, unable to refuse, said, "My son, if that is so, go to the garden in disguise." King Kusa went to the garden, entered the royal lotus pond up to his neck, covered his head with a lotus leaf, and remained there hiding his face with a blooming lotus flower.

King Kusa's mother, the Queen, brought Pabhavatī to the garden in the evening and, enticing her by saying, "Look at these trees, look at these birds, look at these deer," she led her to the edge of the royal lotus pond. When Princess Pabhavatī saw the royal lotus pond covered with five kinds of lotuses, she wished to bathe. While playing in the pond with her attendants, she saw that lotus flower and, wishing to pluck it, she stretched out her hand. When she stretched out her hand, King Kusa pushed aside the lotus leaf, said, "I am King Kusa," and grabbed Pabhavatī by the hand. When Pabhavatī saw King Kusa's face, she cried out, "A yakkha has caught me!" and fainted right there. Then King Kusa released Pabhavatī's hand.

## Pabhavatī Departs

When Pabhavatī regained consciousness, she thought, "King Kusa actually grabbed my hand. This same King Kusa threw lumps of elephant dung at me in the elephant stable and horse dung in the horse stable. This same King Kusa mocked me from behind on the elephant. What use have I for such an ugly husband? If I live, I shall find another husband." She then called the ministers who had come with her and said, "Prepare my carriage, and the elephant and horse carriages. I shall leave this very day."

The ministers reported this matter to King Kusa. King Kusa thought, "If Pabhavatī is not allowed to go, her heart will break. Let her go; I shall bring her back again by my own power." Having thought thus, he gave her permission to return to her own country. Pabhavatī returned to her father's city. The Bodhisatta, King Kusa, also entered the city from the garden and ascended the decorated golden palace.
306:
## Past Deeds and Destiny

This is true. By the power of her past prayer, Pabhavatī did not desire the Bodhisatta, King Kusa. And the Bodhisatta, King Kusa, was ugly due to the power of his past unwholesome kamma. The reason is as follows:

In the past, in a village near the gate of Bārāṇasī, two families lived on the upper street and the lower street. One family had two sons, and the other family had only one daughter. Of the two sons, the Bodhisatta was the younger. That one daughter was given in marriage to the elder brother. The younger brother lived with his elder brother without taking a wife of his own.

## Pabhavatī's Prayer

Then one day, they fried very delicious cakes in that house. The younger brother, the Bodhisatta, had gone to the forest. They set aside the younger brother's portion of the cakes and divided and ate the rest. At that moment, a Paccekabuddha arrived at the door of the house for alms. The elder brother's wife thought, "I will fry another cake for my brother-in-law," and taking his portion of the cake, she offered it to the Paccekabuddha.

The Bodhisatta returned from the forest at that very moment. When he arrived, his sister-in-law said, "Brother, please be joyful in heart; your portion of the cake has been offered to a Paccekabuddha." The brother-in-law became angry, saying, "You ate your own portion and gave away mine! What else shall I eat?" and going after the Paccekabuddha, he took the cake back from his bowl.

The sister-in-law went to her mother's house, brought some freshly clarified butter (ghee) the color of champak flowers, and filled the Paccekabuddha's bowl with it. The ghee emitted a radiance. Seeing that radiance, the Bodhisatta's sister-in-law made a prayer: "Venerable Sir, by the power of this gift of ghee, may my body emit radiance in every life I am born, and may I possess supreme beauty. And may I never have to live in the same place as this vile man." Because of the power of this past prayer, Pabhavatī did not desire King Kusa.

## King Kusa's Prayer

The Bodhisatta also placed that cake back into the ghee and made a prayer: "Even if this sister-in-law of mine lives a hundred leagues away, may I be able to bring her back to serve at my feet."
307:
1. This kingdom is yours, with wealth and vehicles,
With the royal regalia and all desires fulfilled.
Rule this kingdom, Mother;
I am going to where my beloved Pabhāvatī is.

He spoke this first verse:
1. Mother, this kingdom is yours. Mother, rule this kingdom, which is endowed with wealth, with elephant and horse vehicles, with the five royal regalia, and with all that is desirable. I shall go to where my beloved Pabhāvatī is.

## Now They Have Met
Between those two, King Kusa, out of anger, went and snatched the cake. Due to the power of that past unwholesome deed, he became unlovely in appearance. Pabhāvatī, due to the power of her past aspiration, did not desire King Kusa. This is the past cause.

## King Kusa Follows
When Pabhāvatī departed, King Kusa fell into great sorrow. Although all the remaining concubines served King Kusa in various ways, they could not please him. To King Kusa, the entire palace without Pabhāvatī seemed empty.

King Kusa thought, "I shall reach the city of Sāgala this very moment." At dawn, he went to his mother and said, "Mother, I shall bring Pabhāvatī back. You must rule the kingdom." Wishing to entrust the kingdom to his mother—

Queen Sīlavatī, hearing the words of her son King Kusa, said, "Dear son, if you wish to go, be heedful. It is true that women have impure hearts." Having said this, she filled a golden casket with food of various excellent flavors and sent him off, saying, "Eat this food along the way."

King Kusa took the rice casket given by his mother, paid homage to her, performed three circumambulations, and said, "If I remain alive, I shall see you again." He then entered the auspicious chamber, firmly equipped himself with the five weapons, placed a thousand coins along with the rice casket in a bag, took the lute named Kokanada, and departed from the city. As he traveled, being endowed with great strength and power, he covered a distance of fifty yojanas by midday. After eating his meal, he traveled another fifty yojanas during the remainder of the day. Thus, in a single day, he completed a journey of a hundred yojanas and entered the city of Sāgala at nightfall.

As soon as King Kusa entered the city of Sāgala, Pabhāvatī, unable to remain on her bed due to King Kusa's power, descended and lay upon the ground.

## Giving the Lute Sound
A certain woman saw the Bodhisatta King Kusa, whose faculties were weary from travel, and she called him in, washed his feet, and gave him a bed. The Bodhisatta, being exhausted, fell into a deep sleep.
308:
Then, while the Bodhisatta was asleep, that woman prepared a meal and fed him when he woke up. The Bodhisatta, being pleased, gave that woman a thousand coins along with the rice casket.

The Bodhisatta left his five weapons in that house, saying, "I have a place to play the lute." Taking his lute, he went to the elephant stable and said, "Please let me stay here for just one day; I will perform music for you." Having received permission from the elephant keepers, he lay down in a certain spot, slept for a while, and when his fatigue had subsided, he rose, tuned his lute, and sang while playing, thinking, "Let all the inhabitants of Sāgala hear this sound."

Pabhāvatī, lying on the ground, heard that lute sound and thought, "This lute sound is not that of any other; undoubtedly King Kusa has come for my sake." King Madda also heard the lute sound and thought, "He plays most melodiously; tomorrow I shall summon this musician and have him perform for me."

## Presenting the Pottery
The Bodhisatta thought, "It is not possible to see Pabhāvatī while staying in this elephant stable; this stable is not the right place." He departed early in the morning, ate his breakfast at the same house where he had eaten the previous evening, left his lute there, and went to the King's potter. He became an apprentice to that potter and, in a single day, filled the house with lumps of clay. He said, "Teacher, I shall make pots." When told, "Do so," he placed a lump of clay on the potter's wheel and spun it. Once spun, it continued to rotate until after midday.

The Bodhisatta made pots of various colors, both small and large. While making a pot for Pabhāvatī, he created various figures upon it. It is true that the wishes of Bodhisattas are always fulfilled. He made an aspiration: "Let Pabhāvatī alone see these various figures." The Bodhisatta dried all the pots, fired them, and filled the house.

The potter took the various pots and went to the King's palace. When King Madda saw them, he asked, "Who made these pots?" When the potter replied, "Your Majesty, I made them," the King asked again, "I know the pots you make; tell the truth, who made them?" The potter then had to report, "Your Majesty, they were made by my apprentice."

"That person is not your apprentice; he is your teacher. You should learn the craft from him. From this day forward, let him make pots for my daughters. Also, give him this thousand coins." Having ordered the thousand coins to be given, the King said, "Give these small pots of various colors to my daughters."

The potter took those pots to the princesses and presented them, saying, "These small pots are for the princesses to play with." All the princesses came. The potter presented to Princess Pabhāvatī only the pot that the Bodhisatta had made specifically for her.

When Princess Pabhāvatī took the pot and saw her own figure, King Kusa's figure, and the figure of the hunchback nurse upon it, she knew, "No one else could have made this; only King Kusa made it." In anger, she said, "I have no need for this pot; give it to those who want it."

Then her younger sisters, realizing that their elder sister Pabhāvatī was angry, teased her, saying, "Do you think King Kusa made this? King Kusa could not have made this; it was made by the potter. Take the pot."
309:
Pabhāvatī did not tell her sisters that the pottery was made by King Kusa or that he had arrived. The potter gave the Bodhisatta a thousand pieces of money and said, "My dear man, the King is pleased with you. From this day forth, you shall make vessels for the princesses, and I shall carry them to them."

## He Served as a Reed-worker

The Bodhisatta thought, "It is not possible to see Pabhāvatī while staying here." He gave that thousand pieces to the potter and went to a reed-worker who served the King. Becoming his apprentice, for the sake of Pabhāvatī, he wove a palm-leaf fan and depicted various figures on it: a white parasol, a market scene, and Pabhāvatī herself standing and holding a cloth.

The reed-worker took that palm-leaf fan made by King Kusa and other articles he had made and went to the royal palace. When King Madda saw them, he asked, "Who made these fans?" and as before, gave a thousand pieces, saying to the reed-worker, "Give these reed-worker's goods to my daughters."

That reed-worker gave the palm-leaf fan made by the Bodhisatta for Pabhāvatī to Princess Pabhāvatī alone. Other people did not see the various figures on the fan, but Pabhāvatī saw them and, knowing they were made by King Kusa, said in anger, "Let those who wish to take them, take them!" and threw it on the ground. When she threw it down, her remaining sisters mocked her as before. The reed-worker brought the thousand pieces and gave them to the Bodhisatta.

## He Served as a Garland-maker

The Bodhisatta thought, "This is not yet a place for me to stay," and gave the thousand pieces to the reed-worker. He went to the King's garland-maker, became his apprentice, and weaving various kinds of flowers, he wove a beautiful wreath for Pabhāvatī, adorned with various figures. The garland-maker took all of them and went to the royal palace.

King Madda saw them and asked, "Who wove these garlands?" "O King, I wove them," he replied. "I know the garlands you weave. Tell the truth, who wove them?" the King asked again. "O King, my apprentice wove them," he replied. "He is not your apprentice; he is your teacher. You should learn the craft from him. From this day forth, let him weave flowers for the princesses, and give him this thousand pieces." The King gave a thousand pieces and said, "Give these flowers to my daughters."

The garland-maker gave the garlands woven by the Bodhisatta for Pabhāvatī to Princess Pabhāvatī alone. Pabhāvatī saw her own image along with King Kusa's image and various other figures in the wreath. Knowing they were woven by King Kusa, she became angry and threw them on the ground. Her remaining sisters mocked their elder sister Pabhāvatī in the same way. The garland-maker brought the thousand pieces, gave them to the Bodhisatta, and told him the news.

## He Went to Serve as a Cook

The Bodhisatta thought, "This place is also not yet for me," and gave the thousand pieces to the garland-maker. He then went to the King's cook and became his apprentice again.
310:
Then one day, when the cook was bringing special food to the King, he gave the Bodhisatta some bone-meat to cook for himself. The Bodhisatta prepared the bones exactly as the cook had instructed. Then, the aroma of the curry spread throughout the whole city. King Madda smelled the aroma and asked, "Are you cooking another kind of curry in your kitchen?"

"O Great King, I am not. However, I gave my apprentice some rice and bone-meat to cook for himself. That aroma must be from that curry," he replied. King Madda had the curry brought to him and placed a little on the tip of his tongue. At that moment, it pervaded and thrilled his seven thousand taste nerves.

King Madda, bound by the craving for taste, gave a thousand pieces and said, "From this day forth, let your apprentice cook food for me and my daughters. You bring the food for me, and let your apprentice carry it for my daughters." The cook went and told the Bodhisatta.

When the Bodhisatta heard the cook's words, he thought, "Now my heart's desire has reached its fulfillment. Now I shall be able to see Pabhāvatī." He was very pleased and gave that thousand pieces to the cook. The next day, after preparing the royal meal, he sent the King's food bowls and, carrying the yoke with the Princess's food bowls himself, he ascended to the palace where Pabhāvatī resided.

## Pabhāvatī Drove Him Away

When Pabhāvatī saw the Bodhisatta ascending the palace carrying the yoke, she thought, "This King Kusa is performing slave labor that is unsuitable for him; he is doing what should not be done. If I remain silent for two or three days, he will think, 'Now this Pabhāvatī is pleased with me,' and without going anywhere else, he will stay here just to look at me. I will drive this King Kusa away right now."
311:
“Go back quickly to Kusāvatī, Kusa; I do not desire you, who are of ugly appearance, dwelling here.”

She spoke this second verse:

2. Kusa, O Great King. With a mind crooked by passion, carrying a heavy burden, you endure great suffering by day, by night, and at the midnight hour. You, Great King, return quickly to the city of Kusāvatī. I do not want you, who have come to stay here in our city. Why? Because of your ugly appearance.

3. I shall not go from here to Kusāvatī,
O Pabhāvatī, for I am enticed by your beauty.
I delight in the pleasant palace of the Madda king,
Having abandoned my kingdom, devoted to the sight of you.

4. O Pabhāvatī, enticed by your beauty,
I wander the earth in a state of confusion.
I know not the direction from which I came;
I am intoxicated by you, O deer-eyed one.

5. O you who wear garments woven with gold,
With a golden girdle,
O you of beautiful hips, because of my desire for you,
I have no need for a kingdom.

He spoke these three verses:

3. Lady Pabhāvatī, being enticed by the beauty of your loveliness, I shall not go from this city of Sāgala, where you dwell, to our great city of Kusāvatī. I delight in the golden palace of your father, King Madda. Having a heart full of affection and attachment at the sight of you, I delight here. I cannot leave this golden city of Sāgala where you dwell and go away.

4. Lady Pabhāvatī, because I am enticed by the beauty of your form, I wander upon the earth with a mind bewildered by the defilement of attachment. I do not even remember the direction from which I came. I have become intoxicated by my deep affection and attachment for you. (Alternatively) You have made me forget myself.

5. O Lady Pabhāvatī, who has eyes like the dark-green eyes of a newborn fawn, who wears garments woven with golden threads, who wears a golden girdle, and who has a slender and beautiful waist; because of my love and attachment for you, I have no desire for the glory of a kingdom.

Having thought thus, Pabhāvatī opened the door halfway, holding one leaf of the door with one hand and pressing the bolt with the other, intending to scold and lament:

2. Carrying a heavy burden with a crooked mind,
By day, by night, and at the midnight hour.

## If Not Loved, I Shall Not Return

That King Kusa was greatly pleased, thinking, “I have received a word from Pabhāvatī,” and wishing to respond to her:

## Pabhāvatī Did Not Come Out

When King Kusa spoke thus, Pabhāvatī thought: “I mocked this King Kusa thinking he would be displeased, yet he speaks only with attachment for me. Indeed, if he were to proclaim, ‘I am King Kusa,’ and seize my hand, who could prevent him? Someone might hear these words spoken to me.” Thinking thus, she closed the door, bolted it, and remained inside the chamber.

## King Kusa Fell Prostrate

King Kusa then took the yoke with the food and served the princesses. Pabhāvatī sent the hunchback servant, saying, “Go and bring the food cooked by King Kusa.” The hunchback brought it and said, “Please eat.” Pabhāvatī replied, “I will not eat the food cooked by King Kusa. You eat it yourself, take your own portion, cook food, and bring it. Do not let anyone know that King Kusa has come.”

From that day on, the hunchback servant took Pabhāvatī’s portion and ate it herself, and gave her own portion to Pabhāvatī. King Kusa, not seeing Pabhāvatī from that day, reflected again.
312:
7. Whether she is unwilling or willing, if a man obtains the one he loves,
We praise that gain; failure therein is an evil.

He uttered this subsequent verse.

7. Ayye: O Lady Pabhāvatī. Yo naro: whatever man. Akāmaṃ vā: whether unwilling. Sakāmaṃ vā: or willing. Lābhaṃ: that which is obtained. Piyaṃ: the person he loves. Labhate: obtains. Ettha: in thus obtaining the beloved. Pasaṃsāma: we shall praise. Tattha: in that beloved. Alābho: not obtaining. Pāpako: is wretched.

He thought, "Does Pabhāvatī have no love for me, or might she still have love? I will test Pabhāvatī." Having thought thus, after King Kusa had fed the princesses, he carried the rice-yoke and, as he went out, he kicked the palace floor near Pabhāvatī's chamber door, made the pots and pans roll about, and groaning, he fell prostrate as if he had fainted.

## Pabhāvatī Is Spat Upon

When Pabhāvatī heard King Kusa's groaning, she opened the door and saw him pinned down by the yoke. She thought, "This King Kusa is the supreme king in all the land of Jambudīpa. Because of me, he suffers greatly day and night. Because of his delicacy, he lies pinned by the rice-yoke. Is he still alive, or is he not?" Pabhāvatī came out of the chamber and, to test his breath, she stretched out her neck and looked at his face. King Kusa, having filled his mouth with saliva, spat it out. It fell upon Pabhāvatī's body.

Pabhāvatī reviled King Kusa, entered the chamber, and while standing there having closed one leaf of the door, she wished to lament and cry out:

6. It is a misfortune for him who desires one who does not desire him.
O King, you love one who does not love you; you wish to cherish the uncherished.

She uttered this verse.

6. Rāja: King Kusa. Yo koci: whoever. Anicchantaṃ: one who is not desired. Icchati: desires. Akāmaṃ: one who is not liked. Kāmesi: you love. Akantaṃ: one who is not pleasing. Kantuṃ: to be pleased. Icchasi: you wish. Tassa: for that person. So: that desiring, loving, and wishing. Abbhūti: is without benefit (misfortune). Hoti: it is.

## To Obtain Is the Main Thing, Liked or Not

Because King Kusa had a mind full of attachment, even though he was thus reviled and scolded, he did not become displeased, but wishing to speak back to Pabhāvatī:
313:
8. "O King Kusa! Just as one who digs into the heart of a stone with Kanikāra wood, or one who tries to bind the wind with a net, so do you desire me, who does not desire you."

8. O King Kusa! Just as one digs into a solid stone with Kanikāra wood, or just as one traps the wind with a net, in the same way, you desire me, who does not desire you.

9. "Surely a stone has been placed in your heart, O you of soft feminine marks, for I, who have come from a distant land, find no pleasure in you."

10. "Whenever the princess looks at me with a frown, I then become like a cook's servant in the inner palace of King Madda."

11. "Whenever the princess looks at me with a smile, I am no longer a cook's servant; then I am King Kusa."

9. O Pabhāvatī, endowed with very soft feminine marks, has a stone slab surely been placed in your heart? I, who have come from another province, find no happiness in your presence.

10. O Pabhāvatī, endowed with very soft feminine marks, whenever the princess Pabhāvatī looks at me with a frown, at that time, I become like a servant of the cook in the inner palace of King Madda.

11. O Pabhāvatī, endowed with very soft feminine marks, whenever the princess Pabhāvatī looks at me with a smile, at that time, I do not become like a servant of the cook. At that time, when you look with a smile, I become like King Kusa.

## The Dialogue Begins

Even though King Kusa spoke such unpleasant words, Pabhāvatī did not retreat; wishing to drive him away, she spoke even harsher words.

Hearing those words, King Kusa wished to reply.

When Pabhāvatī heard King Kusa's words, she thought, "This King Kusa is excessively attached. I will use a lie as a stratagem to drive him away from our capital." Wishing to drive him away, she spoke.

Hearing her words, King Kusa, wishing to refute her again, said: "Lady Pabhāvatī, when I consulted the diviners in our city of Kusāvatī, those diviners predicted that apart from King Kusa, who has a voice like a lion's roar, there shall be no other husband for you."
314:
12. "If the words of the diviners be true, you shall never be my husband; let them cut my body into seven pieces at will."

12. O King Kusa, if the words of the diviners who know the omens are true, then indeed, even if they were to cut my body into seven pieces, you would never be my husband. Thus they have predicted.

13. "Whether the words of others or my own be true, there is no other husband for you than Kusa, who has a voice like a lion's roar."

13. O Lady Pabhāvatī, if the words of other diviners or my own words are true, then indeed, there is no husband for you other than King Kusa, who has a voice like a lion's roar.

"I have also predicted the omens in this way through the power of my own wisdom," he said, wishing to report that matter.

When Pabhāvatī heard King Kusa's words, she thought, "I cannot make this king feel ashamed, nor can I make him flee. Whether he wishes to flee or stay, what is this King Kusa to me?" She then shut the door and did not show herself.

King Kusa also took up his carrying pole and went down. From that day on, he did not see Pabhāvatī. Performing the duties of a cook, he became very exhausted. After eating his morning meal, he had to split wood. He had to wash the pots and pans. He had to carry water with a carrying pole. When he slept, he slept on a wooden bench used for placing rice. Rising early in the morning, he had to cook gruel and other foods. He had to carry and serve them. He had to feed others. Depending on the passion of lustful attachment for the woman, he underwent extreme suffering.
315:
14. I will have a golden necklace made for you, O hunchback, upon reaching Kusāvatī, if Pabhāvatī, who has thighs like an elephant's trunk, would but look at me.
18. I will have a golden necklace made for you, O hunchback, upon reaching Kusāvatī, if Pabhāvatī, who has thighs like an elephant's trunk, would but touch me with her hands.
He spoke these five verses.
14. O hunchback mother; you who have the mark of thighs like an elephant's trunk; Pabhāvatī; at me; if she would but look. To Kusāvatī; having arrived; for you; a necklace made of pure gold; I will have made.
15. O hunchback nurse; you who have thighs like an elephant's trunk; the princess named Pabhāvatī; at me; if she would but speak. To our city of Kusāvatī; having arrived; for you; a necklace made of pure gold; I will have made.
16. O hunchback mother; you who have thighs like an elephant's trunk; the princess named Pabhāvatī; at me; if she would but smile gently. To the great royal capital named Kusāvatī; having arrived; for you, mother; a necklace made of pure gold; I will have made.
17. The nurse called by the name Khujjā; you who have the mark of thighs like an elephant's trunk, beautiful and tapering; the princess named Pabhāvatī; at me; if she would but laugh heartily. To the great royal capital named Kusāvatī; having arrived; for you; a necklace made of pure gold; I will have made.
18. O hunchback nurse; you who have beautiful thighs like an elephant's trunk, tapering and lovely; the princess Pabhāvatī; me; with her hands; if she would but touch. To our city of Kusāvatī; having arrived; for you; a necklace made of pure gold; I will have made.

## Speaking to the Hunchback
One day, King Kusa saw the hunchback nurse passing by the kitchen door and called her. Because she was afraid of Pabhāvatī, the hunchback nurse did not dare to go to King Kusa and walked as if in a hurry. Then, he quickly approached the hunchback and called out, "Khujjā!" The hunchback stopped, turned around, and said, "Who is it? I did not hear the Great King's voice."
Then he said to the hunchback, "Khujjā, both you and your mistress Pabhāvatī are very hard-hearted. Though I have stayed near you for so long, I have not even received a word asking if I am free from illness, let alone receiving any gift. Let this matter of yours be; indeed, would you be able to make Pabhāvatī tender towards me?"
Then the hunchback nurse agreed, saying, "Very well." Afterwards, he said to the hunchback, "If you are able to show her to me, if you can do this, I will make your hunchback condition straight and give you a golden necklace," and thus he spoke to entice the hunchback nurse.
316:
16. Surely this princess finds no pleasure in Kusa, who serves as a cook and a servant, desiring no wages.
He spoke this verse.
16. O Princess; you, royal daughter; in Kusāvatī; even a slight bit of happiness; do you not find? This King; in the role of a cook; without desiring wages; being a hired man; you, royal daughter; he nourishes.
20. Surely this hunchback deserves to have her tongue cut with a well-sharpened knife for speaking such ill words.
He spoke this verse.
20. Thus, in various ways starting with 'Surely this princess...', ill-spoken words; she who speaks; this hunchback; there is. Of this hunchback; the tongue; with a well-sharpened; knife; the cutting; will she not surely receive? She will certainly receive it.
... etc ...

## The Hunchback's Effort
Upon hearing King Kusa's words, the hunchback nurse said, "O Great King, please go. After two or three days, I will make Princess Pabhāvatī follow your will. Please watch my effort." Having completed what needed to be done, she went to Pabhāvatī. As if cleaning Pabhāvatī's chamber, she removed even the worm castings, leaving nothing behind, and even took out the foot-mats. She swept the entire chamber, set the door-sill apart, and prepared a high seat. She then spread a low stool for Pabhāvatī and said, "Come, dear daughter, I will look for lice on your head." She made Pabhāvatī sit on the low stool, placed Pabhāvatī's head on her own lap, and after scratching it a little, said, "There are so many lice on this princess's head!" She then took lice from her own head, placed them in Pabhāvatī's hand, and said, "Dear daughter, look at the lice that are the impurities from your head." Speaking such pleasant words, she intended to speak of King Kusa's virtues.

## Rebuking the Hunchback
Pabhāvatī became angry with the hunchback nurse. When she became angry, the hunchback nurse grabbed Pabhāvatī by the neck, threw her into the chamber, and staying outside, closed the door and stood hanging onto the door-rope. Pabhāvatī, being unable to catch the hunchback, stood at the door and, wishing to revile her, said:
317:
21. Mā naṃ rūpena pāmesi, ārohena pabhāvatī.
Mahāyaso ti katvāna, karassu rucire piyaṃ.

## The Hunchback's Roar
When Pabhāvatī reviled him in such a manner, the nurse Khujjā stood pulling the door-rope and said, "O foolish and stubborn girl! What will your beauty do for you? Can we even eat your beauty?" Thus, she proclaimed the virtues of King Kusa with thirteen verses, in what is known as "The Hunchback's Roar."
...

Kusarājā ti katvāna, karassu rucire piyaṃ.
She spoke these thirteen verses:

21. O Pabhāvatī, do not despise him for his appearance or his stature. Considering in your heart that he is a king of great fame and power, show love to the beloved King Kusa when you see him.
