## Pabhāvatī Entreats
Hearing these words, Pabhāvatī threatened Khujjā, saying, "Khujjā, you roar too much! When you fall into my hands, I shall make you know who is mistress." Khujjā replied, "As long as I have been looking after you, I have not informed your father of King Kusa's arrival. But now, I shall tell the Great King today!" and she frightened her with a loud voice. Then Pabhāvatī, fearing someone might hear, entreated Khujjā.

## The Seven Kings Come to Ask
King Kusa, unable to see Pabhāvatī and exhausted by seven months of poor food and poor bedding, thought to himself: "What benefit is there for me with this Pabhāvatī? Though I have stayed here for seven months, I have not been able to see her."
318:
“She is exceedingly harsh and oppressive. I shall return to our great city of Kusāvatī and see my mother and father,” he thought thus.

At that moment, Sakka, King of Devas, reflecting, knew the weariness of King Kusa. He thought, “For seven months, King Kusa has not even had a glimpse of Pabhāvatī. I shall create a means for him to obtain her.” Disguising himself as a messenger of King Madda, he sent word to the kings of seven kingdoms: “Pabhāvatī has abandoned King Kusa and returned. Come and take Pabhāvatī.” He sent this message to each king individually.

Those seven kings arrived at the city of Sāgala with great retinues, and upon reaching the city, they were unaware of each other's reasons for coming. Those seven kings asked one another, “Why have you come?” and upon learning the reason, they became angry. “He intends to give one daughter to seven kings! Look at this improper conduct of King Madda; he is insulting us. Let us seize him.” All the kings sent a message: “Will you give us Princess Pabhāvatī, or shall we wage war?” and they surrounded the city.

## Now She Must Be Given

King Madda, hearing this news, was greatly terrified. He summoned his ministers and asked, “What shall we do?” The ministers replied, “Great King, the seven kings have come because of Pabhāvatī. If you do not give her, they will destroy the city walls, enter, kill us all, and take the kingdom. Let us send Pabhāvatī to those kings before they destroy the city.” They wished to report this matter.
319:
34. "These elephants are stubborn; all stand armored. Before they crush the wall, bring forth this Pabhāvatī."

34. "O Great King! These elephants of the seven kings are very fierce. All the seven kings, wearing their armor, stand close to the city. Before they destroy the city wall, let them bring forth this Pabhāvatī."

35. "Having made seven pieces, I shall give this Pabhāvatī to the kshatriyas who have come here to kill me."

35. "O ministers! These seven kings have come here to the Kingdom of Madda to kill me. To those kshatriyas, I will give this Pabhāvatī after dividing her into seven portions."

## Divide into Seven Pieces
Hearing the words of the ministers, King Madda thought: "O ministers, if I send Pabhāvatī to only one king, the remaining kings will wage war. It is not possible to give her to only one. She left King Kusa, the supreme king in all of Jambudīpa, merely because he was 'ugly.' Let her reap the fruit of her coming. I will kill Pabhāvatī, cut her into seven pieces, and send them to the seven kings." Desiring to command this, he spoke:

## Lamenting to the Mother
The words spoken by King Madda became known throughout the entire palace. The attendants went and informed Pabhāvatī: "The King, your father, will divide you into seven pieces and send them to the seven kings." Pabhāvatī, terrified of the fear of death, rose from her seat and, surrounded by her sisters, went to her mother's royal chamber.

To clarify this matter, the All-Enlightened Buddha said:

Pabhāvatī, having gone to her mother and paid homage, wished to lament and wail:

37. "That face, which used to be adorned with..."
320:
36. The Buddha spoke this verse:
36. "The princess arose, she of golden hue, dressed in silk, her eyes filled with tears, surrounded by a group of handmaidens."
(Monks, the princess Pabhāvatī, who possessed a complexion like gold and wore silk garments interwoven with golden threads, arose weeping, her eyes filled with tears, while being surrounded by her retinue of maids.)
...
She spoke these eight verses beginning with "Remember me, O Mother, Pabhāvatī was of such a color."
37. "O Mother, that face of mine, which was gazed upon in a mirror set in a handle of ivory, beautiful, with lovely eyes, stainless and free from blemish, and constantly anointed with the five kinds of powders—surely it will lie abandoned in the forest by the seven kings." Thus she lamented.
38. "O Mother, those soft, dark tresses of mine with curled ends, anointed with the essence of sandalwood and well-ordered—surely in the midst of the cemetery, vultures will drag them about with their feet."
39. "O Mother, those soft arms of mine with copper-colored nails, scented with the essence of sandalwood—when they are cut off and cast away in the forest by the seven kings, surely a crow will seize them and fly wherever it pleases, pecking and devouring them."
40. "O Mother, those breasts of mine, like golden palmyra fruits, hanging low and constantly perfumed with fine Kāsī sandalwood—surely an old jackal in the cemetery will cling to them and suck, just as a young son sucks at his mother's breast."
41. "O Mother, those broad hips of mine, well-formed by being smoothed with a cow's bone and always adorned with golden girdles—when I am abandoned naked in the forest by the seven kings, surely packs of jackals will drag them about."
42. "O Mother, the dogs, the crows, the jackals, and whatever other fanged beasts there are—surely they will become ageless by devouring the flesh of Pabhāvatī."
321:
43. "O Mother, if those kings who have come from afar should carry away my flesh, then please beg for my bones and cremate them near the main road."
44. "O Mother, having made flower beds at the place where I am cremated, please plant Kaṇikāra trees there. When those trees bloom at the end of the winter season, O Mother, when the Kaṇikāra trees are in flower, please remember me, saying, 'My daughter Pabhāvatī was of such a color as these blossoms.'"

[Commentary Section]
In that context, 'kakkūpanisevitaṃ' means anointed with these five powders: mustard powder, salt powder, clay powder, sesame powder, and turmeric powder. 'Ādāsadantātharupaccavekkhitaṃ' means gazed upon in a mirror with an ivory handle, having been adorned while looking therein. 'Subhaṃ' means a beautiful face. 'Virajaṃ' means free from dust, stainless. 'Anaṅgaṇaṃ' means free from defects such as boils or moles. 'Chuddaṃ' means, "O Mother, such a face of mine will surely now be cast away by the kings and lie in the forest, the wilderness," thus she laments. 'Asite' means black. 'Vellitagge' means with curled ends. 'Sīvathikāya' means in the cemetery. 'Parikaḍḍhissanti' means, "Vultures that eat human flesh will surely strike with their feet and drag about such hair of mine." 'Gayha dhaṅko gacchati yenakāmaṃ' means, "O Mother, surely a crow, having seized such an arm of mine, pecking and eating it, will go wherever it pleases."
'Tālūpanibhe' means like golden palmyra fruits. 'Kāsikacandanena' means anointed with fine sandalwood. 'Thanesu me' means, "O Mother, seeing such breasts of mine fallen in the cemetery, a jackal will surely bite them with its mouth and cling to them as if it were a mother's young son." 'Soṇiṃ' means the hips. 'Sukoṭṭitaṃ' means well-enlarged/smoothed by being struck with a cow's jawbone. 'Avatthaṃ' means abandoned [naked]. 'Bhakkhayitvā' means, "O Mother, all these [beasts] will surely become ageless by eating my flesh."
'Sace maṃsāni hariṃsu' means, "O Mother, if those kings, their hearts bound to me, should carry away my flesh, then you should beg for the bones and cremate them near the path," meaning she says to cremate them between the footpaths and the main roads. 'Khettāni' means, "O Mother, having prepared flower beds and the like at the place where I am cremated, plant Kaṇikāra trees in those beds." 'Himaccaye' means at the end of the falling of snow, in the month of Phagguṇa. 'Sareyyātha' means, "Having filled a golden casket with those flowers and placed it on your lap, remember me, saying, 'My daughter Pabhāvatī was of such a color.'"

## Even the Mother Must Weep
While Pabhāvatī was thus lamenting before her mother, terrified by the fear of death, King Madda gave the order: "Let the executioner come, bringing an axe and a meat cleaver!"
322:
Thus, terrified by the fear of death, she lamented in the presence of her mother. King Madda also gave the order, "Let the executioner come here, taking the axe and the block." The news of his coming became known throughout the entire palace. Then, hearing of his arrival, Pabhāvatī's mother, overcome with grief, rose from her seat and went to the King. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:

45. Her mother stood up, the princess of divine beauty, seeing the axe and the block in King Madda's inner palace.

45. Bhikkhus, the mother of Pabhāvatī, who was of royal birth and possessed a complexion like that of a goddess, seeing the axe and the meat-cleaver in the inner palace of King Madda, rose from her seat.

Hearing that the executioner had arrived, Pabhāvatī's mother rose from her seat and, oppressed by sorrow, came to the King.

The All-Enlightened Buddha, wishing to make this matter clear, said:

The Queen Mother, having gone to the King, wished to ask about the matter while lamenting:

46. With this axe, will you indeed kill your daughter of fine features and slender waist, O Madda, and show her to the princes?

46. O King Madda, will you indeed kill your daughter Pabhāvatī, who has fine features and a slender waist, with this axe, and give her to the kings of the seven kingdoms?

When the Queen Mother asked thus, King Madda, wishing to make her understand, said: "O Queen, what are you saying? Your daughter rejected the supreme king of the entire Jambudīpa, saying he was 'ugly'. Before her footprints on the path she took have even vanished, she has brought death upon her own forehead. Now, let her receive such a result because of her own beauty."

## It Would Be Good if King Kusa Were Here

Upon hearing King Madda's words, the Queen Mother went to her daughter Pabhāvatī and, wishing to speak with her while lamenting, said these six verses:

47. You did not follow my words, O daughter, though I desired your welfare. Today, covered in blood, you go to the realm of Yama.
...
In the family of the Kusa princes, O auspicious one, what could be more pleasant than that?

47. O dear daughter Pabhāvatī, you did not follow my words, though I pleaded with you, desiring your welfare. Today, you, my daughter Pabhāvatī, covered in blood, must go to the abode of King Yama.

48. Thus a person meets with misfortune and falls into evil, who does not follow the words of those who are beneficial and see what is good.

48. O dear daughter Pabhāvatī, if a being does not follow the words of those who desire their welfare and who see long-term benefits, that being meets with misfortune in this manner. And meeting with it, they fall only into a state of misery.

49. O dear daughter Pabhāvatī, if you had not followed the whims of your mind, and were today holding a prince born of the royal Kusa, who is of beautiful appearance, adorned with a waist-belt of gold and jewels, and honored by the assembly of kinsmen, you would not be going to the destruction of Yama today.
323:
50. Where the drum sounds and the elephant trumpets, in the family of the Kusa princes, O auspicious one, what greater happiness than that did you see that you came running here?

51. O dear daughter Pabhāvatī, in the family of the Kusa princes, the auspicious horse surrounded by more than a thousand horses is joyful. At the palace gate, the young musician plays and sings. What greater happiness than that did you see that you came running here?

52. O dear daughter Pabhāvatī, in the family of the Kusa princes, it is a place where peacocks and cranes cry out in joy, and where cuckoos constantly warble. What greater happiness than that did you see that you fled and came here?

Thus, the Queen Mother, having spoken with her daughter Pabhāvatī with these many verses, thought: "If King Kusa were here in our country now, he would put these seven kings to flight, release my daughter Pabhāvatī from suffering, and take her away." Wishing to lament and yearn for him, she said:

53. Where indeed is Kusa, the crusher of enemies, the subduer of foreign lands, possessed of great wisdom, who might release us from suffering?

53. Where is that King Kusa, who can suppress enemies and subdue foreign lands, and who possesses great wisdom? How might he release us from this suffering?

## King Kusa Is Here

After that, Pabhāvatī thought: "My mother's mouth cannot contain enough praise for King Kusa's virtues. I shall inform my mother that King Kusa is right here in our city, living and performing the duties of a cook." Wishing to inform her, she said:
324:
54. Right here is he, the crusher of enemies, the subduer of foreign realms. Kusa of great wisdom, who will slay all your [enemies].

54. Mother, he who is the crusher of enemies, the subduer of foreign realms, and who possesses great wisdom—that King Kusa is right here in our city. That King Kusa will slay all those enemy kings.

55. Are you mad that you speak thus? You speak like a blind fool. If Kusa had come, how would we not know it?

55. Dear daughter, are you speaking with a distracted mind? Are you speaking these words because you are extremely foolish and deluded? If King Kusa had come, if such a thing had happened, why would we not know of that King Kusa?

56. That man, the cook, between the maidens' quarters, having firmly tucked up his loincloth, is washing a pot, stooping down.

56. Mother, having firmly tucked up his loincloth and with his head bowed down, he is washing a pot. That cook is indeed King Kusa. Mother, look between the windows of the maidens' quarters where your daughters reside.

57. Are you a basket-maker's daughter, a Caṇḍāla woman, or a destroyer of your clan's reputation? Born in the Madda lineage, how could you take a servant as a lover?

57. Dear daughter, have you become a basket-maker's daughter? Have you become a Caṇḍāla woman? Or else, have you become a woman who destroys her own clan? For what reason, though born in the royal Madda lineage, do you take your own husband as a servant?

## Are you mad?
When she heard this, the Queen Mother, Pabhāvatī's mother, thought, "This Pabhāvatī is merely lamenting out of fear of death," and wishing to question Pabhāvatī, she spoke.

## Look there, Mother
When the Queen Mother questioned her thus, Pabhāvatī thought, "My mother does not believe the words I say. She does not know that King Kusa has come to our city and has lived here for seven months. I will show him to my mother." Taking her mother by the hand, she opened the lion-casement window and, stretching out her hand, she wished to show him.

## How foolish you are
At that time, King Kusa thought, "Today my heart's desire will reach its fulfillment. Without fail, Pabhāvatī, being terrified by the fear of death, will speak of my arrival. I will wash the pots and put them away." Having fetched water, he began to wash the pots.
When the Queen Mother saw this, she wished to revile and lament to her daughter Pabhāvatī.
325:
## Do you think he is a servant?
Then Pabhāvatī thought, "My mother surely does not know that King Kusa has come to live here as a cook because of me," and wishing to inform her mother, she spoke this verse:

58. I am no basket-maker's daughter, nor a Caṇḍāla, nor a destroyer of my clan. He is the son of Okkāka, O lady; do you really think he is a servant?

58. Mother, I am not a basket-maker's daughter. I am not a Caṇḍāla woman. I am not a woman who destroys her clan. Dear mother, do you really think that King Kusa, the son of King Okkāka, is a servant?

Now, Pabhāvatī, wishing to praise the glory and virtues of King Kusa, spoke these five verses:

59. He who always feeds twenty thousand Brahmins... (etc.) ...He is the son of Okkāka, O lady; do you really think he is a servant?

59. Mother, that King who is the son of King Okkāka always feeds twenty thousand Brahmins. Dear mother, do you think that King Kusa, the son of King Okkāka, is a servant?

60. Mother, for that King Kusa, the son of King Okkāka, twenty thousand elephants are always harnessed. Dear mother, do you think that King Kusa, the son of King Okkāka, is a servant?

61. Mother, for that noble King Kusa, the son of King Okkāka, twenty thousand horses are always harnessed. Dear mother, do you think that noble King Kusa, the son of King Okkāka, is a servant?

62. Mother, for that noble King Kusa, the son of King Okkāka, twenty thousand chariots are always harnessed. Dear mother, do you think that noble King Kusa, the son of King Okkāka, is a servant?

63. Mother, for that noble King Kusa, the son of King Okkāka, twenty thousand milch-cows are always milked. Dear mother, do you think that noble King Kusa, the son of King Okkāka, is a servant?

## The Mother reports to the King
When Pabhāvatī thus praised the wealth and retinue of the Bodhisatta King Kusa with these five verses, Pabhāvatī's mother thought, "This Pabhāvatī speaks without any hesitation. Surely, the person in the kitchen is indeed King Kusa as Pabhāvatī says." Believing her, she went to King Madda and reported the matter.
326:
64. "Truly, you have done wrong, you foolish girl, in that you did not tell me that the mighty Khattiya, who is like a noble elephant (nāga) but appeared in the form of a frog, had come here."

64. You foolish girl! It is indeed a great wrong you have committed regarding this King Kusa, a Khattiya of great power. To treat him as if he were of the appearance of a frog is a grave error. Furthermore, your failure to inform me that he had arrived here in our kingdom is also a great impropriety.

65. "O Great King, bull among charioteers, please forgive our offense. Since you came here in an unknown disguise, we did not recognize you."

65. O Great King Kusa, may you forgive our offense. O King, most noble among all those who ride chariots, because you arrived here in the city of Sāgala in an unrecognizable form, we did not know of your arrival.

66. "It was not fitting for one like me to become a cook. May you alone be pleased with me; there is no fault in you, O Deva."

66. O King, it was not fitting for someone like me to serve as a cook. May you, O King, be well-pleased with me. There is no fault or wrong committed by you, O Deva.

67. "Go, foolish girl, and ask for the forgiveness of King Kusa of great power. Once King Kusa has been asked for forgiveness, he will grant you your life."

67. You foolish girl, go! Ask for the forgiveness of King Kusa, who possesses great power. If you ask for his forgiveness, King Kusa will grant you your life.

## Rebuking the Daughter
King Madda went quickly to Princess Pabhāvatī and asked, "Dear daughter, is it true that King Kusa has come to our country?" She replied, "Great Father, it is true. It has been seven months today that King Kusa has been serving as a cook for your daughters." King Madda, not believing his daughter's words, questioned the hunchback nurse. Having heard the truth, he wished to rebuke Princess Pabhāvatī and spoke the verse.

## Paying Homage to King Kusa
After King Madda had rebuked his daughter Pabhāvatī, he went quickly to King Kusa. Having performed the proper courtesies and with hands joined in reverence, he spoke the verse to acknowledge his own fault.

## King Kusa's Forgiveness
Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta thought, "If I speak harsh words, King Madda's heart will break right here. I shall comfort him." Standing among the pots and vessels, he spoke the verse to inform the King.

## Ordering the Daughter to Ask Forgiveness
Having received a friendly response from King Kusa, the King ascended the palace, called Princess Pabhāvatī, and wishing to send her to ask for forgiveness, he spoke the verse.

## Pabhāvatī Asks Forgiveness
When Pabhāvatī heard her father King Madda's command, she went to King Kusa surrounded by her sisters and her retinue of attendants.

King Kusa, still standing in the guise of a laborer, knew she was coming and thought, "Today I shall break Pabhāvatī's pride and make her lie in the mud at my feet." He poured out all the water he had carried and trampled the ground about the size of a threshing floor, turning it into a single patch of mud. Pabhāvatī went to King Kusa, fell at his feet, and lying in the mud, she asked for his forgiveness.
327:
68. Hearing her father's words, Pabhāvatī, who possessed a complexion like that of a goddess, bowed her head at the feet of the mighty King Kusa.

68. Monks, Pabhāvatī, the princess of divine beauty, having heard the words of her father, King Madda, fell at the feet of the powerful King Kusa and paid homage with her head.

69. "O Lord, those nights that have passed without you—I revere your feet with my head; do not be angry with me, O best of charioteers.
70. I confess everything to you, Great King; listen to me. Never again shall I do anything displeasing to you.
71. If you do not grant my request as I thus entreat you, my father will now kill me and give me to the [seven] princes."

69. "O Lord, those nights that have passed while I was separated from you have now reached seven months. O best of charioteers, I revere your feet with my head; do not be angry with me.
70. Great King, I have done what is displeasing to you. I confess all my faults. Great King, please listen to my words. I shall never again dare to do anything displeasing to you.
71. If you do not grant the request of one who entreats you thus, because of your refusal, my father will now kill me and hand me over to the kings of the seven kingdoms."

72. "As you thus entreat me, why should I not grant your request? I am no longer angry with you, O beautiful one; do not be afraid, Pabhāvatī.
73. I forgive all your faults, O Princess; listen to me. Never again shall I do anything displeasing to you.
74. Out of love for you, O fair-hipped one, I have endured much suffering. Though I was capable of slaying the entire Madda clan to take you, Pabhāvatī."

72. "O beautiful Pabhāvatī, endowed with the five beauties, do not be afraid. I am not angry with you. Since you entreat me so, why should I not follow your words? I will certainly follow them.
73. Princess Pabhāvatī, I forgive all your faults. Listen to my words. I shall not do anything displeasing to you again.
74. O Pabhāvatī of the slender and beautiful waist, though I was capable of slaying the entire Madda royal line to take you, it was only because of my desire for you that I endured so much suffering."

To clarify this matter, the All-Knowing Buddha said:
Desiring to pay homage by bowing her head at his feet—

## King Kusa is Satisfied
Hearing Pabhāvatī's words of apology and entreaty, King Kusa thought, "If I say to this Pabhāvatī, 'You shall know for yourself,' her heart will break. I will comfort her." Thus, wishing to accept her plea, he spoke.

## Roaring and Ordering the Army to Prepare
Then, King Kusa, seeing his own retinue which was like the retinue of Sakka, the king of gods, felt his royal pride swell. Like a lion, he paced majestically in the palace courtyard, thinking, "While I am still alive, shall other kings take away my wife?" Wishing to let all the city dwellers know of his arrival, he shouted, roared, and struck his arms in challenge, saying, "Now I shall capture those seven kings alive! Harness the chariots and horses for me!"

Having roared thus, he said, "The task of capturing the enemy kings is my responsibility. Go now, bathe, adorn yourself, and ascend to the palace first." With these words, he dismissed Pabhāvatī.

## Dressing in Battle Array
King Madda also sent his ministers to attend to King Kusa. Those ministers set up a curtained enclosure right at the kitchen gate and had the barbers attend to him. King Kusa, with his beard trimmed and having bathed his head, adorned himself with all kinds of ornaments. Surrounded by the host of ministers, he looked toward the cardinal directions, intending to ascend the palace, and struck his arms in challenge.
328:
75. "Let them harness the horses to the chariots, well-trained and of various colors. Then you shall see my speed as I scatter the enemies."

75. "O friends, harness the horses, which are valiant, steady, and adorned with various ornaments, to the chariots. After that, you shall see my might as I suppress the enemy kings."

76. "They gazed upon him there in King Madda's palace, as he paced like a lion, striking his arms [in challenge]."

76. Monks, they gazed upon King Kusa in that palace of King Madda, as he paced majestically like a lion, shouting and striking his arms in challenge.

Every place he looked upon trembled. King Kusa said, "Now, behold my prowess!"

To clarify this matter, the All-Knowing Buddha spoke the following verse:

## The Lion's Roar
Then, King Madda sent a noble elephant, adorned and shaded by a white umbrella, to King Kusa. King Kusa mounted the back of the elephant, which was well-shaded by the white umbrella, and said, "Bring Pabhāvatī here." He had Pabhāvatī sit behind him and, surrounded by the fourfold army, he went out through the eastern gate. Looking at the enemy forces, he roared three times with a voice like a lion's roar, "I am King Kusa! Let those who desire life lie prostrate on their breasts!" Thus he began the suppression of the enemies.

To clarify this matter, the All-Knowing Buddha spoke these seven verses:

77. "Having mounted the elephant's back and taken Pabhāvatī up..." (and so forth).
329:
Having exited through the eastern gate and observed the enemy army, he roared a lion's roar three times, saying, "I am King Kusa! Let those who desire life lie on their chests!" and crushed the enemy. To clarify this, the Teacher said:

77. "Having mounted the back of an elephant and placed Pabhāvatī upon it, Kusa entered the battle and roared a lion's roar.

78. "Hearing him roar, just as other animals flee from a lion, the kings fled, oppressed by the fear of Kusa's voice.

79. "Elephant riders, cavalry, charioteers, and infantry cut each other down, oppressed by the fear of Kusa's voice."

## The Verocana Jewel

80. "In that vanguard of the battle, Sakka, the Lord of Devas, seeing [the Bodhisatta's prowess] with a delighted heart, gave the Verocana jewel to King Kusa.

81. "Having conquered that battle and obtained the Verocana jewel, the King, mounted on the back of an elephant, entered the city."

## Capturing the Seven Kings

82. "Having captured the seven kings alive and bound them, he presented them to his father-in-law, saying, 'O King, these are your enemies.

## Handing over to the King

83. 'O Great King, all your enemies have been crushed, having been brought under your power. Do with them as you wish; either release them or kill them.'"

## Returning them to King Kusa

Thereafter, King Madda, wishing to entrust all of them back to King Kusa—

## Marriage with the Seven Sisters

When King Madda spoke thus, the Bodhisatta King Kusa thought, "What is the use of killing these seven kings? Let their coming not be in vain. There are seven princesses who are Pabhāvatī's younger sisters; I shall have them given to these seven kings." Wishing to have them given, he said:
330:
The King said:

84. "These enemies are yours alone; they are not my enemies. You alone are our master, O Great King; either release them or kill them."

In that verse, 'you alone are ours' means, "O Great King, you alone are our lord."

When this was said, the Great Being thought, "What is the use of these men being killed? Let their coming not be in vain. There are seven daughters of King Madda, younger sisters of Pabhāvatī; I will give them to these kings." He then spoke this verse:

85. "These seven daughters of yours, O Great King, are beautiful like celestial nymphs. Give one to each [of these kings]; let them be your sons-in-law."

Then the King said to him:

86. "You are the master of us all, both of ourselves and of them. You alone are our master, O Great King; give them [the daughters] if you so desire."

In that verse, 'you are the master of us all' means, "O Great King Kusa, what are you saying? You alone are the master of these seven kings, of myself, and of these daughters—of all of us." 'If you so desire' means, "If you wish, or to whomever you wish to give, give it to them."

When this was said, he had all of them adorned and gave one to each king. To clarify this, the Teacher spoke five verses:

87. "Then Kusa, who has a voice like a lion's roar, gave the daughters of King Madda to those kings, one to each.

91. "Monks, the mother, Queen Sīlavatī, was reunited with her son, the great king. At that time, the royal couple, husband and wife, were also in harmony. They lived prosperously upon the earth, radiant with garments and ornaments."

Identification of the Birth: The All-Knowing Buddha, having delivered this Dhamma teaching of the Kusa Jātaka and revealed the Truths, identified the Birth. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who had become dissatisfied and wished to leave the Order was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

How was the Birth identified? "The mother and father of that time, who were of the noble Sākyan royal family, have now become the mother and father. Anuruddha of today was then Sakka, the king of devas. Ānanda of today was then the younger brother, Prince Jayampati. Khujjuttarā of today was then the nurse Khujjā. The mother of Rāhula today was then Pabhāvatī. The Buddha's assembly today was then the assembly of that time. And I myself was then King Kusa." Thus he identified the Birth.

## Succeed through great effort, analytical wisdom, and perseverance

The Kusa Jātaka is finished.

## 2. Soṇananda Jātaka

## One should support parents without regard for life or wealth

The Present Story: While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Soṇananda Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Devatā nu si gandhabbo," concerning a monk who supported his parents. The present story is identical to the present story in the Suvaṇṇasāma Jātaka.
332:
At that time, the All-Knowing Buddha said, "Monks, do not disparage this monk. In the past, wise men, even when they obtained kingship over the entire Rose-apple Island (Jambudīpa), did not value that kingship but instead supported their parents." Then he recounted the past.

The Story of the Past: Monks, in the past, the city of Bārāṇasī was named Brahmavaḍḍhana. In that city of Brahmavaḍḍhana, a king named Manojava reigned. In that same city, there was a Brahmin of a great family, possessing eighty crores of wealth, who was childless. Then the Brahmin said to his wife, "My dear, I urge you, please pray for a son." The Brahmin woman then prayed for a son. At that time, the Bodhisatta, passing away from the Brahma realm, took rebirth in her womb. When he was born, they named him Soṇakumāra. When Soṇakumāra was able to walk, another being also passed away from the Brahma realm and took rebirth in that same womb. When he was born, they named him Nandakumāra.

## They became ascetics

Having mastered the Vedas and all the arts, and having reached the prime of youth, the old Brahmin, seeing the perfection of his two sons' appearance, called his wife and said, "O Brahmin woman, let us bind our son Soṇakumāra with the bond of marriage." The Brahmin woman agreed, saying "Very well," and informed her son of the matter. Soṇakumāra said, "Mother, I have no desire for household life. I will support you and father as long as you live, and after your passing, I will enter the Himalayas and become an ascetic." The Brahmin woman informed the father of this.

Though the parents spoke to him repeatedly, they could not win Soṇakumāra's heart. They then called the younger brother, Nanda, and said, "Dear Nanda, you should manage this household wealth." When they said this, he replied, "Mother and father, I do not wish to carry on my head the saliva spat out by my elder brother. After your passing, I will become an ascetic along with my brother." When he said this, the parents thought, "These children renounce sensual pleasures even at such a young age. What can be said of us? All four of us shall become ascetics." They then said, "Dears, what is the use of you becoming ascetics only after our death? Let us all become ascetics right now." After informing the king, they gave away all their wealth in charity, freed their assembly of slaves, and gave what was appropriate to their relatives. The family of four then left the city of Brahmavaḍḍhana. Reaching the Himalayan region, they built a hermitage in a delightful forest grove near a lake covered with five kinds of lotuses. Having become ascetics, they lived in that hermitage. The two brothers served their parents.

Early in the morning, they provided their parents with tooth-sticks and water for washing the face, and they swept the cell and the surrounding grounds...
333:
They swept the compound, provided drinking water, and brought various sweet and excellent fruits from the forest to feed their parents. They bathed them with warm or cold water, cleaned their matted hair, and massaged their hands and feet.

## The Younger Hermit's Eager Service
As time passed, Nanda the Wise thought, "I will feed my parents only with the fruits I have gathered." He went out early and brought whatever fruits he could find—whether good or bad—from the places he had gathered them the day before or the day before that, and fed them to his parents. After eating those fruits and rinsing their mouths, the parents observed the Uposatha.

Soṇa the Wise, however, went far away to gather the sweetest and ripest fruits and offered them. Then the parents said to Soṇa, "Dear Soṇa, your younger brother Nanda brought fruits early this morning, and we have already eaten and are now observing the Uposatha. We have no need for them now." Thus, Soṇa's fruits were not consumed and went to waste. This happened again on the following days. Even though Soṇa, possessing the five superknowledges, went far to bring them, the parents would not eat them again.

Then the Great Being thought, "My parents are delicate. My brother Nanda brings whatever fruits he finds, including those that are unripe or poorly ripened, and feeds them. If this continues, they will not live long. I must stop him." He called Nanda and said, "Nanda, from now on, after gathering fruits, wait for my arrival. We shall feed our parents together." Despite being told this, Nanda, desiring his own merit, did not follow his brother's words.

## The Younger Hermit Banished
The Great Being thought, "My brother Nanda does not listen; he is doing what is improper. I shall send him away, and then I alone will look after our parents." He then said, "Nanda, you are uninstructable and do not listen to the words of the wise. I am the eldest; the parents are my responsibility. I alone will care for them. You shall not stay here; go elsewhere." He then snapped his fingers at him.

## Planning to Ask Forgiveness
Being banished and unable to stay near his brother Soṇa, Nanda paid homage to him, informed his parents, and entered his own leaf-hut. There, he practiced meditation on the kasina and, on that very day, attained the five superknowledges and the eight attainments. He thought:

"I could bring jeweled sand from the foot of Mount Sineru and scatter it in my brother's hut and compound to ask for his forgiveness. But that would not be grand enough. I could bring water from Lake Anotatta to ask for forgiveness, but that too would not be grand enough. If I were to ask for forgiveness through the power of the deities, I could bring the Four Great Kings and Sakka to ask for his forgiveness. But even that..."
334:
...would not be grand enough. I shall bring the great King Manojava and other kings from across the whole of Jambudīpa to ask for forgiveness. Then my brother's virtues will spread throughout Jambudīpa and become as famous as the sun and the moon."

## Organizing the Kings
Having thought this, Nanda the Wise immediately traveled by psychic power and stood at the palace gate of King Manojava in the city of Brahmavaḍḍhana. He had someone announce to the King, "A hermit wishes to see Your Majesty." King Manojava thought, "What use is it for me to see a monk? He must have come for food," and sent him a meal. Nanda the Wise did not want the meal. The King sent raw rice; he did not want it. He sent clothes; he did not want them. He sent betel; he did not want it. Then the King sent a messenger to ask, "For what purpose have you come?" When asked by the messenger, Nanda the hermit replied, "I have come to serve the King."

## Winning Over King Manojava
Hearing this, King Manojava sent word, "I have many attendants. Let him just practice his own hermit's duties." Hearing the King's words, Nanda the hermit said, "By my power, I shall seize the sovereignty of all Jambudīpa and give it to Your Majesty." Hearing this, King Manojava thought, "Monks are wise; they must know some means."

He summoned Nanda the hermit, offered him a seat, paid homage, and asked, "Venerable sir, is it true that you will seize the sovereignty of all Jambudīpa and give it to me?" "Yes, Great King," he replied. "How will you take it?" the King asked. "Great King, without causing even as much blood to flow as a small fly might drink, and without causing you any loss of wealth, I shall take it by my psychic power alone. However, there is little to say—we should set out today without delay."

## Winning Over the King of Kosala
King Manojava believed Nanda the Wise and set out surrounded by his army. If the heat became too much for the army, Nanda the Wise used his power to create shade and make it cool. When it rained, he did not let it fall on the army. He blocked cold winds and hot winds. He cleared all dangers such as stumps and thorns from the path. He made the path as smooth as a kasina-mandala. He himself traveled through the air, seated cross-legged on a spread-out piece of leather, surrounded by the army.

In this way, taking the army, he first went to the Kingdom of Kosala. He established a camp not far from the city and sent a messenger to the King of Kosala, saying, "Give us battle or give us the white parasol." The King of Kosala became angry and thought, "Am I not a king?" He replied, "I shall give battle," and came out of the city at the head of his army. The two armies prepared to fight.

Nanda the Wise created a large black antelope skin as his seat between the two armies and spread it out. He caught all the arrows shot by both armies with the skin alone. Not a single soldier was pierced by an arrow. When their arrows were exhausted, both armies stood still, their efforts rendered futile.
335:
Nanda the Wise went to King Manojava and comforted him, saying, "Great King, do not be afraid." Then he went to the King of Kosala and said, "Great King, do not be afraid. There is no enemy opposing you. Your kingdom shall remain yours; only become a follower of King Manojava."

The King of Kosala believed the words of Nanda the Wise and agreed, saying, "Very well." Having obtained his consent, Nanda led the King of Kosala to King Manojava and said, "Great King, the King of Kosala is now under your authority. Let this king's kingdom remain his own."

## Conquering All Kings

King Manojava agreed, saying, "Very well," and brought the King of Kosala under his sway. Then, taking both armies, he went to the kingdom of Aṅga and conquered it. From there, he went to the kingdom of Magadha and conquered it. In this manner, he brought all the kings of the entire Jambudīpa under his authority. Surrounded by all those kings, he returned to the city of Brahmavaḍḍhana. It took seven years, seven months, and seven days for this Nandapaṇḍita to conquer all the kingdoms.

## The King's Gratitude

King Manojava had various kinds of food brought from each royal capital and, together with the one hundred and one kings, he drank a great beverage for seven days. Nandapaṇḍita thought, "As long as King Manojava enjoys the bliss of sovereignty for seven days, I will not show myself to him." He went to Uttarakuru for alms and then stayed for seven days at the entrance of a golden cave in the Himavanta.

On the seventh day, King Manojava, looking at his great glory and prosperity, remembered Nandapaṇḍita, thinking, "This glory was not given to me by my mother or father, nor by anyone else. It arose because of the ascetic Nanda. Indeed, it has been seven days since I last saw that Nanda the Wise. Where is the holy ascetic who gave me this glory?"

Knowing that King Manojava was thinking of him, Nandapaṇḍita came and stood in the air before him. The King saw him and thought, "I do not know if this ascetic is a deity or a human. If he is a human, I will give him the sovereignty of the entire Jambudīpa. If he is not a human but a deity, I will pay him great honor." Desiring to test him, King Manojava spoke this first verse:

92. Are you a deity, a gandhabba, or Sakka Purindada?
Or are you a powerful human? How may we know you?

92. O ascetic, are you a deity of the Cātumahārājika realm? Are you a gandhabba? Or are you Sakka, who has given gifts in the past? Or are you a powerful human? How may we know you?

I am a powerful human; know this, O Bhāradha.

93. O Bhāradha, you who bear the burden of the great kingdom, I am not a deity of the Cātumahārājika realm. I am not a gandhabba. I am not Sakka, the king of gods who gave gifts in the past. I am truly a powerful human. Know this.

Nandapaṇḍita, hearing the words of King Manojava, wished to speak only the truth.

Hearing this, King Manojava thought, "This ascetic, though a human, has done me such great service. I shall satisfy him with great wealth and glory." Desiring to offer him whatever he wished while expressing his gratitude, he spoke these six verses:

## The Journey of the Many Kings

Then King Manojava, wishing to give orders for the journey to the hermit's dwelling, spoke thus.

Having spoken thus, he took one hundred and one kings and, surrounded by a host of twenty-four akkhobhinis, with the wise Nanda leading the way, he departed from the city and went to the hermitage where the hermit Sona resided.

To make this matter clear, the All-Enlightened Buddha, after attaining Buddhahood, spoke this.

107. "Whose is this yoke of Kadamba wood, four inches in the air? It goes without touching the shoulder of the one going to fetch water."

107. "O ascetic! It moves through the air, four inches away, without touching the shoulder. As you go to fetch water, whose is this yoke made of Kadamba wood?"

On the day he was to arrive at the hermitage of the Venerable Ascetic Nanda, the elder brother, the wise Soṇa, reflected: "It has been seven years, seven months, and seven days since my younger brother Nanda left this place." Looking with the divine eye to see where he was now, he saw: "He is coming with an escort of twenty-four akkhobhaṇīs and a hundred and one kings, only to ask for my forgiveness." He then thought:

"These hundred and one kings and this multitude of twenty-four akkhobhaṇīs have seen many miracles of my younger brother Nanda. Not knowing my power, they might disparage me, saying, 'This fraudulent ascetic does not know his own measure; he dares to compare himself with our master.' Thus, they might be headed for the Avīci hell. I shall show them a miracle of psychic power."

Having so thought, the wise Soṇa placed his yoke in the air, about four inches from his shoulder without touching it, and traveled through the sky not far from King Manojava to fetch water from Lake Anotatta. The wise Nanda, seeing his elder brother Soṇa coming, did not dare to show himself; he vanished from his seat and fled into the Himālaya.

## Informing the Father Ascetic
Having thus given directions for the path, he quickly went to Lake Anotatta, fetched drinking water, and arrived before the one hundred and one kings reached the hermitage. Then the younger brother, the ascetic Nanda, thought: "My elder brother is wise, skilled in means, and a preacher of Dhamma. He has broken my entire following and made them his own. Apart from this elder brother, I have no other refuge. I shall beg only him." Desiring to plead, he spoke.

## Permission to Serve Parents

By nature, the Bodhisatta held no anger or malice toward Nanda the Wise.

## Serving the Mother
Then the mother of the hermit Nanda rose from her seat and said, "Wise Soṇa, your younger brother Nanda has been separated from us for a long time. Even though he has been away so long, we did not dare to entreat you. This is true; we depend on you. But now, you have given permission. Then the Bodhisatta said to his mother, "Mother, if that is so, I grant permission. Mother, please go. Embrace your son Nanda, kiss his head, and extinguish the sorrow in your heart." The mother went to her son, the wise Nanda, embraced him in the midst of the assembly, kissed his head repeatedly, extinguished the sorrow in her heart, and wishing to speak with her son, the Bodhisatta, she said:

## The Gratitude of Mothers
The Bodhisatta accepted his mother's words, saying, "Let it be so," and exhorted his younger brother Nanda, "Younger brother Nanda, you have received a great portion. A mother is indeed a great benefactor. Serve her diligently and without negligence." To make the mother's virtues clear, he said:

## Parents Should Be Served
Thus, the Bodhisatta explained the mother's gratitude with two verses. Again, when he returned and sat in the mother's place, he said, "Younger brother Nanda, you have the opportunity to serve a mother who is difficult to serve. Our mother raised both of us with great hardship. Now, serve her diligently and without negligence. Do not let her eat unpalatable fruits." Thus, in the midst of the assembly, he wished to make clear the fact that a mother is difficult to serve.

Thus the Bodhisatta concluded the Dhamma teaching as if rolling the king of mountains, Meru. Having heard this Dhamma teaching, all the one hundred and one kings, along with their retinues, were filled with devotion.

In that context, 'puttaphalaṃ' means the fruit known as a son. 'Devatāya namassatīti' means she pays homage and prays to the deity, saying, "May a son be born to me." 'Pucchatīti' means she asks about the constellations, "A son born under which constellation will be long-lived, and under which will he be short-lived?" 'Utu-saṃvaccharāni cāti' means she asks about the seasons and years, "A son born in which of the six seasons will be long-lived, and in which will he be short-lived? Or a son born to a mother of how many years will be long-lived, and at how many years will he be short-lived?" 'Utumhi nhātāyāti' means bathed after the menses had arisen. 'Vokkamoti' means the descent of the embryo occurs through the meeting of the three factors, and the embryo is established in the womb. 'Tenāti' means because of that embryo, she has pregnancy longings (dohaḷinī). 'Tenāti' means at that time, affection arises for the offspring produced in her womb; for that reason, she is called 'Suhadā' (Kind-hearted). 'Tenāti' means for that reason, she is called 'Janayantī' and 'Janettī' (The Progenitress).

'Aṅgapāvuraṇena cāti' means laying the child between her breasts and letting him feel the touch of her body, using her own limbs as a covering. 'Tosentīti' means pleasing and making him laugh. 'Mamaṃ katvā udikkhatīti' means thinking with a loving heart, "The wind blows upon my son, the heat of the sun strikes him," she looks after him with possessive affection. 'Ubhayampetassāti' means the mother guards both types of wealth for the sake of this son, not showing it to others, keeping it in inner chambers and such. 'Evaṃ putta, aduṃ puttāti' means teaching him, "O foolish son, be diligent in the royal court and such, and do not do that deed," thus the mother is distressed and weary.

Then, he established the one hundred and one kings in the five precepts and exhorted them, saying, "Be diligent in giving alms and other meritorious deeds," and then dismissed them. All those kings ruled righteously and, at the end of their lives, filled the celestial realms. The elder brother, the wise ascetic Soṇa, and the younger brother, the wise ascetic Nanda, served their mother and father for the rest of their lives and were reborn in the Brahma realm.

The Teacher, the All-Enlightened One, having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who supported his parents was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

How did he identify the Jātaka? — "At that time, the mother and father were those who are now the Great Queen Māyā and King Suddhodana of the noble Sākyan clan. The wise ascetic Nanda was Ānanda. King Manojava was Sāriputta. The one hundred and one kings were the eighty Great Elders and other elders. The army of twenty-four akkhobhaṇīs was the Buddha’s present assembly. And I myself was the wise ascetic Soṇa." Thus he identified the Jātaka.

355:
## 1. Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka

## The Teacher Escaping Death Due to a Wise Disciple

The Present Account: While staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the All-Enlightened Buddha told this Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Sumukha," concerning the Venerable Ānanda’s sacrifice of his life for the Blessed One.

This is the story: Among the archers sent by Devadatta to kill the Buddha, the first one sent approached and said, "Venerable Devadatta, I am unable to kill the Blessed One. The Blessed One is of great psychic power and great majesty." Devadatta replied, "Layman, it is not right. Do not kill the ascetic Gotama yourself; I will kill the ascetic Gotama myself." Then, while the Buddha was walking to and fro in the shadow to the west of Gijjhakūṭa Mountain, Devadatta climbed the mountain and, using a mechanical device, hurled a large rock, thinking, "I will kill the ascetic Gotama with this rock."

Two mountain peaks came together and caught that rock. A splinter from the rock broke off and struck the Blessed One’s foot, causing blood to flow. Severe pains arose. Jīvaka lanced the Blessed One’s foot with a small knife, removed the bad blood and the putrid flesh, washed it, applied medicine, and healed the wound. The All-Enlightened Buddha, surrounded by the assembly of monks as before, walked with the great grace of a Buddha.

## Encounter with the Elephant Nālāgiri

Then, seeing the Buddha, Devadatta thought: "When people see the body of Gotama, which has reached the perfection of beauty, no human being is able to approach him to harm him. However, King Ajātasattu has a fierce, cruel, man-killing elephant named Nālāgiri, who knows nothing of the virtues of the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha. That elephant Nālāgiri will bring Gotama to the end of his life." Thinking thus, Devadatta went and informed King Ajātasattu of the matter.

King Ajātasattu agreed, saying "Very well," and summoned the mahout, saying, "Friend mahout, tomorrow make the elephant Nālāgiri drunk and release him early in the morning on the street where the ascetic Gotama is walking." Devadatta also asked the mahout, "Layman, how much liquor does the elephant drink on other days?" When told "Eight pots, venerable sir," he said, "In that case, tomorrow you must give the elephant Nālāgiri sixteen pots of liquor and release him directly onto the path where the ascetic Gotama goes for alms."

The mahout agreed. King Ajātasattu had the drum beaten in the city to announce: "Tomorrow, the elephant Nālāgiri will be made drunk and released in the city. Let all the citizens finish their chores early in the morning and stay off the main roads."
356:
Devadatta also descended from the royal residence and went to the elephant stable. He called the elephant keepers and said, “Friends, we are capable of placing those in high positions into low ones, and those in low positions into high ones. If you desire wealth and prosperity, tomorrow morning, give the elephant Nālāgiri sixteen pots of strong liquor to drink. When the ascetic Gotama arrives, pierce the elephant with spears and goads to make him angry, break him out of the elephant stable, and release him directly onto the path where the ascetic Gotama is walking, so that he may be put to death.” The elephant keepers agreed, saying, “Very well.” That news spread throughout the entire city of Rājagaha.

Upon hearing this, the lay followers who were devoted to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha approached the Teacher and said, “Venerable Sir, Devadatta has conspired with King Ajātasattu and will release the elephant Nālāgiri on the path where you will travel tomorrow. Please do not go out for alms tomorrow; stay here in this Veḷuvana monastery. We will serve alms-food to the assembly of monks headed by the Buddha right here in the monastery.”

The Omniscient Buddha, without saying “I will not go for alms tomorrow,” accepted their offer by saying: “Tomorrow, after taming the fierce elephant Nālāgiri and performing a miracle, and after subduing the heretics, I will not walk for alms in Rājagaha but will return to Veḷuvana surrounded by the assembly of monks. The people living in Rājagaha will also bring many vessels of food and come to Veḷuvana. Tomorrow, the meal will take place only in the monastery.” Knowing that the Buddha had accepted, the citizens departed, thinking, “We will bring vessels of food and give the offering only at the Veḷuvana monastery.”

The Omniscient Buddha preached the Dhamma in the first watch of the night, answered the questions of the deities in the middle watch, and in the first part of the last watch, he took the lion’s posture (sīhaseyya). In the second part, he spent time in the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), and in the third part, he entered the attainment of great compassion (mahākaruṇāsamāpatti). While surveying the beings who were ready to be enlightened, he saw that eighty-four thousand beings would realize the Dhamma upon the taming of the fierce elephant Nālāgiri. When the night turned to dawn, after attending to his physical needs, he called the Venerable Ānanda and said, “Ānanda, inform all the monks in the eighteen great monasteries around Rājagaha to enter Rājagaha with me today.”

Venerable Ānanda did exactly as the Buddha commanded. All the monks gathered at the Veḷuvana monastery. The Omniscient Buddha, surrounded by the assembly of monks, entered the city of Rājagaha. The elephant keepers acted according to Devadatta’s instructions. A great crowd gathered.

People endowed with faith thought, “Today, there will be a battle between the Noble Elephant, the Buddha, and an animal elephant. We shall witness the taming of the fierce Nālāgiri through the incomparable and majestic grace of the Buddha,” and they climbed onto the long pavilions, flat-roofed mansions, and rooftops to watch.
357:
Those who were faithless, lacking devotion, and held wrong views thought, “The elephant Nālāgiri is extremely fierce, violent, and a killer of men. He does not know the virtues of the Buddha and others. Today, that Nālāgiri will destroy the golden-hued body of the ascetic Gotama and bring his life to an end. Today, we shall see the back (defeat) of our enemy,” and they stood upon the pavilions and other high places.

Nālāgiri, seeing the Blessed One approaching, terrified the people, destroyed houses, and crushed carts to pieces. With his trunk raised and his ears and tail erect, he charged like a massive mountain toward the place where the Blessed One was.

Seeing the elephant Nālāgiri approaching, the monks addressed the Omniscient Buddha thus: “Venerable Sir, the elephant Nālāgiri is fierce, violent, and a killer of men. He has entered this street. Indeed, he does not know the virtues of the Buddha and others. Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One retreat; may the Sugata retreat.”

The Omniscient Buddha said, “Monks, do not be afraid. I am capable of taming the fierce Nālāgiri.” When he said this, the Venerable Sāriputta pleaded with the Buddha, “Venerable Sir, the duty that arises for a father is the burden of the eldest son. I myself will tame this fierce elephant.” Then the Omniscient Buddha restrained him, saying, “Sāriputta, the power of a Buddha is one thing, and the power of a disciple is another. Stay where you are.”

In the same way, most of the eighty great disciples also pleaded. The Omniscient Buddha restrained all the disciples. Then the Venerable Ānanda, unable to endure [the danger] due to his strong affection for the Omniscient Buddha, sacrificed his life for the sake of the Buddha and went to stand in front of the Teacher, saying, “Let the elephant kill me first.”

Then the Buddha said to the Venerable Ānanda, “Ānanda, move away. Do not stand in front of me.” The Venerable Ānanda pleaded with the Buddha again, “Venerable Sir, this elephant Nālāgiri is fierce, violent, and a killer of men. He is like the fire at the end of an aeon. Let him kill me first, and only then let him come toward you.” Although he was forbidden three times, he continued to stand right there in front and did not retreat. Then the Blessed One, by the power of his psychic ability, caused the Venerable Ānanda to move back and placed him in the midst of the monks.

## Taming the Elephant
At that moment, a woman, seeing the elephant Nālāgiri and being terrified of death, fled, abandoning her young child whom she had been carrying in her arms, leaving him between the elephant Nālāgiri and the Buddha. The elephant Nālāgiri chased the woman, then turned back and went toward the child. At that time, the child cried out with a loud voice.

The All-Knowing Buddha, directing his attention toward the elephant Nālāgiri, suffused him with loving-kindness and, emitting a sweet voice like that of the Great Brahma, called out: “O Nālāgiri! When they made you drink sixteen jars of liquor to intoxicate you, they did not do so thinking you would catch someone else; indeed, they did so thinking you would catch Me. Do not wander about pointlessly, wearying your legs and body; come here toward Me.”

Upon hearing the Buddha’s words, the elephant Nālāgiri opened his eyes, beheld the glorious beauty of the Buddha’s form, and was struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Through the Buddha’s power, his intoxication from the liquor vanished. Lowering his trunk and drooping his ears, he went and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet. Then the Buddha said to him: “Nālāgiri, you are an animal elephant; I am the Buddha-Elephant. From this day forward, be not fierce, be not harsh, and do not kill humans. Develop a mind of loving-kindness toward all beings repeatedly.” Extending his right hand, he stroked the elephant’s forehead and, wishing to admonish him, spoke as follows:

After he spoke thus and preached the Dhamma, the elephant Nālāgiri’s entire body was continuously suffused with joy. If that elephant Nālāgiri had not been an animal, he would have attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

When the people saw that miracle, they raised a great shout and clapped their hands. Being filled with great joy, they threw various ornaments. Those ornaments of gold, silver, and jewels covered the body of the elephant Nālāgiri. From that time on, Nālāgiri became known as the elephant Dhanapālaka. In that assembly where the fierce elephant Dhanapālaka was tamed, eighty-four thousand beings drank the nectar of the Deathless, Nibbāna.

The All-Knowing Buddha established the elephant Dhanapālaka in the Five Precepts. The elephant Dhanapālaka took dust from the Buddha’s feet with his trunk, sprinkled it upon his head, and retreated respectfully while facing the Buddha. Staying within sight, he paid homage to the All-Knowing Buddha and then returned to the elephant stable. From that time on, he became exceptionally gentle among all tamed elephants and never harmed anyone again.

They spoke thus: “Friends, the Venerable Ānanda performed a most difficult task by sacrificing his own life for the sake of the All-Knowing Buddha. The All-Knowing Buddha, knowing that the conversation was about Ānanda’s virtues, thought, “I should go there.” He emerged from the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), arrived at the hall, and asked: “Monks, what is the subject of your discussion as you sit here now?” When they replied, “We are gathered to discuss such and such a matter,” he said: “Monks, it is not only now that Ānanda has sacrificed his life for my sake; in the past, even when he was born in the animal kingdom, he sacrificed his life for my sake.” He then brought forth the past story.

Story of the Past: Monks, in the long-past time, in the city of Sāgala in the kingdom of Mahimsaka, a king named Sāgala ruled righteously. At that time, in a hunter’s village not far from the city, a certain hunter made his living by catching birds with snares and selling them in the city.

Not far from the city of Sāgala, there was a lake named Mānusiya, twelve yojanas in circumference, covered with five-colored lotuses. Various flocks of birds would descend upon that Mānusiya lotus lake. The bird hunter would set his snares at that Mānusiya lotus lake without targeting any specific bird.

At that time, the Swan King Dhataraṭṭha lived in a golden cave on Mount Cittakūṭa, surrounded by ninety-six thousand swans.

## The Swan King is Trapped

Although the Bodhisatta swan king Dhataraṭṭha refused, saying, "The world of men is full of danger and peril; it is loathsome; do not let it please you," he was repeatedly entreated by those swans. He said, "If it pleases you, let us go," and went to that pond with his retinue.

As the Bodhisatta swan king Dhataraṭṭha descended from the sky, he descended even as he placed his foot into a snare. Then, the snare gripped the Bodhisatta swan king's foot, binding it as if pulling it with an iron band. Then, as the Bodhisatta pulled, thinking, "I will break the snare," at the first pull, the skin tore. At the second pull, the flesh tore. At the third pull, the sinew tore. The snare reached the bone and stayed there. Blood flowed, and intense pains arose.

That Bodhisatta thought, "If I utter the cry of one who is trapped, my relatives will be terrified and, without taking food, will flee with hungry bodies. Due to their weakness, they will fall into the Great Ocean." Having so thought, the Bodhisatta endured the intense pain, and when the swans who were his kin had eaten as much as they desired and were playing, he uttered the cry of one trapped in a snare with a loud voice. Upon hearing that cry, the swans, being terrified by the fear of death, fled in groups toward Mount Cittakūṭa.

## The Return of General Sumukha

While those swans were flying away, the swan general named Sumukha thought, "How is this? Has this danger indeed befallen our Great King? I shall find out." Flying swiftly, he did not see the Bodhisatta among the flock of swans going in front, so he searched the middle flock of swans. Not seeing him in that middle flock either, he searched the rear flock of swans again.

Not seeing him in that flock of swans either, he thought, "Undoubtedly, this danger has befallen our Great King alone." Returning and coming back, he saw the Bodhisatta caught in the snare, smeared with blood, and lying in great pain on the surface of the mud. He said, "Great King, do not be afraid..."

## Rewarding the Hunter
After saying this, King Sāgala looked at an official and, when asked "What shall I do, your Majesty?", he commanded, "Take this hunter, have his hair and beard trimmed, have him bathed and anointed with perfumes, and bring him back adorned with all kinds of ornaments." ## The Goose King Requests Permission to Return

## The Geese's Blessing

Having thus surrounded him, the geese asked, "O Great King, by what means were you released?" The Bodhisatta explained how he was freed because of the General Sumukha, and related the actions of King Sāgala and the hunter.

Hearing the words of the Bodhisatta, the assembly of geese was greatly delighted and made this aspiration: "May the General Sumukha, King Sāgala, and the hunter's son be happy, free from suffering, and live for a long time!"
377:
The Omniscient Buddha, wishing to clarify this matter, concluded the Jātaka. Having delivered this Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka Dhamma teaching, the Omniscient Buddha said, "Monks, not only now has Ānanda sacrificed his life for my sake; in the past too, he sacrificed his life for my sake." He then identified the characters: "At that time, the hunter was Channa; the king was Sāriputta; Sumukha, the golden goose general, was Ānanda; the 96,000 geese were the Buddha's assembly; and I myself was Dhataraṭṭha, the king of the 96,000 geese."
## Sacrificing Life for a Benefactor Leads to Increased Happiness
The Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka ends.
## 2. Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka
## The Teacher's Life is Saved Because of the Wise Disciple
While staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka, adorned with the verse starting with "Ete haṃsā pakkamanti," regarding Elder Ānanda's sacrifice of his life.
The story of the present is similar to what was stated in the Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka above. Specifically, in this Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka, the Buddha told this story of the past.
Story of the Past: Monks, long ago, a king named Saṃyama reigned in Bārāṇasī. He had a chief queen named Khemā. At that time, the Bodhisatta lived on Mount Cittakūṭa, surrounded by 90,000 geese.
## Golden Geese in a Dream
One day, Queen Khemā had a dream at dawn. Golden geese came, sat on the royal throne, and preached the Dhamma in sweet voices. While Queen Khemā was listening to the Dhamma and giving applause, the night turned into day before she was satisfied with the preaching. After preaching the Dhamma, the geese departed through the lion-window.
The queen rose quickly and said, "Catch the fleeing geese! Catch them!" and while stretching out her hands, she woke up. Hearing the queen's words, her attendants laughed a little, asking, "Where are the geese?"
## The Queen's Longing
At that moment, Queen Khemā realized it was a dream and thought: "I would not dream of something that does not exist. Surely, there must be golden geese in this world. However, if I tell the King, 'I wish to hear the Dhamma of golden geese,' he might say, 'We have never seen golden geese before, and the preaching of geese has never happened,' and he will remain indifferent. But if I say it is a pregnancy craving (dohaḷa), he will search for them by some means. If he searches in this way, my heart's desire will be fulfilled." Thinking thus, she pretended to be ill, gave a sign to her attendants, and lay down.
When the King was in his place and did not see the queen at the time he should, he asked, "Where is Queen Khemā?" Hearing that she was ill, he went to her, sat on one side of the bed, and stroking her back, asked, "What is your discomfort, my Queen?" She replied, "Great King, I have no other discomfort, but a pregnancy craving has arisen in me."
378:
"My Queen, if so, tell me. Whatever you desire, I shall have it brought to you quickly," the King said. She replied, "Great King, I wish to worship a golden goose king sitting on a royal throne under a raised white parasol with flowers, scents, and the like, and listen to his Dhamma discourse while giving applause. If I get this, it is well. If not, I shall die."
## The King Searches for Golden Geese
Then the King comforted her, saying, "If they exist in the human world, you shall have them. Do not worry." He left the royal chamber and consulted with his ministers. "O ministers, Queen Khemā says, 'If I get to hear the Dhamma discourse of a golden goose, I shall live; if I do not, I shall die.' Do golden geese exist?" When he asked this, they replied, "Great King, we have never seen nor heard of them." "Who then would know?" he asked. "Great King, the Brahmins would know," they replied.
The King summoned the Brahmins, honored them, and asked, "Teachers, do golden geese exist?" They replied, "Yes, Great King. In our Vedas, it is mentioned that these six types of animals—fish, crabs, turtles, deer, peacocks, and geese—can be golden. Among them, those of the Dhataraṭṭha lineage are wise and endowed with wisdom. Thus, including humans, there are seven types of golden beings."
Hearing this, the King was delighted and asked, "Teachers, where do the Dhataraṭṭha geese live?" When they replied, "We do not know, Great King," he asked, "Then who will know?" They said, "The sons of hunters will know." The King then summoned all the hunters in his kingdom and asked, "Friends, where do the golden Dhataraṭṭha geese live?" One hunter replied, "Great King, it is said in our family lineage that they live on Mount Cittakūṭa in the Himālaya."
"Do you know the means to catch them?" the King asked. "I do not know, Great King," he replied. "Who then will know?" the King asked, and the hunter replied, "Great King, the Brahmins will know."
379:
## Digging the Lake

The King summoned the wise Brahmins and, having heard that there were geese with golden complexions on Mount Cittakūṭa, asked, "Do you know a way to capture those golden geese?"

"Great King, what is the use of going to capture them? We shall lure them near the city by a stratagem and capture them," they replied. When they said this, he asked, "What is this stratagem?"

"Great King, have a lake named Khema dug three leagues north of the city, three leagues in extent. Fill it with water, plant various kinds of grain, and cover it with five-colored lotuses. Entrust it to a wise hunter, and do not allow people to approach. Have a proclamation of safety (abhaya) made at the four corners. Hearing this proclamation, various birds will descend from the ten directions. When they descend, those golden geese will also hear of the safety of the lake through the reports of others and will come. When they come, capture them using hair-nooses (vālapaasa)," they submitted.

Hearing this, the King had the lake dug as described in the place mentioned by the Brahmins. He summoned a skilled hunter, gave him a thousand pieces of money, and said, "From this day forth, do not do your own work. I will support your wife and children. Vigilantly guard Khema Lake, keep people away, proclaim safety at the four corners, and report to me every bird that comes. When the golden geese arrive, you shall receive great honor." He comforted the hunter and entrusted him with Khema Lake.

From then on, the hunter acted according to the King's command. He guarded Khema Lake, and because he guarded it, he became known as "Khema the Hunter."

## The Geese Arrive

From that time, various kinds of birds descended. Through the spreading reports that "Khema Lake is safe and peaceful," various geese came. First, the Grass Geese (Tiṇahaṃsa) came. Because of their cries, the Pale Geese (Paṇḍuhaṃsa) came. Because of their cries, the Cinnabar Geese (Manosilāhaṃsa) came. Because of their cries, the White Geese (Setahaṃsa) came. Because of their cries, the Pāka Geese (Pākahaṃsa) came.

When the Pāka Geese arrived, Khema the Hunter went and reported to the King: "Great King, five kinds of geese have come and are feeding in the lake. Since the Pāka Geese have arrived, the Golden Geese will come in a few days. Do not worry, Great King."

Hearing this, the King had a drum beaten throughout the city, proclaiming: "No one except Khema the Hunter shall go to Khema Lake. Whoever goes there shall suffer the cutting off of hands and feet and the destruction of his house." From then on, no one dared go to the lake.

Not far from Mount Cittakūṭa, in a golden cave, lived the Pāka Geese. They were very strong and lived together with the Dhataraṭṭha clan. Only their body color was different. The daughter of the Pāka Goose King was golden-colored. Thinking she was a suitable match for the Dhataraṭṭha King, he sent her to be his chief queen. The Dhataraṭṭha King loved her dearly. For this reason, the two clans of geese became intimate with each other.
380:
One day, the attendant geese of the Bodhisatta, the Golden Goose King, asked the Pāka Geese, "Where have you been feeding these days?"

"We feed at a lake named Khema, not far from the city of Bārāṇasī. And where do you wander?" they asked. When they replied, "We wander in such-and-such a place," the Pāka Geese said, "Why do you not go to Khema Lake? It is true that Khema Lake is delightful. It is crowded with various kinds of birds, covered with five kinds of lotuses, and full of various grains. It resounds with the humming of various swarms of bees. At its four corners, a proclamation of safety is constantly made. No one dares to approach that lake, let alone cause any harm. It is truly free from danger. Such is the nature of Khema Lake." Thus they praised Khema Lake.

## The Goose King's Prohibition

The attendants of the Bodhisatta Golden Goose King heard the words of the Pāka Geese and said to the general Sumukha, "We hear there is a lake named Khema near Bārāṇasī of such a nature. The Pāka Geese go there and take food. Please report this to King Dhataraṭṭha. If he permits, we too shall go to Khema Lake and take food." General Sumukha reported this matter to his lord, King Dhataraṭṭha.

The Bodhisatta Dhataraṭṭha Golden Goose King thought, "Humans are full of deceit, harsh in their counsel, and skilled in stratagems. There must be a reason for this lake. For so long this lake did not exist, but now it has been made. It must have been made to capture us." Having thought thus, the Golden Goose King said to General Sumukha:

"Sumukha, do not desire to go to that Khema Lake. Humans did not make that lake for the sake of merit; they made it only to capture us. Humans are full of deceit, harsh in their counsel, and skilled in stratagems. You should feed only in your own feeding grounds."

## The Golden Geese Arrive

The Golden Geese told Sumukha a second and a third time that they truly wished to go to Khema Lake. General Sumukha again reported to the Bodhisatta Dhataraṭṭha King that the attendant golden geese wished to go.

When Sumukha reported this, the Bodhisatta thought, "Let my relatives not suffer on my account," and said, "If that is the case, let us go." Surrounded by ninety thousand golden geese, he went to the lake, took food, enjoyed the geese's play, and then returned to Mount Cittakūṭa.
381:
The hunter Khema, when those golden geese had fed and returned, went and reported their arrival to the King. The King was greatly pleased and said, "Friend Khema, strive to catch one or two golden geese; I shall bestow upon you great wealth and happiness." Having provided him with provisions, he sent the hunter forth.

The hunter went to Lake Khema and, staying in a hollow like a large water-jar, investigated the feeding grounds of the geese. Bodhisattas do not feed in a flighty or erratic manner. Therefore, the Bodhisatta, starting from where he landed, fed in order, eating the wild rice as he went. The remaining geese fed here and there as they went.

Then the hunter Khema thought, "This golden goose does not feed in a flighty manner; it is proper to set a snare for this golden goose." On the following day, before the golden geese descended to the lake, he went to that place, stayed in the jar-like hollow, concealed himself within the hollow, and remained watching through a hole. At that moment, the Bodhisatta, the Golden Goose King Dhataraṭṭha, surrounded by ninety thousand geese, descended at the very spot where he had landed the previous day, and having fed within that area, he departed.

## The Golden Goose King
When the hunter Khema looked through the hole of the hollow and saw the body of the Bodhisatta, the Golden Goose King Dhataraṭṭha, which had reached the pinnacle of physical beauty:

"This golden goose has a body the size of a chariot hub; it has a complexion like gold. Its neck is encircled by three red stripes. Three lines descend from the neck and go along the left and right of the breast. Three lines pass through to the back. It is exceedingly beautiful, like a golden mass placed in a mesh of red woolen thread. This golden goose must be the king of those geese; I will catch only this golden goose," he thought.

The Golden Goose King Dhataraṭṭha, having eaten much food and played in the water, departed for Mount Cittakūṭa surrounded by the flock of geese. In this manner, he took food for five days.
382:
89. "These geese are departing, crooked-necked and driven by fear. O Sumukha of golden skin and golden hue, depart at your will."
90. "Leaving me, who has fallen alone into the power of a snare, the flock of kinsmen go without looking back; why do you remain alone?"
91. "O best among those who fly, there is no companionship with one who is bound. Do not let your effort for a painless state fail; depart, Sumukha, at your will."
He spoke these three verses.

90. O friend Sumukha. My kinsmen, the ninety thousand geese, have abandoned me, who has fallen alone into the power of a snare, and have flown away without regard. O Sumukha of golden hue, why do you remain alone?
