## Captured!
On the sixth day, the hunter Khema, having twisted a strong rope made of black horsehair and made a snare on a stick, knowing truly that "Tomorrow the Goose King will descend in this place," set the stick-snare in the water. On the following day, when the Golden Goose King descended, he stepped into the snare as he landed. Then the snare bound and held the Bodhisatta's foot as if pulling it with an iron band.

The Golden Goose King, thinking "I will break the snare," exerted force and pulled. At the first pull, the skin of golden hue was cut. At the second pull, the flesh of crimson hue was cut. At the third pull, the tendon was cut. If he pulled a fourth time, the Bodhisatta Golden Goose King's foot would be severed. For a king, to be deficient in limbs is not appropriate; therefore, he did not make further effort. Intense pains arose.

The Bodhisatta Golden Goose King thought, "If I utter the cry of one caught in a snare, my kinsmen will be terrified in heart, and without taking food, they will flee with hungry bodies and fall into the Great Ocean." Having so thought, the Bodhisatta endured the great pain, and though caught in the snare, he acted as if he were eating the wild rice. After the flock of geese had eaten as much as they desired and it was time for their water-play, he uttered the loud cry of one caught in a snare. Hearing that sound, the geese, terrified by the fear of death, fled in groups toward Mount Cittakūṭa in the manner previously described.

## The Return of General Sumukha
General Sumukha also searched in the manner described below, and not seeing his lord, the Golden Goose King Dhataraṭṭha, in any of the three groups, he thought, "Surely this danger has befallen only our Great King." Returning and coming back, he saw the Bodhisatta lying on the surface of the mud, smeared with blood, suffering and distressed, caught in the snare. He said, "Great King, do not fear; I shall sacrifice my own life to set you free." Descending from the sky and comforting the Bodhisatta, he remained on the surface of the mud.

## The Goose King Sends Him Back
The Bodhisatta thought, "While the ninety thousand geese have abandoned me and fled, this Sumukha alone has come. How is it? When the hunter comes, will he abandon me and flee, or will he not?" To test him, while still smeared with blood and hanging from the snare-stick, he wished to examine General Sumukha.

## A True Friend
Hearing those words, General Sumukha thought, "This Goose King does not know my status as a dear friend; he regards me as a false friend. I shall show him my state of affection as a true friend." Wishing to show this:

94. O Great King, most excellent among the host of geese. I am your companion, conceived, born, and raised together with you on the same day. I am a true and beloved friend, like your right eye. I dwell in your heart and am known as your commander.

95. O Great King, named Dhataraṭṭha. If I go from here, how shall I speak in the midst of my kinsmen? Having abandoned you and gone from your feet, what shall I say of your fate? O Great King, especially noble among the birds. I shall give up my life here at your feet. I do not venture to perform the practice of the ignoble and unrighteous.

## Well Done
When Commander Sumukha spoke these brave words in four verses, the Bodhisatta, wishing to reveal the virtues of Commander Sumukha, said:
384:
## The Hunter Khema Arrives
While the two golden geese were conversing, the hunter's son, standing by the lake, saw the geese fleeing in three groups. Wondering what had happened, he looked toward the place where the snares were set and saw the Bodhisatta, the Golden Goose King, hanging from the snare-post. Filled with great joy, he tucked up his loincloth firmly, took his club, and approached swiftly like the fire at the end of an aeon, treading on the mud with his heels so that it splashed up over his head and fell in front of him.

The All-Knowing Buddha, wishing to clarify this matter, said:

98. "While those noble ones of noble conduct were thus consulting, the hunter took his staff and approached quickly and violently."
... (omitted) ...
"Through that pure effort, you shall soon be released from the snare."
He preached these three verses.

98. Monks, while those two noble golden geese of noble conduct were thus consulting and speaking, the hunter Khema took his staff and spear and approached quickly and forcefully.

99. Seeing that hunter Khema approaching, the golden goose commander named Sumukha reassured the trembling Golden Goose King and stood in front of him, uttering a loud cry.

100. O Great King, most excellent among the host of geese, do not be afraid. Those like you do not fear. I will exert effort, a fitting endeavor based on reason and associated with wisdom and energy. Through that pure effort exerted by me, you, Great King, shall soon be released from the snare.

## The Commander's Plea
Thus, Commander Sumukha, having comforted his lord, the Bodhisatta Dhataraṭṭha the Golden Goose King, went to the hunter and, speaking in a sweet human voice, asked, "Friend hunter, what is your name?" When he replied, "Goose King, I am named Khema," Sumukha asked, "For what purpose have you come?" When the hunter said, "I have come to catch the Golden Goose King," Sumukha said:
385:
“Friend Khema the hunter, do not think that this goose caught in the snare you set is just an ordinary goose. The Golden Goose King named Dhataraṭṭha, who is superior to ninety thousand geese, is caught in your snare. He is endowed with wisdom, virtue, and conduct. He abides in the four bases of social harmony (saṅgaha-dhamma). It is not proper to kill this Golden Goose King. I shall perform whatever tasks, great or small, you require with this body of mine. This Goose King has a complexion like gold, and I too have a complexion like gold. I shall sacrifice my life for the sake of this Goose King. If you, hunter, wish to take the feathers of this Golden Goose King, take my feathers. Furthermore, if you wish to take any of the skin, flesh, sinews, or bones, take them from my body alone. If you wish to make this Golden Goose King a pet to play with, use only me for your play. If you wish to generate wealth by selling him alive, sell me alive and generate that wealth. Do not kill the Golden Goose King who is endowed with virtues such as wisdom. This is the truth: if you kill this Golden Goose King, you shall not escape from hell and other states of misery.” Thus, having intimidated the hunter Khema with the fear of hell and other miseries, and having made him accept his sweet words of Dhamma, Sumukha went back to the Bodhisatta and stood there comforting him.

## The Hunter Pays Homage

Having heard the words of the general Sumukha, the hunter Khema thought, “This being, though an animal, performs such an act of friendship that even humans are unable to do. Even humans cannot abide in such a nature of friendship. Oh, how wonderful this golden goose is! He is endowed with wisdom, speaks sweet words of Dhamma, and is truly a guardian of righteousness.” His entire body became filled with joy and gladness, and with his hair standing on end, he threw away his staff, placed his hands in reverent salutation upon his head, and stood praising the virtues of the general Sumukha as if worshipping the sun.

To make this matter clear, the Omniscient Buddha said:

101. Having heard those well-spoken words of Sumukha, the hunter, with hair standing on end, raised his hands in salutation.

102. “Never have I heard or seen a bird speaking in human tongue, a curved-necked one speaking noble words, uttering human speech.”

103. “What is this bird to you, that you attend to the one who is bound while you are free? Other birds have abandoned him and fled; why do you remain alone?”

101. Monks, the hunter Khema, having heard those well-spoken words of Sumukha, with joyful hair standing on end, paid homage to Sumukha with joined palms.

102. Friend Golden Goose, you are a bird with a curved neck, yet how wonderful it is! Speaking of the noble King of Geese, who is noble in conduct—
386:
“I have never heard nor seen such a thing.” Regarding the phrase “What is this bird to you,” he asks, “What is he to you that you attend to him?”

Being thus questioned by the hunter with a delighted heart, Sumukha thought, “This hunter has become soft-hearted. Now I will show him my virtues to make him even more tender-hearted,” and he said:

104. “He is my King, O friend of birds; he made me his general. I cannot bear to abandon that Lord of Birds in his time of calamity.”

105. “He is the provider for a great flock; let him not come to ruin alone. Thus, friend hunter, as I say, so it is. He is my master, and I delight in being near him.”

104. Friend hunter, this Golden Goose is my King. He appointed me to the position of general. I do not dare to abandon our lord, the King of Geese, when he has met with danger.

105. Friend hunter, this master of mine has a great following. Friend hunter, let him not come to ruin alone. Just as I say, so it is. This is my master, and I delight in his presence.

106. “You are of noble conduct, O curved-necked one, you who respect your provider. I release your master to you; may you both go in happiness.”

106. Noble Golden Goose, you who show respect to the Golden Goose King who is your provider of food, you are endowed with the conduct of the virtuous. I shall release your master. May both of you Golden Geese go according to your desire.

Comforting him, [the hunter said]: “Now I have seen you uttering human speech. Before this time, I have never heard nor seen a bird speaking in human tongue.”

103. Friend Golden Goose, you are free from the snare, yet you approach this Golden Goose King who is bound. What is the relationship between you and this Golden Goose King? Other geese have abandoned the Golden Goose King and fled; why do you remain behind alone?

## The Wisdom of the General

Thus, when questioned by the hunter Khema with a delighted heart, the general Sumukha thought, “This hunter’s heart has softened. Now, to make him even more tender-hearted, I shall show him my virtues.”

## The Golden Geese are Released

When the hunter heard the sweet words of Dhamma based on Sumukha’s account, he reached a state of joy and gladness. With his hair standing on end, he thought, “If I were to kill this Golden Goose King who is endowed with virtues such as morality, I would not escape the four lower realms. Let the King do to me whatever he wishes; I shall release this Golden Goose King as a noble gift to the general Sumukha.” Wishing to release him, he thought thus.

Having said this, the hunter Khema, with a tender heart, approached the Bodhisatta Golden Goose King, lowered his staff, and placed him on the muddy ground. He then loosened the snare from the staff, lifted the Bodhisatta, and took him out of the lake. Placing him on a bed of fresh dabba grass, with great affection and a heart of loving-kindness, he took water, washed away the blood, and stroked him repeatedly.
387:
Having loosened the bound snare gently, and having established a strong affection for the Great Being, the hunter took water with a mind of loving-kindness, washed away the blood, and massaged the wound repeatedly. Then, by the power of his loving-kindness, vein joined with vein, flesh with flesh, and skin with skin; the Bodhisatta's foot became normal, no different from the other foot. The Bodhisatta, having attained comfort, sat in his natural state. When the General Sumukha saw the King of Swans' state of comfort brought about by his own actions, he felt great joy and thought: “This hunter has done us a great favor, yet we have done no favor for him. If he takes us for the sake of the King's high ministers, he will receive much wealth by bringing us to them. If he takes us for his own sake, he will surely receive wealth by selling us. I will ask him first.”

Then, desiring to return the favor, he asked the hunter:

107. “If you set the snare for the swans and other birds for your own sake, friend, we accept your word. This Lake Khemā is a place of sanctuary and a noble lake.”

108. “But if you did not set the snare for the swans and other birds for your own sake, then by releasing us without authority, you would be committing theft, O hunter.”

These were the two verses he spoke.

107. Friend hunter, if you set the snare for the swans and other birds for your own sake, we accept your word. This Lake Khemā is a place of sanctuary and a noble lake.

108. O hunter, if you did not set the snare for the swans and other birds for your own sake, then by releasing us without authority, you would be committing theft.

At that time, by the power of the hunter's loving-kindness, vein joined with vein, flesh with flesh, and skin with skin. The Bodhisatta's foot became normal, no different from the foot that was not caught in the snare. The Bodhisatta, having attained comfort, sat in his natural state.

## Why were they caught?

When the General Sumukha saw the state of comfort of the Bodhisatta, the Golden Swan King, which was due to his own efforts, he was filled with joy and thought: “This hunter has done us a great favor. We have done nothing to favor this hunter. If this hunter catches us for the sake of the King's great ministers and others, he will receive much wealth by bringing us to them. If he catches us for his own sake, he will receive wealth by selling us. I will ask the hunter first.”

Having thought thus, and because he wished to return the favor, he asked:

Upon hearing those words, the hunter Khema said, “I did not catch you, noble Golden Swan Kings, for my own sake. Indeed, I was ordered to catch you by our lord, the King of Bārāṇasī named Saṃyama.” He then related the entire story, starting from the time Queen Khemā had the dream, until the King heard of the Golden Swans' arrival and sent him, saying, “Friend Khema, strive to catch one or two swans; I shall grant you great status,” and gave him provisions for the journey. He reported all these events to General Sumukha.

## Take us to the King

Upon hearing the words of the hunter Khema, General Sumukha thought: “This hunter has performed a difficult task by releasing us without regard for his own life. If we were to go from here only to Mount Cittakūṭa, the power of our lord Dhataraṭṭha the Swan King's wisdom would not be known, my quality of friendship would not be known, the hunter's son would not receive great status, King Saṃyama would not be established in the five precepts, and Queen Khemā's heart's desire would not be fulfilled.” Thinking thus, he said, “Friend hunter Khema, if this is the case, you will not be able to release us.
388:
Having thought thus, he spoke this verse to reveal the matter: “Friend, since this is the case, you cannot release us. Show us to your King; he shall do with us as he pleases.”

109. “To whichever King you are a servant, by all means, take us to that very King. There, King Saṃyama will do as he pleases.”

109. Friend hunter, to whichever King you are a servant, by all means, take us to the presence of that very King, your lord. There, in the King's palace, King Saṃyama—or one who has a restrained heart—will do as he desires.

110. Thus spoken to, the hunter Khema took both golden-colored, golden-skinned [swans] with both hands and placed them in the cages.

111. Taking those two birds in the cages, both of radiant color—Sumukha and Dhataraṭṭha—the hunter departed.

These were the two verses the Teacher (the Buddha) spoke.

110. O Bhikkhus, thus spoken to by General Sumukha, the hunter Khema took both Golden Swan Kings, who had the color of gold and skin like gold, with both his hands and placed them in the cages.

111. Taking those two Golden Swan Kings—General Sumukha and the Golden Swan King Dhataraṭṭha—who were in the cages and endowed with radiant color, the hunter Khema departed.

“Show us to King Saṃyama; let that King do with us as he pleases,” he said, wishing to make this matter clear to the hunter Khema.

Hearing this, the hunter Khema said, “Noblest ones, do not desire to be shown to the King. Kings are full of danger; they might keep you as pet swans or they might kill you.”

When he said this, General Sumukha said to the hunter Khema, “Friend hunter, do not worry about us. I have produced gentleness through Dhamma talk even in a harsh and cruel person like you; why should I not be able to produce gentleness in a king? It is true that kings are wise; they know how to distinguish between good speech and bad speech. Take us quickly to the presence of the King. When you take us, do not take us by binding us. Place us in flower cages and take us. When making the flower cages, make a large cage covered with great white lotuses for our lord Dhataraṭṭha the Swan King, and for me, make a smaller cage covered with red lotuses. Then, placing our lord Dhataraṭṭha in front and me behind and lower, take us and show us quickly to the King.”

Upon hearing the words of General Sumukha, the hunter Khema felt great joy, thinking, “When Sumukha sees the King, he will surely want the King to grant me great status.” He made cages with soft vines, covered them well with lotuses, and following the instructions given, he took the two Golden Swan Kings and departed.

To make this matter clear, the All-Knowing Buddha said:
389:
## Longing for the Female Goose

In this way, when the hunter Khema was carrying away these two golden goose kings, the golden goose king Dhataraṭṭha, remembering his queen who was the daughter of King Pāka, called General Sumukha and lamented through the power of his own defilements.

The All-Knowing Buddha, making that matter clear, said:

112. Harīyamāno dhataraṭṭho, sumukhaṃ etadabravi.
...
Koñcī samuddatīreva, kapaṇā nū na rucchati.

He preached these two verses.

112. Monks. Dhataraṭṭha, the golden goose king who was being carried away by the hunter Khema, said this to General Sumukha: "Friend Sumukha, I greatly fear for the death of Sāmā, who is endowed with noble signs on her thighs and has the color of gold. Having the thought that we are dead, she will surely kill herself, thinking, 'What is the use of my life when my dear husband, the golden goose king, is dead?'"

113. "Friend Sumukha, the queen named Suhemā, who is the daughter of King Pāka and has very beautiful skin like gold thread, will surely weep like a lonely crane bird on the seashore."

## The Faults of Women

Hearing the words of the golden goose king's lament, General Sumukha thought: "This golden goose king, while he ought to be advising others, laments because of a woman through the power of defilement. It has become like water catching fire, or like a fence rising up and eating the crops in the field (instead of protecting them). Indeed, I will show the faults of women through my own power to make this golden goose king understand." Wishing to show this to the golden goose king, he said:

114. Evaṃ mahanto lokassa, appameyyo mahāgaṇī.
...
Tāsu yo vissase poso,
390:
So naresu narādhamo.

He spoke these verses:

114. "O Great King Dhataraṭṭha, though you are so great in the world of beings, though you are endowed with immeasurable virtues, and though you are the leader of a great flock, that you should grieve for a single woman—this grief appears as if you are not a wise man."

115. "O Great King, just as the wind carries both good and bad scents, or as a fool greedy for food eats both raw and ripe fruit, or as a greedy blind man eats whatever food is given—so do women associate with all men, whether they be low or noble."

116. "O Great King, you appear to my mind like a fool who does not know how to distinguish between what is a cause and what is not. Having reached the turn of death, you do not know what should or should not be done."

117. "O Great King, whoever thinks that women are excellent is like a half-mad drunkard who laments. For truly, these women are common to many men, like a tavern for drunkards."

118. "O Great King, these women are like magicians because they are deceitful. They are like mirages because they cannot be grasped by the heart. They cause grief, they cause disease, and they bring many calamities. These women..."
391:
"...are harsh and stubborn because of their anger. They are the cause of bondage. They are the snares of death. They dwell in the cave of the body. Any man who trusts in them is the lowest of men."

## The Virtues of Women

After that, because the golden goose king Dhataraṭṭha had a mind attached to women, he said: "You do not know the virtues of women; only the wise know them. They should not be blamed." Wishing to show the virtues of women, he spoke these seven verses:

119. Yaṃ vuddhehi upaññātaṃ, ko taṃ ninditumarahati.
...
Sopajja saṃsayaṃ patto, atthaṃ paṇhāhi mā mukhaṃ.

He spoke these seven verses:

119. "Friend Sumukha, what has been understood by the elders regarding women, who is worthy of blaming that? In the world..."
392:
In the world, those called women possess great virtues. In the beginning of the era, they appeared first.

120. Sumukha, in those women, playfulness of body and speech is established. In those women, delight in sensual pleasures is also established. In those women, the seeds of Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Noble Disciples, Universal Monarchs, Mandhātā, and others arise. Whatever beings there are, they are born in the wombs of those women. Having risked one's own life for the life of women, what man could be weary of them?

121. Sumukha, you alone are preoccupied with the affairs of women. No one else but you. Now, when danger has arisen for you, wisdom is born out of fear.

122. Indeed, everyone reaches uncertainty. A wise person, even when facing death, endures fear. Only the wise and the great engage in difficult tasks.

123. For this purpose, kings desire a brave and wise counselor. A brave person can ward off whatever danger exists. He can act for his own protection.

124. Sumukha, let the king's cooks not slaughter us in the kitchen today. Just as the fruit that grows depending on the bamboo kills that very bamboo, so let the golden color of your wings not kill you.
393:
126. Sumukha, apply that effort which is appropriate and connected with the Dhamma. Through your pure effort, strive for my life.

127. O Great King, best among those who fly, do not fear. Indeed, those like you do not fear. I shall apply appropriate effort connected with the Dhamma. Through my pure effort, you shall soon be released from the snare of suffering.

125. Sumukha, although you were free from the snare, you did not wish to fly away. You came to captivity yourself. Now I too have reached uncertainty regarding my life. Take up my welfare. Do not think of reasons to disparage women.

## Give Me Life

Thus, the Bodhisatta Golden Goose King, by praising the virtues of women, left General Sumukha with nothing to say. Knowing Sumukha's displeasure, he now sought to encourage him again.

## Stay at Ease

Then General Sumukha thought, 'This Golden Goose King is exceedingly afraid of the threat of death; he does not know the power of my wisdom. Once I see the King of Bārāṇasī and get to speak a few words, he will know. For now, I will comfort him.' Wishing to comfort him, he spoke.

## They Have Reached the Palace

While these two Golden Goose Kings were conversing in the language of birds, the hunter Khema did not understand anything. He simply carried the two Golden Goose Kings on a carrying-pole and entered the city of Bārāṇasī. As it was a marvelous and unprecedented sight, the multitude followed them with hands joined in reverence. When the hunter Khema reached the palace gate, he sent word to the King regarding his arrival.
394:
128. That hunter, with a carrying pole of geese, approached the royal gate. "Report me to the King; I have come for Dhataraṭṭha."

The Teacher spoke this verse:
128. "Bhikkhus, that hunter Khema approached the palace gate with a carrying pole of geese. 'O friends, report to the King: This golden goose king Dhataraṭṭha has arrived.'"

129. Seeing those two, resembling merit, both recognized by their marks, King Saṃyamana addressed the ministers.
130. "Give the hunter clothes, food, and drink; let him have as much gold as he desires."

The Teacher spoke these two verses:
129. "Bhikkhus, the King of Bārāṇasī named Saṃyamana, seeing those two noble geese who possessed merit like his own, indeed addressed the ministers thus:"
130. "'O ministers, give the hunter Khema clothes and garments, rice and drinks, and various kinds of food. Let this hunter be given as much gold as he desires.'"

To clarify this matter, the All-Knowing Buddha said:

## The King Bestows Rewards

The gatekeeper went and reported the matter to the King. The King, filled with joy, said, "Let him come quickly." Surrounded by his host of ministers, seated on the royal throne under the raised white umbrella, he saw the hunter Khema ascending to the upper terrace of the golden palace carrying the two golden geese on a pole. Looking at the two golden geese, he thought, "My heart's desire is fulfilled," and he commanded the ministers to perform the necessary duties for the hunter Khema.

To clarify this matter, the All-Knowing Buddha said:

Having shown his appreciation in this way and being filled with joy, the King said, "Go, adorn that hunter and bring him back." Then the ministers led the hunter down from the palace, trimmed his hair and beard, bathed him, anointed him with perfumes, adorned him with all kinds of ornaments, and presented him to the King. Then the King granted him great wealth and status, including twelve villages that yielded a revenue of one hundred thousand each per year, a chariot harnessed with thoroughbred horses, and a large, decorated house.

Having received such great status, the hunter Khema, wishing to reveal his deed to the King, said, "Great King, I have not brought just any ordinary goose; this is the king of ninety thousand geese named Dhataraṭṭha, and this is the general named Sumukha."
395:
Then the King asked him, "Friend, how were these caught?" To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:

131. Seeing the hunter with a pleased mind, the King of Kāsi then said: "Friend Khema, if this lake of ours is full of geese,"
132. "How did you, with snare in hand, approach the one who is delightful to look at? How did you seize the noble one who was surrounded by a host of kin?"

The Teacher spoke these two verses:
131. "Bhikkhus, the King of Bārāṇasī, the ruler of Kāsi, seeing the hunter Khema with a pleased mind, spoke these words: 'Friend hunter Khema, if this Khema Lake of ours remains full of geese,'"
132. "'How did you, with snare in hand, approach the delightful golden goose king in the midst of the flock? How did you capture the great golden goose king who was surrounded by his host of relatives?'"

133. "Today is my seventh night of waiting at the feeding grounds; seeking his footprints, I waited diligently in a pit."
134. "Then I saw his footprints as he searched for food; there I set the snare, and thus I caught that bird."

The hunter spoke these two verses:
133. "Great King, today is the seventh night since I have been approaching the feeding grounds. Seeking the footprints where the golden goose king treads, I waited diligently, leaning in a pit like a large jar."
134. "Then I saw the footprints of that golden goose king as he wandered in search of food. In the place where I saw those footprints, I set the snare. By setting it thus, I captured that bird."

135. "Hunter, these birds are two, yet you speak of one; is your mind deranged, or what do you intend?"

The King spoke this verse:
135. "Hunter, these golden geese are two. Yet, though there are two, you speak as if there were only one. Is your mind deranged? Or if not, what is your intention?"

The hunter reported, "This golden goose king is the general of the geese named Sumukha."

## How Were They Caught?

Then the King asked the hunter, "Friend hunter, how did you capture these geese?" To clarify this matter, the All-Knowing Buddha said:

The hunter Khema, wishing to explain to the King how he captured the golden goose kings, replied:

## Only One?

Hearing those words, the King thought, "This hunter, even while standing at the gate to report, reported only the arrival of the golden goose king Dhataraṭṭha. Now, too, he says he caught only this one golden goose king. What could be the reason for this?" Wishing to question the hunter, he said:

## One Who Was Captured

Thereafter, the hunter Khema said, "Great King, my mind is not deranged."
396:
He spoke these two verses:

136. He who has red streaks, beautiful like refined gold, which stand touching his breast—he has come into my snare.

137. Then this radiant bird, though unbound, stood by the bound one in distress, speaking like a noble one and uttering human speech.

136. O Great King. To which Golden Goose King the red streaks, three in number, have the beauty of sunlight and stand touching his breast—that Golden Goose King has come into my snare.

137. O Great King. Then, this radiant Golden Goose Commander, who was not caught in the snare, stood comforting the distressed Golden Goose King who was caught in the snare, while uttering speech in the language of humans, like a noble one of virtuous conduct.

He spoke this verse:

138. Now then, Sumukha, why do you stand with your beak closed? Or, having reached my assembly, do you not speak because you are trembling with fear?

138. Sumukha, you are one who speaks pleasant words of Dhamma. That being so, why do you now stand with your mouth closed? How is it? Having reached my assembly, do you not speak because you are afraid of danger?

"I do not wish to give this one Golden Goose to anyone other than your Majesty. Indeed, only one Golden Goose was caught in the snare I set." Saying this, the hunter Khema wished to clearly show the reason and report it to the King:

"O Great King, at that time, knowing that King Dhataraṭṭha was caught in the snare, Sumukha turned back and comforted the King. When I approached, he came to meet me and, while still in the sky, spoke pleasant and polite words to me. He stood there speaking of the virtues of his lord, King Dhataraṭṭha, in human language. Having softened my heart, he stood again in front of the Golden Goose King. O Great King, upon hearing the well-spoken words of the Commander Sumukha, I was filled with a devoted heart and released King Dhataraṭṭha. Thus, the release of King Dhataraṭṭha from the snare and my coming to this palace bringing these two geese were both brought about by the Commander Sumukha alone." Thus, the hunter Khema reported the words of Sumukha's virtues.

## Is Sumukha Afraid?

Hearing that report, the King desired to hear the Dhamma discourse of Commander Sumukha. Even as he was honoring the hunter, the sun set. Lamps were lit. Many people, including nobles, assembled. Queen Khemā also sat on the right side of the King, surrounded by various dancers and attendants. At that moment, the King, wishing to make Sumukha speak, uttered a verse:
397:
He spoke this verse:

139. I am not afraid, O Lord of Kāsi, having entered your assembly. It is not out of fear that I will not speak; I shall speak when such a matter of benefit arises.

139. O Great King, Lord of Kāsi. Having entered your assembly, I am not afraid. It is not that I do not speak because of fear of the assembly. When a matter of such benefit arises, I shall speak.

He spoke these two verses:

140. I see no reinforcements for you, nor chariots, nor infantry. I see no shield or pot-lid, nor armored archers.

141. I see no silver or gold, nor a well-constructed city, with a wide moat, difficult to cross, and strong watchtowers and gates. Entering where, Sumukha, do you not fear what is to be feared?

140. Sumukha, I do not see any armed soldiers as your reinforcements. I do not see chariot-warriors. I do not see infantry. I do not see any shields, nor soldiers holding pot-sherds, nor archers clad in armor.

141. I do not see silver, nor gold, nor a well-established city. I do not see a moat filled with water that is difficult to cross, nor strong watchtowers and gates. I do not see the reason why you, having entered here, do not fear that which should be feared.

He spoke these three verses:

142. I have no need for reinforcements, nor for a city or wealth. We travel by a path that is no path; we are dwellers in the sky.

143. We are heard to be wise, subtle thinkers of meaning. We speak words of benefit, and we are established in truth.

144. Moreover, for you who are untruthful, ignoble, a liar, and cruel, what will even a well-spoken word do?

142. O Great King. I have no need for an entourage or reinforcements. I have no need for a city or wealth. We travel through the sky, which is not a path for feet. We are those who move in the sky.

143. You, O King, have heard of us as being wise. We are subtle and can contemplate the meaning. If we are established only in truth, we shall speak words that are beneficial.

144. O Great King. For you who do not keep the truth, who are not noble, who speak falsehoods, and who are cruel, what will be achieved even if well-spoken words are uttered?

## I Am Not Afraid, Your Majesty

Hearing those words, Commander Sumukha wished to show the King that he was not afraid.

## Why Are You Not Afraid?

Hearing those words, the King, wishing to prolong Sumukha's speech, spoke jokingly again.

## The Basis of Fearlessness

When the King asked, "What is the reason for your fearlessness?", Sumukha wished to tell the King the reason for that fearlessness.

## Being a Wicked King

Hearing those words of Sumukha, the King said, "Why do you call me a wicked man who speaks falsehoods? What have I done?" Then Sumukha said, "O Great King, if that is so, then listen," and wishing to show the King's falsehood, he said:

145. By the word of the Brahmins, you had this Khema [lake] made... (etc.)
398:
Crossing both boundaries, one arises in the unpleasant state.

He spoke these four verses:

145. "Great King, because of the words of the brahmins, you had this Khema lake dug. You proclaimed safety (abhaya) in these ten directions."

146. "Geese came to your Khema lake, which has very cool, clear, and pure water. There is abundant food in that lake, and there is no harming or killing of birds there."

147. "Great King, hearing this proclamation of safety, we have come to your presence. We are now caught in your snare; this statement of yours was a lie."

148. "Great King, when one puts falsehood and evil desire, which is called greed, at the forefront, crossing both boundaries—"
399:
—namely the two types of rebirth in the human and celestial worlds, one passes beyond them and arises in the unpleasant state of hell.

## Desiring to Hear the Dhamma

In this way, he shamed the king in the midst of the assembly. Then the king, wishing to reveal the reason to Sumukha, said, "Friend Sumukha, I did not have you caught because I wanted to kill you and eat your flesh. Indeed, having heard of your wisdom, I had you caught because I wished to hear well-spoken Dhamma."

149. "Sumukha, we will not kill you, nor did I catch you out of greed. You are known as wise and subtle thinkers of hidden meanings."

150. "Perhaps those wise ones who have come here to our palace might speak words endowed with reason. We wish to hear such words. Friend Sumukha, because of that desire to hear words endowed with reason, the hunter was told to catch you."

## The General's Discourse

Hearing the words spoken by King Saṃyama, the general Sumukha said, "Great King, you who wish to hear good Dhamma have done what is improper." To explain this to the king, he spoke these six verses:

151. "O Lord of Kāsi, King Saṃyama, when beings reach the turn of death and their lives are led to the realm of the King of Death, they do not speak words endowed with reason."

152. "Great King, one who kills a wild deer using a decoy deer, or a wild bird using a decoy bird—you have 'bought' a wise preacher of Dhamma using the famous Khema lake as a decoy. What act could be more ignoble than this act of yours?"

153. "Great King, he who speaks the sound of the noble Dhamma with his mouth but practices ignoble conduct with his body—such a person who speaks only with words but acts wickedly—perishes from both worlds, both in this present world and the world beyond."
400:
154. "Great King, one who has attained glory, wealth, and attendants should not be negligent. When facing the doubt of death, one should not be distressed. One should strive only in one's duties and close the openings (of vice)."

155. "Great King, those wise ones of great virtue who have passed from this present world, even though they reached the turn of death, because they practiced merit in this life, they have thus reached the celestial realm."

156. "O Lord of Kāsi, Great King, having heard this Dhamma that I have preached, protect the Dhamma within yourself. And release Dhataratṭha, the most excellent among the geese."

## To Release the Geese

Hearing the words of General Sumukha, King Saṃyama wished to release the Golden Goose Kings. To reveal the virtues of General Sumukha to his ministers and others, he spoke these three verses:

157. "O ministers, bring water for washing the feet, oil for massaging the feet, and a seat worthy of noble ones. I shall release Dhataratṭha, the one of great fame, from the cage."
401:
158. "Sumukha, the general, who is wise, subtle, and a thinker of deep matters, who is happy when his master, the Golden Goose King, is happy, and who is sorrowful when his master is sorrowful."

159. "O ministers, such a one as this Sumukha deserves to eat the master's food; he is a true friend who shares the very life of the King."

## The Geese were Attended to

Hearing the words of King Sanyama, the ministers prepared seats for the two Golden Goose Kings. Having washed the feet of the two Golden Goose Kings seated there with scented water, they anointed them with oil that had been cooked a hundred times. Desiring to make this matter clear, the Teacher said:

160. "Monks, Dhataraṭṭha sat upon a throne made entirely of gold, with eight legs, delightful to the mind, and covered with fine cloth from the kingdom of Kāsi."

161. "Monks, the general Sumukha sat down next to Dhataraṭṭha on a golden couch covered with tiger skin."

162. "Many people of Kāsi, taking golden bowls, offered those two geese excellent food of various flavors sent by King Sanyama."

## The Great King and the Golden Goose King

Those two geese ate the parched rice from the golden bowls and drank the sweet, excellent water. Then, the Bodhisatta Dhataraṭṭha, seeing the food brought by King Sanyama and his devotion, exchanged pleasantries and asked about all matters. King Sanyama answered all the questions asked by the Golden Goose King.

Desiring to make this matter clear, the Teacher said:

163. "Seeing the excellent food sent and brought by the King of Kāsi, the Golden Goose King, skilled in royal duties, then asked immediately:"
402:
The Teacher spoke these seventeen verses:

163. "Monks, seeing the excellent food sent and brought by King Sanyama, the ruler of Kāsi, the Golden Goose King, who was skilled in royal duties, then asked at that time:"

164. "O Great King, are you well? Are you free from illness? Is this kingdom of Kāsi prosperous, and do you rule according to the Dhamma?"

165. "O Goose, I am well and free from illness. Moreover, this kingdom of Kāsi is prosperous, and I rule according to the Dhamma."

166. "O Great King, is there no fault among your ministers? When your affairs arise, do they not disregard their own lives to serve you?"

167. "O Goose, there is no fault among my ministers. Moreover, when my affairs arise, they do not disregard their own lives."

168. "O Great King, are your wives of similar birth, obedient to you as their husband, sweet-spoken, endowed with children, beauty, and wealth, and do they follow your will?"

169. "O Goose King, my wives are of similar birth, they listen to my words, they are sweet-spoken, endowed with children, beauty, retinue, and wealth, and they follow my will."

170. "O Great King, do you rule the kingdom without oppression, without any danger from anywhere, without violence, and with justice and impartiality?"

171. "O Goose King, I do not oppress the kingdom; there is no danger from anywhere. I rule without violence, with justice and impartiality."

172. "O Great King, do you respectfully attend to the virtuous and avoid the wicked? Do you refrain from following unrighteousness by abandoning the Dhamma?"

173. "O Goose King, I respectfully attend only to the virtuous and avoid the wicked. I follow only the Dhamma; unrighteousness is abandoned by me."

174. "O Khattiya, do you look far into the future? Are you heedless in matters of intoxication? Do you not fear the next world?"

175. "O Noble Bird, I look far into the future. Established in the Ten Royal Virtues, I do not fear the next world."
403:
## The Ten Royal Virtues

176. O Goose, Golden King of Geese! Charity (dāna), morality (sīla), self-sacrifice (pariccāga), uprightness (ajjava), gentleness (maddava), austerity (tapa), non-anger (akkodha), non-violence (avihiṃsā), patience (khanti), and non-opposition to the people (avirodhana).

177. Thus, I see these wholesome qualities established within myself. Because I see them so, great joy and immense happiness arise within me.

178. O Goose, Golden King of Geese! This Sumukha, who travels through the sky, without thinking and without knowing the state of our mind, released harsh words.

179. O Goose, Golden King of Geese! That Sumukha, being angry, uttered harsh words improperly. [He spoke of faults] in us...
404:
...which do not exist. He spoke of those faults. This speech of Sumukha does not appear to me like the words of a wise person.

## The General's Apology

Hearing this, Sumukha the general thought, "I have disparaged a king who is endowed with virtue. He is angry with me; I shall ask for his forgiveness." To seek forgiveness, he spoke these two verses:

180. O Lord of Men, O Great King! I have committed this transgression in haste. When my lord Dhata-raṭṭha, the Golden Goose King, was captured, I felt immense sorrow. Because of that distress, I spoke those erring words.

181. O Great King! You are like a father to his children. You are like the earth, the support of all living beings. May you be our refuge. O Noble King, O Chief among Men! Please forgive our offense committed through the power of anger.

## The King's Satisfaction

Sumukha the general descended from his seat, folded his wings in a gesture of reverence, and spoke these words. Then King Saṃyama embraced Sumukha, placed him on a golden pedestal, and wishing to accept his confession of fault, said this verse:

182. O Bird, O Sky-traveler, O friend Sumukha! Because you do not conceal the fault hidden in your heart, we rejoice in your honesty. You have broken through the mental obstruction; you are indeed upright. We rejoice in your removal of this mental thorn and in your uprightness.

183. Whatever treasures there are in the palace of the King of Kāsi—silver, gold, pearls, and many lapis lazuli gems;

184. Many rubies, conch shells, pearls, fine Kāsi cloth, red sandalwood, antelope skins, ivory goods, and much copper and iron—all this wealth I give to you both, O Golden Goose Kings. I relinquish my sovereignty to you.

## The Kingdom is Offered

Having said this, King Saṃyama, being pleased with the Great Being's Dhamma discourse and the general Sumukha's uprightness, thought, "One who is pleased should show signs of pleasure." Wishing to hand over the great city of Bārāṇasī along with his royal splendor to the two Golden Geese, he spoke these verses.
405:
185. "O Bull among charioteers, most excellent among kings! O King of Kings, we have indeed been honored and respected by you. May you be our teacher, practicing in the ways of the Dhamma (the ten paths of wholesome action)."

186. "O Teacher, O Tamer of Enemies, O Lord of the Palace! Having been permitted by you and having known your will, we, having circumambulated you, wish to see our kinsmen."

These two verses were spoken.

185. O Bull among charioteers, most excellent among those who ride chariots. O King of Kings, god among men. You, O Great King, have indeed honored us. We have been respected. We have been honored. You, O Great King, may you be our teacher for us who practice in the Dhamma of the ten paths of wholesome action.

186. O Teacher, standing in the place of a teacher. O Tamer of Enemies, who is able to discipline foes. O Lord of the Palace. You, O Great King, have permitted us. We, who have known your will, having circumambulated you to the right, wish to see our multitude of kinsmen.

187. "The Buddha said: 'O Monks, at that time, the King of Kāsi, having thought and consulted with those two Golden Geese for the whole night as he desired, gave permission to the most excellent of geese.'"

This verse was preached.

187. O Monks, at that time, the King of Kāsi, having thought and consulted with those two Golden Geese for the whole night as he desired, gave permission to the Golden Goose King, who is the most excellent among the multitude of geese.

## The Geese Requesting Permission to Return

After saying these words, he honored the two Golden Geese with a white parasol and offered them the kingship of Bārāṇasī. Then the Bodhisatta, Dhataraṭṭha the Golden Goose, wishing to converse with the king—

## The Golden Geese are Freed

That King Saṃyama permitted the geese to go. While the Bodhisatta Dhataraṭṭha was preaching the Dhamma, dawn broke. To clarify this, the Blessed One said:

When King Saṃyama of Bārāṇasī gave permission, the Bodhisatta exhorted the king: "Rule with diligence and according to the Dhamma," and established him in the Five Precepts. The King of Bārāṇasī offered the two Golden Geese parched rice in golden bowls and sweet, noble water. After they had finished eating, he honored them with flowers and perfumes. The King himself carried the Bodhisatta in a golden basket, and Queen Khemā carried the Commander Sumukha. They opened the noble lion-window at sunrise and released them, saying, "Noble sirs, please proceed."

To clarify this, the Blessed One said:
406:
188. "The Buddha said: 'O Monks, then at the end of the night, at sunrise, while the King of Kāsi watched, those two Golden Geese flew into the sky from the palace.'"

This verse was preached.

188. O Monks, at that time, at the end of the night, at sunrise, while the King of Kāsi watched, those two Golden Geese flew into the sky from the golden palace.

189. "O Monks, at that time, the multitude of geese, seeing those two noble birds arriving free from illness, made their own sound 'Keka'. A great sound arose."

190. "O Monks, those geese, out of respect for their master, seeing their master freed from the hands of the enemy, were delighted and, having found their support, surrounded them on all sides."

These two verses were preached.

189. O Monks, at that time, the multitude of geese, seeing those two noble Golden Geese arriving free from illness, made their own sound 'Keka'. A great sound arose.

190. O Monks, when their master, the Golden Goose King, was freed from the hands of the enemy, those geese, who respect their master, were delighted and, having found their place of support, surrounded them on all sides.

191. "O Monks, just as the two Golden Geese of the Dhataraṭṭha clan, who are good friends, returned to their kinsmen with prosperity, so too for those who have good friends, all their goals result in success."

This verse was preached.

191. O Monks, just as the two Golden Geese of the Dhataraṭṭha clan, who are good friends, returned to their kinsmen with prosperity, so too for those who have good friends, all their benefits result in success.

## Arrival at Mount Cittakūṭa

Among the two Golden Geese, the Bodhisatta flew up from the golden basket, stood in the air, and comforted King Saṃyama of Bārāṇasī, saying, "O Great King, do not worry; practice our exhortation with diligence." Then, taking Commander Sumukha, he went to Mount Cittakūṭa.

At that time, ninety thousand geese came out of the golden cave and, staying on the slopes of Mount Cittakūṭa, saw the two Golden Geese arriving and went out to welcome and surround them. Surrounded by their kinsmen, the two Golden Geese entered the plateau of Mount Cittakūṭa.

To clarify this, the Blessed One said—

## The Geese Sending Metta

Having surrounded them, the geese asked, "O Great King, by what means were you freed?" The Bodhisatta Dhataraṭṭha told them how he was freed because of Commander Sumukha, and about the deeds done by King Saṃyama and the hunter's son.

Hearing this, the multitude of geese were delighted and said, "May Commander Sumukha, King Saṃyama, and the hunter's son be happy, free from suffering, and live a long life."

To clarify this, the Blessed One said—
407:
The Omniscient Buddha, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, said: "Monks, not only now has Ānanda sacrificed his life for my sake; in the past also, he sacrificed his life for my sake." Then he identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the hunter's son was Channa, Queen Khemā was the nun Khemā, King Saṃyama was Sāriputta, the Golden Goose commander Sumukha was Ānanda, the rest of the assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and the Golden Goose King Dhataraṭṭha was I myself."

## Through Gratitude and Sacrifice of Life, Prosperity and Happiness Will Follow

The Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka is concluded.

## 3. Sudhābhojana Jātaka

## On the Elimination of Stinginess and Avarice

The Present Story: While the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, was residing at Jetavana Monastery, he told this Sudhābhojana Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Neva kiṇāmi," concerning a monk who was inclined towards generosity.

That monk, having been a young man of good family in Sāvatthī, heard the Buddha's Dhamma teaching and, with a heart full of faith, went forth into the monkhood. He was one who fulfilled the precepts, was endowed with the virtues of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), practiced the holy life, and possessed a well-developed mind of loving-kindness (mettā). He was diligent in serving the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha three times a day, was perfect in conduct, and was inclined towards generosity. He fulfilled the duties of hospitality (sāraṇīya-dhamma). Even when he had only enough food for himself, if recipients were present, he would give it away, even if it meant he had to go without food. Therefore, his inclination and delight in generosity became well-known among the community of monks.

## The Generous Monk

One day, the monks started a conversation in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, this monk named so-and-so is inclined towards generosity and delights in giving. Even if he receives only a handful of water, he cuts off greed and gives it to his fellow practitioners. His inclination is like that of a Bodhisatta."

The Omniscient Buddha, hearing this conversation with his divine ear (dibbasota), came out from the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) and asked: "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such a discussion," he said: "Monks, in the past, this monk was not of a giving nature; he was stingy and would not give even a drop of oil from the tip of a blade of grass. At that time, I tamed him, made him disciplined, praised the fruits of giving, and established him in generosity. He took a vow in my presence, saying, 'Even if I receive only a handful of water, I will not drink it without giving some away.' Due to the power of that vow taken in the past, he has become inclined towards and delights in generosity." Having said this, being requested by the monks, he related the past story.

The Past Story: Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, there was a wealthy householder with a fortune of eighty crores. At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī appointed that householder to the position of Treasurer (Seṭṭhi).

That householder, being honored by the king, the citizens, and the country folk, one day looked at his wealth and thought: "I did not obtain this glory and wealth in a past life by sleeping, nor by committing bodily misconduct and the like. Indeed, it was obtained by fulfilling virtuous deeds. In the future also, it is proper for me to create a foundation for myself."
408:
Having thought thus, the householder went to the king and said: "Great King, there are eighty crores of wealth in my house; please take that wealth." The king replied: "Treasurer, I have no need for your wealth; my own wealth is abundant. If you wish, you may take wealth from my palace." The treasurer asked: "Great King, how is it? May I be allowed to give away my own wealth?"

Then King Brahmadatta said to the treasurer: "Do as you please with your wealth." The treasurer then had six alms-halls built—at the four city gates, in the center of the city, and at the door of his own residence—and practiced great generosity, distributing six hundred thousand pieces of money every day.

## The Stingy Treasurer

That treasurer gave alms throughout his life and, after instructing his sons, "Do not break this lineage of my generosity," he was reborn as Sakka at the end of his life. His son also gave alms in the same way and was reborn as the god Canda. The second treasurer's son gave alms in the same way and was reborn as the god Suriya. The third treasurer's son gave alms in the same way and was reborn as Mātali. The fourth treasurer's son gave alms in the same way and was reborn as Pañcasikha.

The son of the fifth treasurer, who was the sixth in line, upon attaining the position of Treasurer, became known as Macchariyakosiya. He also possessed a fortune of eighty crores.

## The Extremely Frugal One

This Treasurer Macchariyakosiya thought: "My father and grandfathers were fools; they threw away wealth that was accumulated with great difficulty. As for me, I will guard this wealth and will not give even a little to anyone." Thinking thus, he destroyed the alms-halls, burned them with fire, and became harsh and stingy.

Then, beggars and mendicants gathered at the door of Treasurer Macchariyakosiya's house, raising their arms and crying out loudly: "Great Treasurer, do not destroy the tradition of almsgiving of your own father and grandfathers! Give alms!" Hearing those cries, the people reviled him, saying: "Treasurer Macchariyakosiya has broken his own tradition of almsgiving."

Treasurer Macchariyakosiya, being ashamed, stationed guards to prevent beggars from coming to his house door. Those beggars and mendicants, having no support, no longer looked toward the treasurer's house door. From that time on, the treasurer only accumulated wealth. He did not enjoy it himself, nor did he give it to his wife, children, or others. He ate only broken rice with sour gruel as a second dish. He wore only coarse clothes woven from cotton thread. Carrying a leaf-umbrella over his head, he traveled in an old, dilapidated chariot drawn by old oxen. Thus, the wealth of this base treasurer was like a coconut found by a dog.

## Deprived of Nutrition

One day, while the treasurer was going to serve the king, he thought, "I will go and call the junior treasurer," and went to the junior treasurer's house. At that moment, the junior treasurer, surrounded by his children, was eating milk-rice prepared with fresh ghee, honey, and granulated sugar.
409:
When the junior treasurer saw the Great Treasurer Maccharikosīya, he rose from his seat and said, "Great Treasurer, please come; let us sit on this couch and eat milk-rice together." Upon seeing the milk-rice, saliva formed in the mouth of that Treasurer Maccharikosīya. He desired to eat it. Even though he desired to eat, he thought again: "If I eat this milk-rice, when this junior treasurer comes to my house, I will have to reciprocate with hospitality. If I have to reciprocate, my wealth will be destroyed." Thinking thus, he said, "I will not eat."

Even though he was repeatedly entreated, he said, "I am full now," and did not wish for it. While the junior treasurer was eating, he sat there watching with much saliva in his mouth. At the conclusion of the junior treasurer's meal, he went with him to the King's palace, saw the King, and after descending from the palace and reaching his own home, he was oppressed by the craving to eat milk-rice and thought:

"If I say I want to eat milk-rice, many people will also want to eat it. Much rice and other ingredients will be destroyed. I will not say anything to anyone." Having thought so, that treasurer spent days and nights thinking only of milk-rice, but out of fear of losing his wealth, he told no one and endured the hunger. Gradually, being unable to endure it, he became pale like a withered leaf. Even though he was pale, he did not speak out of fear of losing wealth. Later, becoming weak, he lay down embracing his bed.

## Cooking Milk-Rice in Hiding

Then his wife approached that Treasurer Maccharikosīya and, stroking his back with her hand, asked, "Lord, what is your discomfort?" He replied, "Lady, attend to the discomfort in your own body; I have no discomfort." She said, "Lord, you have become pale like a withered leaf. Do you have some worry? Or is the Great King angry with you? Or have your children shown you disrespect? Or has some craving arisen?"

When he said, "Lady, a craving has arisen in me," she said, "Lord, tell me of the craving that has arisen." He replied, "Lady, I will not tell of that craving." She asked, "Lord, will I be able to fulfill that craving?" He said, "If the time is suitable for it to be fulfilled, I will fulfill it," but even so, he did not dare to speak for fear of losing wealth. When that wife repeatedly pressed and questioned him, he spoke:

"Lady, one day I saw the junior treasurer eating milk-rice well-prepared with fresh butter, honey, and sugar. From that time on, I have desired to eat such milk-rice." When he said this, she said, "O wretched man! What is this? Are you poor? I will cook enough milk-rice for the whole city of Bārāṇasī." When she said that, it was as if the treasurer had been struck on the head with a staff.
410:
The treasurer became angry with his wife and said, "I know you are very wealthy. If you have wealth brought from your parents' house, cook milk-rice with that wealth and give it to all the city dwellers." She said, "In that case, I will cook enough for those living in one street." He replied, "What benefit is there for you in letting those people eat your wealth?" She said, "In that case, I will cook enough for those living in seven houses here and there." He said, "What benefit is there for you from those people?" She said, "I will cook enough for the group of servants living in this house." He said, "What benefit is there for you from those people?"

She said, "In that case, I will cook enough for only our children and relatives." He said, "What benefit is there for you from these children and relatives?" She said, "In that case, I will cook enough for just the two of us, husband and wife." He said, "What would you do with it? It is not suitable for you." When she said, "In that case, I will cook enough for only you, my lord," he replied, "Do not cook for me either. Indeed, if this milk-rice is cooked in this house, many people will desire it. Give me one measure of rice, a quarter measure of milk relative to the rice, a bowl of sugar, a bowl of butter, a bowl of honey, and a pot for cooking milk-rice. I will go into the forest, cook there, and eat." When he said this, the wife did as the treasurer said.

The treasurer had a servant take everything and told him, "Go, stay in such-and-such a place." Having sent the servant ahead, he went alone in disguise to the place he had designated. By the river, he made a fireplace in a hollow, had wood and water brought, and said, "Go and stand on a path; if you see anyone, give me a sign. Come only when I call you." Having sent the servant away, he lit a fire and cooked the milk-rice.

## Sakka Comes to Receive Alms

At that moment, Sakka, King of Devas, looked at his own collection of glory: the decorated celestial city of Sudassana which is a thousand leagues in extent, the golden celestial street of sixty leagues, the Vejayanta palace a thousand leagues high, the Sudhammā celestial hall of five hundred leagues, the Paṇḍukambala stone throne of sixty leagues, the golden flower and white parasol five leagues in circumference, the host of celestial nymphs numbering twenty-five million, and his own decorated and prepared person. Thinking, "By what merit did I obtain such celestial sovereignty and bliss?" he saw the alms-giving he had performed when he was a treasurer in the city of Bārāṇasī.

After that, looking to see where his sons and others were reborn, he saw that his son was reborn as the deva Canda. Canda's son was the deva Suriya. Suriya's son was the deva Mātali. Mātali's son was the deva Pañcasikha. Seeing the rebirth of all of them, he looked to see what the son of the deva Pañcasikha was like, and he saw the cutting off of his lineage.

Then this thought occurred to Sakka, King of Devas: "This wretched man has become stingy; he neither enjoys things himself nor gives to others. This wretched man is cutting off my lineage. When he dies, he will be reborn in hell. By admonishing this wretched man, I will establish my lineage and create the cause for this wretched man to be reborn in this celestial realm of ours."
411:
Having thought thus, the King of the Devas summoned the deity Candana and others, saying, "Friends, come, let us go to the human world. The merchant Maccharikosiya has cut off our lineage. He has destroyed our alms-halls and set them on fire. He neither enjoys his wealth himself nor gives to others. Now, desiring to eat milk-rice, he thought, 'If I cook at home, I will have to give milk-rice to others,' so he entered the forest and is cooking alone. Let us go and discipline that base man, making him understand the benefits of giving. Indeed, if all of us were to beg together, he might die right there. I will go first, and while I am sitting there having asked for the milk-rice, you should come one by one in the guise of brahmins and ask for it." Having given these instructions:

He himself first approached the merchant Maccharikosiya in the guise of a brahmin and asked, "O Merchant, which is the road to Bārāṇasī?" Then the merchant Maccharikosiya said to the King of the Devas, "Are you mad? You do not even know the road to Bārāṇasī. Why have you come here? Go away from here!"

Although the King of the Devas heard the merchant's words, he acted as if he did not hear and approached the merchant, asking, "What did you say?" The merchant shouted, "Hey, deaf brahmin! Why have you come here? Go forward!"

Then the King of the Devas said to the merchant, "O Merchant, why do you cry out? Smoke is seen. Fire is seen. Are you cooking milk-rice? This must be a place where brahmins are invited. I too will receive a little when the food is given to the brahmins. Why do you drive me away?" When the merchant replied, "There is no invitation for brahmins here; you go forward," Sakka said, "If that is so, why are you angry? I will receive a little when you eat."

Then the merchant said to the King of the Devas, "Brahmin, I will not give you even a single mouthful. This milk-rice is only a little; I have cooked just enough for myself. I obtained this only by asking. Why? You go and seek food elsewhere." Referring to the fact that he had obtained it by asking his wife, and wishing to let the brahmin know this, he spoke this verse:

192. I neither buy nor sell, nor do I have a store.
412:
193. From a little, one should give a little; from a medium amount, a medium portion.
From much, one should give much. Not giving is not appropriate.

194. Therefore I tell you, Kosiya, give gifts and enjoy them yourself.
Ascend the path of the noble ones; one who eats alone does not find happiness.

He spoke this pair of verses.

193. Kosiya, O Merchant Kosiya. From a little object, one should give a little object. From half of a small object, one should give a half-portion. From much wealth, one should give much. Not giving should not happen.

194. Kosiya, O Merchant Kosiya. Therefore, I tell you. Ascend well the path traveled by noble persons. Give gifts. Enjoy them yourself too. Even if one eats alone, one will not obtain the three types of happiness.

195. His sacrifice is in vain, and his effort is in vain,
who eats food alone while a guest is sitting there.

196. Therefore I tell you, Kosiya, give gifts and enjoy them yourself.
Ascend the path of the noble ones; one who eats alone does not find happiness.

He spoke this pair of verses.

195. Kosiya, O Merchant Kosiya. Whoever eats food alone while a guest is present, for that person, the gift offered is in vain. The effort spent in accumulating wealth is also in vain.

196. Kosiya, O Merchant Kosiya. Therefore, I tell you. Ascend well the path traveled by the Noble Ones (Ariyas). Give gifts. Enjoy them yourself too. One who eats alone will not obtain the three types of happiness.

197. His sacrifice is true, and his effort is true,
who does not eat food alone while a guest is sitting there.

198. Therefore I tell you, Kosiya, give gifts and enjoy them yourself.
Ascend the path of the noble ones; one who eats alone does not find happiness.

He spoke this pair of verses.

197. Kosiya, O Merchant Kosiya. Whoever does not eat food alone while a guest is present, for that person, the gift is true. The effort to produce wealth is also true.

198. Kosiya, O Merchant Kosiya. Therefore, I tell you. Ascend well the path traveled by the virtuous. Give gifts. Enjoy them yourself too. One who eats alone will not obtain the three types of happiness.

This small amount was obtained with great difficulty;
this bowl of rice is not enough for two.

He spoke this verse.

192. Brahmin, I neither buy nor sell this milk-rice. Nor do I have milk-rice stored up. This milk-rice was sought with great difficulty. It is only a little. This milk-rice is just one bowl's worth. It is not enough for the two of us.

Hearing those words, the King of the Devas said, "I too will recite a verse for you with a sweet voice; listen to that verse." Even as the merchant was forbidding him, saying, "I have no need for your verse"—

The merchant, hearing the words of the King of the Devas, said, "Brahmin, you speak pleasant words. When the milk-rice is cooked, you shall receive a little. Stay." The King of the Devas sat in a suitable place.

## The Arrival of the Deity Candana to Receive Alms

After the King of the Devas had sat down, the deity Candana approached the merchant in the same manner as before, and while the merchant was still forbidding him, he initiated the conversation in the same way—

The merchant, hearing the words of the deity Candana, initiated the conversation in the same manner as before and, with great reluctance, said, "If that is the case, stay. You shall receive a little." That deity Candana went and sat near the King of the Devas.

## The Arrival of the Deity Suriya to Receive Alms

Thereafter, the deity Suriya approached the merchant in the same manner as before, and while the merchant was still forbidding him, he initiated the conversation in the same way—
413:
199. A man offers sacrifice at a lake, and at the many-bodied Gaya, at the Dona and Timbaru fords, in the swift-flowing great river.

200. There his sacrifice is made, there his effort is successful. When a guest is seated, one should not eat food alone.

201. Therefore I tell you, Kosiya: give gifts and enjoy them yourself. Ascend the Noble Path; one who eats alone finds no happiness.

These three verses were spoken.

199. Kosiya, the merchant Kosiya. Poso, a being. Sarañca, approaching a lake. Juhati, offers sacrifice. Bahukāya ca, and at the river named Bahukā. Gayāya ca, and at the lake named Gaya. Hearing these words of the deity Suriya, he reluctantly and with difficulty said, "If that is so, then stay; you shall receive a little." That deity Suriya went and sat near the deity Canda.

## Matali Comes to Beg

Then the deity Mātali approached the merchant in the same manner as before, and while the merchant was still trying to refuse, he spoke these verses—

Hearing the words of the deity Mātali, the merchant felt as if he were crushed by a mountain peak and reluctantly said, "If that is so, then stay; you shall receive a little." The deity Mātali went and sat near the deity Suriya.

## Pañcasikha Comes to Beg

Thereafter, the deity Pañcasikha approached in the same manner as before, and while the merchant was still trying to refuse, he spoke this pair of verses—

202. He swallows a fish-hook with a long line and its attachment, who eats food alone while a guest is seated.

203. Therefore I tell you, Kosiya: give gifts and enjoy them yourself. Ascend the Noble Path; one who eats alone finds no happiness.

He spoke this collection of two verses.

202. Kosiya, the merchant Kosiya. Yo, whoever. Atithismiṃ, while a guest. Nisinnasmiṃ, is staying. Eko, alone. Bhojanaṃ, food. Bhuñjati, eats. So, that person who eats alone while a guest is present. Dīghasuttaṃ, having a long string. Sabandhanaṃ, together with the attachment. Baḷisaṃ, the fish-hook. Nigilati, is like one who swallows.

203. Kosiya, the merchant Kosiya. Taṃ tasmā, therefore. Taṃ, you. Vadāmi, I tell. Ariyamaggaṃ, the path traveled by the virtuous such as the Buddhas. Samāruha, ascend well. Dānāni, gifts. Dehi, give. Bhuñja ca, and enjoy them yourself. Eko, alone. Bhuñjamāno, one who eats. Sukhaṃ, the three kinds of happiness—human, celestial, and Nibbāna. Na labhate, shall not obtain.

## Giving the Milk-Rice

The miserly merchant Kosiya, hearing these words, groaned in distress and said, "If that is so, then stay; you shall receive a little." The deity Pañcasikha went and sat near the deity Mātali.

Thus, as soon as those five Brahmins were seated, the milk-rice was cooked. Then the merchant Kosiya took the milk-rice off the stove and said, "Bring your bowls."

Those five Brahmins did not get up, but while remaining seated, they stretched out their hands and brought Māluva leaves from the Himālaya. The merchant Kosiya, seeing the Māluva leaves, said, "I do not have enough milk-rice to give you in such leaves; bring leaves of the Khadira tree and such."

When he said this, the Brahmins brought those Khadira leaves. Each single Khadira leaf was the size of a chariot floor-board.

The merchant took the milk-rice with a ladle and gave it to all the Brahmins. Even after giving to all the Brahmins, the amount in the cooking pot did not decrease. After giving to the five Brahmins, he himself sat down holding the cooking pot.

At that moment, Pañcasikha arose, discarded his Brahmin form, and having transformed into a dog, went in front of the merchant and urinated. The Brahmins covered their milk-rice with leaves. A drop of urine fell on the back of the merchant Kosiya's hand.

## Chased by the Dog

The Brahmins acted as if they were washing their hands with water from their water-pots and eating the milk-rice. The merchant Kosiya said, "Give me some water too; I will wash my hands and eat."

They replied, "Bring your own water and wash your hands."

He said, "I have given you milk-rice; give me a little water." When he said this, they replied, "We do not perform the act of giving in return (piṇḍapaṭipiṇḍaka)."

He then said, "If that is so, please watch over this milk-rice; I will go wash my hands and return," and he went down to the river.

At that moment, the dog filled the milk-rice pot with urine. When the merchant saw the dog urinating, he took a large staff and came threatening the dog. That dog became the size of a noble steed, and while chasing the merchant, it assumed various colors—sometimes black, sometimes white, sometimes golden, sometimes speckled, sometimes tall, and sometimes short. Thus, having assumed various colors, it chased the miserly Kosiya.
415:
“This is Mātali, the divine charioteer.
I am Sakka, the lord of the Thirty-three.
And this one is called Pañcasikha.”
He spoke these verses.

205. O Great Merchant! The deity Canda and the deity Suriya, both of them have come here. This one is Mātali, the divine charioteer. As for me, I am Sakka, the lord of the gods of the Thirty-three. And this one is known as the deity Pañcasikha.

207. “Those who are miserly and stingy,
And revilers of ascetics and brahmins,
Having cast off the physical body here,
Go to hell upon the dissolution of the body.”
He spoke this verse.

207. O Great Merchant! Those who are miserly, stingy, and deceitful, and all those who revile those who have calmed and abandoned evil (ascetics and brahmins)—having abandoned the physical body here in this human world, after the dissolution of the body, they go to hell.

[The dog] was of black color, and also white; it was of a color like gold, and also spotted; it was tall, and also short. Thus, having various appearances, it followed the merchant Macchariya Kosiya. That merchant, being afraid of death, approached the brahmins. Those brahmins then flew up and stayed in the sky.

## Knowing They Are Devas
Seeing the psychic power of those brahmins, the merchant, wishing to question them, spoke this verse:

204. “O Brahmins, these are indeed of magnificent appearance,
And for what reason does this dog of yours
Manifest various colors and forms?
Tell us, O Brahmins, who are you?”

204. O Brahmins! These brahmins are indeed of very beautiful appearance. O Brahmins, for what reason does this dog of yours manifest various noble and lowly colors? Tell us, who are you?

Hearing the merchant's words, Sakka the King of Devas, wishing to tell the merchant, spoke this verse:

205. “Canda and Suriya, both have come here...”

After speaking this verse, Sakka, wishing to praise the divine bliss of those deities, spoke this verse:

206. “Hand-cymbals, drums, and lutes,
And the Ālambara drums,
Wake me from sleep,
And being awakened, I rejoice.”

206. O Great Merchant! The sounds of hand-cymbals, the Mudinga drums, the Muraja drums, and the Ālambara drums wake me, who am sleeping. And I, being awakened, rejoice.

## The Deceitful Go to Hell
Hearing Sakka's words, the merchant asked, “O King of Devas, by performing what deed do you obtain such divine bliss?” Sakka, showing that those who do not practice giving, who are of evil conduct, and who are miserly and deceitful do not reach the celestial realm but are reborn only in hell, spoke this verse to show the merchant:

## Rebirth in Heaven through Meritorious Deeds
Having spoken this verse about how the miserly go to hell, he spoke another verse to show the attainment of the celestial realm by those who, free from stinginess, are established in the ten courses of meritorious action (kamma-patha):
416:
209. “You were our relative in former births,
That miserly, offensive, and evil-natured person.
We have come here for your benefit alone,
Lest you, being of evil nature, go to hell.”
He spoke this verse.

209. O Great Merchant! You were our relative in former births. You, who are offensive, are miserly and of evil conduct. We have come here for your benefit alone. May you, who are of evil conduct, not go to hell.

208. “Those who desire a good destination,
Standing in Dhamma, restraint, and sharing,
Having cast off the physical body here,
Go to a good destination upon the dissolution of the body.”
He spoke this verse.

208. O Great Merchant! All those who long for a good destination, who are established in the ten courses of meritorious action (Dhamma), in the restraint of body, speech, and mind, and in sharing through giving—having abandoned the physical body here in this human world, after the dissolution of the body, they go to a good destination.

## Telling the Truth
Having shown this, he said, “O Kosiya, we did not come to your presence for the sake of milk-rice; rather, we have come because we wish to protect you out of compassion,” and wishing to inform the merchant of the reason, he spoke.

## Please Instruct Me
Hearing those words, the merchant Kosiya, with a pleased mind, thinking, “These beings indeed desire my welfare; they wish to lift me out of hell and establish me in the celestial realm,” and wishing to urge Sakka to instruct him, spoke these three verses:

210. “Surely you are well-wishers to me, since you instruct me.”
“Having abandoned sense-pleasures according to their limits.”
He spoke these three verses.

210. O Sakka! Surely, you deities are my well-wishers because you instruct me. Because you instruct me so, you desire my welfare. O deities who seek my welfare, I shall follow everything that you have spoken.

211. O Sakka! From this very day, I shall cease from being miserly. I shall do no evil, however slight. There shall be no object, however small, that I will not give. I shall not drink even a palmful of water without giving.

212. O Vāsava! O Sakka! While I am giving in this manner at all times, these riches of mine will be exhausted. O Sakka! When they are thus exhausted, I shall renounce the sense-pleasures of various kinds and become an ascetic.
417:
Sakka, the king of devas, having admonished the treasurer Macchariya Kosiya and made him disciplined, taught him the Dhamma to make him understand the fruits of giving. He established him in the five precepts and returned to the celestial city together with those four devas.

## Becoming an Ascetic
The treasurer Macchariya Kosiya, having entered the city and obtained permission from the king, gave away his wealth to beggars and solicitors, filling whatever vessels they brought. He said, "Take as much as you desire." When his wealth was exhausted, he renounced the world and went to the forest. Between the Ganges and a lake called Jātasara on the southern side of the Himālaya, he built a leaf-hut and became an ascetic. Subsisting on forest roots and fruits, he lived there in the Himālaya for a long time and reached old age.

## The Ascetic Nārada Creates a Dispute
At that time, Sakka had four daughters: Āsā, Saddhā, Sirī, and Hirī. These four goddesses took many celestial flowers and went to Lake Anotatta to play in the water. After playing there, they sat on a Manosilā stone slab.

At that moment, a brahmin ascetic named Nārada went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven for his day-rest. After resting in the Nandana and Cittalatā groves, he carried a Pāricchattaka flower like an umbrella for shade and was traveling above the stone slab where the goddesses were sitting, heading toward his dwelling in a golden cave. Then, those four goddesses saw the Pāricchattaka flower in the hand of the ascetic Nārada and asked for it.

The Buddha, wishing to clarify this matter, spoke these five verses:

213. "On the noble mountain Gandhamādana, the best of mountains..." and so on, ending with "Whichever among you is the best, let her wear it."

213. Monks, on the noble mountain named Gandhamādana, the best of mountains, those four goddesses protected by Sakka, the king of devas, were joyfully playing in the water. The noble ascetic Nārada, who is capable of traveling to all worlds (human and celestial), arrived at this place carrying a well-blossomed branch of the Pāricchattaka tree.

214. Monks, this Pāricchattaka flower is pure, fragrant, honored by the Tāvatiṃsa devas, and frequented by the noble immortals. It is not obtainable by mortals or even by the Dānavas; it is suitable only for those devas.
418:
