215. Monks, then those four goddesses, whose skin was like the color of gold, the best among women—Āsā, Saddhā, Sirī, and then Hirī—stood up from their places and spoke these words to the sage, the brahmin Nārada.

216. "O Brahmin, O Great Sage, if this flower of the Pāricchattaka tree has not been designated for anyone by you, please give it to us. May all your heart's desires be fulfilled. May you be to us just like Vāsava, our father."

217. Monks, observing the goddesses who were begging for the Pāricchattaka flower, the ascetic Nārada considered and spoke these words, uttering a speech that would cause a dispute: "O daughters of devas, I have no need for these Pāricchattaka flowers. Whichever among you four is the most excellent, let her wear it."

[Commentary]: He explains, "I have no use for these flowers because I have abstained from wearing garlands." "Whichever among you is the best" means whichever among you is the eldest or most superior. "Let her wear it" means let her adorn herself with it.

Upon hearing his words, those four goddesses spoke this verse to the ascetic to test his judgment of who was superior or inferior:

218. "O Nārada, you yourself should observe who is the most excellent. To whomever you wish, please give it. O Nārada, to whomever among us you give it, she alone shall be considered the best among us."

219. "O goddesses of beautiful form, these words of yours are not proper for me. What brahmin would stir up a dispute? If you do not know who is superior or inferior here, go from here and ask your father, the Lord of Beings (Sakka), himself."

220. Those goddesses, greatly provoked by Nārada and intoxicated by the pride of their beauty, went to the presence of the Thousand-Eyed One and asked the Lord of Beings, "Father, who among us is the most excellent?"
419:
218. "O Nārada, you yourself should observe who is the most excellent. To whomever you wish, please give it. O Nārada, to whomever among us you give it, she alone shall be considered the best among us."

219. "O goddesses of beautiful form, these words of yours are not proper for me. What brahmin would stir up a dispute? If you do not know who is superior or inferior here, go from here and ask your father, the Lord of Beings (Sakka), himself."

220. Monks, those goddesses, having been addressed by the ascetic Nārada, became greatly provoked and, intoxicated by the pride of their beauty, went to the presence of the Thousand-Eyed One (Sakka) and asked the Lord of Beings, "Father, who among us is the most excellent?"

[Commentary]: "Whichever among you is the most excellent, let her wear these Pāricchattaka flowers."

Hearing the words of Nārada, those four goddesses, wishing to have the ascetic himself judge their superiority, replied to him.

## Asking Sakka
Hearing the words of those goddesses, the ascetic Nārada called them and directed them to ask Sakka.

Then the goddesses went and asked their father Sakka. The Buddha, wishing to clarify this matter, spoke the verse beginning with "Tā Nāradena...".

Sakka, seeing his daughters, asked, "Dear daughters, who caused your dispute?" The Buddha, wishing to clarify this matter, spoke the verse.

Then the daughters, wishing to report clearly to their father Sakka, spoke.
420:
221. Seeing them with anxious minds, Purindada, the lord of gods to whom they paid homage with joined palms, spoke thus: "You all appear equal in beauty, O blessed ones; who then has stirred up this quarrel?"

221. Bhikkhus, monks. Seeing those goddesses with anxious and preoccupied minds, Purindada, the lord of gods to whom the deities pay homage with joined palms, spoke these words: "O daughters of beautiful form, you all appear equal to one another. O blessed ones, who in this place has stirred up this quarrel?"

222. "The Great Sage who wanders through all the worlds, Nārada, who is established in Dhamma and of true endeavor, spoke to us on the noble mountain Gandhamādana: 'Go and ask the Lord of Beings himself; if you do not know who is superior or inferior here.'" This verse was spoken.

222. O Lord of Beings, lord of the deities, dear father. There is a Great Sage named Nārada, who is able to travel through all the worlds of men and gods, who is established in the practice of Dhamma, and who possesses unerring effort. That Great Sage spoke to us on the noble mountain named Gandhamādana: "If you do not know who is superior or inferior in this place, go and ask only your father, the Lord of Beings, the King of the Gods." Thus did the sage Nārada speak to us.

## Going to Ask the Hermit Kosiya

Upon hearing the words of his daughters, the father, Sakka, thought: "These four goddesses are all my daughters. If I say that one among these four is endowed with virtue and is superior, the remaining daughters will be angry with me. I cannot decide this case myself. I will send these daughters of mine to the hermit Kosiya in the Himālaya; that hermit Kosiya will decide their case."

Thinking thus, he said: "I will not decide the quarrel of my dear daughters. There is a hermit named Kosiya in the Himālaya. I will send him divine ambrosia (sudhā). That hermit Kosiya does not eat without giving to others; he eats only after giving. Even when giving, he discriminates and gives only to those who possess virtue. Among you four, whichever goddess receives the divine ambrosia from the hand of that hermit Kosiya shall be the superior one." Desiring to inform his daughters of this matter, he spoke.

After the King of the Gods had sent his daughters to the hermit Kosiya, he called the young deva Mātali, desiring to send him also to the hermit.
421:
223. "That Great Sage who wanders in the vast forest does not eat his meal without having given to others, O fair-limbed ones. Kosiya gives gifts after discriminating; she to whom he gives shall be the best."

223. O dear daughters of noble form. That Great Sage named Kosiya, who dwells in the great forest, does not eat his meal without giving to others. He eats only after giving. The hermit Kosiya gives gifts after careful selection and discrimination. It is true; to whichever goddess that hermit Kosiya gives, she alone is exceptionally superior.

224. "He dwells in the southern direction on the bank of the Ganges, on the slopes of the Himālaya. That Kosiya has food and drink hard to obtain. O divine charioteer, deliver this ambrosia to him."

224. O Mātali, the divine charioteer. That hermit named Kosiya dwells in the southern direction on the slopes of the Himālaya, by the bank of the river Ganges. That hermit Kosiya possesses food and drink that are difficult to obtain. O Mātali, go and offer this divine ambrosia to that hermit Kosiya.

## The Divine Ambrosia is Received

The young deva Mātali took the divine ambrosia and offered it to the hermit Kosiya. Desiring to make this matter clear, the All-Enlightened Blessed One spoke this verse:

225. Sent by the lord of gods, Mātali mounted the chariot drawn by a thousand horses. Quickly reaching the hermitage, he offered the ambrosia to the Sage while remaining invisible.

225. Bhikkhus, monks. At that time, Mātali, sent by the King of the Gods, mounted the chariot drawn by a thousand Sindh horses. Very swiftly reaching the hermitage of the hermit Kosiya, he offered the divine ambrosia to the hermit while his body remained invisible.

Holding the bowl of divine ambrosia and standing there, the hermit Kosiya, desiring to ask Mātali about the matter, spoke these two verses:
422:
226. "While I was worshipping the sun, the light-maker, the supreme dispeller of the world's darkness, after performing the fire-oblation... who was it that placed this ambrosia in my hands?"
227. "Like a conch shell, white, of incomparable sight, pure, fragrant, pleasant, and wonderful; never before seen by my eyes—which deity placed this ambrosia in my hands?"

226. O friends. After performing the water and fire oblations, while I was worshipping the sun—the light-maker, the supreme dispeller of darkness in the world—who was it that, surpassing all beings, placed this divine ambrosia in my hands? Was it Vāsava?

227. This divine ambrosia is like a conch shell, brilliantly white, of incomparable appearance, pure, fragrant, pleasant to behold, and marvelous. Truly, it has never been seen before by my eyes in this life. Which deity placed this in my hands?

Thereafter, Mātali, desiring to explain the matter to the hermit Kosiya, spoke these two verses:

228. "I am sent by Mahinda, the seeker of great virtue. I have brought this ambrosia swiftly, O Great Sage. Know me as Mātali, the divine charioteer. Eat this supreme food; do not refuse it."
229. "When eaten, it destroys twelve evils: hunger, thirst, discontent, fatigue, exhaustion, anger, malice, strife, slander, cold, heat, and sloth. This is the supreme flavor."

228. O Great Sage, seeker of noble virtues. I am sent by the King of the Gods, Mahinda. I have brought this divine ambrosia swiftly. Know me as Mātali, the divine charioteer. Please partake of this excellent ambrosia; do not refuse it.

## The Power of Divine Essence

229. Venerable sir. When this divine ambrosia is consumed, it removes hunger for food...
423: 230. It is not fit for me to eat, Mātali, without having given first; this is my supreme vow. Thirst, discontent, distress and fatigue, anger, malice, strife, slander, cold, heat, and sloth—in this way, it dispels the twelve wicked and evil consequences. This divine ambrosia is of supreme taste. Hearing these words, the ascetic Kosiya, wishing to reveal his practiced vow, spoke this verse: 'Eating alone is not praised by the Noble Ones, and one who does not share does not find happiness.' 230. Mātali, it is not fit for me to eat without having given first. I have undertaken this supreme vow. Even eating alone is not praised by the virtuous ones such as the Buddha. One who is not in the habit of sharing does not obtain the happiness of men, gods, or Nibbāna. Having spoken this verse, Mātali asked: 'Venerable sir, what fault did you see in eating without giving to others that you undertook this vow?' To inform Mātali of the reason, he spoke these two verses: 231. Those who are killers of women, those who are adulterers... [etc.] ...they are regarded as pure and truthful. 230. Mātali, those who are killers of women, those who are adulterers, those who betray their friends, those who curse virtuous ascetics and brahmins, and those for whom stinginess is the fifth—all these are base. Therefore, I would not consume even water without giving to others. 232. Mātali, I will surely give the gift praised by the wise to a woman or a man. In this world, those who are faithful, who know kind words, and are free from stinginess...
424:
...endowed with faith. *Vadaññū*, knowing the right words (charitable). *Vītamacchara*, free from stinginess. *Ete*, these people. *Suci*, are pure. *Saccasammata*, are regarded as noble persons. *Bhavanti*, they are.

## The Hermit and the Goddesses
Hearing those words, the young deva Mātali stood with a visible body. At that moment, the four goddesses stood in the four directions. Goddess Sirī stood in the eastern direction. Goddess Āsā stood in the southern direction. Goddess Saddhā stood in the western direction. Goddess Hirī stood in the northern direction.

The Omniscient Buddha, wishing to make this matter clear, spoke these five verses:

233. *Atho matā devavarena pesitā,*
...
*Taṃ maṃ sudhāya varapañña bhājaya.*

233. Monks, *atho*, thereafter. *Devavarena*, by Sakka, the king of devas. *Matā*, permitted. *Pesitā*, sent. *Kanakattacupamā*, having skin like the color of gold. *Āsā ca*, Āsā. *Saddhā ca*, Saddhā. *Sirī ca*, Sirī. *Tato*, and furthermore. *Hirī ca*, Hirī. *Iti*, thus. *Catasso kaññā*, the four goddesses. *Yattha*, where. *Kosiya*, the hermit Kosiya. *Atthi*, is. *Taṃ assamaṃ*, to that hermitage. *Āgamum*, they came.

234. Monks, *subhena vaṇṇena*, with a beautiful appearance. *Aggino sikhāriva*, like the flame of a fire. *Catuddisā*, in the four directions. *Caturo*, endowed with beauty. *Catasso tā kaññā*, those four goddesses. *Disvā*, having seen. *Kosiya*, the hermit Kosiya. *Sabbo paramappamodito*, being entirely delighted without exception. *Mātalinno sammukhāva*, in the very presence of the young deva Mātali. *Iti-idaṃ*, these words. *Abravi*, he spoke.

235. *Devate*, O goddess. *Tvaṃ*, you. *Purimaṃ disaṃ*, in the eastern direction. *Pabhāsi*, shine brightly. *Kā*, who are you? *Alaṅkatā*, being adorned. *Tāravarā osadhīva*, like the morning star, the most excellent of all stars. *Kañcanavelliviggahe*, having a body like a golden statue. *Devate*, O goddess. *Taṃ*, you. *Pucchāmi*, I ask. *Tvaṃ*, you. *Katamā devatā*, which goddess. *Asi*, are you? *Tvaṃ*, you. *Me*, to me. *Ācikkha*, please tell.

## Goddess Sirī
236. *Varapañña*, O hermit of great wisdom. *Ahaṃ*, I. *Sirī devī*, am the goddess named Sirī. *Ahaṃ*, I. *Manujehi*, by humans. *Pūjitā*, am worshipped. *Sadā*, always. *Apāpasattūpanisevinī*, am associated with only noble beings. *Sudhāvivādena*, because of the dispute over the Sudhā food...
425: ...I have come to your presence. Therefore, please grant me a share of the ambrosia. 237. O Great Sage, I desire the ambrosia for that man who then rejoices in all desires. O supreme among those who offer sacrifices, know me as Sirī. O one of supreme wisdom, grant me a share of the ambrosia. Hearing this, the ascetic Kosiya, wishing to reject the words of the goddess Sirī, spoke these three verses: 238. Goddess, men endowed with arts such as training elephants and horses, with knowledge and conduct known as the three Vedas, with wisdom, and with their own diligent efforts, they obtain happiness. But being devoid of you, they do not obtain even a small amount of wealth. This thing that you have done is not good. 239. I see a person who is lazy, gluttonous, of very low birth, and ugly. Yet, being protected by you, Sirī, he commands a man who is of noble birth, wealthy, and happy, as if he were a slave.
426:
240. "Therefore, I know you as one who does not keep her word, who does not associate with discrimination, who is foolish, and who does not follow the wise. One such as you does not even deserve a seat or water. How could you deserve divine ambrosia? I do not like you. Go away!"

## Goddess Āsā

That Goddess Siri vanished right there. Then, wishing to speak with Goddess Āsā, he spoke these two verses:

241. "O Goddess, you with pure white teeth, wearing jeweled earrings, adorned with various seven-fold gems, and wearing smooth golden ornaments—who are you? You shine, wearing a divine white robe like a stream of poured water, and adorned with a garland of Asoka buds as red as a flame of kusa-grass."

242. "O Goddess with gentle eyes, you look like a frightened doe that a hunter with bow and arrow has missed. You look as if you are smiling. Who is your companion here, O gentle-eyed one? Are you not afraid, alone in this great forest?"
427:
243. "O Kosiya, I have no companion here. I am a goddess born in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. I, named Āsā, have come to you, O Lord, because I desire divine ambrosia. O wise one of excellent wisdom, therefore, please grant me the divine ambrosia."

Then, Goddess Āsā wished to explain the reason for her coming to the ascetic.

Hearing the words of Goddess Āsā, the ascetic Kosiya said, "You fulfill the fruits of hope only for those you like, and you do not give hope to those you do not like. You are not impartial; you destroy equality." To show this reason, he spoke these five verses:

244. "O Goddess, merchants seeking wealth travel because of hope. They board ships and cross the great ocean. There, they sometimes sink, or at other times, they return with lost wealth and ruined capital."

245. "O Goddess, farmers plow the fields because of hope. They sow seeds and perform their tasks with various means. Yet, due to the arrival of pests—such as harmful winds, rats, locusts, parrots, or insects—or due to drought, they obtain no harvest of grain from those fields."

246. "Furthermore, men seeking happiness perform their duties for their masters, placing hope at the forefront. For the sake of their master's interests, they are severely oppressed by enemies, and again, without obtaining even a little wealth, they flee in all directions."

247. "O Goddess, those seeking happiness, with minds set on heaven, abandon grain, wealth, and kinsmen because of hope. They practice even harsh austerities for a long time. Taking the wrong path, they go to woeful states."
428:
248. "O Goddess, because of hope, these beings go to woeful states. You, named Āsā, are known as a deceiver. O Āsā, give up your own hope for divine ambrosia. One such as you does not even deserve a seat or water. How could you deserve divine ambrosia? I do not like you. Go away!"

## Goddess Saddhā

That Goddess Āsā, being rejected by the ascetic Kosiya, vanished right there. Then, wishing to speak with Goddess Saddhā, he spoke this verse:

249. "O Goddess with a body like a golden vine, shining with glory and possessing a great retinue, you stand facing the direction called the 'hindmost' (the West). I ask you, O Goddess: who are you? Tell me, which goddess are you?"
429:
Then she spoke this verse:

250. "I am the goddess Saddhā, worshipped by men, always associating with non-evil beings. I have come to you because of the dispute over the ambrosia (sudhā). O one of excellent wisdom, share that ambrosia with me."

250. O Varapañña, hermit of excellent wisdom, I am named Saddhā. I am a goddess who is always worshipped by men. I am associated with by noble beings. O Varapañña, hermit of excellent wisdom, I have come to your presence because of the dispute over whether or not I should receive the celestial ambrosia. Therefore, please share the celestial ambrosia with me.

Then, that goddess Saddhā wished to inform the hermit Kosiya of the reason—

At that time, the hermit Kosiya, wishing to reject the goddess Saddhā, said:

251. "Sometimes, taking up faith, they practice giving, self-control, generosity, and restraint. But again, led astray by you, some commit theft, lying, fraud, and slander."

251. O Goddess, some people, based on faith, occasionally practice giving (dāna), restraint of the senses (dama), generosity (cāga), and the observance of virtue (saṃyama). But some others, led astray by you, again commit theft, lying, fraud in weights and currency, and slander.
430:
252. "O Goddess, a man full of desire, even if he has wives of equal status, endowed with virtue and devoted to their husband, might abandon his desire for noble women and place his faith in a slave girl."

253. "O Saddhā, you alone cause the practice of adultery; you cause evil and neglect merit. One such as you does not deserve even a seat or water, let alone the ambrosia. Go away, you do not please me."

252. O Goddess, a man possessed of craving (taṇhā), even if he has wives of equal status in terms of birth and lineage, who are endowed with virtue and devoted to their husband, might abandon his desire for such noble women and again place his faith in the words of a slave girl.

253. O goddess Saddhā, you alone cause the practice of adultery; you commit evil and have no desire for merit. One such as you does not deserve even a seat or water. How could you deserve the celestial ambrosia? I do not like you. Go away.

## The Goddess Hirī

When the hermit Kosiya said, "These beings, believing someone's words, do more of what should not be done than what should be done when they perform such actions; all that is caused by you," the goddess Saddhā disappeared right there. Then, the hermit Kosiya, wishing to speak with the goddess Hirī who stood in the north, spoke these two verses:

254. "O Goddess, appearing at the end of the night when the dawn rises, possessing excellent beauty and complexion, you appear to me like that [goddess of the east]. Tell me, which celestial nymph (accharā) are you?"

255. "O Goddess, like a dark creeper in the heat, like a flame, moved by the wind..."

254. O Goddess, at dawn when the sun rises, you appear like the goddess who stands in the east, possessing a noble physical form. This goddess standing here appears to me just like that goddess of the east. Tell me, what is your name? Which celestial nymph are you?

255. O Goddess, like a dark creeper in the summer, or like...
431:
256. "I am the goddess Hirī, worshipped by men, always associating with non-evil beings. I have come to you because of the dispute over the ambrosia. But I do not dare to beg for the ambrosia. For a woman, begging is like exposing her nakedness (kopīna)."

256. Venerable sir, I am the goddess named Hirī. I am worshipped by men. I always associate only with noble beings. I have come to your presence because of the dispute over whether or not I should receive the celestial ambrosia. I, such as I am, do not dare to beg for the ambrosia. For a woman, begging is like being shameless.

...moved by a gentle breeze. Like a flame, wearing a garland of red leaves, looking like a gentle deer, you stand there. Who are you? Though you seem to want to speak with me, you do not utter a word.

Then, the goddess Hirī wished to inform the hermit Kosiya of the reason—

Having heard the words spoken by the goddess Hirī, the hermit Kosiya, wishing to give her the ambrosia while praising her, spoke these two verses:

257. "O goddess of beautiful form, you shall receive it by right and by reason. For this is the Dhamma; the ambrosia is not [to be gained] by begging. I invite you who do not beg; I give you whatever you desire of the ambrosia."

258. "Today you are invited by me to my own hermitage, O you with a body like a golden creeper. You are worthy of my worship with all flavors. Having worshipped you, I shall eat the ambrosia."

257. O goddess of beautiful form, you shall receive it by nature and by reason. To receive it in this way is the right way (Dhamma). Since the ambrosia is not to be obtained by begging, therefore, to you who do not beg...
432:
...Not asking. You. I invite. Whatever divine food you desire, that divine food I shall give to you.
258. O Hiri goddess, whose form is like a golden vine, I invite you today to my own hermitage. Truly, I should honor you with all flavors. Having honored you, I shall eat the remaining divine food.

## The Hermitage of the Hermit
Thereafter, the goddess Hiri, endowed with glory and power and permitted by the hermit Kosiya, entered the hermitage of the hermit Kosiya, which was delightful, well-supplied with water, food, and fruit, honored by the virtuous, and always frequented by noble beings.
The Buddha, wishing to clearly show that matter along with the praise of the hermit Kosiya’s hermitage, after his enlightenment, spoke these ten verses:
259. 'O Monks, at that time, the radiant goddess Hiri, permitted by the hermit Kosiya, indeed entered the hermitage of the hermit Kosiya, which was delightful, well-supplied with water and fruit, honored by the virtuous, and always frequented by noble beings.
260. O Monks, in this hermitage of the hermit Kosiya, there are many well-blossomed forest trees bearing flowers and fruits. There are mango trees, piyāla trees, jackfruit trees, and kiṃsuka trees. The sobhañjana trees, loddha trees, and also padmaka trees, keka trees, bhanga trees, and tilaka trees are well-blossomed.
261. Around this hermitage of the hermit Kosiya, there are many sāla trees, karerī trees, and jambu trees. There are assattha, nigrodha, and madhuka trees, as well as vetasa trees, uddālaka trees, pāṭalī trees, and sinduvārika trees. There are also pleasant-smelling mucalinda and ketaka trees.
262. O Monks, around this hermitage, there are beans, bamboo seeds, wild beans, and tinduka fruits. There are sāmāka and nīvāra grains, and also cīnaka millet, wild bananas, domestic bananas, many types of sāli rice, paddy, ābhūjina trees, and husked rice.
263. O Monks, on the northern side of that hermitage, there is a lotus pond that arose naturally, with water free from the smell of rotting fish or shells and free from moss, without steep slopes, excellent, and with water of a non-repulsive scent.
264. In that pond, there are fish that are very delighted, safe, and have plenty of food. There are singū fish, savanka fish, sankula fish, satavanka fish, and rohita fish. There are also āḷivaggara fish, kākiṇṇa fish, pāṭhīna fish, and kākamacchaka fish.'
433:
265. O Monks, in that natural pond, there are flocks of birds that are very delighted, safe, and have plenty of food. There are swans, cranes, peacocks, ruddy sheldrakes, and kukkuhu birds. There are many cuckoos, and beautiful crested birds and jīvajīvaka birds.
266. O Monks, in that natural pond, many groups of various animals come to drink water. Lions, tigers, boars, bears, hyenas, and leopards come to drink water.
267. O Monks, rhinoceroses, gavaja (gayals), buffaloes, rohita deer, ruru deer, eṇeyya deer, boars, gaṇin deer, and nīkasūkara (sheep or bears) come to drink water in that natural pond.
268. O Monks, around that hermitage of the hermit Kosiya, there are many kadalimiga (marsh deer), cats, hares, and small deer. There is a stone slab as level as the ground, well-spread with beautiful flowers. It is a place where flocks of birds chirp and play, a place frequented by flocks of birds.
With these aforementioned verses, the Buddha praised the hermitage of the hermit Kosiya. Now, the Buddha, wishing to show the entry of the goddess Hiri into that hermitage, etc...

In those verses: jutīmatā means endowed with power. yassamaṃ means entered the hermitage; the 'y' is a euphonic consonant. udakavantaṃ means well-supplied with water in various places. phalaṃ means endowed with many fruits. ariyapūjitaṃ means praised and honored by the Noble Ones who are free from the defilements of the hindrances and possessors of meditative absorptions (jhāna). rukkhaggahaṇā means a thicket of trees bearing flowers and fruits. sobhañjanā means siggu trees. loddhamathopi paddhakā means loddha trees and paduma trees. kekā ca bhaṅgā are simply trees of those names. karerī means kareri trees. uddālakā means vātaghātaka trees. mucalindaketakā means mucalinda trees and five kinds of ketaka trees. hareṇukā means types of legumes. veḷukā means types of bamboo seeds. keṇū means wild beans. tindukā means timbaru trees. cīnakā means small royal beans. mocā means seeded bananas. sāliyော means various types of sāli rice growing near the natural lake. pavīhayော means various types of paddy. ābhūjinော means bhujapatta (birch) trees. taṇḍulā means naturally grown rice heads free from red powder and husks.
tasseva means, O Monks, on the northern side of that very hermitage. pokkharaṇī means a natural lotus pond covered with five kinds of lotuses. akakkasā means free from the roughness of fish shells, moss, etc. apabbhārā means with banks that are not broken, having level shores. appaṭigandhikā means endowed with water that has no repulsive smell. tattha means in that pond. kheminော means safe...
434:
269. 'Sā suttacā nīladumābhi-lambitā...' and so on, up to 'Navamhi kocchamhi yadā upāvisi.' The Buddha preached these five verses.

269. Monks, that goddess Hirī, who has beautiful skin, appeared as if hanging from dark-green trees. She entered the hermitage like a flash of lightning during a great rainstorm. Kosiya spread a noble seat (koccha) at the door of the leaf-hut—a seat well-made, woven with kusa grass and fragrant roots, pure, scented, and adorned with antelope skin. He said to the goddess Hirī, who possessed the five beauties: "O beautiful one, sit here on this pleasant seat."

270. Monks, the great sage named Kosiya, who wore matted hair and possessed radiant power, then quickly brought celestial food (sudhā) with water in his own hands, using fresh, green lotus leaves plucked from the lotus pond, for the goddess Hirī who was seated on the noble seat and desired the food.

271. She received the celestial food with both hands and, being delighted, said to the matted-haired ascetic Kosiya: "O Brahmin, now that I have been honored by you and have become a winner, I shall return to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven."

272. Monks, permitted by the radiant ascetic Kosiya, she, intoxicated with the pride of her beauty...
435:
...went to the presence of the Thousand-Eyed Sakka and said: "Vāsava, father Sakka, this celestial food is for me; grant me victory."

273. Monks, then Sakka also honored that goddess Hirī. When that goddess Hirī, who is honored by gods and humans, sat on the new noble seat with her hands joined in reverence, then the gods along with Sakka honored the noble celestial maiden Hirī with Pāricchattaka flowers and other offerings.

## Attributes of the Goddess Hirī

Thus, after Sakka had honored the goddess Hirī, he thought: "For what reason did the ascetic Kosiya give the celestial food only to this goddess Hirī, and not to the others?" Having thought this, Sakka sent the celestial youth Mātali again to discover the reason.

To make this matter clear, the Blessed One said:

274. 'Tam-eva saṃsī punadeva mātaliṃ...' and so on. The Buddha preached this verse.

274. Monks, Sakka, the Thousand-Eyed Lord of the Tāvatiṃsa gods, spoke again to that same Mātali: "Mātali, go and speak my words to the ascetic Kosiya. Ask him: 'O Kosiya, for what reason did Hirī obtain the celestial food instead of Āsā, Saddhā, or Sirī?'"
436:
Mātali accepted the words of his lord Sakka and, mounting the Vejayanta chariot, went to the ascetic Kosiya. To make this matter clear, the Blessed One spoke these six verses:

275. 'Taṃ supplavattaṃ udatārayī rathaṃ...' and so on, up to 'Hirī sudhaṃ kena malattha hetunā.'

275. Monks, he prepared the Vejayanta chariot, which was extremely swift, radiant, like a palatial building, made of Jambu-river gold, shining like refined gold, decorated and adorned with various precious jewels.

## The Vejayanta Chariot

276. Monks, on this Vejayanta chariot, there were many golden peacock-tail patterns. Figures of elephants, bulls, horses, kinnaras, tigers, and leopards made of gold, silver, and rubies, as well as figures of Eṇī deer and various birds made of diverse jewels, stood in order as if they were about to fly. On this chariot, figures of deer and other wild animals made of lapis lazuli were arranged as if they were engaged in combat.

277. Monks, to that Vejayanta chariot, they harnessed a thousand noble Sindhu horses of golden hue, which were like young elephants, decorated with golden nets and breast-ornaments, wearing ear-ornaments, moving by sound alone without the use of a whip, and moving without obstruction.

278. Monks, then Mātali, mounting that most excellent vehicle, made the ten directions resound. He caused the sky, the mountains, the lords of the forest, the groves, and the earth along with the oceans to tremble.
437:
279. Monks, that Matali the deva-son, having quickly approached the hermitage of the hermit Kosiya, placing his robe over one shoulder and raising his hands in salutation, spoke thus to the noble hermit Kosiya, who was learned, great in virtue, and well-disciplined in conduct.

280. "Hermit Kosiya, listen to the words of Indra. I am his messenger. Purindada (Indra) asks you: 'Hermit Kosiya, for what reason did the goddess Hirī obtain the divine ambrosia (sudhā) over Āsā, Saddhā, and Sirī?'"

Having heard the words asked by Matali the deva-son, the hermit Kosiya, wishing to explain the reason to him—
438:
281. "O Matali, Sirī appears to me as blind.
O Charioteer of the Gods, Saddhā is indeed unstable.
Āsā is regarded by me as deceptive.
But Hirī is established in noble virtue."

281. O Matali, Charioteer of the Gods, the goddess Sirī appears to my wisdom as blind. The goddess Saddhā is unstable. As for the goddess Āsā, I regard her as one who speaks falsely. But the goddess Hirī is firmly established in noble virtue.

Now, wishing to praise the virtues of the goddess Hirī again—

282. "There are young maidens protected by their lineage...
...Report this to Indra, O Charioteer of the Gods."

282. Matali, there are young maidens who protect their lineage, there are elderly women who are widows, and there are women who are married. All these women, recognizing the intense desire and passion for other men that arises in them, restrain their own minds through Hirī (shame).

283. Matali, at the front of the battle where arrows and spears clash, those who are defeated, falling, or fleeing, give up their lives through Hirī and turn back. Those who have a sense of shame (hirīmanā) accept their duty again.

284. O Matali, Charioteer of the Gods, just as the shore restrains the force of the ocean's waves, so does this goddess Hirī restrain all beings from evil. In all the worlds of men and devas, that Hirī is praised by the Noble Ones (Ariyas) such as the Buddhas. Report this matter to Indra.

Having heard these words, Matali the deva-son, wishing to acknowledge what the hermit Kosiya said—
439:
285. "Hermit Kosiya, who gave you this view?
Was it Brahmā, Mahinda, or Pajāpati?
Among the gods, Hirī is indeed regarded as the best.
She is the daughter of Mahinda, a seeker of great virtue."

285. Hermit Kosiya, why have you taken up this view? Was it Indra (Mahinda), who is the Great One, or was it Pajāpati, the lord of beings? This goddess Hirī, the daughter of the great Indra and a seeker of noble merit, is regarded as especially excellent among the gods.

## The Hermit Kosiya Becomes a Deva

While Matali the deva-son was speaking, the nature of passing away (death) arose for the hermit Kosiya. Then Matali, wishing to take him to the celestial realm, said: "Venerable sir, your life-force is relinquished. The time for your passing has arrived. What use is the human world to you? Let us go to the deva world."

286. "Come now, depart for the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Mount this beloved chariot of mine.
Indra, who is of the same lineage as you, desires your presence.
Go this very day to the companionship of Indra."

286. Hermit of the same lineage as Indra, I urge you: Come! Now, depart for the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Mount this beloved Vejayanta chariot. Indra desires your presence. Go this very day to the companionship of Indra.

While Matali was speaking with the hermit Kosiya, the hermit passed away and was reborn as a deva by spontaneous rebirth (upapātika), and he stood upon the Vejayanta celestial chariot.

## Marriage to the Goddess Hirī

Then Matali the deva-son brought the Kosiya-deva to Indra. When Indra saw the Kosiya-deva, he was greatly pleased and gave his daughter, the goddess Hirī, to the Kosiya-deva to be his chief queen.
440:
287. *Evaṃ visujjhanti apāpakammino,*
*Atho suciṇṇassa phalaṃ na nassati.*
*Ye keci maddakkhu sudhāya bhojanaṃ,*
*Sabbeva te indasahabyataṃ gatā.*

He spoke this concluding verse.

287. Monks, *evaṃ*, in this aforementioned manner. *Apāpakammino sattā*, beings who do no evil. *Visujjhanti*, are especially purified. *Atho*, furthermore. *Suciṇṇassa*, of a well-performed deed. *Phalaṃ*, the fruit. *Na nassati*, is not lost. *Ye keci*, all those people. *Sudhāyabhojanaṃ*, the divine Sudhā food. *Hirī*, to the goddess Hirī. *Diyyamānaṃ*, being given. *Addakkhu*, saw. *Te sabbeva*, all those people. *Taṃ dānaṃ anumoditvā*, because of rejoicing in that gift. *Indasahabyataṃ*, to the companionship of Sakka, the king of devas. *Gatā*, they went.

That young deva Kosiya came to possess immeasurable and great wealth and attendants; the Omniscient Buddha, knowing this matter, said, "The deeds of noble beings are thus purified," and wishing to make that matter clear, he identified the Jātaka:

The Omniscient Buddha, having brought this Sudhābhojana Jātaka Dhamma teaching, said, "Monks, not only now have I tamed this monk who was not delighted in giving and was stubborn and stingy; in the past also, I have tamed this monk." He then identified the birth: "At that time, Uppalavaṇṇā was the goddess Hirī. This monk, who is now a donor delighted in giving, was then the hermit Kosiya. Anuruddha was then the young deva Pañcasikha. Ānanda was then the young deva Mātali. Mahā Kassapa was then the deva Suriya. Mahā Moggallāna was then the deva Canda. Sāriputta was then the hermit Nārada. I myself was then Sakka, the king of devas."

## The Stingy One takes Hell, the Donor goes to Heaven
The Sudhābhojana Jātaka is finished.

## 4. Mahākuṇāla Jātaka
## On why one should not quarrel
The Omniscient Buddha, who is the teacher of the world including the devas, while staying at Lake Kuṇāla, spoke this Mahākuṇāla Jātaka, adorned with verses beginning with "Evamakkhāyati," concerning five hundred monks who were oppressed by discontent. In this context, the following is the sequential account.
441:
The Sakyans and the Koliyans, having dammed the river named Rohiṇī with a single dam between the city of Kapilavatthu and the city of Koliya, cultivated their crops.

## Conflict at the Meeting

Then, in the month of Jeṭṭhamūla, when the crops were withering, the laborers of both cities gathered. Among them, the Koliyans said, "If this water is drawn by both of us, it will not be enough for you, nor will it be enough for us. Our crops, however, will ripen with just one more watering. Give this water to us." The Sakyans said, "If you fill your granaries and remain [prosperous], we will not be able to go to your doors with baskets and sacks in hand, taking gold, silver, blue sapphires, rubies, and black coins (kahāpaṇas). Our crops will also ripen with just one more watering. Give this water only to us."

"We will not give it!" "We too will not give it!" Saying thus, they increased the quarrel, and one man rose up and struck another. That person also struck another. Thus, by striking one another, they insulted the lineage of the royal families and caused a conflict to break out.

The laborers of the Koliya city said, "You, taking the side of the Sakyan youths living in Kapilavatthu, boast loudly—those who, like dogs and jackals, cohabited with their own sisters. What will their elephants, horses, and weapons do to us?" The laborers of the Sakya city said, "You now boast loudly, taking the side of the princes of the leper lineage, who, being outcasts and helpless like animals, lived in Kola trees. What will the elephants, horses, and weapons of those Koliya kings do to us?"

Those two groups of laborers went and reported to the ministers in charge of the work. The ministers reported to the royal families. Then the Sakyans, saying, "We will show the strength and power of those who cohabit with their sisters," went out prepared for battle. The Koliyans also, saying, "We will show the strength and power of those who live in Kola trees," went out prepared for battle.

★ Note ★
Other teachers say that the slave women of the Sakyans and Koliyans went to the river to fetch water, and while they were sitting and talking pleasantly after placing their head-coils (cumbatas) on the ground, one woman took another's head-coil, thinking it was her own. Based on that head-coil, they argued, "My head-coil, your head-coil," and as the quarrel progressed, the slave laborers, village headmen, ministers, and viceroys of both cities all went out prepared for battle.

However, the former account is found in many Great Commentaries (Mahā-aṭṭhakathā) and is more appropriate. Therefore, only that former account should be accepted.

Those Sakyan and Koliyan kings went out in the evening, prepared for battle.

## The Buddha Brings Peace

At that time, the Omniscient Buddha, while residing in Sāvatthī, surveyed the world of beings at dawn and saw these Sakyan kings who had gone out prepared for battle. Having seen them, He reflected, "If I go there, will this quarrel be settled or not?"
442:
"I shall go to that place and preach three Jātakas to settle that quarrel. Through that preaching, the quarrel will subside. When it has subsided, I shall preach two Jātakas to illustrate unity, and then I shall preach the Attadaṇḍa Sutta. Having heard the Dhamma teaching, the inhabitants of both cities will each offer two hundred and fifty princes. I shall ordain those five hundred princes, and there will be a great assembly." Having made this resolution—

In the early morning, after attending to his bodily needs, he entered Sāvatthī for alms. After returning from the alms round, in the evening, he departed from the Gandhakuṭi without informing anyone. Taking his bowl and robes himself, he sat cross-legged in the air between the two armies. To inspire awe in the two armies, he emitted dark rays from his hair to create darkness during the day.

Then, revealing himself to the two armies whose minds were filled with awe, he emitted the six-colored Buddha-rays. When the inhabitants of Kapilavatthu saw the Blessed One, they thought, "Our noble kinsman, the Teacher, has arrived. Has he seen that we are quarreling?"

They thought, "Indeed, while the Teacher has arrived, it is not proper for us to strike others with weapons. Let the inhabitants of Koliya kill us or bind us." Thus, they discarded their weapons. The inhabitants of Koliya did likewise.

Then the All-Enlightened One descended from the sky and sat upon the noble Buddha-seat prepared on a pleasant sandbank, radiant with incomparable Buddha-glory. Those two kings also paid homage to the All-Enlightened One and sat down.

As they were seated, the All-Enlightened One, though he already knew, asked those two kings, "Noble kings, for what reason have you come?" "Venerable Sir, we have not come to see the river, nor for play. Indeed, we have come to this place intending to wage war." 

"Noble kings, on what account are you quarreling?" "Venerable Sir, it is on account of water." "Noble kings, how much is water worth?" "Venerable Sir, it is of little value." "Noble kings, how much is the earth worth?" "Venerable Sir, the earth is of inestimable value." "Noble kings, how much are kings worth?" "Venerable Sir, kings are of inestimable value."

"Noble kings, why do you destroy kings of inestimable value on account of water which is of little value? There is no such thing as happiness in quarreling. Noble kings, this is true; through the power of quarreling, a certain deity of a Phandana tree bore a grudge against a bear, and even this entire world reached destruction." Having said this, he preached the Phandana Jātaka. (This Phandana Jātaka was preached in the Terasa Nipāta.)
443:
Then he said, "Noble kings, one should not blindly follow and believe the words of others. This is true; by following the words of another, because of the words of a single young hare, the entire host of four-footed animals in the three-thousand-league wide Himavanta forest rushed into the great ocean. Therefore, one should not be a follower of others' words." Having said this, he preached the Daddara Jātaka. (This Duddubha Jātaka was preached in the Catukka Nipāta.)

Then he said, "Noble kings, sometimes even a weak person can see the vulnerability of a strong person. This is true; even a small quail could kill a noble elephant." Having said this, he preached the Laṭukika Jātaka. (This Laṭukika Jātaka was preached in the Pañcaka Nipāta.)

Thus, he preached three Jātakas to settle the quarrel, and furthermore, he preached two Jātakas to illustrate unity. "Noble kings, this is true; no one is able to see a flaw or an opening in those who are united." Having said this, he preached the Rukkhadhamma Jātaka. (This Rukkhadhamma Jātaka was preached in the Ekaka Nipāta.)

Furthermore, he said, "Noble kings, no one is able to see a division in those who are united. But when they quarreled with one another, a certain hunter brought those quails to their end and took them away. There is no such thing as happiness in quarreling." Having said this, he preached the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka. (This Vaṭṭaka Jātaka was preached under the name Sammodamāna Jātaka in the Ekaka Nipāta.)

## Five Hundred Princes Ordain

Thus, having preached these five Jātakas, at the conclusion, he preached the Attadaṇḍa Sutta. Then the Sakyan kings were inspired with faith and thought, "If the Blessed One had not come, we would have killed one another and caused a river of blood to flow. Because of the Teacher, we have received our lives. If the Teacher had remained in the household life, the sovereignty over the four great islands with their two thousand small islands would have come into his hands. Indeed, he would have had over a thousand sons. Because of his sovereignty over those four great islands, he would have traveled with a retinue of kings. The Blessed One renounced such Universal Sovereignty, went forth, and attained All-Enlightenment. Now, let him travel with a retinue of noble kinsmen." Thus, the inhabitants of both cities offered two hundred and fifty princes each.

The All-Enlightened One ordained those five hundred princes and went to the Mahāvana forest. From the following day, surrounded by those five hundred Sakyan prince-monks, he went for alms sometimes in the city of Kapilavatthu and sometimes in the city of Koliya. Thus, he traveled in both cities. The inhabitants of both cities performed great offerings and honors. Because they had ordained out of deep respect for the Buddha and not by their own desire, dissatisfaction (anabhirati) arose in them.
444:
Dissatisfaction arose in those five hundred monks who had not gone forth by their own will but out of great respect for their families. Their former wives, in order to cause dissatisfaction, sent messages mentioning various matters. Those monks became exceedingly weary.

When the All-Enlightened Buddha reflected, he knew the state of dissatisfaction of those five hundred Sakyan princes who had become monks. He considered, "These monks are weary even while living with a Buddha like me; what kind of Dhamma discourse would be suitable and appropriate for them?" While investigating, he saw the Kunāla Jātaka Dhamma teaching.

Then, this thought occurred to the Buddha: "I shall take these five hundred monks to the Himalayas, and by revealing the faults of women through the Kunāla Jātaka Dhamma teaching, I will remove their dissatisfaction and grant them the Fruit of Stream-entry." Having had this thought, the Buddha dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robes, and entered Kapilavatthu for alms. After returning from the alms round and finishing his meal, at that very time, he addressed the five hundred monks, "Monks, have you ever seen the delightful region of the Himalayas?"

## Journey to the Himalayas

"Venerable Sir, we have never seen the Himalayas," they replied. When he asked, "Shall we go for a wandering in the Himalayas?" they answered, "Venerable Sir, we do not possess psychic powers; how can we go?" He asked, "If someone were to take you, would you go?" They replied, "Yes, Venerable Sir, we would go."

The All-Enlightened Buddha, taking all those five hundred monks by his own psychic power, ascended into the sky and went to the Himalayas. Standing in the firmament, he showed them various mountains in the delightful Himalayan region: the Golden Mountain, the Silver Mountain, the Gem Mountain, the Vermilion Mountain, the Antimony Mountain, the Crystal Mountain, and the Plateau Mountain.

He also showed them the five great rivers—the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Mahī, and Sarabhū—and the seven great lakes: Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, Rathakāra, Sīhapapāta, Chaddanta, Tiyaggala, Anotatta, and Kunāla. The Himalayas are vast, being five hundred yojanas in height and three thousand yojanas in width. By his own majesty, he showed them this one delightful part of the Himalayas.

He also showed them some of the four-footed animals dwelling there, such as lions, tigers, and elephants. He showed the delightful groves and such, trees bearing flowers and fruits, various flocks of birds, water-flowers and land-flowers, the golden plateau on the eastern side of the Himalayan mountain, and the vermilion plateau on the western side.

From the time they saw such delightful sights, the strong lustful desire for their former wives was abandoned by those five hundred monks.
445:
## The Kuṇāla Bird King
Then the Omniscient Buddha, taking those five hundred monks, traveled through the sky and descended to the western side of the Himavanta. There, on the Maṇisilā stone slab which was sixty leagues in extent, beneath a Sal tree seven leagues high that lasts for an entire aeon, he sat upon a Maṇisilā stone throne three leagues in size. Surrounded by the five hundred monks, the Buddha emitted the six-colored rays, causing the vast ocean to tremble. Sitting there like the radiant sun, he addressed the monks in a melodious voice: “Monks, ask about anything in this Himavanta region that you have never seen before.”

At that moment, two beautiful female cuckoos, holding a stick at both ends with their beaks, seated their husband, the Kuṇāla King, in the middle. They were accompanied by other beautiful cuckoos—eight in front, eight behind, eight on the left, eight on the right, eight below, and eight above—providing shade. Thus, surrounding the Kuṇāla King, they flew through the sky.

Seeing that flock of birds, the monks asked the Buddha: “Venerable Sir, what kind of birds are these?” “Monks, this flock of birds is of my ancient lineage; it is a tradition established by me. In the past, they used to serve me in this manner. At that time, the flock was very large; three thousand five hundred female birds served me. Having gradually declined, it has now become only this many.” “Venerable Sir, how did those female birds serve you in such a forest grove?”

[The Story of the Past] Then, the Omniscient Buddha, wishing to bring forth the past and show it to those monks, said, “Monks, listen then,” and establishing their mindfulness, he spoke these verses beginning with *Evamakkhāyati, eva manusūyati*.

## Animals of the Himalayas
The meaning of those verses is as follows:

Friends, O monks! Indeed, in such a delightful forest grove, there lives a bird named Kuṇāla, who is exceedingly beautiful in color and covered with exceedingly beautiful wings. This forest grove is known as the *Sabbosadha-dharaṇīdhara* (the earth-bearer of all medicinal herbs). It is spread with many flowers that bloom for fruit and flowers not meant for wearing. It is frequented by elephants (*gaja*), wild oxen (*gavaja*), buffaloes (*mahiṃsa*), ruru deer (*ruru*), yaks (*cāmara*), antelopes (*pasada*), rhinoceroses (*khagga*), elks (*gokaṇṇa*), lions (*sīha*), tigers (*byaggha*), leopards (*dīpi*), bears (*accha*), hyenas (*koka*), panthers (*taraccha*), otters (*uddāra*), kadalī-deer, cats (*biḷāra*), rabbits (*sasa*), and deer (*kaṇṇikā*). It is inhabited by herds of small and large elephants of the ten noble lineages. It is the resort of bears (*issamiga*), monkeys (*sākhamiga*), sarabha deer, eṇī deer, wind-deer (*vātāmiga*), antelopes (*pasada*), *purisālu* (wild-men), various types of Kinnaras such as Deva-kinnara, Canda-kinnara, and Duma-kinnara, Yakkhas, and Rakkhasas. It is adorned with many flowering trees with buds and stalks, whose tips are touched with blossoms.

It is constantly and beautifully filled with the songs of flocks of intoxicated birds such as ospreys (*kurara*), partridges (*cakora*), elephant-cranes (*vāraṇa*), peacocks (*mayūra*), cuckoos (*parabhata*), pheasant-birds (*jīvañjīvaka*), *celāvaka* birds, *bhiṅkāra* birds, and *karavīka* birds.

## Minerals and Jewels
It is a region decorated and constantly permeated with many minerals such as collyrium (*añjana*), red arsenic (*manosilā*), yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), cinnabar (*hiṅgulaka*), gold (*hema*), silver (*rajata*), and other forms of gold (*kanaka*). In such a delightful forest grove, the bird king named Kuṇāla dwells. That forest grove where the Kuṇāla King lives is described in this manner and heard of in this manner.

Friends, O monks! Indeed, that bird king named Kuṇāla has three thousand five hundred female birds as his attendants. 

Friends, O monks! Then, two female birds, biting a stick with their beaks and seating the Kuṇāla King in the middle, fly through the air, thinking in their hearts: “Let not fatigue trouble the Kuṇāla King on the long journey.”
446:
Five hundred bird-maidens fly below, thinking: 'If this bird king named Kunāla should fall from his seat, we will catch him with our wings.'

Five hundred bird-maidens fly above, thinking: 'May the heat of the sun not distress the bird king named Kunāla.'

Five hundred bird-maidens fly on both sides, thinking: 'May cold, heat, grass, dust, wind, or dew not touch the bird king named Kunāla.'

Five hundred bird-maidens fly in front, thinking: 'May cowherds, shepherds, grass-cutters, wood-gatherers, or forest-workers not strike the bird king named Kunāla with wood, potsherds, hands, clods, sticks, weapons, or gravel; and may this bird king named Kunāla not collide with bushes, creepers, trees, branches, posts, stones, or powerful birds.'

Five hundred bird-maidens fly behind, attending to him with smooth, lovely, pleasant, and sweet words, thinking: 'May this bird king named Kunāla not become bored in his seat.'

Five hundred bird-maidens fly in all directions, bringing various kinds of fruits from many trees, thinking: 'May this bird king named Kunāla not suffer from hunger.'

O monks, then those bird-maidens quickly brought that bird king named Kunāla from grove to grove, from garden to garden, from river-crossing to river-crossing, from mountain peak to mountain peak, from mango grove to mango grove, from rose-apple grove to rose-apple grove, from breadfruit grove to breadfruit grove, from coconut grove to coconut grove, for the sake of his pleasure.
447:
...from garden to garden, from river-crossing to river-crossing, from mountain peak to mountain peak, from mango grove to mango grove, from rose-apple grove to rose-apple grove, from breadfruit grove to breadfruit grove, from coconut grove to coconut grove, they quickly brought him for the sake of his pleasure.

O monks, then the bird king named Kunāla, surrounded all day by those three thousand five hundred bird-maidens, reviled them thus: 'Perish, you outcasts! Perish, you outcasts, thieves, rogues, unmindful ones, fickle-minded ones, ungrateful ones, who go wherever you desire like the wind!'
448:
Having spoken these words, the Buddha said: 'Monks, in this way, even when I was born in the animal kingdom, I knew the ingratitude, the great deceit, the misconduct, and the immorality of women. At that time, I did not follow the will of those women, but made them follow my will.' Having said this, he dispelled the dissatisfaction of those monks with these verses and remained silent.

## The Phussa Cuckoo King

At that moment, two black cuckoos came to that place, carrying their husband with a stick, with four female cuckoos on the lower side and other sides. The monks saw those birds and asked the All-Enlightened Buddha. The Blessed Buddha said: 'Monks, in the past, there was a Phussa cuckoo named Punnamukha who was my friend. This is the lineage of that Punnamukha cuckoo.' Being asked by the monks in the same manner as before, wishing to answer...
449:
He spoke this verse: 'In the eastern region of that very king of mountains, Himavā, there are rivers that are very subtle and clear, originating from the mountains and flowing with currents mixed with green grass.'

O monks, in the eastern region of that very king of mountains, Himavā, rivers that have very subtle and clear water, flowing from the mountains and having currents mixed with green grass, flow forth.

Now, having praised the rivers that flow into Lake Kunāla, and wishing to praise the flowers found in that Lake Kunāla, he spoke this verse:

'In the region where blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, lilies, hundred-petalled lotuses, fragrant lotuses, and Mandālaka flowers are newly blossomed, possessing a pure fragrance and charming the heart...'

O monks, in the lake which is endowed with a region that binds the heart with pure fragrances that have well arrived, the blue lotus, the red lotus, the white lotus, the lily, the hundred-petalled lotus, the small lotus, and the bell-shaped lotus bloom.

Having praised the various types of lotuses in Lake Kunāla, the All-Enlightened Buddha, wishing to describe the trees and other things around Lake Kunāla, as well as the splendor and retinue of the Phussa cuckoo, spoke these twenty-six verses:

'Kuravaka, Mucalinda, Ketaka, Vedisa, Vañjula... [etc.] ...that affliction of the cuckoo was subsided.'

## Various Trees
Kuravaka tree, Mucalinda (King-of-trees), Ketaka (Screw-pine), Vedisa tree, Vañjula (Reed), Punnāga (Alexandrian laurel), Bakula, Tilaka, Piyaka (Kadamba), Asana (Padauk), Saḷala (Pine), Campaka, Asoka, Nāga (Ironwood), Tirīṭi tree, Bhujapatta (Birch), Loddha, and forests of Red Sandalwood.

Kāḷāgaru (Black aloe), Padmaka (Cherry), Piyaṅgu, Devadāru (Cedar), and thickets of plantains. Kakudha, Kuṭaja, Aṅkola, Kaccikāra, Kaṇikāra, Kaṇṇikāra, Koraṇḍaka, Kovilāra (Mountain ebony), Kiṃsuka (Flame-of-the-forest), Yodhikā (Jasmine), Vanamallikā (Wild jasmine), Anaṅgaṇa tree, Anavajja tree, Bhaṇḍi (Gardenia). It also bears the very delightful Bhaginī flowers.

Jāti-sumana (Spanish jasmine), Madhugandhika, Dhanu, Takkarī, Tālīsa, Tagara, Musira, and it is adorned with clusters of flowers. It is a region decorated with various flowering vines such as Atimuttaka.

## Various Birds
It is a place where swans (Haṃsa), Pilava ducks, and Kādamba geese cry out. It is inhabited by groups of Vidyādharas, Siddhas, monks, and ascetics. It is a region frequented by noble Devas, Yakkhas, Rakkhasas, Dānavas, Gandhabbas, Kinnaras, and Mahoragas (great serpents).
450:
In such a delightful forest grove, O monks, there truly dwells a Phussa cuckoo named Puṇṇamukha, who has an exceedingly sweet voice and eyes that are beautiful and red like those of one intoxicated.

## How the Female Birds Serve Him
O monks, that Phussa cuckoo named Puṇṇamukha has three hundred and fifty female birds as his attendants.

O monks, then, two female birds, holding a wooden stick in their beaks and seating the Phussa cuckoo Puṇṇamukha in the middle, fly along, thinking: 'Let not the Phussa cuckoo Puṇṇamukha be exhausted on the long journey.'

Fifty female birds fly below, thinking: 'If this Phussa cuckoo Puṇṇamukha should fall from his seat, we will catch him with our wings.'

Fifty female birds fly above, thinking: 'Let not the heat of the sun scorch the Phussa cuckoo Puṇṇamukha.'

Fifty female birds fly on both sides, thinking: 'Let not cold, heat, grass, dust, wind, or dew touch the Phussa cuckoo Puṇṇamukha.'

Fifty female birds fly in front, thinking: 'Let not cowherds, shepherds, grass-gatherers, wood-gatherers, or forest workers strike the Phussa cuckoo Puṇṇamukha with wood, potsherds, hands, clods of earth, sticks, weapons, or gravel; and let not this Phussa cuckoo Puṇṇamukha collide with bushes, vines, trees, branches, posts, stones, or powerful birds.'

Fifty female birds fly behind, addressing him with smooth, friendly, pleasant, and sweet words, thinking: 'Let not this Phussa cuckoo Puṇṇamukha become weary in his seat.'

Fifty female birds fly in all directions, bringing various kinds of wonderful fruits from many trees, thinking: 'Let not this Phussa cuckoo Puṇṇamukha suffer from hunger.'

Then, O monks, those female birds carry the Phussa cuckoo Puṇṇamukha from grove to grove, from garden to garden...
451:
To a garden. From one river bank to another river bank, from one mountain peak to another mountain peak, from one mango grove to another mango grove, from one rose-apple grove to another rose-apple grove, from one breadfruit grove to another breadfruit grove, from one coconut grove to another coconut grove, they quickly reach for the sake of delighting in sensual pleasures.

O monks, then indeed, Punnamukha the Phussa-cuckoo, surrounded all day by those female birds, praised them thus: 'Excellent, excellent, sisters! This service you provide to your husband, sisters, is fitting for you as well-born daughters.'

## Going to Kunala the Bird King

O monks, then indeed, Punnamukha the Phussa-cuckoo approached where Kunala the bird king was. The female birds, the attendants of Kunala the bird king, saw Punnamukha the Phussa-cuckoo coming from afar. Seeing him, they approached Punnamukha the Phussa-cuckoo and said this to him: 'Friend Punnamukha, this Kunala bird is exceedingly harsh and speaks exceedingly harsh words. Perhaps through you, we might receive pleasant speech.' Saying, 'Perhaps, sisters,' he approached where Kunala the bird king was. Having approached and exchanged friendly greetings with Kunala the bird king, he sat to one side. Sitting to one side, Punnamukha the Phussa-cuckoo said this to Kunala the bird king:

## Good Women

'Friend Kunala, why do you behave wrongly toward these well-born women of the same species who behave rightly? Friend Kunala, it is true that even if women speak unpleasantly, men should be those who speak pleasantly, let alone when they speak pleasantly.'

## Go Away, You Who are Conquered by Your Wife

When this was said, Kunala the bird king rebuked Punnamukha the Phussa-cuckoo thus: 'Perish, you wretched outcaste! Perish, you wretched outcaste! Who is as clever as you, who are conquered by a wife?' Being thus rebuked, Punnamukha the Phussa-cuckoo turned back from that very place.
452:
## Phussa-cuckoo Falls Ill

O monks, then indeed, after some time, not long after, a severe illness arose for Punnamukha the Phussa-cuckoo. Severe, life-threatening pains of bloody diarrhea occurred.

## The Wives Come to Kunala

O monks, then indeed, the female birds who were the attendants of Punnamukha the Phussa-cuckoo had this thought: 'This Punnamukha the Phussa-cuckoo is afflicted by illness; we do not know if he will recover from this illness.' Leaving him alone and without a companion, they approached where Kunala the bird king was.

## Rebuking and Sending Away

Kunala the bird king saw those female birds coming from afar. Having seen them, he said this to those female birds: 'You outcaste women, where is your husband?' They said: 'Friend Kunala, Punnamukha the Phussa-cuckoo is afflicted by illness; we do not know if he will recover from that illness.'

When this was said, Kunala the bird king rebuked those female birds thus: 'Perish, you outcaste women! Perish, you outcaste women! You thieves, deceivers, unmindful ones, fickle-minded ones, ungrateful ones, who go wherever you please like the wind!'

## Treating Phussa

Having said this, he approached where Punnamukha the Phussa-cuckoo was. Having approached, he said this to Punnamukha the Phussa-cuckoo: 'Friend Punnamukha, are you still alive?' He said: 'Friend Kunala, I am alive.'

O monks, then indeed, Kunala the bird king, supporting Punnamukha the Phussa-cuckoo with his wings and his beak, raised him up and made him drink various medicines. O monks, then indeed, that illness of Punnamukha the Phussa-cuckoo subsided.
453:
## The Preaching of Kunala, the Bird King

Those female birds also returned when the Phussa cuckoo named Punnamukha was free from illness. Kunala, the bird king, also provided Punnamukha with various large and small fruits to eat for two or three days. When the cuckoo regained his strength, Kunala said, "Friend, you are now free from illness. Remain here with your attendants. I shall return to my own place."

Then, Punnamukha said to Kunala, the bird king, "Friend, these women abandoned me when I was severely ill and fled. I have no desire for these women who are obsessed with sensual pleasures."

Hearing these words, the Bodhisatta Kunala, the bird king, said, "Friend, if that is the case, I shall preach to you about the wickedness of women." He then took Punnamukha and sat upon the Manosilā rock slab on the side of the Himalayas. Punnamukha sat on one side with his own retinue.

The entire host of deities in the Himavanta forest also proclaimed: "Now, Kunala, the bird king, sitting upon the Manosilā rock slab in the Himalayas, will preach the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha. Listen to that Dhamma!" As the proclamation spread from one to another, the deities of the six celestial realms heard it and mostly gathered at that Manosilā rock slab.
454:
The deities also proclaimed that matter to many Nāgas, Supaṇṇas, Kinnaras, and Vijjādharas. At that time, a vulture king named Ānanda lived on Mount Gijjhakūṭa, surrounded by ten thousand vultures. Hearing the great clamor, that vulture king Ānanda also came with his retinue to listen to the Dhamma and sat in a suitable place.

An ascetic named Nārada, endowed with the five supernormal powers, also lived in the Himalayan region surrounded by ten thousand ascetics. Hearing the proclamation of the deities, he thought, "My friend Kunala, the bird king, will speak about the lack of virtue in women. There will be a great assembly. It is proper for me also to listen to that discourse." Thus, he went there by psychic power along with his ten thousand ascetics and sat in a suitable place.

There was a great assembly, similar to the assembly for the preaching of the Fully Enlightened Buddhas. Then, the Bodhisatta Kunala, the bird king, through his knowledge of past lives (jātissara-ñāṇa), preached the events he had seen in previous existences concerning the faults of women, using Punnamukha as a witness. To clarify this matter, the Fully Enlightened Buddha said:
455:
The Buddha preached these fourteen verses beginning with "Atha khalu bho Kunālo sakuṇo..." and ending with "nāsayanti ghare bhogaṃ, ratanantakaritthiuyo."

Bho, O monks! Atha, at that time. Khalu, indeed. Sakuṇo, the bird king named Kunālo. Gilānavuṭṭhitaṃ, who had risen from illness. Gelaññā aciravuṭṭhitaṃ, who had not long risen from the state of being ill. Punnamukhaṃ phussakokilaṃ, to that Phussa cuckoo named Punnamukha. Etaṃ, these words. Avoca, he said.

## The Wicked Woman Kaṇhā-devī
Friend Punnamukha. Dvepitikā, who had two fathers. Pañcapatikāya, who had five husbands. Kabandhe, who was like a short-necked peta. Pīṭhasappimhi, who was a cripple. Chaṭṭhe purise, in the sixth man. Cittaṃ paṭibandhantiyā, who was attached in mind. Yadidaṃ—yā esā Kaṇhā-devī, this Kaṇhā-devī. Atthi, there is. Sā Kaṇhā-devī, that Kaṇhā-devī. Mayā, by me. Diṭṭhā, has been seen. Ettha, in this matter. Anuttaraṃ vākyañca, an incomparable verse. Bhavati, there is.

Atha, then. Ajjuno, Prince Arjuna. Nakulo, Prince Nakula. Bhīmaseno, Prince Bhīmasena. Yudhiṭṭhilo, Prince Yudhiṭṭhila. Sahadevo ca rājā, and Prince Sahadeva. Ete pañcapatikā, these five husbands. Aticca, having transgressed against. Nārī, the princess named Kaṇhā-devī. Khujjavāmanakena pīṭhasappinā saddhiṃ, with a hunchbacked, dwarfish cripple. Pāpaṃ, an evil deed. Akāsi, she committed.

## Saccatapāpī
Friend Punnamukha. Mayā diṭṭhā, I have seen. Saccatapāpī nāma, one named Saccatapāpī. Susānamajjhe vasantī, who lived in the midst of a cemetery. Catutthabhattaṃ pariṇāmayamānā, who let the meal of the fourth day pass. Seta-samaṇī, a white-robed female wanderer. Atthi, there is. Sā, she. Surādhuttakena saha, with a drunkard. Pāpaṃ akāsi, committed an evil deed.

## Kākavatī
Friend Punnamukha. Mayā diṭṭhā, I have seen. Samuddamajjhe vasantī, living in the midst of the ocean. Bhariyā, the wife of King Brahmadatta. Kākavatī nāma devī, the queen named Kākavatī. Venateyyassa naṭakuverena saddhiṃ, with the musician and lute player named Naṭakuvera of Venateyya. Pāpaṃ akāsi, committed an evil deed.

## Kuruṅga-devī
Friend Punnamukha. Mayā diṭṭhā, I have seen. Lomasundarī, who had a beautiful belly like fur. Eḷikakumāraṃ kāmayamānā, who desired the youth Eḷika. Kuruṅgadevī nāma, the princess named Kuruṅgadevī. Chaḷaṅgakumāra-dhanantevāsina saddhiṃ, with the teacher named Chaḷaṅgakumāra and the attendant named Dhanantevāsī. Pāpaṃ akāsi, committed an evil deed.

## The Mother of King Brahmadatta
Friend Punnamukha. Brahmadattassa etaṃ mātaraṃ, that mother of King Brahmadatta. Mayā evañca ñātaṃ, has been known by me in this way. Sā mātā, that mother of King Brahmadatta. Kosalarājaṃ ohāya, having abandoned King Kosala. Pañcālacaṇḍena pāpaṃ akāsi, committed an evil deed with Pañcālacaṇḍa.

## Do Not Trust Women
Etā ca, these five women. Aññā ca, and others besides these five. Pāpaṃ akaṃsu, have all committed evil. Tasmā, therefore. Ahaṃ, I. Itthīnaṃ na vissase nappaṃsaṃse, do not trust nor praise women. Jagati, in the world. Samānaraṭṭā, having equal passion. Vasundharā, the source of all treasures. Itarītarapatiṭṭhā, the support of both the noble and the base. Mahī, the earth. Sabbasahā, which can endure all evils. Aphandanā, which is unmoving. Akuppā, which is without anger. Yathā hoti, just as it is. Tathā, in the same way. Itthiyo, women. Itarītarapatiṭṭhā, are the support of both the noble and the base. Sabbasahā, they can endure all evils. Aphandanā, they are unmoving. Akuppā, they are without anger. Honti, they are. Tāyo, those women. Naro, a man. Na vissase, should not trust.
456:
Lohitamaṃsabhojano: one who eats flesh and blood. Vālāmigo: a wild beast. Pañcāvudho: one with five weapons. Suruddho: very fierce. Pasayhakhādī: one who habitually eats by force. Just as a lion (sīho) delights in harming others (parahiṃsane rato), so too do women delight in harming others. A man should not trust those women.

## The Faults of Women

Friend Puṇṇamukha, these women are not called merely 'prostitutes' (vesiyo), 'women' (nāriyo), 'accessible ones' (gamaniyo), or 'unchaste women' (bandhakiyo). In their true nature, they are 'husband-slayers' (vadhikāyo).

Like a thief, they braid their hair. They are like poisoned liquor (diddhā madirā). Like a merchant, they praise only with words. Like the swiftness of a bear (issasingamiva), they are quick to turn (changeable). Like a snake, they are double-tongued. Like a cesspool (sobbhamiva), they are hidden. Like the Pātāla abyss in the ocean, they are hard to fill. Like an ogress (rakkhasī), they are hard to satisfy.

Like Yama, they truly take away. Like fire (sikhī), they consume everything, good or bad. Like a river, they carry everything away. Like the wind (anilo), they go wherever they desire. Like Mount Neru, they make no distinction. Like a poisonous tree (visarukkho), they are always fruiting. In this regard, there is this peerless verse:

293. Just as a thief, just as poisoned liquor, like a boasting merchant, like the turning of a bear, double-tongued like a snake.

294. Hidden like a cesspool, hard to fill like the abyss, hard to satisfy like an ogress, like Yama who truly takes away.

295. Like fire, a river, or the wind, like Mount Neru, like a poisonous tree always fruiting, women who bring about the end of jewels destroy wealth in the home.

(In these Pali verses, the story of the five women beginning with Kaṇhādevī, which is taught in brief, is explained in detail in the Commentary as follows:)

## (1) Kaṇhādevī

The story of the first one, Kaṇhādevī, who, despite having five husbands endowed with birth, lineage, appearance, wealth, and retinue, committed misconduct with a sixth man, a hunchback:

In the past, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi, having a complete army of elephants and horses, conquered the kingdom of Kosala, killed the King of Kosala, took his pregnant chief queen to Bārāṇasī, and made her his own chief queen. Later, she gave birth to a daughter. King Brahmadatta naturally had no sons or daughters of his own.

The King was very pleased and said, 'My dear Queen, choose a boon.' She accepted and set it aside. They named the young daughter Kaṇhādevī.
457:
When Kaṇhādevī reached the proper age, the Chief Queen said to her daughter, 'Dear daughter, your father granted you a boon, which I have kept for you. Choose the boon that pleases you.' Kaṇhādevī replied, 'Mother, I have no lack of other possessions. For the sake of taking a husband, let me choose the boon myself.' Because of her great lust, she cast aside shame and fear (hiri-ottappa) and spoke thus to her mother.

The Queen informed King Brahmadatta. The King said, 'Let her take the husband she desires,' and he had the choice proclaimed. Many men, adorned with all kinds of ornaments, gathered in the royal courtyard.

## Five Husbands

Princess Kaṇhādevī, taking a flower casket and standing at the northern lion-window, looked out but did not like even one of them.

At that time, the five sons of King Paṇḍu—Prince Ajjuna, Prince Nakula, Prince Bhīmasena, Prince Yudhiṭṭhila, and Prince Sahadeva—having completed their education under a world-renowned teacher in Takkasilā, were traveling to learn the customs of various regions. Arriving in Bārāṇasī, they heard the commotion in the city, and upon inquiring and learning the reason, they said, 'We shall go too.' The five Paṇḍu princes, whose appearance was like golden statues, went to the royal courtyard and stood in line.

Then Princess Kaṇhādevī, seeing the five brothers, felt her heart bound to all five. She cast flower garlands upon the heads of all five and said, 'Mother, grant me these five men as my boon.' The Queen informed King Brahmadatta.

Because he had already granted the boon, King Brahmadatta did not say, 'You shall not have them.' Though displeased, he asked, 'Of what lineage are they? Whose sons are they?' Upon learning they were Paṇḍu princes, he honored them and gave his daughter Kaṇhādevī to them. Princess Kaṇhādevī took them to a seven-storied palace, driven by lust.

## Kaṇhādevī's Infidelity

Princess Kaṇhādevī had a servant who was a hunchback and a cripple. Having taken the five princes through the power of lust, whenever she found an opportunity when the five princes had gone out, being consumed by lust, she committed misconduct with the hunchback.

While speaking with the hunchback, she would say, 'I have no one as dear as you. I will have the princes killed and wash your feet with the blood from their throats.' When she was intimate with the eldest prince, she would say, 'I love only you more than these other four. I would even sacrifice my life for your sake. When my father the King passes away, I will give the kingship only to you.' When she was intimate with the remaining four princes, she spoke in the same manner.

The princes thought, 'This princess loves us very much; our wealth and happiness depend on her,' and they were exceedingly pleased with her.
458:
One day, Princess Kaṇhādevi fell ill. At that time, one prince sat massaging her head while surrounding her. The other princes each massaged a hand or a foot. The hunchback sat at the soles of her feet.

Princess Kaṇhādevi gave a sign with her head to the eldest brother, Prince Ajjuna, who was massaging her head, saying, "There is no one I love more than you. If I live, I shall live for you. After my father's passing, I will give the kingdom to you," thus winning him over.

She gave similar signs with her hands and feet to the other four princes. To the hunchback, however, she gave a sign with her tongue, saying, "Only you do I love; I shall live for your sake."

Because of what had been said before, they all understood the meaning through those signs. Among them, those other than Prince Ajjuna understood only through the signs given to them.

Prince Ajjuna, however, seeing the movements of her hands, feet, and tongue, thought, "Just as she gave a sign to me, she must have given signs to the others as well; there must also be an intimacy between her and the hunchback." Having thought this, he called his younger brothers, went outside, and asked them.

## The Five Princes Renounce the World

"Did you see the woman with five husbands making a movement with her head toward me?" he asked. When they replied, "Yes, we saw it," he asked again, "Do you know the reason?" They said, "We do not know." "This is the reason here. But do you know the reason for the signs given to you with the hands and feet?" They replied, "Yes, we know." "She gave me a sign for the same reason. Do you know the reason for the sign given to the hunchback with the movement of the tongue?" When they said, "We do not know," he then informed his brothers of the reason, saying, "This woman commits evil deeds even with this hunchback." When the four brothers did not believe him, he had the hunchback summoned and questioned him.

The hunchback told the whole story. Upon hearing his words, the princes became free from desire and lust for her, saying, "Oh, how evil and immoral are women! They abandon princes like us, who are of noble birth and endowed with beauty, to commit evil deeds with such a loathsome and repulsive hunchback. What wise man would delight in such shameless and wicked women?" After censuring women in many ways, saying, "We have no need for household life," the five men entered the Himalayas, went forth as ascetics, practiced the kasiṇa meditation, and at the end of their lives, passed away according to their deeds. At that time, the bird king Kunāla was Prince Ajjuna. Therefore, showing the reason he had seen himself, he spoke the two verses beginning with 'Diṭṭhā mayā' (Seen by me).
459:
At that time, the bird king Kunāla was the eldest brother, Prince Ajjuna. Therefore, wishing to show the matter he had seen, he spoke the two verses beginning with "Diṭṭhā mayā."

## (2) Saccatapāpī

The story of the second female ascetic named Saccatapāpī is as follows:

In the past, depending on the city of Vārāṇasī, a white-clad female ascetic named Saccatapāpī had a leaf-hut built in a cemetery and lived there, eating only after passing four meals. She became as famous throughout the city of Vārāṇasī as the sun and the moon. All the inhabitants of Vārāṇasī, even when sneezing or slipping, would say, "Homage to Saccatapāpī!"

## The Bet of One Thousand

Then, on the first day of a festival, goldsmiths gathered in a group, built a pavilion in a certain place, brought fish, meat, liquor, perfumes, and so on, and began drinking liquor. At that time, as one goldsmith was pouring from a liquor jar, he said, "Homage to Saccatapāpī!" A wise man among them said, "O you great fool! You pay homage to a woman of wavering mind. How foolish you are!" The other replied, "Friend, do not say such a thing; do not perform an act that leads to hell."

Then the wise man said to that goldsmith, "You of little wisdom, be quiet! Make a bet of a thousand pieces. On the seventh day from today, I will sit in this very pavilion, and I will have your Saccatapāpī, fully adorned, carry a jar of liquor here for me to drink. There is no such thing as a woman of stable virtue." The goldsmith said, "You will not be able to do it," and made a bet of a thousand pieces with the wise man.

## Wooing in the Guise of an Ascetic

After informing the other goldsmiths, the wise man entered the cemetery early the next morning in the guise of an ascetic and stood worshipping the sun not far from the dwelling of the female ascetic Saccatapāpī. As she was going for alms, she saw the wise man disguised as an ascetic and thought, "This must be an ascetic of great power. I live on the edge of the cemetery, but this ascetic lives in the very middle of it. There must be the Dhamma of peace within him. I shall pay homage to him." She approached and paid homage. The ascetic neither looked at her nor spoke. On the second day, he did the same. On the third day, when she paid homage, he looked down and said, "Go away."

On the fourth day, he spoke to her, saying, "How is it? Are you not tired from seeking alms?" The female ascetic was very pleased, thinking, "I have gained speech with him," and departed. On the fifth day, having gained much conversation, she stayed for a while and then left.
460:
