On the sixth day, Saccatapāpī came and paid homage. He asked her, "Sister, why is there such a great sound of singing and music in Bārāṇasī today?" She replied, "Venerable sir, do you not know? A festival has been proclaimed in the city of Bārāṇasī. This is the sound of people playing at that festival." Pretending not to know that this was the sound of a festival, he asked, "Sister, how many meals have you skipped?" She replied, "Venerable sir, I have skipped four days of meals." Then she asked, "And how many have you skipped, venerable sir?" He replied, "Sister, I have skipped seven days." He said this falsely, for he ate every night.

He then asked the female ascetic (paribbājikā), "Sister, how many years (vassa) has it been since you ordained?" She replied, "It has been twelve years." When she asked, "And how many years for you, venerable sir?" he said, "This is my sixth year."

Then he asked her, "Sister, have you attained the Dhamma of peace (Nibbāna)?" She replied, "No, venerable sir." When she asked, "Have you attained it, venerable sir?" he said, "Sister, neither have I. Sister, we obtain neither the pleasure of the senses nor the pleasure of renunciation. Is it only for us that hell is hot? Let us do as the common people do. I shall become a layman. I have wealth inherited from my parents. I cannot endure this suffering."

## The Female Ascetic Disrobes

Hearing his words, the female ascetic, because of her own wavering mind, became attached to him and said, "Venerable sir, I too am weary. If you will not abandon me, I too shall become a laywoman." Then the wise man, disguised as an ascetic, said, "Come, sister, I will not abandon you. You shall be my wife." He took her to the city, went to a tavern, made Saccatapāpī carry the liquor pot, and drank. The goldsmith lost a thousand pieces of wealth. Saccatapāpī, depending on that drunkard, increased her family with sons and daughters.

At that time, the bird-king Kuṇāla was a drunkard. Therefore, wishing to reveal what he had seen, he spoke the verse beginning with "Diṭṭhā māyā".

## (3) Queen Kākavatī

The story of the past regarding the third case, Queen Kākavatī, has been detailed in the commentary on the Kākavatī Jātaka in the Catu-nipāta. At that time, the bird-king Kuṇāla was the king of the Garudas. Therefore, wishing to reveal what he had seen, he spoke the verse beginning with "Diṭṭhā māyā".

## (4) Princess Kurungadevī

The story of the fourth, Princess Kurungadevī, is as follows:

In the past, King Brahmadatta killed the King of Kosala and seized his kingdom. He took the pregnant chief queen of the King of Kosala and returned to Bārāṇasī. Although he knew she was pregnant, he made her his own chief queen.
461:
## Abandoning the Son

When the queen reached full term and gave birth to a son with a complexion like gold, she thought, "The King of Bārāṇasī will think, 'This prince is the son of my enemy; what use is he to me?' and will have him killed. Let my son not die at the hands of another." She called a nurse and said, "Mother, wrap this child in old rags, lay him in the cemetery where corpses are discarded, and return." The nurse did as the queen said, bathed, and returned.

## Being Set Adrift in the Water

The King of Kosala, having died, was reborn as the guardian deity of his son. Through the power of that deity, while a certain goat-herd was grazing his goats in that area, a she-goat saw the prince and, feeling affection for him, gave him milk. After grazing for a while, she returned and gave him milk two, three, or four times.

Seeing the behavior of the she-goat, the goat-herd went to that spot, saw the child, and feeling the love of a father, took him, bathed him, and gave him to his wife. His wife was childless and therefore had no breast milk. So, they fed the child only goat's milk.

From that day on, two or three she-goats died every day. The goat-herd thought, "If we continue to raise this child, all the she-goats will die. What benefit is this child to us?" He laid the child in a clay pot, covered it with a lid, sealed the opening with bean flour so there were no gaps, and set it adrift in the river.

## Becoming the Son of a Caṇḍāla

A Caṇḍāla, who repaired old things at the royal palace, was washing clothes with his wife at a downstream landing place. Seeing the pot drifting by, he went quickly, retrieved it, and brought it to the bank. When he opened it to see what was inside, he saw the child. The Caṇḍāla's wife was also childless, so she felt the love of a mother for the child. They took him home and raised him. From the age of seven or eight, whenever the parents went to the royal palace, they took him along.

## Winning the Princess

From the age of sixteen, the youth himself went frequently to perform the repairs on old things.

The King's chief queen had a daughter named Kurungadevī, who possessed supreme beauty. From the moment she saw the youth, Princess Kurungadevī became attached to him and found no delight elsewhere. She would only go to the place where the youth was working.
462:
Seeing each other constantly, those two developed lustful hearts for one another, and misconduct occurred in a secluded place within the royal palace. As time passed, the female attendants found out and informed the Great King, the father. The Great King became angry, assembled his ministers, and said: "This Caṇḍāla boy has committed such an act. Decide what should be done to this Caṇḍāla boy." The ministers said: "This man's crime is great. He should be subjected to various and diverse royal punishments and then executed."

At that moment, the guardian deity of the prince entered the body of the prince's mother, the Chief Queen. Through the power of the deity, the Queen approached the King and said: "Great King, this youth is not a Caṇḍāla. This youth is the Prince of Kosala, born from my womb. I spoke a lie to Your Majesty, saying 'My son is dead.' I gave this prince to the nurses, telling them he was the son of Your Majesty's enemy, and had him discarded in the cemetery where corpses are thrown. Then, a certain shepherd looked after the boy. When his she-goats died, that shepherd set him adrift in the river. Then, a Caṇḍāla who repairs old and decayed things in Your Majesty's palace saw the boy drifting in the river and raised him. If you do not believe me, summon all of them and ask."

The King summoned everyone, starting with the nurse, and upon questioning them, he learned the truth exactly as the Queen had said. Pleased, thinking "This prince is indeed of noble birth," he had the prince bathed and adorned, and gave him his own daughter, Kurungadevī.

## The Queen's Misconduct

They named the prince Eḷikakumāra because of the death of the she-goats. Then, the King gave the prince an army along with elephants and horses, and sent him away, saying: "Go and take the kingdom of Kosala and the city of Sāvatthī, which belong to your father."

That Prince Eḷika took Princess Kurungadevī, went there, and was established in the kingship of Kosala. Then, the King of Bārāṇasī, thinking "This Prince of Kosala has not yet learned the arts," sent a teacher named Chaḷaṅgakumāra to teach him the arts. The Prince gave the position of General to the teacher Chaḷaṅgakumāra, thinking "This man is my teacher."

Later, Kurungadevī committed misconduct with that teacher Chaḷaṅgakumāra. That General Chaḷaṅga also had a servant named Dhanantevāsī. The General gave clothes, ornaments, and so on into the hands of that servant to be sent to Kurungadevī. That Kurungadevī also practiced wicked conduct with Dhanantevāsī, the servant of the General.

At that time, Kuṇāla, the king of birds, was the teacher Chaḷaṅgakumāra. Therefore, wishing to bring forth and show that matter which he had seen, he spoke the verse beginning with "Diṭṭhā māyā".

## (5) The Mother of King Brahmadatta

The story of the fifth one, the mother of King Brahmadatta, is as follows:

In the past, the King of Kosala, having seized the city of Bārāṇasī, made the pregnant Queen of the King of Bārāṇasī his own Chief Queen and returned to his own city. Later, that Chief Queen gave birth to a son. Because the King of Kosala had no son of his own, he raised him with the love of a father, had him taught all the arts, and when he reached maturity, sent him away, saying: "Go and take the city of Bārāṇasī, which belongs to your father." That Prince Brahmadatta went to the city of Bārāṇasī and ruled as king.
463:
## The Mother's Misconduct

Then, the Chief Queen, the mother of Prince Brahmadatta, thinking "I wish to see my son, Prince Brahmadatta," asked permission from the King of Kosala and traveled to the city of Bārāṇasī with a large retinue. On the way, she took up residence in a market town (nigama) between the two kingdoms of Kāsi and Kosala.

In that market town, there was a Brahmin youth named Pañcālacaṇḍa. He was very handsome. That Brahmin Pañcālacaṇḍa presented gifts to the Queen. Upon seeing the Brahmin Pañcālacaṇḍa, the Chief Queen's heart became infatuated. She practiced wicked conduct with that Pañcālacaṇḍa, spent two or three days in that market town, then went to Bārāṇasī, saw her son, and quickly returned. Again, she stayed in that same market town, practiced misconduct with that Pañcālacaṇḍa for two or three days, and then went back to the kingdom of Kosala.

From that time on, before long, she would speak of various reasons and ask the King's permission, saying "I will go to my son's presence." Whether going or coming, she would stay in that market town for as long as half a month and practice misconduct with that Pañcālacaṇḍa.

At that time, Kuṇāla, the king of birds, was Pañcālacaṇḍa. Therefore, wishing to bring forth and show that matter which he had known and seen, he spoke the verse beginning with "Evañcetaṃ mayā ñātaṃ".

The meaning of the verses beginning with "Etā ca aññā ca akaṃsu pāpaṃ" is explained in detail in the Commentary as follows:

## That All Women are Wicked

"Friend Puṇṇamukha, do not think: 'Only these five women practiced wicked conduct; women other than these five do not practice wicked conduct.' In truth, both these five women and many other women are doers of evil deeds."

"Just as this earth, called Jagati, has an equal attraction to all things because it is without anger, and is the support for all things, both low and excellent; even so, women, by the power of defilements (kilesa), are the support for all men, both low and excellent. This is true: those women, if they get the opportunity, will practice wicked conduct with anyone."

"Just as this earth endures everything, does not tremble, and does not perish; even so, women endure all men, both low and excellent, by the power of delighting in defilements."

"If a certain man is established in the hearts of those women, when he is thus established in their hearts, they do not tremble even slightly, do not move, and do not make a commotion in order to protect that man. Just as this earth does not perish and does not tremble, even so, women do not perish and do not tremble through the practice of sexual intercourse; they are unable to be satiated by that practice of sexual intercourse."
464:
They are illusions, mirages,
Sorrow, disease, and calamities.
They are harsh, they are bonds,
The snares of Death, dwelling in the cave [of the body].
The man who trusts in them
Is the lowest among men.
This is shown by the verse from the Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka.

## Women's Similarity to a Lion
Just as a very cruel, fierce, and harsh lion that catches and drinks the blood and flesh of all animals possesses five weapons—namely, its four limbs and its snout—likewise, women possess five weapons: visible forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles.

Just as that lion, when seizing animals as its food, catches them with those five weapons, likewise, women, when they wish to take the food of defilements (kilesa), strike and seize them with the five weapons of visible forms and so on.

Just as that lion is fierce and harsh, eating by force, likewise, women are also fierce and harsh, eating by force. This statement is indeed true. These women, by their own power, use force even against virtuous men and cause the destruction of their virtue.

Just as that lion delights in harming others, likewise, women, through the power of defilements, delight in harming others. A man should not be intimate with such women who are endowed with these evil qualities. "Friend Puṇṇamukha, those names such as 'Vesī' and so on given to women are not their names by nature. They are not called Vesī, Nārī, Gamanī, or Bandhakī by nature."

(These terms like Vesī and so on are merely synonymous terms for women.)

## Foolish Men Who Follow Women's Desires
Those women are not merely called Vesī, Gamanī, or Bandhakī. By nature, women are called husband-slayers; they kill their husbands. Regarding that meaning—

The meaning of the verse is:
'Etā itthiyo'—these women. 'Māyā'—are deceptive. 'Marīcī'—are like mirages. 'Sokā'—they cause worry and anxiety. 'Rogā'—they cause disease. 'Upaddavā ca'—and they cause dangers. 'Etā'—these women. 'Kharā ca'—are harsh through anger. 'Bandhanā ca'—are the cause of killing and binding. 'Etā'—these women. 'Maccupāsā'—are called the snares of Death. 'Guhāsayā'—they dwell in the cave of the body. 'Tāsu'—in those women. 'Yo poso'—whichever man. 'Vissase'—should become intimate. 'So poso'—that man. 'Naresu'—among men. 'Narādhamo'—is the lowest of men. 'Hoti'—he is.

## Women's Three Types of Insatiability
Just as a thief standing in the forest with his hair tied up plunders wealth, likewise, these women lead men into the realm of defilements and plunder and destroy them. Just as liquor mixed with poison causes derangement, likewise, these women, having minds infatuated with other men, do not know what should or should not be done; while doing one thing, they do another and display derangement.

Just as a merchant speaks only of the virtues of his own goods, likewise, these women conceal their own lack of virtue and display only virtues. Just as a bear turns back quickly, likewise, women, because of their fickle minds, are those who turn back quickly. Just as a snake has a double tongue, these women, because of their habit of lying, are called double-tongued.

Just as a cesspit covered with planks, likewise, these women go about covered with clothes and ornaments. Just as a pit covered with rubbish causes suffering to another when stepped upon, likewise, these women, when associated with through intimacy, cause suffering to others.
465:
Just as the mouth of the Pātāla (the abyss) in the great ocean is difficult to fill with water (Pātālamukha is indeed Balavamukha), likewise, women are difficult to satisfy in these three things: sexual intercourse, childbirth, and adornment.

Therefore, the Omniscient Buddha taught: "Tiṇṇam, bhikkhave, dhammānaṃ atitto mātugāmo," and so on.

"Bhikkhave"—O monks. "Tiṇṇam dhammānaṃ"—in three things: sexual intercourse, childbirth, and adornment. "Atitto"—being insatiable. "Mātugāmo"—a woman. "Kālaṃ karoti"—dies.

## Poison and Women
Just as a Rakkhasī (ogress), because of her craving for flesh, cannot be satisfied with wealth, and rejecting even much wealth, craves only flesh, likewise, these women, because of their craving for sexual intercourse, cannot be satisfied even with much wealth. Disregarding wealth, they crave only sexual intercourse. Just as Yama, the King of Death, is truly investigative and spares no one, likewise, women do not spare anyone among those endowed with high birth and so on. They lead all men, through the power of defilement, to the destruction of virtue and so on, and at the turn of the second rebirth-consciousness, they lead them to hell.

Just as fire burns everything, whether pure or impure, good or bad, likewise, these women consort with all men, whether low or noble. Just as a river carries away all things, good or bad, likewise, these women associate with all men, low or noble. Just as the wind blows to whatever place it desires, likewise, these women run to whatever place they desire.

In the Himālayas, there is a golden mountain named Neru. Crows that reach that golden mountain also become golden in color. Just as that golden mountain named Neru makes no distinction and makes those who reach it identical, likewise, these women make no distinction and look upon the men who come to them as identical.

The poison tree named Kimpakka, which resembles a mango tree, always bears fruit. It is also endowed with beauty and so on. Therefore, people eat those poison fruits without suspicion and die; likewise, these women, because they are always fruiting through the power of beauty and so on, appear as if they are delightful. They cause heedlessness in those who consort with them and cast them into the four lower realms (apāya).

Therefore, the Omniscient Buddha taught:
"One who indulges in sensual pleasures,
Not knowing the future danger,
They are killed when the result matures,
Like eating the Kimpakka fruit."
466:
Monks, whoever indulges in sensual pleasures without knowing the danger in the future, those sensual pleasures kill that person, just like the ripened Kimpaka fruit when eaten.

Women cause danger to the treasures and wealth acquired with great hardship by their husbands, the masters of the house. They give away those treasures and wealth acquired with hardship to others and engage in immoral conduct.

(Thus it is explained in detail in the Commentary.)

## Four Causes of Ruin

Following this, the Kunāla bird king, beautifying his Dhamma discourse, wishing to show to Punnamukha the four things that lead to ruin along with those women, spoke these three verses beginning with "Cattārimāni, samma Puṇṇamukha."

Friend Punnamukha, there are these four things which, when a need arises, become useless. These four things should not be kept in another's house: an ox, a milch-cow, a vehicle, and a wife. These four are the wealth that a wise man should not allow to be away from his home. Furthermore, there is this verse:

An ox, a milch-cow, a vehicle, and a wife in the house of relatives—these four things one should not let stay away from one's own home. Those who have no vehicle of their own will break the carriage; by over-loading, they kill the bull; by over-milking, they kill the calf; and a wife staying in the house of relatives becomes corrupted.

## Six Causes of Ruin

Having shown the four causes of ruin, wishing to show the six causes of ruin, he spoke these two verses including the division beginning with "Chayimāni, Puṇṇamukha."

Friend Punnamukha, there are these six things which, when a need arises, bring about misfortune:

A bow without a string, a wife in the house of relatives, a boat on the far shore, a vehicle with a broken axle, a friend who is far away, and an evil companion—these six things, when a need arises, bring about misfortune.

## Eight Reasons for Despising a Husband

Having shown the six causes of ruin, wishing to show the eight reasons why those women despise their husbands, he spoke these two verses beginning with "Aṭṭhahi khalu, samma Puṇṇamukha."

Friend Punnamukha, indeed, for eight reasons a woman despises her husband: because of his poverty, because of his being afflicted by illness, because of his old age, because of his being a drunkard, because of his extreme foolishness, because of his negligence, because of his compliance with her in all matters, and because of his giving her all his wealth. Friend Punnamukha, for these eight reasons, a woman despises her husband. In this regard, there is this peerless verse:
467:
Women despise their husbands for eight reasons: poverty, affliction by disease, old age, addiction to liquor, intoxication, falling into a state of confusion, being lustful and neglecting all duties by following a woman's will, and by granting every desire.

Having shown the eight reasons for despising a husband with these verses, he wished to show the nine reasons for bringing offense upon a husband, and thus spoke these three verses starting with "Navahi khalu samma puṇṇamukha ṭhānehi."

## 9 Ways of Bringing Offense

Friend Puṇṇamukha, indeed, by nine ways a woman brings offense to her husband: she is in the habit of going to parks; she is in the habit of going to gardens; she is in the habit of going to riverbanks; she is in the habit of going to her relatives' houses; she is in the habit of going to others' houses; she is habitually devoted to grooming herself with mirrors and clothes; she is a drinker of liquor; she is in the habit of looking out [from windows]; and she is in the habit of standing in doorways [showing herself]. Friend Puṇṇamukha, indeed, by these nine ways a woman brings offense to her husband. In this regard, there is this peerless verse:

She is in the habit of going to parks, gardens, riverbanks, her relatives' houses, and others' houses; she is devoted to grooming herself with mirrors and clothes, and she is a drinker of liquor.

She is in the habit of looking out [from windows], and she is in the habit of standing in doorways [showing herself]; by these nine ways, women bring offense to their husbands.

## 40 Feminine Wiles

Having shown the nine reasons for bringing offense upon a husband with these verses, he wished to show the forty wiles by which women behave to overcome men, and thus spoke the passage starting with "Cattālīsāya khalu samma puṇṇamukha."

Friend Puṇṇamukha, indeed, by forty ways a woman behaves to overcome a man: she stretches; she bends; she acts gracefully; she acts shy; she scratches nail against nail; she steps on foot with foot; she scratches the ground with a stick; she lifts a child or has one lifted; she lifts [a child]; she plays or has one play; she kisses or has one kiss; she eats or has one eat; she gives; she begs; she imitates what is done; she speaks loudly; she speaks softly; she laughs with dancing, singing, music, weeping, grace, or adornment; she speaks clearly; she speaks privately; she laughs loudly; she looks askance; she moves her waist; she moves her private parts; she reveals her thigh; she covers her thigh; she shows her breast; she shows her armpit; she shows her navel; she blinks her eyes; she raises her eyebrows; she bites her lip; she sticks out her tongue; she loosens her cloth; she readjusts her cloth; she loosens her hair; she binds her hair. Friend Puṇṇamukha, by these forty ways a woman behaves to overcome men.
469:
She behaves perversely and does what should not be done. She listens to the voice of another man speaking. She destroys wealth and possessions. She forms intimate associations through lust. These are the signs of a corrupt woman.

Wealth that was gained with difficulty, brought with hardship, and accumulated with pain—she destroys such riches. She forms intimate associations with neighbors. These are the signs of a corrupt woman.

She has restless feet and wanders the streets at unseemly hours of the night. She always has a mind to wrong her husband. She is an adulteress and is devoid of respect. These are the signs of a corrupt woman.

She stands frequently at the threshold of the door, showing her breasts and armpits. With a fluttering heart, she looks here and there. These are the signs of a corrupt woman.

All rivers are winding; all forests are made of wood; all women would commit sin if they found a secluded place.

If they should find the opportunity, or a secret place, or if they should find such a person who would seduce them; all women would commit sin; if they find no other, even with a cripple.

In women who cause discontent to men, who are fickle-minded and unrestrained; even if there be delight in every way, one should not trust them; for women are like a public landing place.

By these Pali verses, the Buddha taught the great deceitfulness and the many faults of women. In the Commentary, this story is presented. The story presented is as follows—
470:
## Kinnara Devī
In the past, in the city of Bārāṇasī, King Kaṇḍarī reigned and possessed a radiant complexion. Every day, a thousand ministers brought him a thousand perfume caskets. Therefore, within the palace grounds, they would split the perfume caskets and use the fragrant wood as fuel to cook rice. The king's chief queen was also exceedingly beautiful, named Kinnara Devī.

The king had a chaplain of the same age named Pañcālacaṇḍa, who was endowed with wisdom. Adjacent to the king's palace, within the city walls, stood a Jambu tree. Its branches hung over the wall. In the shade of that Jambu tree lived a loathsome and ugly cripple.

One day, Queen Kinnara Devī looked out through a window and, seeing the cripple, became filled with lust. At night, after entertaining the king with sensual pleasures and waiting until he fell into a deep sleep, she quietly rose from her bed. She placed various delicacies of excellent flavor into a golden bowl, carried it in her waistband, and descended from the window using a cloth rope. She climbed the Jambu tree, descended by its branches, fed the cripple, and committed misconduct with him. Then, returning by the same path to the palace, she anointed her body with perfumes and lay down with the king.
471:
In this manner, she constantly committed misconduct with the cripple. The king, however, was unaware. One day, while making a clockwise procession around the city and entering the palace, the king saw the cripple in a pitiful state under the shade of the Jambu tree and said to the chaplain, "Teacher, do you see this wretched being?" When the chaplain replied, "I see him, Your Majesty," the king asked, "Teacher, would any woman ever approach such a loathsome person out of lustful desire?"

Hearing these words, the cripple became arrogant and thought, "What is this king saying? He seems not to know that his own wife, Kinnara Devī, comes to me." He then raised his hands in reverence to the Jambu tree and said, "O guardian deity of the Jambu tree, please listen. Except for you, O deity, no one else knows of this matter."

The chaplain, observing the cripple's behavior, thought, "Without a doubt, the chief queen must be going by way of the Jambu tree to commit misconduct with this cripple." Thus, the chaplain asked the king, "Your Majesty, how does the chief queen's body feel to your touch during the night?" The king replied, "Teacher, I notice nothing unusual, but at midnight, her body feels very cold." The chaplain then reported, "Your Majesty, if that is so, setting aside other women, your own chief queen, Kinnara Devī, is committing misconduct with this cripple."
472:
The king said, "Teacher, what are you saying? Why would such a beautiful and graceful chief queen take delight in this exceedingly loathsome cripple?" The chaplain replied, "Your Majesty, if that is the case, please investigate the queen." The king agreed, and after having dinner, he lay down with the queen. Intending to investigate her, he pretended to be in a deep sleep at the usual time.

The queen then rose and acted just as before. The king followed her tracks and stood near the shade of the Jambu tree. The cripple, angry with the queen, said, "You have come very late today!" and struck her ear, which was adorned with an earring, with his hand. Then, she said to the cripple, "Lord, please do not be angry with me; I had to wait for the king to fall asleep," and she behaved toward the cripple as if she were his wife.

Due to the blow, the queen's lion-faced earring slipped from her ear and fell at the king's feet. Thinking, "This much will suffice," the king took the earring and left. The queen, after committing the transgression with the cripple, returned by the same way and attempted to lie down with the king.

The next day, the king sent a message saying, "Let Kinnara Devī come adorned with all the jewelry I have given her." Kinnara Devī replied, "My lion-faced earring is with the goldsmith," and did not come. When sent for again, she came wearing only one earring.

The king asked, "Where is your other earring?" When she replied, "It is with the goldsmith," the king summoned the goldsmith and asked, "Why have you not returned the queen's earring?" The goldsmith replied, "Your Majesty, I did not take it." The king, becoming angry with the queen, said, "You wicked outcaste woman! Should someone like me be your goldsmith?" He then threw the earring down in front of the queen and said to the chaplain, "Teacher, what you said is very true."
473:
"Go, cut off that queen's head," he said.

## The Corrupted Maiden

The chaplain placed the queen in a certain part of the palace and approached the king, saying, "Great King, do not be angry with Queen Kinnarā. All women are of such a nature. If you wish to know the lack of virtue in women, I will show you their wicked conduct and great deceit. Come, let us travel through the countryside in disguise."

The king agreed, saying "Very well," and entrusted the kingdom to his mother before setting out on a journey with the chaplain. When they had reached a distance of about one league (yojana) and were resting by the main road, a certain wealthy man (kuṭumbika) was taking a bride for his son, seating her in a covered carriage and traveling with a large retinue.

Seeing this, the chaplain said to the king, "Great King, if you desire, I can make this maiden commit a wicked act with you." The king asked, "Teacher, what are you saying? She has a large retinue; it would not be possible." The chaplain replied, "Great King, then just watch." He went ahead, set up a curtain screen not far from the road, placed the king inside, and sat by the roadside weeping.

Then the wealthy man saw the chaplain and asked, "Friend, why are you weeping?" "Father, my wife is heavily pregnant and I was taking her to her parents' house. Her labor pains started on the way. She is suffering greatly inside the curtain screen, and there is no woman with her. I cannot go in there myself."
474:
"I do not know what will happen. It would be good if I could get a woman to help." The wealthy man said, "Friend, do not weep. I have many women; one shall go."

"Father, if that is so, let this maiden go. It will be an auspicious omen for her as well." The wealthy man thought, "This brahmin speaks the truth. I want an auspicious omen for my daughter-in-law. By this sign, she will be blessed with many sons and daughters." So he sent the daughter-in-law herself.

The maiden entered the curtain screen, and as soon as she saw the king, her heart was filled with lust, and she committed a wicked act. The king gave her a signet ring. When the business was done and she came out of the screen, they asked her, "What was born?" She replied, "A son with a golden complexion." The wealthy man took the maiden and went on his way.

The chaplain went to the king and asked, "Great King, you have seen how even a maiden can commit such a wicked act. What then can be said of other women? Indeed, did you give her anything?" The king replied, "Teacher, I gave her a ring." The chaplain said, "I will not let her keep that ring," and ran quickly to stop the carriage.

When asked, "Who is stopping this carriage?" he replied, "This maiden has taken a ring placed at the head of my brahmin wife and is leaving with it. Dear daughter, give back the ring." When the maiden gave the ring, she scratched the brahmin's hand with her nails and said, "Thief, take it!" as she handed it over.
475:
“Having seen what happened to Kaṇḍarī and Kinnarā, all women do not delight in the home. Having abandoned such a man, the wife, seeing another man, a cripple [committed sin].”

This is the verse he recited. 

'Ve' means indeed. 'Kaṇḍarīkinnarānaṃ' refers to King Kaṇḍarī and Queen Kinnarā. 'Yañca' means the cause which, 'disvā' having seen, 'jānitabbaṃ' should be known. 'Sabbitt hiyō' means all women, 'agāre' in the husband's house, 'na ramanti' do not delight. 'Aññaṃ' another, 'parapurisaṃ' another man who is a 'pīṭhasappi' cripple, 'disvā' having seen, 'tādisaṃ' such a one who is skilled in pleasure, 'taṃ maccaṃ' that King Kaṇḍarī, 'cajitvā' having abandoned, 'bhariyā' the wife Kinnarā, 'manussapete' with that human-pet cripple, 'saddhiṃ' together, 'pāpaṃ' evil, 'akāsi' committed.

In this way, the chaplain showed the King many other unfaithful women through various means and said, “Let this be enough for here, O King, let us go elsewhere.” The King replied, “Even if we travel through the whole of Jambudīpa, all women will be of this nature. What use have we for them? Let us return.” Returning to Bārāṇasī—

“Great King, women are of such evil nature; this is their natural disposition. Forgive Queen Kinnarā, O King,” being thus entreated by the chaplain, the King forgave her but expelled her from the royal residence. He removed her from her position and appointed another as chief queen. He also expelled the cripple and had the rose-apple branch cut down.

At that time, the Kunāla bird was the brahmin Pañcālacaṇḍa. Thus, wishing to show what he himself had seen, he brought forth this story:

## Pañcapāpī

Another story: In the past, a king named Baka ruled Bārāṇasī righteously. At that time, a poor man living at the eastern gate of Bārāṇasī had a daughter named Pañcapāpī.

## Evil Deeds of a Past Life

In a previous life, Pañcapāpī was also the daughter of a poor man and was plastering a wall with clay. Then, a Paccekabuddha, thinking, “Where shall I get clay to plaster my cave?” and deciding “It can be obtained in Bārāṇasī,” robed himself, took his bowl, entered Bārāṇasī, and stood near that young woman.
476:
The young woman, becoming angry and looking at him with a corrupt mind, said, “He even begs for clay!” The Paccekabuddha stood motionless. Then, seeing him standing still, she felt devotion again and said, “Venerable sir, do you not even get clay?” She took a large lump of clay and placed it in his bowl. The Paccekabuddha used that clay to plaster his cave.

Not long after, she passed away from that life and was reborn in the womb of a poor woman in a gate-village outside that same city. After ten months, she was born. Due to the merit of giving the lump of clay, her body possessed a divine touch. However, because she had looked at the Paccekabuddha with anger, her hands, feet, mouth, eyes, and nose were ugly and deformed. Therefore, she was known as “Pañcapāpī” (Five-Evils).

## The King Falls in Love

One day, the King of Bārāṇasī went to inspect the city at night in disguise and reached that place. Pañcapāpī, playing with the village children, unknowingly caught the King's hand. Due to the touch of her hand, the King could not maintain his composure; it was as if he had been touched by a divine touch.

Infatuated by the lust of touch, even though she was so deformed, he held her hand and asked, “Whose daughter are you?” When she replied, “A gate-dweller's,” he asked if she had a husband. He said, “I will be your husband. Go and get permission from your parents.”

Pañcapāpī approached her parents and said, “Mother, Father, a man saw me and desires me.” They replied, “That man must also be poor; if he desires even one like you, it is well.” She then went and informed the King of her parents' permission.

The King stayed with Pañcapāpī in that very house and returned to the palace early in the morning. From then on, he went to that house regularly in disguise, having no desire to look at any other woman.

## Planning to Bring Her to the Palace

One day, Pañcapāpī's father fell ill with dysentery. The cure for this illness was choice milk-rice mixed with milk, ghee, honey, and sugar. Being poor, they were unable to obtain such medicine. Then Pañcapāpī's mother said to her, “Dear daughter, how is it? Can your husband provide the milk-rice?” She replied, “Mother, my husband must be even poorer than us; nevertheless, I will ask him. Do not worry.” When the King arrived, she sat as if she were unhappy.

When the King came to Pañcapāpī, he asked, “Lady, why are you unhappy?” Pañcapāpī told him the reason. Hearing this, the King thought, “Lady, where shall we get this delicious medicine?” and pondered:

“I cannot keep coming like this forever; there are dangers to be seen on the road. If I bring this woman to the palace, those who do not know Pañcapāpī's divine touch will mock me, saying the King has brought an ogress. I will let the whole city experience her touch first to avoid reproach.” Thinking thus—
477:
Then, the King said to Pañcapāpī, "Lady, do not worry; I will bring milk-rice for your father." After enjoying her company, he went to the palace. On the following day, he had such milk-rice prepared and had leaves brought to make two bundles. In one bundle, he placed the milk-rice, and in the other, he placed a jeweled crest-pin. After tying them, he went to her during the night and said, "Lady, we are poor; this was obtained with great difficulty. Tell your father to eat the milk-rice from this bundle today, and give him the other bundle tomorrow."

Pañcapāpī did exactly as the King had said. Then, Pañcapāpī's father ate a little of the milk-rice, which was full of nutritious flavor, and became satisfied. He gave the remainder to the mother and ate some himself. All three of them were satiated. They set aside the bundle containing the jeweled crest-pin for the next day.

## The Crest-Pin Thief

The King went to the palace, washed his face, and said, "Bring me my jeweled crest-pin." When the attendants said, "Your Majesty, we do not see it," he ordered, "Search throughout the entire city." Although the royal officers investigated and searched, they did not find it. "If that is the case," the King said, "search the houses of the poor outside the city, starting with their rice bundles." While searching, they saw the jeweled crest-pin in Pañcapāpī's house, and they bound Pañcapāpī's parents as thieves and brought them away.

Then, Pañcapāpī's parents submitted to the King, "Your Majesty, we did not steal it; another person brought this jeweled crest-pin." When asked, "Who brought it?", they replied, "Our son-in-law brought it." When asked, "Where is that son-in-law?", they replied, "Our daughter knows."

Thereafter, the father spoke with his daughter. "Dear daughter, do you know your husband?" he asked. When she replied, "I do not know him," he said, "If you do not know him, our lives are at an end." She then said, "Father, my husband comes only when it is dark and leaves while it is still dark. Therefore, I do not know his appearance. However, I am able to recognize him by the touch of his hand." Pañcapāpī then informed the royal officers.

## Ordering the Search for the Thief

Those royal officers also reported this to the King. The King, pretending not to know, said, "If that is the case, place that woman inside a curtain in the palace courtyard. Make a hole in the curtain just large enough for a hand to pass through. Assemble all the city dwellers and let her catch the thief by the touch of his hand."
478:
The royal officers, intending to do as the King commanded, went to Pañcapāpī. Upon seeing her appearance, they became displeased and disgusted, saying, "Is this a ghoul haunting the road?" and did not dare to touch her. However, they brought her and placed her inside a curtain in the palace courtyard and assembled all the city dwellers.

As each person came, Pañcapāpī held the hand extended through the hole in the curtain and said, "This person is not the thief." The men, becoming captivated by her touch, which was like a divine touch, were unable to leave. They thought, "Even if this woman deserves royal punishment, we will pay the fine or even become her slaves just to have her in our homes." Then, the royal officers beat them with sticks and made them flee. All the men, starting from the Sub-king (Uparāja), became like madmen.

## The Thief is Caught

Then the King thought, "What if it were I?" and extended his hand into the curtain. As soon as she held the King's hand, she cried out loudly, "I have caught my thief!"

The King asked the assembled city dwellers, "What did you think when this woman held your hands?" The city dwellers reported the truth. Then the King said to them:

"I did this in order to bring this woman to the palace. I thought, 'Those who do not know the touch of this woman might revile me.' Therefore, I have let all of you know. Speak now, in whose house is it proper for this woman to reside?" They replied, "Your Majesty, it is proper for her to reside in your palace."

## Becoming the Chief Queen

Then, he consecrated Pañcapāpī and made her his Chief Queen. He also granted great wealth and status to her parents. From that time on, because he was so enamored with Pañcapāpī, he did not attend to legal judgments, nor did he look at any other woman.

## Becoming Chief Queen Again

Then, the other women sought an opportunity against Pañcapāpī. One day, Pañcapāpī saw an omen in a dream about being the Chief Queen of two kings and reported it to the King. The King summoned dream interpreters and asked, "When such a dream is seen, what will happen?"

Those dream interpreters, having taken bribes from the other women, said, "Great King, the fact that the Queen dreamed of sitting on the back of an all-white elephant is a portent of your death. Dreaming of touching the moon while on the elephant's back is a portent of you being taken away by enemy kings." When asked, "What should be done now?", they replied, "Your Majesty, it is not possible to kill the Queen; it is proper to place this Queen on a boat and release her into the river."

The King, during the night, placed her on a boat along with food, clothing, and ornaments, and released her into the river. As the Queen floated down the river, she arrived in the presence of King Bāvarika, who was playing in the water with his boat downstream. King Bāvarika's general saw the boat and said, "This boat is mine." The King said, "The treasures in the boat are mine."
479:
The wife of one who followed excessive desires,
Committed misconduct with one who followed her own will;
What other woman would not transgress against such a man?

He spoke this verse.

Bakañca rañño: of King Baka. Bāvarikassa ca rañño: and of King Bāvarika. Accantakāmānugata: of one who truly followed her desires. Avācarī: she who has vile conduct. Bhariyā: the wife. Paṭṭhavasānugassa: with one who followed her own will and longing. Saddhiṃ: together with. Pāpaṃ: vile conduct. Akāsi: committed. Kaṃ vā: what. Aññaṃ: other. Taṃpi: even that man. Itthī: women. Nāticaré: would they not transgress against?

When the boat arrived, he saw Pañcapāpī and asked, "You look like an ogress; what is your name?" Pañcapāpī smiled and, speaking of her status as the Chief Queen of King Baka, told King Bāvarika the whole story. This queen was famous throughout the entire Jambudīpa as Pañcapāpī. Then King Bāvarika took Pañcapāpī by the hand and lifted her up. As soon as he touched her, he was overcome by the passion of touch (phassarāga); he lost all perception of other women as women and established Pañcapāpī in the position of Chief Queen. She became as dear to King Bāvarika as his own life.

## The Chief Queen of Two Kings

King Baka heard of this matter and said, "I will not allow her to be the Chief Queen of King Bāvarika." He gathered his army, built a residence at the river landing, and sent a message to King Bāvarika: "Will you give me my wife, or will you fight?" King Bāvarika replied, "I will give you war, but not the wife," and made preparations for battle.

The ministers of the two kings consulted: "There is no reason to face death because of a woman. Since he was her first husband, this queen should belong to King Baka. Since she was found in a boat, she should also belong to King Bāvarika. Therefore, let her stay for seven days at a time in each king's palace." They informed the two kings of this. Both kings were pleased and lived in cities they built on opposite banks of the river. Pañcapāpī served as the Chief Queen for both kings. Both kings were exceedingly devoted to her.

## Taking a Paramour

After staying seven days in one king's palace, while she was traveling by boat to the other king's palace, she committed misconduct in the middle of the river with an old, hunchbacked fisherman who was rowing the boat.
480:
At that time, the bird-king Kuṇāla was King Baka of Bārāṇasī. Therefore, wishing to illustrate the matter he had seen himself, he spoke this verse:

Bakañca bāvarikassa ca rañño...

## Queen Pingiyānī

Another story: In the past, Queen Pingiyānī, the Chief Queen of a certain King Brahmadatta, opened the lion-window and looked out. Seeing the royal groom, she descended from the palace through the window when the king was asleep. After committing misconduct with the groom, she climbed back up, perfumed her body, and lay down with the king.

One day, the king wondered, "Why is the body of this Chief Queen cold at midnight? I shall investigate her." One day, pretending to be asleep, he followed the queen as she left and saw her committing misconduct with the horse-trainer. He returned and went to bed. The Chief Queen also returned after the act and lay down on a low bed.

The next morning, the king summoned the queen in the midst of his ministers and revealed the matter. Saying, "All women are of evil nature," he forgave her the punishment she deserved—death, imprisonment, or mutilation—but demoted her from her position and made another woman his Chief Queen.

At that time, the bird-king Kuṇāla was King Brahmadatta. Thus, to show what he had seen, he spoke this verse:

Pingiyānī sabbhalokissarassa,
Raño piyā brahmadattassa bhariyā.
Avācarī paṭṭhavasānugassa,
Taṃ vāpi sā nājjhagā kāmakāminī.

Brahmadattassa: of the one named Brahmadatta. Sabbhalokissarassa: of the king who rules over all people. Rañño: of the king. Bhariyā: the wife. Piyā: the beloved. Pingiyānī: the Chief Queen named Pingiyānī. Paṭṭhavasānugassa: with the horse-trainer who followed her will and longing. Avācarī: committed misconduct. Kāmakāminī: desiring sensual pleasures. Sā: that queen. Taṃ vāpi: either that desired sensual pleasure. Mahesiṭṭhānaṃ vā: or the position of Chief Queen. Nājjhagā: she did not attain. Ubhato: from both. Bhaṭṭhā: she fell and was ruined.

## Women Not to be Associated With

Thus, the Bodhisatta Kuṇāla, having shown the faults of women through these past stories, spoke these twelve verses to further explain their faults:

Luddhānaṃ lahucittānaṃ, akataññūna dubbhinaṃ...
...Etitthiyo pañca na sevitabbā.

Luddhānaṃ: of those who are greedy. Lahucittānaṃ: of those with fickle minds. Akataññūnaṃ: of those who are ungrateful. Dubbhinaṃ: of those who betray their friends. Itthīnaṃ: of women. Sīlavantavādaṃ: the claim of being virtuous. Saddhātūṃ: to believe. Adevasattō: a man not possessed by the deity of lust. Na arahati: is not fit.

Tā: those women. Kataṃ: a favor done for them. Nappajānanti: they do not know. Kiccaṃ: the duty of gratitude. Nappajānanti: they do not know. Mātaraṃ: neither mother. Pitaraṃ: nor father.
481:
Furthermore, they do not recognize a brother or a sister. They are un-noble, having no shame in evil conduct. They are of a nature to transgress the Dhamma. They follow only the whims of their own minds.

Even if they have lived together for a long time, they abandon a husband who is dear, pleasing, compassionate, and as precious as life itself, due to dangers or various affairs. Therefore, I do not trust women.

Truly, the mind of women is like that of a monkey. Like the shadow of a tree that falls upon whoever comes by, the heart of women is extremely unstable; it revolves like the rim of a chariot wheel.

When they see and observe the desirable wealth of a man, they lead him away with smooth words, just as the people of Kamboja lead a horse with water-weeds.

When they see and observe that a man's desirable wealth is gone, they avoid him from all sides, just as one who has crossed to the other side of a river leaves the raft behind.

Women are like birdlime; they are like fire that consumes everything, good or bad. They possess sharp cunning like a swift-flowing river. Truly, just as a boat serves both this shore and the other shore, they serve both the man they love and the man they hate.

They do not belong to just one or two; they are like an open market shop. Any man who thinks, 'She is my wife,' would be trying to catch the wind with a net.

In this world, women are of such a nature: like a river landing, like a main road, like a tavern, like a public hall, or like a water-stand; there is no fixed time or limit for them.

They are like fire; they are like the head of a cobra. Like cows that search for the best grass outside, they seek out whatever seems better.
482:
Fire, an elephant, a cobra, a consecrated king, and all women—a man should associate with these five with constant mindfulness. Indeed, the entire nature of these five is difficult to know.

## Women Who Should Not Be Associated With

One should not associate with a woman who is exceedingly beautiful. One should not associate with a woman who is desired by many. One should not associate with women who are skilled in dancing and singing. One should not associate with another's wife. And a woman who associates with one only for the sake of wealth, even if she has no owner, should not be associated with. These five types of women should not be associated with.
483:
## The Discourse on Women by the Vulture King Ānanda

When this was preached, the people praised the Bodhisatta Kuṇāla, saying, 'Oh, how wonderful! It is well preached.' Having preached the faults of women through these many reasons, the Bodhisatta Kuṇāla remained silent.

Having heard the Dhamma talk of the Kuṇāla bird, the Vulture King Ānanda said, 'Friend Kuṇāla, I too shall preach the faults of women through my own power of wisdom,' and he made an effort to speak about the faults of women.
484:
Desiring to show this matter, the Omniscient Buddha preached the fifteen verses beginning with 'Atha khalu bho Ānando gijjharājā'.

O monks! Then, indeed, the Vulture King named Ānanda, having understood the beginning, middle, and end of the speech of the Bird King named Kunāla, recited these verses at that time:

326. Even if a man were to give this earth filled with wealth to a woman he cherished, she would despise him if she found the opportunity. One should not fall under the power of such immoral women.

327. Even if he is energetic, of steady conduct, a beloved and pleasing husband of her youth, they abandon him in times of danger or for various needs. Therefore, I do not trust women.

328. A man should not trust, thinking 'She desires me,' nor should he trust, thinking 'She weeps in my presence.' They serve both the dear and the undear, just as a boat serves both this shore and the other.

## Four Things Not to be Trusted

329. One should not trust an old spread of branches. One should not trust an old friend who has become a thief. One should not trust a king, thinking 'He is my friend.' One should not trust a woman, even if she is the mother of ten children.
485:
330. One should not trust women who delight in fools, who are excessive in their conduct, and who are unrestrained. Even if a wife is one of extreme devotion, one should not trust her. Truly, women are like a river landing.

331. They might kill, they might cut, or they might even have one killed; they might cut the throat and drink the blood. One should not place affection in women of low desires, the unrestrained, who are like the landings of the Gaṅgā.

## A Woman's Truth is but a Lie

332. To them, a lie is like the truth, and the truth is like a lie. They are like cows searching for the best grass outside.

333. They entice with their gait, with their looks, and with their smiles; also with improper dress and with sweet speech.

334. Truly, they are thieves, harsh-hearted, and fierce; yet they are sweet-tongued like sugar through useless talk. They know every deception that exists among humans; there is nothing they do not know.

335. In the world, those called women are immoral and heedless. There is no limit to them. They are always full of lust and are bold; they are like an all-consuming fire.

336. To women, there is no such thing as 'dear,' nor does 'undear' exist. Truly, they serve both the dear and the undear, just as a boat serves both this shore and the other.

337. To women, there is no such thing as 'dear,' nor does 'undear' exist. For the sake of wealth, they entwine themselves around a man, like a creeper clinging to a tree.

## What Women Desire

338. Women follow after an elephant-trainer, a horse-trainer, an ox-herd, an outcaste who burns corpses, or a scavenger who removes flowers; they follow any group of men who possess wealth.
486: 339. Women abandon even a well-born man if he is penniless. For the sake of wealth, they follow and pursue even one who is like an outcaste dog-eater, provided he has riches.
487:
## The Discourse of the Hermit Nārada on Women

Thus, the vulture king named Ānanda, established in his own wisdom, having preached the faults of women, remained silent.

Hearing the words of the vulture king Ānanda, the hermit Nārada also, established in his own wisdom, preached the faults of those women. To make this matter clear, the All-Knowing Buddha preached the twelve verses beginning with "Atha khalu bho Nārada."

O monks! Then, indeed, the hermit Nārada, who was a noble brahmin, having understood the beginning, middle, and end of the speech of the vulture king named Ānanda, recited these verses at that time:

## Things That Cannot Be Filled

O Cuckoo, the king of birds! Listen to my words which I shall speak. The ocean, the brahmin, the king, and the woman—these four can never be filled.

Whatever rivers exist on earth flow into the sea. Those rivers cannot fill the ocean. Because of its vastness, it is never full.

A brahmin, even after studying the four Vedas with the Itihāsa as the fifth, would still desire more learning. Because of his great desire for knowledge, he is never full.

A king, even after conquering the entire earth including the oceans and the mountains of the universe, and possessing various jewels, still yearns for the other shore of the ocean. Because of his great greed, he is never full.

Even if a single woman were to have eight husbands, each of whom is brave, powerful, and capable of providing all sensual pleasures, she would still have desire for a ninth husband. Because of her great sensual craving, she is never full.

All women are like fire, consuming everything. All women are like rivers, carrying everything away. All women are like thorny branches. All women go to another man for the sake of wealth.
488:
If a man were to surrender his whole being to women, that man might as well try to catch the wind with a net, bale out the great ocean with a single hand, or produce a sound with his own hand.

Truth is very difficult to find in those women, who are like thieves and possess many wiles. The nature of women is hard to know, like the path of a fish in water.

They are insatiable; they never say "enough" regarding three things. They are soft-spoken. They are hard to fill like a river because they are difficult to satisfy with sensual pleasures. Knowing that women sink into the four woeful states, one should avoid them from afar.

Women are great deceivers and are like a conjurer's trick. They destroy the holy life. Knowing that they sink into the four woeful states, one should avoid them from afar.

Whether these women serve a man out of affection or for the sake of wealth, they quickly consume the man who associates with them, just as fire consumes its own place.
489:
## The Discourse of Kuṇāla the Cuckoo on Women

Thus, when the hermit Nārada had shown the faults of women, the Great Being, the cuckoo king Kuṇāla, further revealed their faults in detail. To make this matter clear, the All-Knowing Buddha preached the twenty verses beginning with "Atha khalu Kuṇālo."

O monks! Then, indeed, the bird king named Kuṇāla, having understood the beginning, middle, and end of the speech of the hermit Nārada, the noble brahmin, preached these verses at that time:

A wise man might speak with one who holds a sharpened sword in hand, or even with a wrathful demon. He might even touch a snake of fierce power. But he should never speak alone with a woman in a secluded place.

## The Weapons of Women

For indeed, women agitate the minds of the world. Having dancing, singing, speech, and smiles as their weapons, they oppress the man of unestablished mindfulness, just as a group of ogresses devours merchants on an island.
490:
353. "They have no discipline, no restraint; they delight in liquor and meat and are unrestrained. They swallow the wealth painfully gathered by a man, just as the Timiṅgala fish in the ocean swallows a Makara."

354. "Their range is the pleasure of the five cords of sensual desire; they are haughty, unstable, and unrestrained. Women approach negligent men just as rivers flow into the salt-water ocean."

## Enticements of Women

355. "Whatever man women entice, whether through affection, through delight in sensual pleasures, or for the sake of wealth, those women—who oppress with lust and hatred—burn that man, even if he is as brilliant as fire."

356. "Knowing a man to be wealthy and of great means, they approach him, giving their own wealth and their very selves. They completely entangle that man whose mind is infatuated, just as the Māluva creeper entangles a Sāl tree in the forest."

357. "Adorned and with faces like beautiful images, they approach with various desires. Women laugh loudly and laugh softly; they are like Sambara, skilled in a hundred deceits."

358. "Adorned with gold, gems, and pearls, and honored in their husbands' homes, women, if not guarded, transgress against their husbands, just as the woman kept inside the heart of the Dānava transgressed against him."

359. "Even a powerful man, wise, honored, and worshipped by many, does not shine when he falls under the power of women, like the moon seized by Rāhu."
491:
360. "Whatever ruin an angry and corrupt-minded person might inflict upon an enemy who has come into his power, a man who yearns for women and falls under their power meets with even greater ruin than that."

361. "Though threatened by the pulling of hair and scratching with nails, and though beaten with feet, hands, elbows, ropes, and sticks, women still resort to the low. They delight in the low, just as flies delight in a corpse."

362. "In families, in the streets, or in royal cities and market towns, they set the snare and trap of Namuci (Mara). A man with vision who desires happiness should avoid them."

363. "He who abandons the virtue of asceticism, which is called merit, and practices ignoble conduct in sensual pleasures, will be led to hell by the deities, just as a merchant takes a counterfeit gem after giving a hundred thousand in wealth."

364. "That foolish man, censured here and in the next world, destroyed by his own evil deeds, falls from the human and celestial realms and wanders for a long time in the states of deprivation, like a chariot drawn by a wicked donkey going off the path."

## Hell for the Lustful

365. "He goes to the great hell named Patāpana and to the iron forest of sword-leafed silk-cotton trees. Having lived in the animal realm, he is not released from the realm of Petas and Asuras."

366. "Women destroy the divine sports and delights in the Nandana Grove and the status of a Universal Monarch among humans for negligent men, and they cause them to reach the four states of deprivation."
492:
367. "Divine sports and delights are not hard to obtain, nor is the status of a Universal Monarch among humans, nor the nymphs dwelling in golden mansions, for those men who live the holy life, having no desire for women."

368. "The destination that transcends the sensual realm and the state in the fine-material realm are not hard to obtain; nor is rebirth in the Pure Abodes for those who are free from lust and live the holy life, having no desire for women."

369. "Even Nibbāna—the peaceful, the absolute, the unshakable, the unconditioned, which transcends all suffering—is not hard to obtain for those pure ones who have extinguished defilements and live the holy life, having no desire for women."

Regarding "converses" (sallape): even if one stands with a sword and says, "If you converse with me, I will cut off your head," or if a demon stands there in anger saying, "As soon as you speak, I will eat you and end your life," one might converse with them. One might even approach a fierce snake and touch it. But a man should never speak alone in private with a woman. "Disturbers of the world's mind" means they destroy the mind of the world. "A group of Rakshasas on an island": just as Rakshasas on an island entice merchants by taking human form and then eat them once they are under their power, so too these women bring beings to great ruin by bringing them under their power through the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Vinaya" means conduct. "Saṃvara" means restraint. "A man's wealth" means wealth gathered with difficulty. "Aniyatā" means having an unstable mind. "Loṇatoyavatiyaṃ" means the ocean which has salt water. "Āpakā" means rivers. Just as rivers flow into the ocean, so women approach the negligent. "Chandasā" means through affection. "Ratiyā" means through delight in the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Dhanena vā" means because of wealth. "Jātaveadasadisaṃ" means even one who shines like fire with the accomplishment of virtues.
493: Thus, the Bodhisatta Kuṇāla, leading [the audience] to the deathless Nibbāna, concluded his Dhamma teaching. The Kinnaras, Nāgas, and others dwelling in the Himālaya region, as well as the deities established in the sky, gave praise and applause, saying, "Oh, how wonderful! He teaches with the grace of an Omniscient Buddha!"
494: The vulture king named Ānanda, the ascetic Nārada, and the cuckoo named Puṇṇamukha took their respective followers and returned to their own places. The Bodhisatta Kuṇāla also went to his own place. However, the vulture king Ānanda, the ascetic Nārada, and the cuckoo Puṇṇamukha would visit the Bodhisatta Kuṇāla from time to time to receive his instructions. By establishing themselves in those instructions, they were destined for the heavenly realm.
495:
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka by reciting these concluding verses:

"I was Kuṇāla then, and Udāyī was the cuckoo Puṇṇamukha.
Ānanda was the vulture king, and Sāriputta was Nārada.
The assembly was the Buddha’s assembly; thus remember the Jātaka."

Bhikkhave, O monks. Etarahi, now. Ahaṃ, I. Tadā, at that time. Kuṇālo, was the bird-king Kuṇāla. Etarahi, now. Udāyī, Udāyī. Tadā, at that time. Phussakokilo, was the cuckoo named Puṇṇamukha. Etarahi, now. Ānando, Ānanda. Tadā, at that time. Gijjharājā, was the vulture king named Ānanda. Etarahi, now. Sāriputto ca, and Sāriputta. Tadā, at that time. Nārado, was the ascetic Nārada. Etarahi, now. Buddhaparisā, the Buddha’s assembly. Tadā, at that time. Parisā, was the assembly of the bird-king Kuṇāla. Evaṃ, thus. Jātakaṃ, the identification of the Jātaka. Dhāretha, you should remember.

The Omniscient Buddha, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka in this way.

Those five hundred Sakyan princes went [to the forest] by the power of the Teacher, but returned by their own power. The Teacher taught them the meditation subject in the Mahāvana forest. All of them attained Arahantship on that very day. There was a great assembly of deities. At that great assembly of deities, the Blessed One taught the Mahāsamaya Sutta.

## By knowing the many faults of women, one attains happiness.

The Mahākuṇāla Jātaka is concluded.

## 5. Mahāsutasoma Jātaka

## Fulfillment of Desires through Wisdom

The Teacher, the Omniscient One who disciplines the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Mahāsutasoma Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Kasmā tuvaṃ", concerning the taming of the Elder Angulimāla.

The life story and the ordination of the Elder Angulimāla should be understood in detail as stated in the Commentary on the Angulimāla Sutta. Specifically, the Elder Angulimāla, by making an Act of Truth, brought safety to a woman who could not give birth. From then on, he easily obtained alms-food and, while cultivating meditation, later attained Arahantship and became famous as one of the eighty Great Elders.

At that time, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, how wonderful! The Omniscient Buddha performed a difficult task by taming such a cruel, bloody-handed great robber like Angulimāla, making him harmless without using a rod or a weapon. Indeed, the Omniscient Buddhas are performers of difficult tasks!"

The Blessed One, staying in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), heard the monks' conversation with his divine ear. Knowing that "My visit to the Dhamma Hall today will be of great benefit to beings; a great Dhamma teaching will take place," he went to the Dhamma Hall with the incomparable grace of a Buddha and sat on the prepared noble seat.
496:
"Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" he asked. When they replied, "For such and such a discussion," he said, "Monks, it is no wonder that I, having now attained supreme Enlightenment, have tamed the Elder Aṅgulimāla. In the past, while practicing the conduct for Buddhahood and established in partial knowledge (padesañāṇa), I also tamed that Aṅgulimāla." Having said this, being requested by the monks, he brought forth the past.

In the past, monks, in the city of Indapatta in the Kuru kingdom, a king named Korabya ruled according to the ten kingly virtues. At that time, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of King Korabya's chief queen. After ten months, the queen gave birth to a son with a complexion like gold. Because he possessed the delightful wealth of learning, they named the prince "Sutasoma."

When King Korabya saw that his son Prince Sutasoma had come of age, he gave him a thousand pieces of gold (nikkhas) and sent him to Takkasilā to study under a world-renowned teacher. Prince Sutasoma took the thousand nikkhas for the teacher's fee, departed from the city, and set out on his journey.

At that time, in the city of Bārāṇasī, Prince Brahmadatta, the son of the King of Kāsi, was also sent by his father, the King of Kāsi, for the same purpose. He departed from the city and set out on the same journey. Prince Sutasoma, traveling along the way, sat down to rest at a rest house by the gate of Takkasilā.

## Two Prince Friends

Prince Brahmadatta also arrived and sat on the same bench with Prince Sutasoma. Then, Prince Sutasoma, wishing to converse with Prince Brahmadatta, spoke thus:

"Friend, are you tired from the journey? Where have you come from?" he asked. When the other replied, "I have come from Bārāṇasī," he asked, "Whose son are you?" When he replied, "I am the son of the King of Kāsi," he asked, "What is your name?" When he replied, "I am Prince Brahmadatta," he asked, "For what reason have you come here?" Prince Brahmadatta replied, "I have come to study." Then he asked Prince Sutasoma in the same manner, "Are you also tired from the journey? Where have you come from?" Prince Sutasoma also told him everything.

The two of them thought, "We are both of the warrior caste (khattiya); let us go to study under the same teacher." Having made a friendship with each other, they entered the city, went to the teacher's house, paid homage to the teacher, made their lineage known, and explained that they had come to study. The teacher accepted them, saying, "Very well." The two princes paid the teacher's fee and began their studies.

## Finished Education and Returned

It was not only these two princes; at that time, there were one hundred and one other princes from across Jambudīpa who were also studying under that teacher.
497:
Prince Sutasoma was the senior pupil among those princes, and while studying, he reached completion in a short time. Prince Sutasoma did not go to anyone else but went only to Prince Brahmadatta, thinking, "Prince Brahmadatta is my friend," and acted as an assistant teacher (piṭṭhi-ācariya) to teach him.

For the other princes as well, their studies gradually reached completion. After they had mastered the difficult parts, they paid homage to the teacher and, surrounding Prince Sutasoma, departed from Takkasilā.

## When They Became Kings

Then, Prince Sutasoma, standing in the middle of the road and wishing to send them off, said, "You will all demonstrate your knowledge to your respective parents and be established in kingship. Once established, follow my advice." When they asked, "Teacher, what is it?" he instructed them, "On the Uposatha days of the waxing and waning fortnights, observe the Uposatha and do not take the lives of beings; make this a regular practice." The princes agreed, saying, "Very well."

The Bodhisatta, Prince Sutasoma, because he was renowned in the art of physiognomy (aṅgavijjā), knew that "In the future, a great danger will arise in Bārāṇasī because of Prince Brahmadatta." Having given this advice to the princes, he sent them away.

All those princes went to their respective countries, demonstrated their knowledge to their parents, and were established in kingship. To let him know of their establishment in kingship and their adherence to his advice, they sent letters along with gifts. Hearing this news, the Bodhisatta sent back letters saying, "Be only heedful."

## The King of Bārāṇasī Eating Human Flesh

Among those princes, the King of Bārāṇasī would not eat his meal without meat. For the King of Bārāṇasī, meat had to be bought and kept for the Uposatha day. Then one day, the cook was negligent with the meat kept in this way, and the dogs raised in the palace ate it. The cook, not seeing the meat and going around with coins (kahāpaṇas) to search for it, was unable to obtain any. He thought, "If I serve the meal without meat, my life will be no more. What shall I do?" and then he devised a plan.
498:
Thinking, "This is the way," he went to the cemetery at night, took the thigh meat of a man who had just died, cooked it well, and served it to the king. As soon as the piece of meat touched the tip of the king's tongue, the flavor pervaded his seven thousand taste nerves. His whole body was thrilled.

Why was this? Because King Brahmadatta had eaten human flesh in a past life, his whole body was stirred. In his immediately preceding life, King Brahmadatta had been a yakkha and had eaten much human flesh. Therefore, he had a craving for human flesh.

King Brahmadatta thought, "If I eat this in silence, this cook will not tell me about this meat," and so he spat it out on the ground along with his saliva. When the cook said, "Your Majesty, the meat is faultless; please eat," the king dismissed the attendants and asked, "I too know that the meat is faultless. But what kind of meat is this?"

"Your Majesty, it is the same meat as consumed in previous days," the cook replied. "In other times, this meat did not have such flavor," the king said. "Your Majesty, it was cooked well today," the cook submitted. "Was it not cooked in the same way in previous days?" the king asked. Seeing the cook remain silent, he said, "Speak the truth. If you do not speak the truth, your life is no more."

The cook asked for immunity and then reported the truth. King Brahmadatta said, "Do not make a sound; keep quiet. You eat the meat cooked normally, but for me, cook only human flesh." "Your Majesty, human flesh is difficult to obtain," the cook submitted. "Do not be afraid; it is easy to get," the king replied. "Your Majesty, where can it be obtained regularly?" "Are there not many people in the prison?" the king said.

## When the People Agitated

From then on, the cook did as the king commanded. Later, when the people in the prison were exhausted, he submitted, "Your Majesty, what shall I do now?" "Throw a bundle of a thousand coins in the middle of the road. Whoever takes that bundle, seize him as a thief, kill him, and cook him," the king said. The cook did as the king commanded.
499:
Thinking, "Or does he kill at the word of another?" and wishing to ask about the matter, the General spoke the first verse:

371. "Why, Rasaka, do you do such things, deeds so very cruel? You kill women and men, O deluded one; is it for the sake of meat, or for the sake of wealth?"

371. Friend Rasaka, O cook. You, such as these, very cruel deeds, why do you do them? Being deluded, do you kill women and men? Is it for the sake of meat? Or else, is it for the sake of wealth?

373. "If you are employed in your master's interest and do such cruel deeds, then having reached the inner palace early in the morning, speak this in the presence of my King."

373. Friend Rasaka. You, being engaged in your master's welfare, if you do such very cruel deeds, then having done so, early in the morning, having reached the inner palace, in the presence of the King, my lord, speak these words to me.

Later, because they feared the King's punishment, the cook saw no one even looking at the thousand-piece bribe and asked again, "Great King, what shall I do now?" The King replied, "At midnight, when the whole city is disturbed by thieves, stand at a fence, a main road, or a crossroads, kill a person, and take the meat." From that day on, the cook did as the King said, taking fat meat and departing.

Seeing corpses in various places, the people's cries were heard: "My mother is missing, my father is missing, my brother or sister is missing." The citizens were terrified and looked about, wondering, "Has a lion eaten these people? Has a tiger eaten them? Or has an ogre eaten them?" Seeing the stab wounds, they realized, "A certain man-eating thief is eating these people."

The people gathered at the palace courtyard and cried out. King Brahmadatta asked, "Friends, what is it?" They submitted, "Great King, there is a man-eater in this city; please have that man-eater caught." The King said, "How can I know that thief? What then, shall I go around guarding the city myself?"

## The Killer is Caught

The people said, "This King has no concern for the country; let us inform the General named Kālahaṭṭhi." They reported the matter to the General and said, "It is proper for you to search for the thief."

The General said, "Very well, wait for seven days; I will find the thief and give him to you." He dismissed the people, called his men, and ordered, "Friends, it is said there is a man-eater in the city. You must hide in various places and catch that thief." The men agreed and investigated the city from that day on.

The cook, hiding by a fence, killed a woman and was trying to fill his meat basket with solid meat. Then the King's men caught the cook, beat him, bound his hands behind his back, and made a great noise, shouting, "The man-eater is caught!" Many people surrounded the cook. Then, having bound him firmly and hung the meat basket around his neck, they brought him and showed him to the General.

## Why Do You Kill?

Seeing the cook, the General thought, "How is this? Does this man eat this human flesh? Or does he mix it with other meat to sell? Or does he kill at the word of another?" Wishing to ask about the matter:

## The King Commanded Me

Thereafter, the cook, wishing to explain the matter to the General, spoke this second verse:

372. "Not for my own sake, nor for the sake of wealth, nor for children, wife, friends, or kin. My master, the fortunate lord of the earth, he eats meat such as this, O venerable one."

372. Lord General, may it be well with you. I do not kill for my own sake. I do not kill for the sake of wealth. I do not kill for the sake of wife and children. I do not kill for the sake of friends and kin. My master, who provides my food, the fortunate lord of the earth, that King exists. That King eats meat of this kind.

## Answer in the King's Presence

Hearing those words, General Kālahaṭṭhi wished Rasaka to speak of that matter in the presence of the King.

Then Rasaka, wishing to agree to speak thus, spoke this verse:

374. "I will do so, venerable one, just as you say, Kālahaṭṭhi. Having reached the inner palace early in the morning, I will speak this in the presence of the King for you."

374. Venerable Kālahaṭṭhi of pleasant countenance. As you say, so I will do. Early in the morning, having reached the inner palace, in the presence of the King, I will speak these words to you.

After this inquiry, General Kālahaṭṭhi kept Rasaka bound just as he was and let him sleep. When dawn broke, he consulted with the ministers and citizens. When all were of one mind, he placed guards in all places, took control of the city, and led Rasaka to the King's palace with the meat basket hanging from his neck. The whole city shouted.
500:
375. Then, at the break of night, towards the rising of the sun, Kāḷa, taking Rasaka, approached the King. Having approached the King, he spoke these words.

376. "Is it true, O Great King, that Rasaka was sent by you? He kills men and women, and you eat their flesh."

The Teacher preached these verses:

375. Bhikkhus, monks. Tato—at that time. Ratyā, when the night. Vivasāne, had dawned. Suriyuggamanam pati, at the time of sunrise. Kāḷo, the general Kāḷahatta. Rasakaṃ, Rasaka. Ādāya, having brought. Rājānaṃ, to King Brahmadatta. Upasaṅkami, approached. Upasaṅkamma, having approached. Rājānaṃ, to King Brahmadatta. Idaṃ vacanaṃ, these words. Abravi, he said.

376. Mahārāja, O Great King. Tayā, by you. Rasako, Rasaka. Pesito, was sent. Saccaṃ kira, is it true? Ayaṃ Rasako, this Rasaka. Itthī ca, women. Purise ca, and men. Hanati, kills. Tuvaṃ, you, O Great King. Maṃsāni, human flesh. Khādasi kira, eat, it is said. Saccaṃ, is it true?

King Brahmadatta, having eaten his breakfast the previous day, had not received any meat in the evening. Saying, "Rasaka will come now, Rasaka will come now," he spent the night sitting up. Thinking, "Even today Rasaka does not come, and a great noise of the citizens is heard; what could this be?" he looked through the palace window and saw Rasaka being brought in that manner. Thinking, "This matter has become public," he established mindfulness and remained seated on his royal throne.

## The General's Petition

General Kāḷahatta approached the King and investigated the matter. The King also spoke to General Kāḷahatta. Desiring to make the matter clear, the Blessed One said:

## The King's Answer

Having heard those words, King Brahmadatta admitted his deed and, wishing to blame General Kāḷahatta, spoke these verses:

377. "Even so, O Kāḷa, Rasaka was sent by me. Why do you revile him who is doing my work?"

377. Kāḷa, Kāḷahatta. Evam eva, it is exactly as you say. Tathā, in that manner. Rasako, Rasaka. Mayā, by me. Pesito, was sent. Mama, my. Atthaṃ, benefit/interest. Karontassa, while he is performing. Etaṃ, this Rasaka. Kiṃ, why. Paribhāsasi, do you revile?

Having heard this, General Kāḷahatta thought, "This King admits it with his own mouth. How reckless! For such a long time, these people have been eaten by this King. I will stop him." He then urged, "O Great King, do not do this; do not eat human flesh."

"Kāḷahatta, what are you saying? I am unable to abstain from this human flesh," the King replied. "O Great King, if you do not abstain from this human flesh, you will destroy both yourself and the entire kingdom," the General said. "Kāḷahatta, even if it leads to such destruction, I am unable to abstain from that human flesh," the King insisted.
