Then, General Kāḷahatta, to make the King understand, brought forth and showed this story:

## The Great Fish Ānanda

O Great King, in times past, there were six great fish in the great ocean. Among those six great fish, the fish named Ānanda, the fish named Timinanda, and the fish named Ajjhāroha—these three great fish were each five hundred yojanas in length. The fish named Timingala, the fish named Timirapingala, and the fish named Mahātimirapingala—these three great fish were each one thousand yojanas in length. All those great fish ate only rock-moss and algae.

Among those six great fish, the great fish Ānanda lived on one side of the great ocean. Many fish came to visit that great fish Ānanda. One day, a thought occurred to all those fish: "Among two-legged humans and four-legged beasts, a king is known. We have no king. We shall make this great fish Ānanda our king." Having so thought, all the fish, being of one mind, consecrated the great fish Ānanda as their king.
501:
From that time on, those fish went to serve the great fish Ānanda every evening and morning.

Then one day, while the great fish Ānanda was eating rock-moss on a certain mountain, he unknowingly ate a fish, mistaking it for moss. As he ate that flesh, his entire body was thrilled with the taste. The great fish Ānanda thought, "Why is this food so exceedingly delicious?" and upon looking at what he had spat out, he saw a piece of fish. He thought, "For so long a time, I did not eat this because I did not know. In the evening and morning, when the fish come to serve me and then depart, I will eat one or two fish. If I eat them openly, not a single fish will approach me; they will all flee. I will act in secret, and as the fish retreat, I will strike and eat the one at the very end."

Realizing that their numbers were dwindling, the fish pondered, "From where does this danger to our kinsmen arise?" Then a certain wise fish thought, "I do not like the behavior of Ānanda; I will investigate him." When the fish went to serve him, he remained hidden near Ānanda's ear-fin.

After Ānanda dismissed the fish, he ate the fish that was going last of all. When the wise fish saw that action, he informed the other fish. All of them, trembling with fear, fled away.

## Died from Eating One's Own Kind

From that time on, because of his greed for fish flesh, the great fish Ānanda did not take any other food. Being oppressed by hunger and exhausted, he searched for those fish, wondering, "Where have these fish gone?" Seeing a mountain, he thought, "I suppose they are living in reliance on this mountain out of fear of me. I will encircle the mountain and investigate." He then wrapped himself around both sides of the mountain with his tail and his head.
502:
He ate with a crunching sound, and painful feelings arose. Attracted by the smell of blood, other fish gathered and bit and ate him until they reached his head. Because of his great body, he was unable to turn over and reached the end of his life right there; his heap of bones became like a mountain range. Ascetics, wanderers, and humans traveling through the air told people about it. People throughout the whole of Jambudīpa came to know of it. To illustrate this matter, the commander Kāḷahatta said:

378. Ānanda, greedy for taste, having eaten all the fish,
When his retinue was exhausted, died eating himself.

379. Thus, one who is negligent, attached to the importance of taste,
A fool who does not perceive the future,
Having destroyed children and abandoned relatives,
Will wander about and eat only himself.

380. Having heard this, may your desire vanish;
Do not eat human flesh, O King.
Do not make this entire kingdom empty,
O Lord of bipeds, just like the fish [Ānanda].

He spoke these three verses.

378. O Great King! The great fish Ānanda, who was greedy for taste, having eaten all the fish, when his followers were exhausted, died eating himself.

379. In this same way, O King, if you, being negligent and attached to the nature of the taste of human flesh, being unwise, do not realize the suffering that will arise in the future; if you do not realize this, you will destroy your children and abandon your relatives. Wandering throughout the city, when you do not obtain human flesh, you will eat only yourself.

380. O Great King! Having heard this matter, I wish for your desire for human flesh to vanish. O King! Do not eat human flesh. O Great King, Lord of humans! Do not make this kingdom of Kāsi empty, just like the fish Ānanda made the ocean empty.

After that, thinking, "If I stay at this mountain, they will flee," as he circled the mountain, he saw his own tail. Thinking, "This fish is circling me and staying near the mountain," he became angry and firmly seized his own tail, which was fifty yojanas long, mistaking it for another fish, and ate it, tearing it into pieces. Intense and painful feelings arose.

Because of the smell of blood, fish gathered and tore at his flesh, eating until they reached his head. Because of his great body, he was unable to turn over and reached the end of his life there. The heap of bones became like a mountain.

Ascetics, monks, and wanderers traveling through the air saw that heap of bones and told the people. People living throughout the whole of Jambudīpa knew of it. Wishing to bring forth and show this story, the commander Kāḷahatta said:

## Dying for the Love of Jambu Fruit

Upon hearing these words, King Brahmadatta said, "Friend Kāḷahatta, do you alone know similes? I also know them." Wishing to bring forth and show an ancient story because of his greed for human flesh, he said:

The story of the householder Sujāta, which is shown in brief in this verse, is shown in detail in the Commentary as follows:

In the past, in the city of Bārāṇasī, a householder named Sujāta supported five hundred ascetics who had come from the Himalayas to seek salt and acidic foods, letting them stay in his garden. In his house, there was a constant supply of alms for five hundred.
503:
381. Sujāta by name, his own legitimate son,
Died upon the exhaustion of that rose-apple, not having obtained it.

382. Even so, O Kāḷa, having eaten the food of supreme taste,
Not obtaining human flesh, I think I shall lose my life.

He spoke these two verses.

381. O Kāḷa! There was a householder named Sujāta. His own legitimate son, not having obtained a Jambu fruit, died because that Jambu fruit was finished.

382. O Kāḷa! In this same way, I, having first eaten the food that is supreme among all tastes, think I shall lose my life because of not obtaining human flesh.

Those ascetics sometimes went into the countryside for alms. Sometimes they brought and ate large Jambu fruits. At the time when those ascetics brought and ate the Jambu fruits, the householder Sujāta thought, "The venerable ones have not come for three or four days now; where could they have gone?" That householder, leading his young son by the hand, went to the monastery at the time the ascetics were taking their meal.

When the householder arrived, at the time the senior ascetics were washing their mouths, he gave them water, and the youngest ascetic was eating a Jambu fruit. Sujāta paid homage to the ascetics and, while sitting, asked, "Venerable sirs, what are you eating?" When they replied, "Lay follower, we are eating Jambu fruit," the young boy, hearing this, developed a craving for it.

Then, the senior ascetic, the leader of the group, gave a small piece of the Jambu fruit to the boy. Having eaten that fruit, the boy became intensely attached to the sweet taste and repeatedly begged, "Give me Jambu fruit! Give me Jambu fruit!"
504:
The householder, while listening to the Dhamma, deceived the boy, saying, "Dear son, do not cry; you shall eat it when we reach home." Thinking, "The venerable ones might become annoyed because of this boy," he comforted the boy and went home without taking leave of the assembly of ascetics. From the time they reached home, the householder's son lamented, "Give me Jambu fruit! Give me Jambu fruit!"

Sujāta the householder went to the garden, thinking, "I will tell the ascetics." But the assembly of ascetics, thinking, "We have stayed here a long time," had already returned to the Himalayas. Not seeing the ascetics in the park, he gave the boy pieces of rose-apple, mango, jackfruit, banana, and so on, mixed with honey and sugar. As soon as those things were placed on the tip of the boy's tongue, they were like deadly poison to him. That boy, having gone without food for seven days, reached the end of his life.

King Brahmadatta, wishing to bring forth and show this reason, spoke the two verses beginning with "Sujāta by name." (This is shown in detail in the Commentary.)

After that, the commander Kāḷahatta thought, "This king is excessively greedy for taste; I will bring forth other examples for him," and said, "O Great King, desist!" The King replied, "I am unable to desist." "Sire, if you do not desist, you will fall away from your circle of relatives and from your royal glory. In the past, O Great King, right here in Bārāṇasī, there was a family of the Sotthiya caste who kept the five precepts..."
505:
383. Young man, you are handsome, born in a Sotthiya family. It is not fitting for you, dear son, to consume what should not be consumed.

383. Māṇava, young man; Tāta, dear son. Tvaṃ, you; abhirūpo, are very handsome. Asi, you are. Sotthiye, in a Sotthiya; kule, family; jāto, you were born. Asi, you are. Tāta, dear son; tvaṃ, you; abhakkhāṃ, that which should not be consumed; bhakkhayetave, to consume; na arahesi, it is not fitting.

Your Majesty will fall away from your kinsmen and from the glory of your kingdom; that word is true.

## The Sotthiya Drunkard

Great King, in the past, in this very city of Bārāṇasī, there was a Sotthiya family that observed the five precepts. That Sotthiya family had an only son. He was dear and pleasing to his parents, wise, clever, and had mastered the three Vedas.

He wandered about in a group with young men of his own age. The rest of the group ate fish and meat and drank liquor (surā). The young man did not eat meat and did not drink liquor. They consulted among themselves: "Because this young man does not drink liquor, he does not give us money. Let us make him drink liquor by a trick." Having gathered together, they said, "Friend, let us play at the festival." He said, "Friends, you drink liquor; I do not drink liquor. You go ahead." They said, "Friend, we will have milk brought for you to drink." The Sotthiya young man agreed, saying, "Very well."

The rogues went to the park and placed strong liquor tied in lotus leaves. Then, at the time of their drinking, they brought milk to the young man. Then one rogue said, "Friends, bring the lotus honey (pokkharamadhu)!" and having had it brought, he made a hole in the bottom of the lotus-leaf wrap, placed it to his mouth with his fingers, and sucked it. In the same way, the other rogues had it brought and drank.

The young man asked, "What is this?" When they said, "It is called lotus honey," he said, "Friends, I too would like to have a little; please give me some." They gave it to him. Thinking it was lotus honey, he drank the liquor. Then they gave him meat roasted on coals, and he ate that too.

As he drank again and again, when he was intoxicated, they said, "This is not lotus honey; this is liquor." The young man said, "For all this time, I did not know such a sweet taste."
506:
384. This liquor is one of the best among tastes. Why would you restrain me? I shall go to that place where I can obtain such a taste.
385. I shall depart; I will not live in your presence. You do not rejoice at the sight of me, O Brahmin.

384. Brāhmaṇa, father Brahmin. Etaṃ, this liquor; rasānaṃ, among all tastes; aññataraṃ, is a superior and distinct taste. Hoti, it is. Kasmā, why; maṃ, me; tvaṃ, you, father; nivāraye, do you restrain? Brāhmaṇa, father Brahmin. Yo ahaṃ, I who; yattha, in whatever place; edisaṃ, such a taste; lacchāmi, shall obtain; tattha, to that place; so ahaṃ, I shall; gamissāmi, go.

385. Brāhmaṇa, father Brahmin. Tvaṃ, you, father; yassa-me, of me; dassanena, by seeing; nābhinandasi, do not rejoice. So ahaṃ, I; te, your; santike, in the presence; na vacchāmi, shall no longer live. Nippatissāmi, I shall depart.

386. We shall surely obtain other children who are worthy of inheritance, young man. And you, vile one, go to ruin in a place where we shall not hear of you.

386. Māṇava, young man. Dāyāde, worthy of inheritance; aññepi, others besides you; putte, children; addhā, surely; lacchāma, we shall obtain. Jamma, vile one. Yatta, to whatever place; pattaṃ, you have gone; taṃ, of you; na suṇe, we shall not hear. Tattha, to that place; tvaṃ, you; vinassasu, go to ruin.

"Friends, bring the liquor!" he said. The rogues brought it again and gave it to him. His craving and thirst grew great.

Then, when he asked again, they said, "It is finished." The young man said, "Friends, bring that liquor now!" and gave them his ring. He drank with them the whole day, and being intoxicated, with bloodshot eyes, trembling and lamenting, he went home and lay down.

Then his father, knowing he had drunk liquor, said when the intoxication had passed, "Dear son, you have done what is improper. Being born in a Sotthiya family, it is not fitting to drink liquor. Do not do this again." He asked, "Father, what fault is there in my drinking liquor?" When told that drinking liquor was improper, he said, "Father, what are you saying? For all this time, I have never before obtained such a sweet taste."

The Brahmin father pleaded with him again and again. The young man said, "I am unable to desist." Then the Brahmin father, thinking, "If this is so, our lineage will be cut off and our wealth will be destroyed," wishing to admonish his son, spoke these words:

## Dying for the Love of Liquor

After speaking these words, he said, "Dear son, desist. If you do not desist, I will leave this house, and I will have you banished from the country." The young man said, "Father, even if you banish me, I cannot give up drinking liquor." To inform his father of this, he spoke these words.

After saying this, he said, "I will not desist from drinking liquor. Do whatever you please." Then the Brahmin father, saying, "If you abandon us, we too shall abandon you," spoke this verse.

Then the Brahmin father took that vile son to the place of judgment, declared him no longer his son, and had him expelled. Later, being without support and destitute, wearing worn-out rags and carrying a bowl in his hand, he wandered for alms and died leaning against a certain wall.
507:
387. "Even so, O King, lord of bipeds, listen to me. They will banish you from the kingdom, just as a drunken youth is banished."

387. Lord of bipeds, you who rule over two-legged humans. Great King. You. My. Word. Listen. A drunken. Youth. Just as they banish from the country. Even so. You. From the kingdom. They will banish.

Presenting this matter, General Kāḷahatthi showed it to King Brahmadatta, saying, "Great King, if you do not follow our words, we will perform the act of banishing you from the country," and wishing to inform the King of this matter, he said:

## The One Who Died Longing for a Celestial Nymph

Although General Kāḷahatthi presented this example and illustration, King Brahmadatta was unable to abstain from human flesh. Wishing to show another example to General Kāḷahatthi, he said:

388. "There was a disciple of the five hundred ascetics with developed minds, Sujāta by name. Longing for a celestial nymph, he neither ate nor drank.

389. "Taking water with the tip of a blade of kusa grass and comparing it to the water in the ocean—such are human pleasures in the presence of divine pleasures.

390. "Even so, Kāḷa, having eaten food of supreme flavor, if I do not obtain human flesh, I think I shall lose my life."

388. Kāḷa, Kāḷahatthi. Of those with developed minds. Of the five hundred ascetics. A disciple and donor. By name. Named Sujāta. That householder. Exists. That householder. A celestial nymph. Longing for. Did not eat. He, that householder. Did not drink.

389. Kāḷa, Kāḷahatthi. With a blade of kusa grass. Water. Taking. In the ocean. Water. Just as one compares. Even so. Human. Pleasures. Of divine pleasures. In the presence. They are.

390. Kāḷa, Kāḷahatthi. Even so. I. Having a flavor superior to all other flavors. Food. Having eaten. Human flesh. Because of not obtaining. My. Life. I think I shall have to give up.

In these verses, the story of the householder Sujāta, which is presented in brief, is presented in detail in the Commentary as follows:

## The One Who Had to Die Longing for a Celestial Nymph

The householder named Sujāta mentioned above, knowing that the five hundred ascetics did not come at the time of eating rose-apples, thought, "Why do the noble ones not come? If they have gone to some place, I shall know. If they have not gone to another place, I shall listen to the Dhamma in the presence of those noble ones." He went to the park, paid homage to the group of ascetics, and while sitting and listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the head of the group, the sun set.

Although those ascetics dismissed him, he said, "I will stay in this monastery today," and having paid homage to the group of ascetics, he entered the leaf-hut and lay down. During the night, Sakka, the king of gods, surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs, came with his attendants to pay homage to the group of ascetics. The entire monastery grounds became illuminated all at once.
508:
391. Just as those Dhataratṭha swans, who travel through the sky, all came to destruction by consuming what should not be consumed.
392. Even so, O King, lord of men, listen to me. You have eaten what is not to be eaten, O King; therefore, they will banish you from the kingdom.
This refers to the collection of these two verses.
391. O lord of men, O King who rules over two-legged humans, may you listen to my words. There are those swans of the Dhataratṭha breed who are accustomed to flying through the sky. All those golden swans, just as they reached destruction because they consumed food that should not be consumed.
392. Even so, O King, because you have eaten food that should not be eaten, therefore, they will banish you from the country.
Sujāta the householder rose and looked through the door of the monastery, asking, "What is this light?" He saw Sakka, the King of Devas, surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs who had come to pay homage to the group of sages. As soon as he saw the nymphs, his mind became stained with passion. Sakka stayed in that monastery, listened to the delightful Dhamma, and then departed to his own abode in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
On the following morning, Sujāta the householder paid homage to the sages and asked, "Venerable sirs, who was that person who came to pay homage to you during the night?" When they replied, "Lay disciple, it was Sakka," he asked, "Who were those women who sat surrounding that Sakka?" Upon being told, "Lay disciple, those women were celestial nymphs," the householder paid homage to the sages and went home. From the moment he reached home, he lamented, "Give me a nymph! Give me a nymph!" His relatives surrounded him and snapped their fingers, wondering, "Is he possessed by a spirit?"
The householder said, "I am not possessed. I am not speaking of these women; I am speaking only of the nymphs of Tāvatiṃsa." Even when shown his own wife or a courtesan adorned like a nymph, he would look at them and lament, "This is not a nymph; this is an ogress. Give me a nymph!" Refusing to eat, he reached the end of his life right there.
"Friend Kāḷahatthi, if a person were to take water with the tip of a blade of kusa grass and compare it with the water in the great ocean, saying 'Let the water in the great ocean be this much,' he would only be making a mere comparison. The water taken with the grass is extremely minute. In the same way, human pleasures are like the water on the tip of a grass blade when compared to divine pleasures. Therefore, that Sujāta the householder died while longing only for a nymph, without looking at any other woman. Just as that householder gave up his life because he did not obtain divine pleasures, even so, I too will give up my life if I do not obtain human flesh, which is the supreme flavor."
## The Golden Swans that Ate Their Own Kind
Having heard this illustrative example presented by King Brahmadatta, the commander Kāḷahatthi thought, "This king is excessively greedy for flavor. I shall make him understand." Desiring to show his master, King Brahmadatta, that even the golden swans who fly through the sky perished because they ate the flesh of their own kind, he said:
(In this illustrative example, the story of the golden swan kings who reached destruction because they ate the flesh of their own kind is presented in detail in the Commentary.)
In the past, ninety thousand golden swans lived in a golden cave of jewels on Mount Cittakūṭa. Those golden swans did not go outside for the four months of the rainy season. If they were to go out, they would be unable to fly with wings soaked with water and would fall into the great ocean.
509:
Therefore, they do not go out. When the rainy season approaches, they bring self-sown rice from Lake Jātassara, fill the golden cave, and live there eating the rice.

At the entrance of the golden cave of those golden swans, a spider named Uṇṇanābhi, the size of a chariot wheel, weaves a web every month. Each thread of that spider's web is as thick as a cow's leading rope. Thinking, "He will break that web," the swans give a young swan double portions of food. When the rains cease, that young swan goes ahead of all the others and breaks the web. The remaining swans follow that path.

Once, at another time, it rained for five months. When the swans ran out of food, they consulted each other, "What shall we do?" and thinking, "If we live, we shall have eggs again," they first ate the eggs. After that, they ate the young swans. Then they ate the old swans. After five months, when the rain ceased, the spider had woven five layers of web.

Because the swans had eaten the flesh of their own kind, they became weak. The young swan, who received double portions, struck the webs and broke four layers, but could not break the fifth and got stuck right there. Then the spider pierced the young swan's head and drank its blood.

Others also came and struck the web, but they too got stuck. In this way, the spider drank the blood of all the swans. At that time, the Dhataraṭṭha lineage was destroyed.

"Just as these swans ate the flesh of their own kind, which should not be eaten, so do you eat human flesh. The whole city is in terror. Desist, O Great King! Because you eat the flesh of your own kind, which should not be eaten, these citizens will banish you from the kingdom." Thus it was demonstrated.

## Banishment from the Country

King Brahmadatta wished to tell another parable. But the citizens rose up and said, "Lord General, what are you doing? Why do you go about with this man-eating thief? If he does not desist, banish that king from the country!" and they did not allow him to speak. King Brahmadatta, hearing the words of many people, was afraid and could not speak again.
510:
Again, General Kāḷahatthi asked King Brahmadatta, "O Great King, will you be able to desist from eating human flesh, or will you not?" When he replied, "I cannot," the General said, "Look at all these harem women, and your sons and daughters, adorned with all kinds of ornaments." He continued, "O Great King, look at this circle of kinsmen, the assembly of ministers, and the royal glory. Do not let them perish. Desist from eating human flesh!"

King Brahmadatta said, "I do not love these possessions more than human flesh." When told, "In that case, O Great King, depart from this city and this kingdom," he replied, "Friend Kāḷahatthi, I have no need for kingship. I will depart from the city. But give me a sword, Rasaka, and a pot for cooking human flesh."

Then, having given him a sword, a pot for cooking human flesh, a basket for carrying it, and Rasaka, they performed the act of banishment from the country.

## The Cook Rasaka

Taking the sword and Rasaka, the King left the city and palace, entered the forest, and made a dwelling at the foot of a banyan tree. Living there, he stood on the forest path, killed people, brought them back, and gave them to the cook Rasaka. Rasaka cooked the human flesh and served it to the King. Thus, the two of them made their living.

When capturing people, he would announce his name, "I am the man-eating thief Porisāda!" and when Porisāda emerged, no one could remain standing in their natural state; everyone fell to the ground. Among those people, whomever he desired, he would take—holding them feet-up and head-down—and strike and kill them, then give them to Rasaka.

One day, Porisāda returned from the forest without finding any human flesh and said, "Set the pot on the stove." When Rasaka asked, "O King, where is the meat?" he replied, "I shall get the meat." Rasaka, trembling and thinking, "Now my life is no more," lit the fire and set the pot on the stove. Then Porisāda struck Rasaka with his sword, cooked his flesh, and ate it. From then on, he was alone and cooked for himself. It became famous throughout the whole of Jambudīpa that "Porisāda kills and eats those who travel the paths."

## Porisāda is Pricked by a Stake

At that time, a wealthy Brahmin merchant was traveling from the eastern end to the western end with five hundred wagons. The Brahmin thought, "They say a thief named Porisāda kills people on the road. I will cross that forest by giving wealth." Having thought so, he spoke to the people living at the edge of the forest, "You all, help me cross the forest," and gave them a thousand pieces of money, then set out on the journey with them.

As they went, the Brahmin sent all the wagons ahead. He himself, having bathed and anointed himself with perfumes, adorned with all ornaments, sat in a comfortable carriage drawn by white oxen. Surrounded by the forest guards, he followed behind everyone else.

At that moment, Porisāda climbed a tree and was scouting for people. Seeing the approaching Brahmin, he lost all desire for the other people, thinking, "What is there worth eating in these others?" From the moment he saw the Brahmin, his saliva flowed because of his desire to eat him. When the Brahmin came near him, Porisāda descended from the tree, announced his name three times, "Hey friends, I am Porisāda!" and ran toward them, brandishing his sword as if to fill their eyes with sand.
511:
Not a single person was able to stand their ground. All of them lay prostrate on the ground on their chests. That Porisāda seized the Brahmin, who was sitting in a comfortable carriage, by the feet and slung him over his back, hanging him upside down. Striking the Brahmin's head with his ankles, he picked him up and set off.

Then those men rose up and said, "O friends, we have taken a thousand coins from the Brahmin's hand. What kind of manhood do we possess? Whether we are able or not, let us pursue him for a while." Saying this, they followed Porisāda. Porisāda, looking back and seeing no one, walked slowly. At that moment, a certain brave man, endowed with great strength, quickly caught up with him.

Seeing that brave man, Porisāda leaped over a fence and stepped on a khadirā stump. The stump pierced through the sole of his foot and came out through the top. He continued to leap and run even as blood flowed. Then the brave man, seeing him, said, "Friends, I have wounded this Porisāda. You just follow from behind; I will capture him." Knowing his weakness, they pursued Porisāda.

## Supplicating the Banyan Tree Deity

When Porisāda realized he was being pursued by those people, he released the Brahmin and secured his own safety. From the moment the hired men recovered the Brahmin, they turned back from that place, saying, "What use have we for the thief?"

Porisāda went to his own place at the foot of the banyan tree, entered between the hanging roots, and lay down. He made a supplication: "O noble deity of the banyan tree, if you can heal my wound within seven days, I will wash your trunk with the throat-blood of one hundred and one kings from the whole of Jambudīpa. I will encircle it with their entrails and perform a sacrificial offering with meat of the five sweet flavors."

Because he did not get food, drink, or meat, his body withered, but within seven days, the wound healed. Porisāda attributed this healing to the power of the deity. After eating human flesh for two or three days to regain his strength, he thought, "This deity has done me a great favor; I shall fulfill my vow to her." Taking his sword, he set out from the foot of the banyan tree, saying, "I will bring the kings."

## The Padalakkhaṇa Mantra

At that time, a Yakkha, who had been his companion in a previous life when they were both man-eaters, saw Porisāda wandering about. Recognizing him, the Yakkha thought, "This person was my friend in a past life," and asked, "Friend, do you recognize me?" "I do not," Porisāda replied. Then the Yakkha told him of their past connection. Porisāda then recognized him and engaged in conversation.

When asked, "Where were you born?", Porisāda told him everything: his birthplace, the reason for his banishment from the kingdom, his current dwelling place, the incident of being pierced by the khadirā stump, and his journey to fulfill the vow to the deity. He then said, "Friend, you should also help me accomplish this task. Friend, let us both go together."
512:
"Friend, I will not go. However, I have a certain task. I know a mantra called Padalakkhaṇa, which is of great value. It can provide strength, speed, glory, and a powerful voice. Take this mantra." Porisāda agreed, saying, "Very well." The Yakkha gave him the Padalakkhaṇa mantra and departed.

## Capturing the Kings

Porisāda mastered the mantra, and from then on, he became as swift as the wind and exceedingly brave. Within seven days, whenever he saw the one hundred and one kings going to their gardens or elsewhere, he would rush forth with the speed of the wind, announcing his name: "Hey, friends, I am the man-thief Porisāda!" Shouting and roaring, he would strike terror into them, seize them by the feet, hold them upside down, strike their heads with his heels, and carry them away with the speed of the wind. He pierced holes in their palms, strung them together with rope, and hung them from the banyan tree so that only their toes touched the ground.

All those kings, when the wind blew, swung back and forth like withered garlands of kuranda flowers. Porisāda thought, "King Sutasoma was my teacher. If I capture him, the whole of Jambudīpa will be empty." Thus, he did not take King Sutasoma. Porisāda then lit a fire and sat sharpening stakes, thinking, "I shall perform the sacrificial offering to the deity."

## Causing the Capture of King Sutasoma

The deity of the banyan tree, seeing these actions, thought, "This Porisāda is going to perform a sacrifice for me. I have not done anything to heal his wound. Now he will cause great destruction to these kings. What should I do?" Thinking, "I will not be able to stop Porisāda," the deity went to the Four Great Kings, explained the matter, and said, "Please stop this Porisāda."

When the Four Great Kings said, "We are not able to stop Porisāda's actions," the deity asked, "Who will be able to?" Hearing that Sakka, the king of gods, would be able, the deity approached Sakka, explained the situation, and said, "Please stop this Porisāda." Sakka also said, "I am not able to stop him, but I will tell you who can."

When asked who that was, Sakka replied: "In this world with its devas, there is no other equal. In the city of Indraprastha in the Kuru kingdom, there is a noble king named Sutasoma, the son of King Koravya. He will tame Porisāda, making him harmless, and will grant life to the kings. He will also make Porisāda abstain from eating human flesh. He will sprinkle the cool water of the Dhamma like nectar throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. If you wish to save the lives of the kings..."
513:
393. "'Stand!' I said, yet you go forward. You say 'I am standing' while not standing, O practitioner of the holy life. Is this fitting for an ascetic? Do you think my sword is like a heron's wing?"

393. "Ascetic, stand!" Thus I spoke. Yet you run away towards another direction. O ascetic, practitioner of the holy life, while not standing, you say "I am standing." You speak these unfitting words. Do you think my sword is as soft as a heron's wing?

"It is proper to bring King Sutasoma and perform the sacrifice," the deity said.

The tree-spirit accepted, saying "Very well," and quickly approached Porisāda in the guise of an ascetic. Hearing the sound of footsteps, Porisāda thought, "Some king must be escaping," and looking back, he saw the tree-spirit. He thought, "Ascetics are indeed of the warrior caste (khattiya); I will seize this one to complete the one hundred and one kings and perform the sacrifice to the deity." He rose and chased with sword in hand. Although he chased for three yojanas, he could not catch the ascetic, and sweat poured from his body.

Porisāda thought, "In the past, I could chase and catch even a running elephant, horse, or chariot. Now, though I run with all my strength, I cannot catch this ascetic who is walking at his natural pace. What could be the reason?" Then he thought, "Ascetics are known to be obedient to words. I will tell him 'Stand' and then catch him while he is standing." So he said, "Stand, ascetic!"

"I have stood; it is you who are striving to run," the ascetic replied. Then Porisāda said, "O ascetic, those called ascetics do not tell lies even for the sake of their lives. But you are telling a lie." To make him understand, the tree-spirit, wishing to inform Porisāda of the matter, spoke these two verses:

394. "I am standing in my own Dhamma, O King; I do not change my name or lineage. In the world, they call a thief 'one who does not stand,' who, having passed away from here, is destined for the states of misery and hell.

395. If you believe me, O King, seize Sutasoma, O khattiya. By sacrificing with him, you shall thus go to heaven."

394. "O King, I am standing in the ten courses of meritorious action (kusalakamma-patha). I do not change my name or lineage. O Great King, in this world, only the thief who, after passing away from this human realm, will be reborn in the states of misery and hell, is called 'one who does not stand.'

395. O khattiya, Great King who rules the land, if you believe my words, seize King Sutasoma. By sacrificing with that King Sutasoma, you shall thus reach the heavenly realm."
514:
## Porisāda Descending into the Pond

After speaking these words, the tree-spirit vanished the ascetic guise and stood in the sky in its own form, radiant like the morning sun. Porisāda heard the deity's words, looked at the form, and asked, "Who are you?" When the deity replied, "I am the deity born in this banyan tree," Porisāda was greatly delighted and said, "I have seen my own deity! Lord deity, do not worry on account of King Sutasoma. Please enter your banyan tree."

While Porisāda was watching, the tree-spirit entered the banyan tree. At that moment, the sun set and the moon rose. Porisāda was skilled in the Vedas and knew the movements of the constellations. Looking at the sky, he thought, "Tomorrow the moon will be in the Phussa constellation. King Sutasoma will go to the park to bathe. I will catch him there. His protection will be great; all the city dwellers within three yojanas will be guarding him. Before the guards are stationed, I will go to the Migāzina park in the first watch of the night and wait, having descended into the auspicious pond."

Thinking thus, he went to the Migāzina park, descended into the auspicious pond, and stayed there covering his head with a lotus leaf. Due to Porisāda's power, the fish, turtles, and other creatures moved away and gathered in groups only at the edges of the water.

How did Porisāda obtain such power? He obtained it through the power of past merit. This statement is true.
515:
396. In what kingdom is your birthplace?
And for what purpose have you come here?
Tell me, O Brahmin, this matter;
What do you desire? I shall give you what you wish today.

He spoke this verse.

396. 'O Brahmin! In what kingdom is your birthplace? For what reason have you arrived here? O Brahmin, being thus questioned, tell me this matter. What do you desire? O Brahmin, I shall give you today the object you have longed for.'

That Porisāda, during the time when the Kassapa Buddha appeared, had offered milk-rice (khīrasalākabhatta). Because of that, he possessed great strength. He also built a fire-hall (aggisālā) and offered fire, wood, wood-cutting knives, and axes for the monks to dispel the cold. Because of that, he possessed great power (teja).

Thus, after Porisāda had entered the Migāzina Garden, at the time of dawn, guards were stationed for three yojanas all around.

## King Sutasoma Sets Out

King Sutasoma, having eaten his breakfast early in the morning, mounted his noble, adorned elephant and departed from the city surrounded by his fourfold army.

At that time, a Brahmin named Nanda from Takkasilā, taking four verses worth a hundred each (sataraha), traveled a distance of one hundred and eighty yojanas and reached the city of Indapatta. Having stayed in a gate-village, he entered the city at sunrise. Seeing King Sutasoma departing through the East Gate, he stretched out his hand and offered a blessing of victory. King Sutasoma, traveling with his eyes fixed ahead, saw the Brahmin standing on high ground with his hand stretched out. Approaching the Brahmin on his elephant, he wished to ask him—

When he was thus questioned, the Brahmin Nanda, wishing to report the reason for his arrival to King Sutasoma—

Having reported thus, he said, 'Great King, these verses were taught by the Blessed One. Having heard that Your Majesty delights in learning (sutavittaka), I have come to recite these four verses worth a hundred each to Your Majesty.' King Sutasoma was greatly pleased and said, 'Teacher, your coming is a welcome arrival.'
516:
Then he spoke this verse to him:

397. There are four verses, O Lord of the Earth,
Deep in meaning, like the noble ocean.
For your sake alone have I come here;
Listen to the verses associated with the highest good.

397. 'O Lord of the Earth (Dharaṇīmahissara), Ruler of the Land (Bhūmipāla), there are four verses which have very deep meanings and are like the noble ocean. For your sake alone have I arrived here. Listen to these verses associated with the highest good (paramattha).'

'I cannot turn back now. I have come today to wash my head as the moon is in the Phussa constellation. I will come and listen tomorrow. Do not be weary, Teacher.' Having said this, he commanded his ministers, 'Go, prepare a bed and place to stay in such-and-such a house for the teacher Brahmin, and provide him with food and clothing,' and then he entered the garden.

That garden was surrounded by a wall eighteen cubits high. Elephants stood around the garden, their temples touching one another. Beyond them were horses, then chariots, then archers, and then infantry. The host of soldiers made a resounding noise like the great ocean stirred by the force of the wind.

Then King Sutasoma removed his heavy ornaments, had his hair and beard trimmed, and with a light body, bathed with royal splendor in the Mangala Lotus Pond. Having emerged from the water, he stood wearing his undergarment. Then they offered King Sutasoma robes, perfumes, and ornaments.

## The King is Captured

Porisāda thought, 'When King Sutasoma is adorned, he will be heavy. I will capture him only when he is light.' Thinking thus, shouting and roaring, causing the fish in the water to tremble, and brandishing his sword above his head like a flash of lightning, he proclaimed his name, 'Hey, you people! I am Porisāda, the man-eater (manussacora)!' Placing a finger on his forehead, he emerged from the water. Hearing his voice, the elephant riders [fled] with their elephants...
517:
398. The wise, the intelligent, and the learned, who contemplate many matters, do not indeed weep. For this is the supreme lamp for men, that the wise are dispellers of sorrow.

399. Is it for yourself, your relatives, or your wife and children? Is it for grain, wealth, silver, or gold? For what, Sutasoma, do you grieve? O best of the Koravyas, let us hear your word.

He spoke these two verses.

398. Sutasoma, Great King Sutasoma. Those who are wise are endowed with the wisdom to know what is beneficial and what is not, what is a cause and what is not. They possess the wisdom of investigation. They are learned and bear much knowledge. They are capable of contemplating many special matters. Those wise ones, indeed, do not weep. Sutasoma, Great King Sutasoma. For those wise ones, that state of non-sorrowing exists. That non-sorrowing is indeed the supreme refuge for men. Those wise ones are dispellers of sorrow.

399. Koravya, O noble one of the Koravya lineage. Great King Sutasoma. Do you grieve for yourself? Or is it for your relatives? Do you grieve for your wife and children? Do you grieve for grain? Do you grieve for wealth? Do you grieve for silver? Do you grieve for gold? Sutasoma, Great King Sutasoma. For what exactly do you grieve? We wish to hear that word of yours.

Upon hearing the voice of Porisāda, the elephant riders fell from their elephants. The horse riders fell from their horses. The chariot riders fell from their chariots. The entire host of soldiers discarded the weapons they were holding and lay prostrate on the ground with their chests to the earth. Porisāda picked up King Sutasoma and took him.

## Does the Great King Cry Out of Fear?

As for the other kings, he grabbed them by their feet, held them upside down, and struck their heads with his heels as he went. But approaching the Bodhisatta, King Sutasoma, he bent down, gently picked him up, and placed him on his shoulder.

That Porisāda thought, "If I go out through the garden gate, it will take a long time," and so, in the direction he was facing, he leaped over the garden wall which was eighteen cubits high. He stepped on the frontal globes of rutting elephants in front of him, making them fall as if toppling mountain peaks. With the speed of the wind, he stepped on the backs of mules, causing them to fall. Stepping on the poles and frames of chariots, he made them spin as if they were revolving. Trampling many armed men as if treading on banyan leaves, he traveled a distance of three yojanas in a single burst of speed. Thinking, "Is there anyone following for the sake of King Sutasoma?" he looked back and saw no one. As he walked slowly, he saw drops of water from King Sutasoma's hair falling on his chest. Thinking, "There is no one who does not fear death; even King Sutasoma is likely weeping because he fears the death he must face," he wished to ask about the reason and said:

## Release Me Now, I Will Return

King Sutasoma, wishing to inform Porisāda of the reason, spoke these two verses:

400.
518:
400. I do not lament for myself, nor for my wife and children, nor for wealth, nor for the kingdom. But there is the ancient practice of the virtuous; I grieve for that promise made to the Brahmin.

401. A promise was made by me to a Brahmin while I was established in the sovereignty of my own kingdom. To fulfill that promise to the Brahmin, I, a guardian of truth, shall return again.

He spoke these two verses.

400. Friend Porisāda. I do not grieve for myself. I do not grieve for my wife and children. I do not grieve for wealth. I do not grieve for the kingdom. But there is an ancient Dhamma practiced by the virtuous. Because I made a certain promise (sangara) to the Brahmin Nanda, I grieve for that promise alone.
519:
402. I do not believe this at all: that a man who has reached happiness, having been released from the mouth of death, would return again to the hands of an enemy. O best of the Koravyas, you will not come back to me.

403. Having been released from the hands of Porisāda, and having gone to your own palace, seeking sensual pleasures, and having regained your sweet and dear life, O King, why would you come back to me?

He spoke these two verses.

402. Koravya, O noble one of the Koravya lineage. Great King. A man who has been released from the mouth of death and is in a state of happiness, would he return again to the hands of an enemy? I do not at all believe in such a return. You will not come to me.

403. Great King. Having been released from the hands of the man-eater, and having gone to your own palace, you who desire the sought-after sensual pleasures, having regained your sweet and dear life, why would you come back to me?

401. Friend Porisāda. While established in the sovereignty of my own country, I made a certain promise to the Brahmin Nanda. Having fulfilled that promise to the Brahmin Nanda, I, who guard the truth, shall return.

(The meaning is: I am a guardian of truth. That Brahmin came from Takkasilā bringing four verses worth a hundred, taught by the Kassapa Buddha. I performed the duties of a host for him and made a promise, saying, "I will come and listen after I have bathed; wait until my arrival." But you captured me before I could hear those verses. If you release me, I will hear that Dhamma and, as a guardian of truth, I shall return.)

## Will You Really Return?

Then Porisāda, not believing the words of King Sutasoma, wished to reply:

## I Will Really Return

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta King Sutasoma, being fearless like a lion king, wished to state the reason again to Porisāda:
520:
404. A person of pure virtue would prefer death; a life of censured evil is not better. For that lie which one might tell, for whatever reason, does not protect that man from the miserable states (duggati).

404. Friend Porisāda. A person of pure virtue, even for the sake of life, if he were to tell a lie, for that person, death would be better; living would not be better. A person of censured and evil nature, for whatever reason, if he were to tell a lie, that lie does not protect that man from the miserable states.

After saying this, wishing to inform Porisāda of his avoidance of false speech:

405. Even if the wind should carry away a mountain,
And the moon and the sun should fall to the ground,
And all the rivers should flow upstream,
O King, I would never tell a lie.

406. Even if the sky should split, the ocean dry up,
And the earth, the supporter of beings, should turn upside down,
And Mount Meru, the king of mountains, should be uprooted with its foundation,
O King, I would never tell a lie.

He spoke these two verses.

405. Friend Porisāda. Even if the wind coming from the eight directions could blow away a great mountain; even if the moon and the sun should fall to the earth; even if all the rivers should flow against the current; O King, I would never tell a lie.

406. Friend Porisāda. Even if the sky should split; even if the great ocean should dry up; even if the face of the earth, the supporter of beings, should turn upside down; even if Mount Meru, the king of mountains, should be uprooted with its foundation; O King, I would never tell a lie.

## I Shall Swear an Oath

Even though the Great King Sutasoma spoke thus, Porisāda still did not believe him. Then the Bodhisatta King Mahāsutasoma thought, "This Porisāda does not believe me; I will make him believe by swearing an oath." He said, "Friend Porisāda, let me down from your shoulder; I will make an oath to make you believe." When Porisāda set King Sutasoma on the ground, the Bodhisatta, wishing to swear the oath, said:

Guarding the truth, I shall return.
521:
407. I touch the sword and the spear;
I also make an oath to you, friend.
Having been released by you and being free from debt,
408. The promise you made with the brahmin,
While established in the sovereignty of your own kingdom.
Fulfill that promise to the brahmin,

He spoke this verse.

407. Friend Porisāda. I touch the sword and the spear. I also make an oath to you. Having been released by you, I, being free from debt and guarding the truth, shall return.

## Do Truly Return

Then Porisāda thought, "This King Sutasoma makes an oath that should not be made by those of the Khattiya race. What use is there for this King Sutasoma? Whether he comes or not, I too am a Khattiya king who rules the land. I will perform the sacrificial offering to the deity using the blood from my own arm. This King Sutasoma is greatly exhausted." Wishing to release King Sutasoma, he spoke this verse:

Guarding the truth, do return.

408. Friend Sutasoma. The promise you made with the brahmin while established in the sovereignty of your own kingdom—fulfill that promise to the brahmin and, guarding the truth, do return.

## I Shall Return After Hearing the Dhamma

Then the Bodhisatta King Sutasoma said to Porisāda, "Friend Porisāda, do not worry. After hearing the four verses worth a hundred (Satāraha) and making an offering to the preacher of the Dhamma, I shall return early in the morning." To make this known, he spoke this verse:

Guarding the truth, I shall return.

409. Friend Porisāda. The promise I made with the brahmin Nanda while established in the sovereignty of my own kingdom—having fulfilled that promise to the brahmin Nanda, I, guarding the truth, shall return.
522:
409. “The promise I made to the Brahmin, while established in my own kingdom's power, that promise I shall fulfill to the Brahmin; protecting the truth, I shall return.”

## Alright, go then
Then Porisāda said to King Sutasoma, “Great King, you have made an oath that should not be made by those of the Khattiya (warrior) caste; remember that oath.” Sutasoma replied, “Friend Porisāda, you have known me since I was young. I have never spoken a lie even in jest. Now, established in kingship and knowing what is right and wrong, why would I speak a falsehood? Believe me, I will return tomorrow in time for your sacrificial ritual.” Having made him believe, Porisāda said, “In that case, go, Great King. If you do not return, the sacrificial ritual to the deity will fail. Even the deity will not accept the offering without you. Do not cause an obstacle to my sacrifice.” Thus, he sent the Bodhisatta King Sutasoma away.

## Upon returning to the palace
That King Sutasoma, like the moon released from the mouth of Rāhu, was endowed with strength and power like a noble elephant, and quickly reached the city. His army, thinking, “Our Lord King Sutasoma is wise and a sweet speaker of Dhamma. If he gets the opportunity to speak one or two verses, he will tame Porisāda and return like a rutting elephant released from a lion's mouth. If we return having given the King to Porisāda, the people will blame us,” had set up camp and waited outside the city.

Seeing the Bodhisatta King Sutasoma coming from afar, they went to meet him, paid homage, and asked, “Great King, did Porisāda trouble you?” When they asked, he replied, “Porisāda has done for me what even parents find hard to do. Even though he is such a fierce, violent, and oppressive person, he released me after hearing my Dhamma talk.” After saying this, they adorned King Sutasoma, placed him on the back of an elephant, and entered the city in procession. Seeing King Sutasoma, all the citizens were greatly delighted.

## Requesting the Dhamma
Because of his great respect for the Dhamma and his thirst for hearing it, without seeing his mother and father first, thinking “I will see them later,” he entered the palace. Sitting on the royal throne, he summoned the Brahmin Nanda and ordered that the Brahmin’s hair and beard be groomed. When the grooming was finished, the Brahmin was bathed, anointed with perfumes, and dressed in fine clothes and ornaments. When the Brahmin was brought and presented, the King himself later bathed and anointed himself, gave the Brahmin his own food, and after the Brahmin had eaten, the King ate. He then seated the Brahmin Nanda on a magnificent throne fit only for noble persons. Out of respect for the Dhamma, he honored him with flowers and perfumes, and sitting on a lower seat himself, he requested, “Teacher, I wish to hear the Sataraha verses that you have brought for me.”
523:
410. “Released from the hands of Porisāda, he went and spoke thus to the Brahmin: ‘I shall hear the Sataraha verses, which I have heard would be for my benefit, O Brahmin.’”

The Teacher (the Buddha) spoke this verse to clarify that matter:
410. Bhikkhus, at that time, the noble King Sutasoma, having been released from the hands of the man-eater Porisāda, went to his palace and said these words to the Brahmin Nanda: “O Teacher, I shall hear those Sataraha verses which I have heard would be for my benefit.”

411. “Only once, Sutasoma, does association with the good occur.
That association protects him; association with the wicked, even if frequent, does not.”

412. “One should associate only with the good; one should cultivate intimacy with the good.
Knowing the true Dhamma of the good, one becomes better, not worse.”

413. “Indeed, the ornate royal chariots wear out;
Likewise, the body also reaches old age.
But the Dhamma of the good does not reach old age;
The virtuous indeed proclaim this to the good.”

414. “The sky is far and the earth is far;
They say the other shore of the ocean is also far.
But indeed, they say the distance between the Dhamma of the good and that of the wicked is even further, O King.”

He spoke these four verses.

411. Great King Sutasoma, the association that occurs even once with the virtuous (santo) protects that person. The association that occurs many times with the non-virtuous (asanto) does not protect that person.

412. One should associate only with the virtuous. One should cultivate intimacy with the virtuous. Knowing the true Dhamma of the wise, such as the Buddhas, one becomes exceptionally noble; one does not become base.

413. Great King, the ornate royal chariots indeed wear out and decay. Furthermore, the physical body also reaches old age. The virtuous, such as the Buddhas, indeed praise the Dhamma of Nibbāna. The Dhamma of the virtuous, which is Nibbāna, does not reach old age.

414. O King, the sky is far from the earth, and the earth is far from the sky. They say the yonder shore of the ocean is far from this shore. But indeed, wise ones such as the Buddhas say that the Dhamma of the virtuous and the Dhamma of the non-virtuous are even further apart than the distance between the sky, the earth, and the shores of the ocean.

To clarify this matter, the Omniscient Buddha said:

## The Brahmin Nanda's 4 Verses
Then the Brahmin Nanda, when requested by the Bodhisatta King Sutasoma, rubbed his hands with perfumes, took out a delightful golden manuscript from his bag, held it with both hands, and said, “Great King, I urge you. Listen to these four Sataraha verses taught by the Kassapa Buddha, which crush the intoxication of passion and lead to the deathless Great Nibbāna.” Looking at the golden manuscript, wishing to preach, he said:

“Knowing the true Dhamma of the good, one becomes better, not worse.”
524:
## Honoring with Four Thousand Kahāpaṇas

Nanda the Brahmin recited these four Satāraha verses according to the method taught by the Blessed Kassapa Buddha and then remained silent. Having heard these four Satāraha verses, the Bodhisatta King Sutasoma, with a joyful heart, thought, "My coming here has indeed been fruitful." He reflected, "These verses were not spoken by disciples, nor by hermits, nor by any ordinary person; they were spoken only by the Omniscient Buddha. How much are they worth?" He considered that even if one were to fill the entire universe up to the Brahma realm with the seven kinds of jewels and give them as an offering, it would not be a fitting price for these verses. "Indeed," he thought, "I am able to give this Brahmin Nanda the kingship of the Kuru kingdom, which is three hundred leagues in extent, and the city of Indapatta, which is seven leagues. Does this Brahmin Nanda have the merit to rule as a king?"

Looking with the power of the science of bodily marks (Aṅgavijjā), he did not see the merit for kingship. Then, looking for the merit of a general and other such positions, he did not even see the merit to be a village headman. Looking for the merit of wealth, starting from a crore of wealth, he saw only the merit for four thousand kahāpaṇas. Thinking, "I will honor him with this much," he had four bags of a thousand kahāpaṇas each brought out and asked, "Teacher, when you recite these verses to other kings, how much wealth do you receive?"

"Great King, for each verse I receive one hundred. That is why they are known as Satāraha (worth a hundred)," the Brahmin replied.

Then the Bodhisatta said to the Brahmin Nanda, "Teacher, you do not know the value of the goods you sell. From this day forward, let each verse be worth a thousand." Wishing to inform the Brahmin Nanda of this, he said:
525:
415. These verses are worth a thousand;
These verses are not worth a hundred.
O Brahmin, take these four thousand
Quickly.

He spoke this verse:
415. "Brahmin, teacher. These verses are worth a thousand kahāpaṇas each. These verses are indeed not worth a hundred each. Brahmin, you should take these four thousand kahāpaṇas quickly."

## The Father's Reproach

Then, giving the Brahmin Nanda a comfortable carriage, he commanded his men, "Escort the teacher Nanda safely to his home," and sent the Brahmin away. At that moment, a great sound of applause arose: "King Sutasoma has honored the Satāraha verses by making them Sahassāraha (worth a thousand). Sadhu! Sadhu!"

When the King's mother and father heard this sound, they asked, "What is this sound?" and upon hearing the truth, they became angry with the Great Being, their son, because of their own greed for wealth. After sending the Brahmin away, the Great Being went to his parents, paid his respects, and stood there.

As he stood there, the King's father did not even offer a friendly greeting (paṭisanthāra), such as asking, "My son, how did you escape from the hands of such a violent robber?" Instead, because of his greed for wealth, he asked, "My son, is it true that I hear you gave four thousand kahāpaṇas after hearing four verses?" When the son replied, "It is true," the father, wishing to reproach the Great Being Sutasoma, spoke this verse:

416. There may be verses worth eighty or ninety,
And there may be verses worth a hundred.
Sutasoma, know for yourself:
Where is there a verse worth a thousand?

416. "Sutasoma, my son. There might be a verse worth eighty. There might also be a verse worth ninety. There might also be a verse worth a hundred. My son Sutasoma, know for yourself. Where and with whom is there a verse known as being worth a thousand?"

## Knowledge Should Be Desired

Then, the Bodhisatta Sutasoma, wishing to make his father understand, said, "Father, I do not desire growth in wealth; I only desire growth in learning (suta)," and spoke three verses beginning with:

417. "I desire for myself the growth of learning..."

417. "O best of kings, my father. I desire for myself the growth of learning (knowledge)."
526:
420. This kingdom is yours, with wealth and vehicles,
With royal regalia and endowed with all sensual pleasures.
Why do you reproach me for the sake of sensual desires?
I go to the presence of the Porisāda.

He spoke this verse:

420. Dear Father, Great King. With wealth: together with treasures and riches. With vehicles: together with elephant-vehicles and horse-vehicles. With royal regalia: together with the royal ornaments. Endowed with all sensual pleasures: complete with all objects of sensual desire. This kingdom of yours: please govern this kingdom of yours, Great King. Dear Father, Great King. For the sake of sensual desires: because of the cause known as objective sensuality. Why do you reproach me? I shall go to the presence of the Porisāda.

I desire to increase my own learning; may good men associate with me. Like the great ocean with flowing rivers, I am not satiated, dear Father, with well-spoken words.

418. O best of kings, dear Father. Just as fire burning grass and wood is not satisfied, and just as the ocean is not satisfied by rivers, even so, indeed, wise men are not satiated with well-spoken words after hearing them.

419. O King, ruler of men, dear Father. When I hear a meaningful verse even from my own slave, I listen to it with great respect; indeed, Father, there is no satiety for me in the Dhamma.

## Must Go to Porisāda
Having spoken these words, he said, "Father, do not reproach me for the sake of wealth. I have come after making an oath to the Porisāda that I would return after hearing the Dhamma. Now I must go to the presence of the Porisāda. Please take this kingdom of yours." Thus, wishing to hand over the kingdom to his father, he spoke the verse:

## The Father Will Suppress the Enemy
When Prince Sutasoma handed over the kingdom in this way, the King's heart became very hot with distress. That Great King, wishing to inform his son of his intention, said, "Dear Sutasoma, why do you speak such words? We shall capture the man-eating thief with the fourfold army," and spoke this verse to his son:

421. Some exist for self-protection,
527:
Elephant riders, charioteers, and infantry.
Horse riders and those who are archers,
Let us employ the army and kill the enemy.

He spoke this verse:

421. Dear Sutasoma. Some wise ones exist for the purpose of self-protection. There are elephant riders, charioteers, infantry, horse riders, and archers. Let us employ this entire army and kill the enemy.

422. Porisāda did what is very difficult,
He captured me alive and then released me.
Remembering such a previous favor,
How could I betray him, O King?

He spoke this verse:

422. O King, ruler of men, dear Father. The Porisāda performed a deed that is extremely difficult to do. He captured me alive and then released me. Remembering that previous favor of such a nature, how could I commit a wrong against that Porisāda?

## The Whole Palace Wept
At that time, the mother and father of Prince Mahāsutasoma, with faces full of tears, wept and lamented, pleading, "Dear Sutasoma, do not go; you shall not be allowed to go." The sixteen thousand court ladies and the remaining attendants also wailed, "O Great King, where are you going, leaving us without a protector?"

In the entire city, not a single person could remain composed, and the whole city was in an uproar, saying, "Friends, it is said that King Sutasoma came after giving his word to the Porisāda. Now, after hearing the four verses worth a hundred each, making offerings to the Dhamma-preacher, and paying respects to his mother and father, he is said to be going back to the man-eating thief."

## Cannot Avoid Going
Mahāsutasoma, having heard the words of his mother and father, wished to explain the reason to them.

## Departing for Porisāda
That King Sutasoma comforted his mother and father, saying, "O Mother and Father, do not worry about me. I have performed good deeds. For me, the bliss and sovereignty of the six sensual heavens is not difficult to attain." After paying respects to his mother and father and comforting the rest of the people, he departed for the presence of the Porisāda.

To make this matter clear, the All-Knowing Buddha said:

Mahāsutasoma stayed in the palace for that whole night. At dawn the next day, he paid respects to his mother and father, comforted the rest of the people, and departed from the city and palace, escorted by a great multitude of people, including the court ladies, who were weeping with tearful faces in various ways.
528:
423. Having paid homage to his father and mother, and having advised the merchants and the army, the speaker of truth, guarding the truth, went to where Porisāda was.

423. Bhikkhus, monks. At that time, that King Sutasoma, having paid homage to his mother and father, and having advised the assembly of townspeople and the army, that noble King Sutasoma, being a speaker of truth and wishing to guard the truth, went to the place where Porisāda was.

424. A promise was made by me to the Brahmin while I stood in my own kingdom's sovereignty. To fulfill that promise to the Brahmin, I, guarding the truth, have returned. Perform your sacrifice, eat me, O Porisāda.

424. Friend Porisāda, while I was established in the sovereignty of my own kingdom, I made a certain promise to the Brahmin Nanda. Having first fulfilled that promise to the Brahmin, I, who am a guardian of truth, have returned to you. Friend Porisāda, if you wish to kill me and perform the sacrifice, then sacrifice me. If you wish to eat me, then eat me.

Being unable to turn back the multitude of people, he drew a line across the road with his staff and said, "If you have affection for me, do not cross this line." The people, not daring to transgress the command of the virtuous and powerful King, wept with a loud voice. Watching the Great King Sutasoma as he departed with the gait of a lion, they entered the city wailing in unison once he had passed beyond their sight.

## I Have Returned After Hearing the Dhamma

King Sutasoma went to Porisāda by the same path he had come. At that time, Porisāda thought: "If my friend King Sutasoma wishes to come, let him come; if he does not wish to come, let him stay. Let the deity of the banyan tree do to me as she wishes. I will kill these kings and perform the sacrifice with the five kinds of choice meat." Having gathered wood and lit a fire, he sat sharpening his spits, saying, "Let there be a heap of embers first." At that moment, King Sutasoma arrived.

Then Porisāda, seeing King Sutasoma, was pleased in heart and asked, "Friend Sutasoma, did you go to the city and perform the task that was to be done?" The Great Being replied, "Great King, I have done so. I have heard the verses preached by the Kassapa Buddha, the One of Ten Powers, and I have also paid honor to the preacher of the Dhamma. Therefore, going to the city and performing the task is indeed accomplished." To show the reason to Porisāda, he spoke the verse:
529:
426. You have acted unrighteously, O Porisāda; you have fallen from your kingdom for the sake of your belly. These verses proclaim the Dhamma.

427. For the unrighteous and cruel one, whose hands are always bloody, there is no truth—how then can there be Dhamma? What will you do with what you hear?

426. Friend Porisāda, you have acted unrighteously and practiced cannibalism. For the sake of your belly, you have fallen from your kingdom. Friend Porisāda, these verses proclaim only the ninefold Supramundane Dhamma. Where do the practice of the virtuous and the practice of the wicked meet?

427. Friend Porisāda, for you who are unrighteous, cruel, and whose hands are constantly stained with blood, there is not even the slightest truth in speech. How then can there be Dhamma? Such as you are, what will you do with what you have heard?

## Preach the Dhamma to Me

Hearing those words, Porisāda thought: "This King is not afraid; he speaks being free from the fear of death. What kind of power and majesty is this fearlessness?" He then decided: "There can be no other power; this King Sutasoma says, 'I have heard the verses preached by the Kassapa Buddha.' It must be the power of those verses. I too shall become fearless." Wishing to hear those verses, he spoke this verse:

425. Eating [you] later will not be lost to me; this pyre is still smoky. Meat cooked on smokeless [embers] is well-cooked. I shall listen to the verses worth a hundred.

425. Friend Sutasoma, eating you later will not be a loss for me. First, let this pyre become smokeless. Meat roasted on a smokeless heap of embers is well-cooked. Friend Sutasoma, I shall listen to the verses that are worth a hundred (satāraha).

## The Righteous and Unrighteous Do Not Match

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta King Sutasoma thought: "This Porisāda has wicked conduct. I will preach to him after rebuking him slightly and making him feel ashamed." Wishing to rebuke him, he said:

426. You have acted unrighteously, O Porisāda...
530:
## What is the difference between eating humans and killing humans?

Even though Sutasoma spoke thus, Porisāda did not get angry. Why did he not get angry? It was because of the greatness of the Great Being Mahāsutasoma’s cultivation of loving-kindness (mettā). Then, saying to Sutasoma, “Friend Sutasoma, what is this? Am I the only one who is unrighteous?” and wishing to inform Sutasoma of this matter, he spoke this verse:

428. “Whichever king goes hunting for the sake of meat,
Or whichever king kills for his own purpose,
Both of them are equal in the afterlife.
Why do you call only me unrighteous?”

428. Friend Sutasoma. Whichever king goes to the forest for deer because he desires meat; and whichever king kills a human being for his own affairs; both those kings become equal in the afterlife. Why do you say that I alone am unrighteous?

429. “Five five-clawed animals are not to be eaten by a Khattiya who knows.
O King, you have eaten what is not to be eaten; therefore, you are unrighteous.”

429. Great King. For a Khattiya who knows the conduct of kings, five types of five-clawed animals are not fit to be eaten as food. Yet, you eat human flesh, which is not to be eaten. Therefore, you have become unrighteous.

430. “You were released from the hands of Porisāda,
And having gone to your own palace, O seeker of desires,
You have come again into the hands of the enemy.
O King, you are not skilled in the Khatta-dhamma (statecraft).”

430. Great King. Having been released from the hands of the man-eater, you, who have desires and longings, went to your own palace and have now come back to the hands of the enemy. Great King, you are not skilled in the Khatta-dhamma, which is called political guile.

Dhamma and Adhamma, where do they ever meet?
531:
431. “Those who are skilled in the Khatta-dhamma,
Mostly they become denizens of hell.
Therefore, having abandoned the Khatta-dhamma,
I have returned, protecting the Truth.
Offer your sacrifice or eat me, Porisāda.”

431. Friend Porisāda. Those kings who are skilled in political guile (Khatta-dhamma) mostly become denizens of hell. Therefore, I have abandoned political guile and, being one who protects the Truth (Sacca), I have returned. Friend Porisāda, if you wish to offer a sacrifice by killing me, then offer it; or if you wish to eat me, then eat.

432. “Palatial dwellings, lands, cattle, and horses,
Desirable women, Kāsī silks, and sandalwood;
All these you obtain there through your sovereignty.
What benefit do you see in the Truth?”

432. Friend Sutasoma. Those golden palatial dwellings, those cattle and horses on the land, those women who are the cause of sensual pleasure, and those Kāsī cloths and red sandalwood—all these many things you obtain in that city of Indapatta to enjoy because of your sovereignty. Yet, what benefit do you see in the Truth?

## You have failed in kingly conduct

Hearing those words, the Great Being Mahāsutasoma, wishing to destroy Porisāda’s view, spoke:

## You do not know political guile

Thus, when Porisāda was rebuked and saw no other refuge, wishing to conceal his own evil, he spoke:

## Political guile is food for hell

Then, Mahāsutasoma said to Porisāda, “Friend Porisāda, one who is skilled in political guile should be like me; that is true. I know that political guile, but even though I know it, I do not practice for the sake of that political guile.” Wishing to inform Porisāda of this matter, he spoke:

## What benefit is there in keeping the truth?

Hearing those words, Porisāda, wishing to ask Sutasoma about the benefit of protecting the Truth, spoke:

## Attaining Nibbāna by standing in Truth

Mahāsutasoma, wishing to preach the benefit of Truth to Porisāda, spoke:
532:
433. “Whatever tastes there are on this earth,
Truth is the sweetest of all those tastes.
Recluses and Brahmins established in Truth,
Cross to the other shore of birth and death.”

433. Friend Porisāda. Whatever tastes of this nature exist on the surface of the earth, the taste of Truth is more excellent than those tastes. Recluses and Brahmins who are established in the Dhamma of Truth can cross to the other shore of rebirth and death.

434. “You were released from the hands of Porisāda,
And having gone to your own palace, O seeker of desires,
You have come again into the hands of the enemy.
Surely you have no fear of death, O Lord of men,
You are of undaunted mind, O speaker of truth.”

434. Great King, ruler of men. Having been released from the hands of the man-eater, you, who have sensual desires, went to your own palace and have returned to the hands of the enemy. Great King, speaker of truth, it seems you have no fear of death. You seem to have a mind that does not shrink back.

## Are you not afraid to die?

In this way, King Mahāsutasoma preached the benefits and advantages of Truth to Porisāda. After that, Porisāda looked at the face of King Mahāsutasoma, which was like the glory of a newly blossomed lotus or the full moon, and thought: “This King Sutasoma sees the heap of glowing coals and sees the sharpening of the meat-spit, yet there is not even a bit of terror in his mind. How is this? Is this fearlessness the power of the verses worth a hundred (Satāraha-gāthā), or is it the power of Truth, or is it the power of something else?” Thinking, “I will first ask King Sutasoma,” he spoke:

## Not afraid of death because of many merits

Hearing those words, the Great Being Mahāsutasoma, wishing to inform Porisāda of the reason why he was not afraid, spoke these eight verses beginning with “Katā me kalyāṇā anekarūpā”:

435. “Many kinds of good deeds have been done by me,
And great sacrifices have been offered, praised by the wise.
The path to the next world has been cleared;
Who like me, established in Dhamma, would fear death?”

435. Friend Porisāda. I have performed many various good deeds. I have offered those sacrifices which are extensive and praised by wise and virtuous people. I have cleared the path to the afterlife. What person like me, who is established in the Dhamma of merit, should fear the danger of death?
533:
436. "Friend Porisāda, I have performed many various good deeds. I have offered great sacrifices that are extensive and praised by the wise. I shall go to the next world without regret. Friend Porisāda, having killed me, offer me as a sacrifice or eat me if you wish."

437. "Friend Porisāda, I have dutifully served my father and mother. I have ruled the kingdom according to the ten royal virtues (Dasa-rājadhamma). The path to the next world has been cleared. Who like me, established in the Dhamma, would fear death?"

438. "Friend Porisāda, I have dutifully served my father and mother. I have ruled the kingdom according to the ten royal virtues. I shall go to the next world without regret. Having killed me, offer me as a sacrifice or eat me if you wish."

439. "Friend Porisāda, I have done favors for my relatives and friends. I have ruled the kingdom according to the ten royal virtues. The path to the next world has been cleared. Who like me, established in the Dhamma, would fear death?"

440. "Friend Porisāda, I have done favors for my relatives and friends. I have ruled the kingdom and villages according to the ten royal virtues. I shall go to the next world without regret. Having killed me, offer me as a sacrifice or eat me if you wish."

441. "Friend Porisāda, I have given many gifts in many ways to many people. I have satisfied ascetics and brahmins. I have cleared the path to the next world. Who like me, established in the Dhamma, would fear death?"

442. "Friend Porisāda, I have given many gifts in many ways to many people...
534:
...I have given many gifts. I have satisfied ascetics and brahmins. I shall go to the next world without regret. Having killed me, offer me as a sacrifice or eat me if you wish."

## Preach the Satāraha Verses

Hearing these words, Porisāda thought, "This Great King Sutasoma is a virtuous person, endowed with wisdom, and a speaker of sweet Dhamma. If I were to eat this Great King Sutasoma, my head would split into seven pieces, or the earth would open up and swallow me." Being terrified, he said, "Friend, Great King Sutasoma, you are not of a nature to be eaten by me." Desiring to let the Great King Sutasoma know this reason, he spoke this verse:

443. "A man who knowingly eats poison,
Or a venomous snake of blazing and fierce power,
His head would split into seven pieces,
Who would eat such a truth-speaker?"

443. "Friend Sutasoma, if a man knowingly eats poison that causes immediate death; if a man catches a venomous snake of blazing and fierce power; that man would surely meet destruction. If one were to eat a truth-speaker like you, his head would split into seven pieces."

Thus, Porisāda compared the Bodhisatta, King Mahāsutasoma, to deadly poison and said, "Who would eat you?" Desiring to hear those Satāraha verses, he entreated King Mahāsutasoma. To instill respect for the Dhamma, King Sutasoma refused, saying, "Friend Porisāda, you are not a fit vessel for such faultless verses." Nevertheless, Porisāda thought, "In the whole of Jambudīpa, there is no wise man like this King Sutasoma. Having been released from my hands, he went and heard those verses, honored the Dhamma-preacher, and taking death upon his forehead, he has returned to me."
535:
444. Having heard the Dhamma, men distinguish between good and evil. Even by hearing these verses, my mind may find delight in the Dhamma.
This verse was spoken.
444. Friend Sutasoma, having heard the Dhamma, men come to know what is good and what is evil. Perhaps by hearing these verses, my mind might also find delight in the Dhamma of the path of wholesome actions.
Then the Great Being thought, "Now Porisāda wishes to listen; I shall speak." He said, "In that case, friend Porisāda, listen well." Making Porisāda pay attention, he praised the verses in the same manner as they were spoken by the Brahmin Nanda. While the deities of the six heavens of the sensual realm raised a simultaneous clamor and gave cries of "Sādhu," the Bodhisatta King Mahāsutasoma, wishing to preach the Dhamma to Porisāda, spoke these four verses beginning with:
445. O Great King, meeting with the virtuous even once protects a person; frequent association with the unvirtuous does not protect.
446. One should associate only with the virtuous; one should cultivate intimacy with the virtuous. Having known the true Dhamma of the wise, one becomes better, not worse.
447. O King, well-decorated royal chariots indeed wear out; likewise, the body also reaches old age. But the Dhamma of the virtuous (Nibbāna) does not reach old age. The peaceful ones, the Buddhas and others, indeed praise this to the virtuous.
448. O King, the sky is far from the earth, and the earth is far from the sky. They say the other shore of the ocean is also far. But they say the Dhamma of the virtuous and the Dhamma of the unvirtuous are even further apart than that.
## Four Boons Granted
Because King Sutasoma had preached so well to him, and because of his own wisdom, Porisāda reflected, "These verses are as if spoken by an Omniscient Buddha." His entire body was filled with the five kinds of joy.
536:
