449. "These verses are meaningful and well-phrased; having heard them well-spoken by you, O King of men, I am delighted, joyful, glad, and satisfied. I give you four boons, my friend."

449. O Janinda, ruler of all people. Friend Sutasoma. These verses, which have good meaning and good phrasing, well-spoken by you—having heard them, I am delighted, I am joyful, I have a glad mind, I am satisfied. I, such as I am, give you four boons.

450. "You who do not understand your own death, nor what is beneficial or harmful, nor hell or heaven; obsessed with the taste [of human flesh] and established in evil conduct—what boon will you give, O wicked one?"

451. "And if I should say to you, 'Give me a boon,' and you, having given it, should not fulfill it; what wise man, knowing this, would enter into such a visible quarrel and dispute?"

450. O wicked one, friend Porisāda. You who do not know your own death. You do not know what is beneficial or harmful, nor the fall into the states of misery, nor heaven. Obsessed with the taste of human flesh, established in evil conduct—what boon will you give?

451. O wicked one, friend Porisāda. And I might say to you, 'Give me a boon.' And you, having given it by word, might not fulfill it as requested. What wise man, knowing for certain, would approach and enter into this visible dispute involving hesitation?

452. "A person does not deserve to give a boon which, having given, he would not fulfill. Choose, friend, without wavering; even at the cost of my life, I will surely give it."

He felt a tender heart toward King Mahāsutasoma. He regarded King Mahāsutasoma like a father who gives a white parasol.

That Porisāda thought, "I do not see any gold or silver to give to King Mahāsutasoma. I will give him one boon for each verse." Desiring to give boons, he said:

## Will you give a verbal boon?

Then, King Mahāsutasoma, wishing to rebuke Porisāda, said, "Friend Porisāda, what kind of boon will you give?"

Thereafter, Porisāda, wishing to promise so that King Sutasoma would believe him, said:

452. O Khattiya, lord of the land...
537:
453. "The friendship of the noble meets with the noble; the friendship of the wise meets with the wise. May I see you healthy for a hundred years; this I choose as the first of the boons."

453. Friend Porisāda. The friendship of a noble person meets with a noble person. The friendship of one endowed with wisdom meets with one endowed with wisdom. Friend Porisāda, I wish to see you without illness for a hundred years. Among the four boons you have offered, I choose this as the first boon.

454. "The friendship of the noble meets with the noble; the friendship of the wise meets with the wise. May you see me healthy for a hundred years; this I give as the first of the boons."

454. Friend Sutasoma. The friendship of a noble person meets with a noble person. The friendship of one endowed with wisdom meets with one endowed with wisdom. Friend Sutasoma, may you see me without illness for a hundred years. Among the four boons I have offered, I give this as the first boon.

455. "Those Khattiyas here who are lords of the land, consecrated on the head and given special names—do not eat such lords of the land; this I choose as the second of the boons."

455. Friend Porisāda. Those Khattiyas who are here, rulers of the land, who have been consecrated on their heads and have special names—do not eat those kings. Among the four boons, I choose this as the second boon.

Friend Sutasoma, a person who, even after giving a boon, does not fulfill it as requested, that person is not worthy to give that boon. Friend Sutasoma, choose without wavering; even if I must sacrifice my life, I will surely give it.

## (1) May you live a hundred years

Then King Mahāsutasoma thought, "This Porisāda speaks with great courage; he will follow my words. I will take the boons. However, if I first forbid him from eating human flesh, he will be greatly distressed. I will first take the other three boons and later take the boon of abstaining from eating human flesh." Desiring to take the boons, he said:

## Live for a hundred years

Porisāda, having heard those words, thought, "This King Sutasoma, though I have destroyed his prosperity and am now a great robber who desires to eat human flesh and causes such great harm, yet he wishes for my life. How wonderful! He truly desires my welfare." With a delighted heart, not realizing that King Sutasoma was taking the boons strategically, and wishing to give that boon, he said:

## (2) Release the captured kings

Thereafter, King Mahāsutasoma, wishing to take another boon, said:
538:
456. "Friend Sutasoma, those kings here who are lords of the earth,
Consecrated on the head and having received their titles,
Such lords of the earth I shall not eat;
Of the boons, I grant this as the second."

456. Friend Sutasoma. Here, in this place. Those who are lords of the earth. Those who have been consecrated on the head. Those who have special names bestowed upon them. Those kings who exist. Such kings as those. I shall not eat. Among the four boons. This second boon. I grant.

457. "Friend Porisāda, more than a hundred kings have been captured by you,
With palms pierced and strung together, weeping with tearful faces;
Restore them to their own kingdoms;
Of the boons, I choose this as the third."

457. Friend Porisāda. By you. Captured. Those whose palms are strung together with cord; or, those whose palms have been pierced and strung together with cord. Those whose faces are filled with tears. Weeping. More than a hundred. Those kings who exist. Those kings. To their own. To their respective kingdoms. Please restore/send them. Among the four boons you have offered. This third boon. I choose.

458. "Friend Sutasoma, more than a hundred kings have been captured by me,
With palms pierced and strung together, weeping with tearful faces;
I shall restore them to their own kingdoms;
Of the boons, I grant this as the third."

458. Friend Sutasoma. By me. Captured. Those whose palms are strung together with cord. Those whose faces are filled with tears. Weeping. More than a hundred. Those kings who exist. Those kings. To their own. To their respective kingdoms. I shall restore/send them. Among the four boons offered. This third boon. I grant.

## Releasing the hundred kings
In this way, while accepting the second boon, the Great Being Sutasoma accepted the boon of life for more than a hundred kings. Porisāda, wishing to grant the boon to Sutasoma, spoke the verse.

## (3) Please send back the hundred kings
How was it? Did those more than a hundred kings hear the sound of the conversation between the Great Being Sutasoma and Porisāda, or did they not? They did not hear everything.

That is true. Porisāda, fearing the danger of smoke damaging the banyan tree, moved away and lit a fire. The Great Being sat between the fire and the tree and spoke with Porisāda. Therefore, not hearing everything, they heard only fragments (half and half).

Those more than a hundred kings comforted one another, saying, "Now the Great Sutasoma will tame Porisāda; do not be afraid." At that moment, the Great Being, wishing to take another boon, spoke this verse:

## I will send them back
In this way, while taking the third boon, the Great Being Sutasoma took the boon of returning those kings to their own kingdoms. Why did he take this boon? Because even if Porisāda did not eat them, out of fear of enmity, he might keep all those kings as slaves in the forest, or he might kill and discard them, or he might take them to the borders and sell them. Therefore, he took the boon to have them sent back to their own kingdoms.

Porisāda, wishing to grant the boon to Sutasoma, said:
539:
Taking the fourth boon, the Bodhisatta spoke this verse:

459. Your kingdom is full of holes, shaken by fear;
Many people have entered hiding places.
O King, abstain from human flesh;
This is the fourth of the boons I choose.

459. Friend Porisāda. Because of the fear that the man-eating thief will come now, your kingdom is shaken and trembling with fear, and it remains empty. Many people have entered hiding places to conceal themselves. O King, abstain from human flesh. Among the four boons you have granted, I choose this fourth boon.

## (4) Abstain from Eating Human Flesh

Then, as Mahā Sutasoma wished to take the fourth boon—

## Request Another Boon

When Sutasoma spoke thus, Porisāda clapped his hands and laughed, saying, "Friend Sutasoma, why do you say this? How shall I give you this boon? If you wish to take a boon, take another." Desiring to reject that boon, he spoke this verse:

460. Indeed, that food is dear to me;
For its sake, I entered the forest.
How can I abstain from it?
Choose another as the fourth of the boons.

460. Friend Sutasoma. Indeed, that food is food that delights my heart. For the sake of that food, I have entered the forest. Such as I am, how can I abstain from this food? Friend Sutasoma, among the four boons I have granted, choose another as the fourth.

## The Self is Most Supreme

Then Mahā Sutasoma said to Porisāda, "Friend Porisāda, you say that because you love human flesh so much, you are unable to abstain from it. That is true. He who does evil depending on a beloved object is called a fool." Desiring to preach this matter to Porisāda, he spoke this verse:

461. O Lord of men, one like you should not serve
What is dear by discarding the self.
The self alone is better, even better than the highest;
What is dear can be obtained later by one who has cultivated the self.

461. O Lord of men, friend Porisāda. One like you should not serve beloved objects by discarding the self, thinking, 'This object is dear to me.' For what reason? The self alone is especially noble. Than what is it more noble? It is more noble even than the most supreme object. For what reason? Because one who has a developed mind and body can obtain beloved objects later. Therefore, the self alone is especially noble.
540:
In that verse, 'one like you' (tādiso) means, O Lord of men, one who is young, handsome, and of great fame. One should not serve beloved objects by discarding the self through greed for such objects, thereby falling away from all happy states and special happiness and falling into hell. 'Even better than the highest' (paramā ca seyyo) means that for a man, the self is more excellent than even the most supreme beloved object. For what reason? 'Beloved objects can be obtained' (labbhā piyā) means that by the power of the senses and by merit, one who has cultivated and developed the self can obtain beloved objects after attaining the prosperity of gods and men in both this life and the next.

When this was said, Porisāda became terrified. Thinking, "I am unable to make King Sutasoma give up the boon he has taken, nor can I abstain from human flesh; what shall I do?", he spoke this verse with eyes full of tears, lamenting and wishing for him to take another boon:

462. Human flesh is dear to me, Sutasoma, know this.
I am unable to refrain from it;
Friend, choose another boon.

462. Sutasoma, O King Sutasoma, please know this. I am very fond of human flesh. I am unable to refrain or abstain from human flesh. Friend Sutasoma, you should take another boon.

## Request Another Boon

When Mahā Sutasoma spoke thus, Porisāda became filled with fear and trembling. "I myself am unable to make the noble King Sutasoma give up the boon he has taken, nor can I abstain from human flesh. What shall I do?" Thus, crying with eyes full of tears, he wished for him to take another boon.

## Fault and Benefit

Then Mahā Sutasoma, wishing to preach the Dhamma by showing the fault in doing evil to Porisāda, spoke these verses:

463. He who, protecting what is dear, serves what is dear
By discarding the self,
Is like a drunkard drinking a poison-mixed drink;
Because of that, he becomes miserable in the hereafter.

464. But he who here, having reflected, gives up what is dear
And serves the Noble Dhamma even with difficulty,
Is like a sick man drinking medicines;
Because of that, he becomes happy in the hereafter.

463. Friend Porisāda. Just as a drunkard drinks liquor mixed with poison and, because of that very act of evil, becomes miserable in the hereafter, so too, whoever serves beloved objects by discarding the self, protecting what is dear and thinking, 'Indeed, this is dear to me,' that person, because of that very act of evil, becomes miserable in the hereafter.

464. Friend Porisāda. In this world, he who, having reflected, gives up beloved objects and serves the Noble Dhamma even with hardship and difficulty, just as a sick man drinks various medicines, that person, because of that very act of merit, becomes happy in the hereafter.

## Porisāda Must Cry

When this was said, Porisāda wished to weep a piteous cry.

## Porisāda's Double-Sided Words

Then Mahā Sutasoma wished to rebuke Porisāda's words.

## How Shall I Give It?

Then Porisāda, weeping again, wished to grant that boon.
541:
When this was said, Porisāda, lamenting piteously, spoke this verse:

465. "Having abandoned my father and mother, and the five pleasant strands of sensual pleasure, I entered the forest for the sake of this [human flesh]. How can I give you that boon?"

In that verse, 'for the sake of this' means for the sake of human flesh. 'How can I give' means in what way can I grant that boon?

Then the Great Being spoke this verse:

466. "The wise do not speak with a double tongue; the virtuous are true to their promise. You said to me, 'Friend, choose a boon,' but what you say now does not agree with that."

In that verse, 'double tongue' means, friend Porisāda, that those who are wise do not say one thing and then speak a second time in contradiction. 'You said to me' means you spoke to me thus: "Friend Sutasoma, choose a boon." 'But what you say now' means therefore what you said then does not agree with what you say now.

Lamenting again, he spoke this verse:

467. "I have incurred demerit, ill-fame, and infamy; I have fallen into much evil, misconduct, and defilement for the sake of human flesh. How can I give you that boon?"

In that verse, 'evil' (pāpa) refers to that which has not reached the path of action (kammapatha). 'Misconduct' (duccarita) refers to that which has reached the path of action. 'Defilement' (kilesa) means suffering. 'For the sake of human flesh' means because of human flesh. 'I have fallen into' means I have approached. 'That to you' means how can I give that boon to you? Do not stop me, have compassion and pity on me, and choose another boon.

## Porisāda’s Inconsistency

Then, King Mahāsutasoma, wishing to bring forth the boon that Porisāda had previously granted, spoke this verse:

468. "Friend Sutasoma, a person who, having granted a boon, would not fulfill it as requested, is not worthy of giving that boon. Friend Sutasoma, choose without hesitation; I will give it even if I must sacrifice my life. Thus you spoke to me. But having spoken so, you now say you cannot give it. Your words do not agree; they are inconsistent."
542:
Then the Great Being said:

468. "A person should not give a boon which, having given, he would not fulfill. Friend, choose without hesitation; I will give it even if I must sacrifice my life."

Having thus brought forth and shown the verse previously spoken by him, and encouraging him to grant the boon, he spoke these verses:

471. "From whomsoever a person may learn the Dhamma, and those virtuous ones who remove his doubts—that person is his island and his refuge. A wise man should not destroy friendship with him."

In that verse, friend Porisāda, a wise man should know the cause that shows benefit and harm from whatever person. And those virtuous ones who remove the doubts of that person—that very person is his island of reliance and his place of refuge. One should not destroy the state of friendship with such a person who is one's teacher.

## Everything Should Be Sacrificed for the Dhamma

Thus, having brought forth the verse previously spoken by Porisāda and wishing to make him strive in granting the boon, he spoke these two verses:

469. "The virtuous sacrifice their lives but not the Dhamma; the virtuous are true to their promise. Having granted the boon, fulfill it quickly, O excellent King; be endowed with this truth.

470. "One should sacrifice wealth for the sake of a precious limb; one should sacrifice a limb to preserve one's life. But a man, mindful of the Dhamma, should sacrifice limbs, wealth, and even life itself—everything."

469. O excellent King, friend Porisāda, the virtuous sacrifice their own lives, but they certainly do not sacrifice the Dhamma. The virtuous are only those who are true to their promise. O excellent King, friend, because you have granted me a boon, fulfill that boon quickly as requested. Be endowed with that Truth-Dhamma.

470. O excellent King, friend Porisāda, a wise man should sacrifice wealth for the sake of a precious limb. Wishing to protect his life, he should sacrifice a precious limb. But one who is mindful of the noble Dhamma should sacrifice limbs, wealth, and even life itself—everything.

## Friendship with a Teacher Should Not Be Broken

In this way, the Bodhisatta King Mahāsutasoma, having established Porisāda in the Truth through these reasons, now wished to show Porisāda his status as a teacher.
543:
472. Indeed, that food is dear to me,
For its sake I entered the forest.
If you ask me for this thing,
I grant you this boon too, friend.

He spoke this verse. 

472. O Anantakitti, you of infinite fame. Friend Sutasoma, Great King Sutasoma. Addhā hi, truly. So bhakkho, that food which is human flesh. Mama, to me. Manāpo, is a pleasing food. Etassa, of this food. Hetu, for the sake. Vanaṃ, into the forest. Paviṭṭho, I have entered. Amhi, I am. Etam-atthaṃ, for the sake of this boon which is this food. Maṃ, from me. Sace ca, if indeed. Yācasi, you ask. Etam-pi, that boon as well. Te, to you. Dadāmi, I grant.

## No Longer Eating Human Flesh

After saying these words, King Mahāsutasoma said, "Friend Porisāda, it is not proper to break the word of a virtuous teacher. In our youth, I was your mentor and taught you many arts. Now, with the grace of a Buddha, I have preached the Sataraha verses to you. Therefore, you ought to follow my words."

Hearing this, Porisāda thought, "This King Sutasoma is indeed my teacher and a wise man. I have also granted him a boon. What can be done? In a single existence, death is certain. Even if I die, I will no longer eat human flesh; I will grant the boon to King Sutasoma." Thus, with tears flowing, he rose and prostrated at the feet of King Mahāsutasoma, and wishing to grant the boon, he spoke the verse.

## Porisāda Undertakes the Precepts

Then King Mahāsutasoma said to Porisāda, "Friend Porisāda, for one established in virtue, even death is noble. Friend Porisāda, you accept the boon given. From this day forth, you are established in the noble path. Even so, I request you further: if you have affection for me, undertake the five precepts." Porisāda replied, "Friend Sutasoma, very well, give me the five precepts; I shall undertake them." Then Porisāda worshipped the Bodhisatta King Mahāsutasoma with the five-point prostration and sat in a suitable place. King Mahāsutasoma then established him in the five precepts.

At that moment, the earth-dwelling deities (Bhumma devas) who had gathered there, feeling joy toward King Mahāsutasoma, made the entire forest echo with a great sound of applause (Sādhu-kāra), saying, "From Avīci to the highest point of existence (Bhavagga), there is no one other than King Mahāsutasoma capable of restraining this Porisāda from eating human flesh. How wonderful! King Mahāsutasoma has performed a most difficult task." Hearing the sound of those earth-dwelling deities, the deities of the Realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā) also gave applause.

## The Hundred Kings Will Be Released

In this manner, a tumultuous sound arose simultaneously up to the Brahma realm. The kings who were suspended from the banyan tree also heard the sound of the deities' applause. The deity guarding the banyan tree, staying in his own celestial mansion, also gave applause. Thus, only the sound of the deities was heard, but their forms were not seen.

Hearing the sound of the deities' applause, the many kings thought, "Because of King Mahāsutasoma, we have regained our lives. King Mahāsutasoma has performed a difficult task by taming Porisāda." Thus, they praised King Mahāsutasoma.
544:
The tumultuous sound reached as far as the Brahma realm. The kings hanging on the tree also heard the sound of the deities' applause. The tree deity, staying in his own mansion, also gave applause. Thus, only the sound of the deities was heard, but their forms were not seen. Hearing the sound of the deities' applause, the kings thought, "Because of Sutasoma, we have gained our lives. Sutasoma has done a difficult thing in taming Porisāda," and they praised the Bodhisatta. Porisāda worshipped at the feet of the Great Being and stood in a suitable place. Then the Bodhisatta said to him, "Friend, release the kshatriyas (kings)."

Porisāda thought, "I am the enemy of these kings. If I release them, they might say, 'Seize our enemy,' and harm me. Yet, even at the cost of my life, I cannot break the precepts I have taken from Sutasoma. I will go together with Sutasoma and release them; in this way, there will be no danger for me."

Having thought thus, he worshipped King Mahāsutasoma and, wishing to release them, said, "Friend Sutasoma, let us both go and release those kings," and spoke this verse:

473. You were my teacher and my friend,
I have followed your word, friend.
You too, friend, follow my word,
Let us both go and release them.

473. Friend Sutasoma, you are my teacher (Satthā) because you showed the path to heaven, and you have been my friend (Sakhā) since our youth. Friend Sutasoma, I have followed your word. Friend Sutasoma, you too follow my word. Friend Sutasoma, let us both go and release them.

When he spoke thus, King Mahāsutasoma, wishing to release them together with Porisāda, spoke this verse:

474. I am your teacher and your friend,
You have followed my word, friend.
I too, friend, follow your word,
Let us both go and release them.

475. You who were oppressed by Kammāsapāda,
Bound through the palms, weeping with tearful faces.
Never bear malice against this king,
Promise me this truth.
545:
476. We have been oppressed by Kammāsapāda, our palms pierced and threaded, weeping with tearful faces. We shall never harm this king.

474. Friend Porisāda, I am your teacher and your friend. Friend Porisāda, you have followed my words. Friend Porisāda, I too shall follow your words. Let us both go and release them.

## Mahāsutasoma Takes the Pledge
The Great Being, King Mahāsutasoma, having agreed with Porisāda saying, "Let us both go and release them," thought: "Kings are by nature proud and stubborn. As soon as they are freed, they might strike or even kill Porisāda, thinking, 'We were oppressed by this man.' However, this Porisāda will not wrong them. I shall go alone first and obtain their pledge from those kings."

Having thought thus, he went to that place and saw those kings threaded through their palms, their toes barely touching the ground, hanging from the branches of the banyan tree. When the wind blew, they swung like garlands of dried Kuranda flowers hanging from elephant tusks.

Upon seeing Mahāsutasoma, they all cried out loudly at once, "Now we are safe!" Then the Great Being, Mahāsutasoma, comforted them, saying, "Great Kings, do not be afraid. I have tamed Porisāda and secured your safety. Therefore, follow my words." Having said this, wishing to make them pledge, he recited this verse:

"Listen to my truthful pledge."

475. O Kings, you have been oppressed by Kammāsapāda, with your palms pierced and threaded, weeping with tearful faces. Even though you have been so oppressed, do not ever harm this king. Listen to my truthful pledge.

Wishing to give their pledge, they recited this verse:

"We listen to your truthful pledge."

476. O Great King, refuge of beings, we have been oppressed by Kammāsapāda, with our palms pierced and threaded, weeping with tearful faces. Even though we have been so oppressed, we shall never harm this king. We listen to your truthful pledge.
546:
## Treating Porisāda as a Father
Then the Great Being, Mahāsutasoma, wishing to have them pledge, said: "O Kings, if that is so, give your pledge." He then recited this verse:

477. Just as a father or a mother is compassionate and desires the welfare of their children, so may this king be to you, and may you be like sons to him.

477. O Kings, just as a father or a mother is compassionate and desires the welfare of their children, so may this king be like a father to you, and may you all be like sons to this king.

Wishing to give their pledge, they recited this verse:

478. Just as a father or a mother is compassionate and desires the welfare of their children, so may this king be to us, and we shall be like sons to him.

478. O Great King, refuge of men, best of kings, just as a father or a mother is compassionate and desires the welfare of their children, so may this king be like a father to us, and we shall be like sons to him.

## The Release of the Kings
Thus, Mahāsutasoma, having taken the pledge of those kings, called Porisāda and said, "Come, friend Porisāda, release these kings." Porisāda took a sword and cut the bonds of one king. That king, having been without food for seven days and suffering great pain, fainted and fell to the ground as soon as the bonds were cut.

Seeing him fall, Mahāsutasoma felt compassion and said, "Friend Porisāda, do not cut them like this." He firmly held another king with both hands, embraced him against his chest, and said, "Friend Porisāda, now cut the bonds." Porisāda cut them with the sword. Because Mahāsutasoma was endowed with great strength, he let the king rest against his chest and, with a gentle heart as if towards his own son, lowered him and laid him on the ground.

In this manner, he laid all the kings on the ground, washed their wounds, and gently pulled out the ropes just as one might pull a thread from a child's newly pierced ear. He washed away the pus and blood, making the wounds clean. Then he said, "Friend Porisāda, grind the bark of a certain tree on a stone and bring it here." Having it brought, he made an Act of Truth and smeared it on the palms of the kings. At that very moment, the wounds were healed.

Porisāda took rice and cooked a thin gruel without solid grains. Mahāsutasoma and Porisāda fed the hundred-odd kings with the gruel. Thus, while they were satisfying all the kings with gruel, the sun set.

On the following day, in the early morning, at noon, and in the evening, they fed them only gruel. On the third day, they fed them gruel with rice grains. By the third day, the kings were free from illness. Then Mahāsutasoma asked them, "Will you be able to travel?" When they replied, "We can go," he said, "Come, friend Porisāda, let us go to our own kingdoms."

Then Porisāda, weeping, fell at the feet of King Mahāsutasoma and said, "Friend Sutasoma, you alone take these kings and go. As for me, I shall live right here in this forest, eating roots and fruits." Sutasoma said, "Friend Porisāda, what will you do in this forest? Your country is very delightful. Go and rule in Bārāṇasī."
547:
"Friend Sutasoma, what are you saying? I cannot go to that city of Vārāṇasī. It is true that all the people living in the city are my enemies. All those city dwellers will revile me, saying, 'Porisāda has eaten my mother, he has eaten my father, he has eaten my brothers and sisters. Seize this thief!' They will bring my life to an end with sticks and stones. Moreover, I have established myself in the precepts (sīla) under your majesty. Even for the sake of my life, I cannot kill another. Therefore, I will not follow you. Since I must abstain from human flesh, how long shall I live? Now, there is no more seeing your majesty." Thus he wept and said, "May your majesty alone depart."

## Porisāda's Entry into the City

Then the Great Being, King Mahāsutasoma, stroked Porisāda and said, "Friend Porisāda, do not worry. I, known as Sutasoma, have been able to tame even one as fierce and harsh as you; what is there to say about taming those who dwell in Vārāṇasī? I will establish you in the kingship of Vārāṇasī. If I am unable to do so, I will divide my own kingdom and give half to you." When he said this, Porisāda replied, "In your majesty's city too, there are surely my enemies." The Great Being thought, "This Porisāda has done a difficult thing by following my word. By what means can I establish this Porisāda in his former glory?" Desiring to entice Porisāda, he praised the prosperity of Vārāṇasī and spoke these verses beginning with "Catuppadaṃ sakuṇañcāpi maṃsaṃ."

## Fine Foods

479. "Great King, in that city of Vārāṇasī, the meats of quadrupeds and birds are well-prepared and finished with various seasonings by the chefs. Having enjoyed them like Indra enjoying celestial ambrosia, how can you delight in the forest alone after leaving them?"

## Beautiful Women

480. "Great King, in that city of Vārāṇasī, princesses adorned with complexions like masses of pure gold and possessing slender, beautiful waists, used to surround and delight you, just as celestial nymphs surround and delight Indra among the gods. Having left those princesses, how can you delight in the forest alone?"

## Excellent Bedding

481. "Great King, in that city of Vārāṇasī, you used to sleep in a beautiful bed provided with red pillows, many rugs, and all kinds of coverings in a multi-storied palace. Having slept comfortably in the midst of such a bed, how can you delight in the forest alone after leaving it?"

## Music and Singing

482. "Great King, in that city of Vārāṇasī, at night, the sounds of gongs and drums, and indeed music played by women, along with much sweet singing and well-played melodies, used to delight you. Having left such prosperity, how can you delight in the forest alone?"
548:
## The Noble City

483. "Great King, in that city of Vārāṇasī, your city is very delightful, endowed with gardens and ponds, and filled with many flowers. It is endowed with the Migāzina garden. Therefore, it is very delightful. Your city, endowed with the Migāzina garden, is very delightful because it is filled with horses, elephants, and chariots. Having left that city of Vārāṇasī, how can you delight in the forest alone?"

Thus the Great Being thought, "Perhaps he will desire to go if he remembers the tastes of the enjoyments he experienced before." He first enticed him with food, second with sensual pleasures, third with bedding, fourth with dance, song, and music, and fifth with gardens and the city. 

## Come, Let Us Go

Having enticed him with these five means, he said, "Great King, come! I will take you and establish you in the kingship of Vārāṇasī, and afterwards I will go to my own kingdom. If you do not obtain the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, I will give you half of my kingdom. What benefit is there for you in living in the forest? Follow my word."

## Porisāda Enters the City

When Porisāda heard the words of King Mahāsutasoma, he desired to go and thought, "King Sutasoma desires my welfare and is compassionate. It is true; first he established me in goodness, and now he says, 'I will establish you in your former glory.' This Sutasoma will surely be able to establish me. It is proper to go with this Sutasoma. What benefit is there for me in living in the forest?" With a joyful heart, and wishing to speak in praise of Sutasoma's virtues, he said, "Friend Sutasoma, there is nothing more noble than associating with a good friend, and nothing more base than associating with a wicked friend." Desiring to inform King Mahāsutasoma of this matter...
549:
484. He spoke these seven verses beginning with 'Kāḷapakkhe yathā cando'.

## The Importance of Associating with the Virtuous

484. O Rathesabha, noble among those who ride chariots! O Great King! Just as the moon in the dark fortnight (kāḷapakkha) wanes day by day, so too does association with the wicked resemble the dark fortnight.

485. O Bhūnātha, Refuge of beings! O King of kings! Because of the cook named Rasaka, a most base man, I committed that evil deed by which I would go to a state of misery.

486. O Raṭṭhādhipati, Lord of the land! O Great King! Just as the moon in the bright fortnight (sukkapakkha) waxes day by day, so too does association with the virtuous resemble the bright fortnight.

487. O Sutasoma, bearer of the kingdom's burden! Please know this: because of you, I shall perform those meritorious deeds by which I will go to a happy destination.

488. O Janinda, Ruler of men! O Bhūmipāla, Lord of the earth! Just as rainwater falling on dry land does not last long and is not enduring, so too is association with the wicked like water on dry land—it is not lasting.

489. O Naravīraseṭṭha, noble among men through effort! O Janinda, King of men! Just as rainwater falling into the great ocean remains for a long time, so too is association with the virtuous like water in the ocean—it is long-lasting.

490. O Rājādhirāja, King of kings! O Most Excellent King! Association with the virtuous is undecaying. For as long as it lasts, that friendship remains the same and does not perish. But association with the wicked perishes quickly...
550:
...perishes quickly. Therefore, the Dhamma of the virtuous is far from the wicked.

Thus Porisāda praised the virtues of the Great Being Sutasoma with these seven verses. The Great Being then took Porisāda and those kings and arrived at the border of Indrapatta in the Kuru kingdom. When the border inhabitants saw the Great Being, they went to the city of Indrapatta and informed the ministers. The ministers took the army and went to escort him.

King Sutasoma, with that retinue, proceeded to the city of Vārāṇasī. Along the way, the country folk presented gifts to King Sutasoma. With a great following, he reached Vārāṇasī.

## The City Gates are Closed

At that time, Porisāda's son was reigning as king, and the commander-in-chief was Kāḷahatthi. The citizens reported to the king: "O Great King, it is said that King Sutasoma has tamed Porisāda and is bringing him to Vārāṇasī. We will not allow that Porisāda to enter the city." They quickly closed the city gates and stood armed.

King Sutasoma, knowing the gates were closed, left Porisāda and the hundred-plus kings behind and approached with two or three ministers, saying, "I am King Sutasoma; open the gates!" The attendants went and informed the king. The king ordered, "Open the gates quickly!" Sutasoma entered the city. The king and General Kāḷahatthi welcomed King Sutasoma and escorted him to the golden palace.

## King Sutasoma

King Sutasoma sat on the royal throne, summoned Porisāda's chief queen and the remaining ministers, and spoke to Kāḷahatthi: "Friend Kāḷahatthi, why did you not allow the king to enter the city?" Kāḷahatthi replied, "O Great King, while he was ruling, he ate many people in this city. He committed deeds that kings should not do. He caused the whole of Jambudīpa to be without a king. Such was his wicked conduct; therefore, we did not allow him to enter."

## Taming and Preaching the Dhamma

"Friend Kāḷahatthi, now that Porisāda will no longer do such things. Do not worry. I have tamed him and established him in the precepts (sīla). Even for the sake of his life, he will not harm anyone. You have nothing to fear from him. Do not act in this way. It is said that children should respectfully care for their parents. This is true: sons and daughters who respectfully care for their parents reach the heavenly realm..."
551:
491. He is not a king who conquers those who should not be conquered,
He is not a friend who conquers a friend.
She is not a wife who does not fear her husband,
They are not children who do not support the aged.

492. That is not an assembly where there are no virtuous ones,
They are not virtuous ones who do not speak the Dhamma.
Having abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion,
Only those who speak the Dhamma are virtuous ones.

493. They do not know a wise man when he is silent,
While he is mixed with fools.
But they know him when he speaks,
Teaching the state of the Deathless.

494. One should speak and illuminate the Dhamma,
One should uphold the banner of the seers.
Well-spoken words are the banner of the seers,
For the Dhamma is indeed the banner of the seers.

“Children who do not respectfully serve their parents go to the state of misery and hell,” thus King Mahāsutasoma gave advice to the prince, the son of Porisāda, who was sitting in a lower place.

“Friend Kāḷahatthi, you are the king's friend and also a minister who serves the king. The king has established you in great wealth and prosperity. You, too, should act for the king's benefit,” thus he advised General Kāḷahatthi.

“Queen, you also came from your parents' house and reached the position of chief queen in the presence of that king, and have prospered with children. You, too, should undertake to act for the king's benefit,” thus he advised the chief queen. Desiring to preach the Dhamma to bring that matter to a conclusion, he spoke these four verses:

## The Foolish Wife and Children
491. O Kings! That king who conquers those who should not be conquered—one's parents—is not called a king. That friend who conquers another friend is not called a friend. That wife who does not fear her husband is not called a wife. Those children who do not support their aged parents are not called children.

## The Fool and the Wise
492. That assembly where there are no wise and virtuous ones is not called an assembly. Those virtuous ones who do not speak the truth and Dhamma are not called virtuous ones. Only those wise ones who, having abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion, and being compassionate for the welfare of others, speak the truth, are called virtuous ones.

493. O Kings! When a wise man who is mixed and associating with fools does not speak, they do not know him as a wise man. Only when he speaks, teaching the Deathless Nibbāna, do they know him as a wise man.

494. Therefore, one should speak the Dhamma and make it shine. Those virtuous ones, such as the Buddhas, have the well-spoken Dhamma as their banner. One should uphold that banner of the Dhamma of those virtuous ones. Indeed, the Dhamma is called the banner of the virtuous ones like the Buddhas.

## Porisāda Becomes King
Upon hearing these words of King Mahāsutasoma, the King (Porisāda), the General, and the Queen were exceedingly pleased and said, “Great King, let us go and bring him back.”
552:
After addressing King Mahāsutasoma, they had the drum beaten throughout the city of Vārāṇasī and assembled the citizens, saying, “Do not be afraid. It is said that our lord the king is now established in the Dhamma. Come, let us bring our lord the king back.” Taking the multitude with them and placing King Mahāsutasoma at the head, they went to Porisāda. They paid homage to him and had the barbers attend to him. When his hair and beard were trimmed, he bathed, was anointed with perfumes, and was well-adorned. They then placed the king upon a heap of treasures, consecrated him, and brought him into the city.

After becoming king, Porisāda offered great honor and hospitality to the more than one hundred kings and to King Mahāsutasoma.

“It is said that the noble King Mahāsutasoma has tamed Porisāda and established him in the kingdom.” Thus, a great stir and excitement arose throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa.

In the city of Indapattha, the people sent a messenger saying, “May our lord, the noble King Mahāsutasoma, return to us.” King Mahāsutasoma stayed in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī for about a month and then advised Porisāda, “Friend Brahmadatta, we shall go. May you be diligent. Have five alms-halls built—at the four city gates and one in the center of the palace. Without violating the Ten Royal Virtues, avoid the four wrong paths of prejudice (agati).” Thus he advised Porisāda.

## King Sutasoma Returns
From more than a hundred royal capitals, a great host of troops mostly assembled. Surrounded by that host of troops, King Mahāsutasoma departed from the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. Porisāda also departed from the city and returned only after accompanying him halfway. King Mahāsutasoma provided elephant-vehicles and horse-vehicles to those kings who had no transport and sent them on their way. Those kings also rejoiced with King Mahāsutasoma, paid him homage, and returned to their respective provinces.

## Worshipping the Banyan Tree Deity
When King Mahāsutasoma reached his capital, he entered the city of Indapattha, which was decorated like a city of the gods. He paid respects to his mother and father, engaged in pleasant conversation, and ascended to the upper level of the golden palace.

While ruling the kingdom in accordance with the Dhamma, King Mahāsutasoma thought, “The deity of the banyan tree has been of great help to me; I shall make an offering to him.”
553:
Thinking, "I shall perform offerings and honors to this banyan tree deity," King Mahāsutasoma had a large reservoir constructed not far from the banyan tree and sent many people to establish a village. That village became great, adorned with eighty thousand shops. Because it was the place where the spotted-footed Porisāda was tamed, that village was named the market town of Kammāsadamma.

He also had the ground around the foot of that banyan tree leveled, starting from the edge of the branches, and provided it with surrounding railings, gateposts, door-leaves, and arches. The banyan tree deity was greatly pleased. All those kings, established in the advice of the Bodhisatta King Mahāsutasoma, performed meritorious deeds such as giving and, at the end of their lives, filled the heavenly realms.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, said, "Monks, not only now have I tamed Aṅgulimāla; in the past also, I tamed him," and he identified the Jātaka.

How did he identify it? "Monks, at that time Porisāda was Aṅgulimāla. The commander Kāḷahatthi was Sāriputta. The brahmin Nanda was Ānanda. The banyan tree deity was Mahākassapa. Sakka was Anuruddha. The remaining kings were the Buddha's assembly. The mother and father, who are now of the noble Sākyan royal lineage, were the mother and father then. King Mahāsutasoma, however, was I myself." Thus he identified the Jātaka.

## Eating the flesh of one's own kind leads to ruin

The Mahāsutasoma Jātaka is concluded.
